openers.hadean-eon: Earth began as dust. A supernova seeded a dense corner of the Milky Way with heavy elements, a hydrogen cloud collapsed into the Sun, and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies until one of them was our planet. Then came violence: iron sank to the core, a Mars-sized body called Theia struck, and a magma ocean about 200 km deep covered the surface. Yet zircon crystals show that liquid water and an atmosphere existed by 4.404 billion years ago, astonishingly soon after Earth formed. This first eon is the story of how a molten ball became a world with seas.
openers.archean-eon: The Archean is the eon of the oldest rocks that still stand intact. Zircons in Canada's Acasta Gneiss crystallized about 4.03 billion years ago, and Greenland's Isua belt holds the oldest known banded iron formations. Around 3,800 million years ago the first cratons, whole continental masses built of granite blocks, appeared. Over this stretch the carbon cycle took its basic form, the last great impacts faded, and life left its first faint chemical traces.
openers.eoarchean-era: The Eoarchean opens with Earth's oldest known felsic crust, the Acasta Gneiss, about 4.03 billion years old. Impacts stayed frequent, with the final phase of the Late Heavy Bombardment placed at about 3,920–3,850 million years ago. Meanwhile the first cratons began to form: the Pilbara of Western Australia, the Yangtze Block of South China, the first rocks of the East European Craton. In Greenland, graphite low in carbon-13 and the oldest banded iron formations hint that life may already have been at work.
openers.paleoarchean-era: The Paleoarchean is where life stops being a maybe. Stromatolites in the Pilbara's Dresser Formation, laid down about 3,483–3,479 million years ago, are the earliest direct evidence of life, and microbes may already have lived around hot springs on land. Meanwhile the continents were taking shape: the Wyoming and Dharwar cratons began, and the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents. Above it all hung a stable atmosphere of nitrogen, methane and carbon dioxide, and below it, spherule layers at Barberton record giant impacts still striking.
openers.mesoarchean-era: In the Mesoarchean, Earth learned to make oxygen. Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesizers appears about 3.2 billion years ago, and a brief rise in oxygen followed around 2,980–2,960 million years ago. The planet was warm, perhaps very warm, yet it also saw the Pongola glaciation, the oldest known on Earth. Continental crust grew fast, the hypothetical supercontinent Ur may have formed, and plate tectonics may have begun, though its timing is still debated.
openers.neoarchean-era: The Neoarchean is the age of supervolcanoes and stitched-together continents. In Ontario and Quebec the Abitibi greenstone belt formed, home to the Blake River Megacaldera Complex, the first known Precambrian supervolcano, and around 2,705 million years ago a possibly global eruption of komatiite lava may mark an overturn of the mantle. Cratons welded together: the Kaapvaal and Zimbabwe along the Limpopo Belt, and many more into the hypothetical supercontinent Kenorland. Meanwhile, about 2,700 million years ago, another pulse of oxygen hinted at the great change to come.
openers.proterozoic-eon: The Proterozoic is the eon in which Earth's air changed for good. Free oxygen built up in the air and shallow seas, turning a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change never reversed. It reshaped everything it touched: banded iron formations precipitated across most continents, new minerals multiplied, and the gas proved toxic to many of the anaerobic microbes that had ruled until then. Ice spread in the Huronian glaciations, and a supercontinent began to rift apart above plumes of magma.
openers.paleoproterozoic-era: The Paleoproterozoic opens with the planet rusting. Massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents as oxygen met the iron dissolved in seawater, and the Great Oxygenation Event set off explosive growth in mineral diversity. Life paid a price, since free oxygen was toxic to a biosphere built of anaerobes. On land, rifting began to split a low-latitude supercontinent, giant swarms of dikes cut the cratons, and a series of glaciations left their boulder beds near Lake Huron.
openers.siderian-period: The Siderian takes its name from the Greek word for iron, and iron is its signature. Banded iron formations piled up across most continents, their red layers made of oxidized iron. At the same time oxygen began to build up in the air for the first time, an irreversible change that may have wiped out many early organisms. Plume-driven rifting cracked a supercontinent, the Mistassini dikes cut the Superior Craton, and the first of the Huronian ice ages began.
openers.rhyacian-period: The Rhyacian is the period of the first complex cells. Eukaryotes are thought to have arisen when an Asgard archaeon took in an alphaproteobacterium, and sexual reproduction probably appeared too. Oxygen surged, leaving the largest carbon isotope excursion known and the first continental red beds, while the Makganyene ice may have frozen the planet as far as the tropics. By the period's end, collisions in West Africa and South America had begun gathering Earth's continents into the supercontinent Columbia.
openers.orosirian-period: The Orosirian is a period of giant blows and great collisions. An asteroid perhaps 20–25 km wide struck South Africa's Kaapvaal craton, and nearby, magma rose to form the largest layered intrusion in Earth's crust. Around the world, mountain belts stitched cratons together: Baltica from three blocks, Laurentia through the Trans-Hudson orogeny, Atlantica from West African and South American cratons. Meanwhile, black chert on the shore of Lake Superior preserved microbes like cyanobacteria.
openers.statherian-period: The Statherian marks the start of a long, quiet stretch sometimes called Earth's Middle Ages, a span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago of tectonic stability, steady climate and slow evolution. Quiet did not mean idle. The oldest sand seas spread across several cratons, island arcs crashed into proto-North America, and in what is now Gabon, uranium deposits ran as natural nuclear reactors. In North China, the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes appear in the rocks.
openers.mesoproterozoic-era: The Mesoproterozoic is when the first algae turned sunlight into food. Around 1.6 billion years ago some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria and gained photosynthesis, and India's Chitrakoot Formation preserves the earliest known red algae. Oxygen may have risen briefly to about 4% of present levels. Columbia began to break apart, great igneous provinces flooded the continents, and in Africa a series of orogenies ran on until Rodinia was assembled about 1,000 million years ago.
openers.calymmian-period: The Calymmian is a period of new life and a fraying supercontinent. Eukaryotes took cyanobacteria inside their cells and became the first algae, and odd forms like Horodyskia, a string of beads on a thread, appeared. Oxygen may have pulsed briefly upward. Meanwhile Columbia began to fragment, rifts opened along the margins of Laurentia and other continents, and a deep rift basin on Laurentia's edge filled with the mud of the Belt Supergroup.
openers.ectasian-period: In the Ectasian, one supercontinent finished falling apart and the next began to form. A large igneous province about 1,380 million years ago marks Nuna's breakup, and from about 1,270 million years ago a massive igneous event spread across 2.7 million km² of the Canadian Shield. Fragments of the old supercontinent then began colliding to build Rodinia. Through it all, stromatolites reached their greatest abundance and diversity.
openers.stenian-period: The Stenian is the period of sex, failed rifts and growing supercontinents. Bangiomorpha, a red alga from Arctic Canada, carries the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction, and the earliest known fungus appears in shale nearby. In the middle of North America, the crust began to split along a rift 2,000 km long, then stopped. Mountain building in Scandinavia and the Grand Canyon's first layers record a world assembling Rodinia, while an impact in Scotland left its debris but no crater anyone has found.
openers.neoproterozoic-era: The Neoproterozoic is the era in which life began to get big. Eukaryotes, long inconspicuous, diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago, green algae became multicellular, and sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 million years old may be the oldest animals. A second great rise in oxygen swept the air and oceans. Meanwhile Rodinia began to rift apart, island arcs built the Arabian-Nubian Shield, and the pieces of a new southern continent, Gondwana, started to come together.
openers.tonian-period: The Tonian is when eukaryotes finally stepped forward. They diversified rapidly around 1 billion years ago, dominated fresh water in Scotland's Torridon lakes, and by about 800 million years ago left fossils notably more complex and numerous. Oxygen began its second great rise, and the first possible animals appear as sponge-like fossils. Under it all, the supercontinent Rodinia started to break apart, opening new oceans as old ones closed.
openers.cryogenian-period: The Cryogenian is the age when the planet nearly froze solid. It opened with magma flooding more than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland, and soon after came a worldwide glaciation that lasted some 57 million years. The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that the surface froze nearly completely, twice, in the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations. Yet life did not stop. Shelled amoebae, sponges and seaweeds appear in these rocks, and red and green algae took over the ocean plankton.
openers.ediacaran-period: The Ediacaran begins at a layer of limestone laid directly on top of the last great glacial deposits. What follows is a world in motion: mountains rose in Antarctica, Australia and the Baltic Shield, and the Pan-African orogeny welded continents into Gondwana. A mantle plume pushed Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean. By about 600 Ma enough oxygen had built up to form an ozone layer. In the rocks of South China appear embryo-like animals and some of the oldest large, complex fossils known.
openers.cambrian-period: Few stretches of time changed life as much as the Cambrian. Beginning about 538.8 Ma, animals diversified suddenly, and the first members of most modern phyla appeared. An asteroid about 1 km across struck what is now Estonia, and the first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma. Under the seafloor, carbon and pyrite were buried in waters short of oxygen, and the chemistry of the sea rose and fell with each pulse. The period is the stage on which the animal kingdom took its modern shape.
openers.terreneuvian-epoch: The Terreneuvian is the Cambrian's first epoch, named for Newfoundland, where Fortune Head marks its base. Its rocks hold small shelly fossils, mineralized tubes and plates, in a nearly continuous record. Gondwana completed its southern half as the Kalahari and Mawson cratons met. Carbon and sulphur isotopes trace pulses of oxygen that spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas. Around 529 Ma a carbon spike and two new molluscs mark the epoch's first internal boundary.
openers.cambrian-series-2-epoch: Trilobites define this epoch: their body fossils first appear around 521 Ma, with exoskeletons of calcite. Radiodonts, the giant predators of the Cambrian, and eocrinoid echinoderms join them. China's Maotianshan Shales preserve an extremely diverse fauna, soft tissues and all, and among them the earliest known vertebrates. Mountains rose in Antarctica and South Australia. The epoch ends in crisis: the Sinsk Event, the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, removed over 60% of animal species.
openers.miaolingian-epoch: The Miaolingian opens with a die-off: the first major trilobite extinction removed the olenellids, eodiscids and most redlichiids. In their place, Paradoxides, the largest trilobites of the Cambrian, spread around the world. Conodonts, eel-like jawless animals known mainly from their teeth, make their first appearance, and the Paleo-Tethys Ocean begins to open along Gondwana's northern margin. Meteorites left craters from Norway to North Dakota. By its end, around 497.05 Ma, the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event had already begun.
openers.furongian-epoch: The Furongian is the Cambrian's last epoch, and it was a hard one. One extinction cut species diversity by 45%, and after a brief recovery another cut it by 55.2%. A global carbon event, SPICE, ran between about 497 and 494 Ma. Yet new things arrived: Plectronoceras, the earliest undisputed cephalopod, and the first brittle stars. Mountain building began that would raise the Caledonides and reshape South America, and the epoch closed with another extinction at the boundary with the Ordovician.
openers.ordovician-period: In the Ordovician, the sea filled up. Marine animal life radiated through the period, and the Cambrian fauna gave way to one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers. Nautiloids reached their peak variety, starfish and brittle stars appeared, and new reef builders brought reefs back after a long lull. The Iapetus Ocean, over 4,000 km wide at the start, began to narrow. The period opens with a single conodont species, Iapetognathus fluctivagus, appearing in the rock record.
openers.early-ordovician-epoch: The Early Ordovician was a time of rising water and new arrivals. Sea level climbed almost without pause, and shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana. Into them came phacopid trilobites, starfish, reef-building stromatoporoid sponges and strophomenid brachiopods. Several invertebrate lineages took to open water and started new food chains. Morocco's Fezouata Shale preserves the soft-bodied animals of this world, while trackways in Western Australia may record animals walking on land.
openers.middle-ordovician-epoch: The Middle Ordovician is when the climate turned. Oxygen isotopes in conodonts show the shift from greenhouse to icehouse beginning, and a long ice age followed. On land, the spores of the first plants appear about 470 million years ago, and atmospheric oxygen began a long rise. In space, the break-up of an asteroid sent fragments toward Earth, and craters from Iowa to Quebec date to this time. The first sea urchins appear in the seas below.
openers.late-ordovician-epoch: The Late Ordovician begins with continents on the move and ends in catastrophe. Terranes split from Gondwana, Avalonia struck Baltica, and huge eruptions blanketed Laurentia in ash. Impacts scarred Sweden and Estonia, and a brief warming built reef mounds across Europe. Arthropods left the oldest clear evidence of animals on land. Then extinction rates began to climb, several million years before a great glaciation.
openers.silurian-period: The Silurian is the period of fish and the first green coasts. Jawed fish diversified into placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish, while armored jawless fish reached their height. Nematophytes, strange land organisms, towered over the small plants beside them. Old groups bowed out, from asaphid trilobites to eocrinoid echinoderms. Far to the south, the Rheic Ocean opened to its greatest width, about 4,000 km.
openers.llandovery-epoch: The Llandovery opens on a recovering world. Its base lies at Dob's Linn in southern Scotland, just after the end-Ordovician extinctions, and as melting ice re-flooded the shelves, life rebounded. Reefs spread, land plants covered much of the land surface, and the oldest unambiguous jawed vertebrates appear in China. Milder glaciations came and went. Meanwhile Baltica and Laurentia began their slow collision in the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny.
openers.wenlock-epoch: The Wenlock is short and turbulent. It opens with the Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, which lasted about 200,000 years. Carbon and oxygen isotopes swung after it, and two more crises followed, the Lundgreni and Mulde events. Yet the epoch also saw the first scorpions and the start of a long rise in oxygen, as vascular plants and fungi began to colonize dry land.
openers.ludlow-epoch: In the Ludlow, the land was still nearly empty, but the first settlers had arrived. Clubmoss-like lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving plant lineages, date to about 425 million years ago, and so do the oldest definite millipedes, from Kerrera in Scotland. At sea, the story turned harsher. A final glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian and is tied to the Lau event, the last of three Silurian extinctions, which may have ended the ancient palaeoscolecid worms. Sea scorpions and the earliest sac fungi were close behind.
openers.pridoli-epoch: The Pridoli, the last and shortest epoch of the Silurian, saw the land come alive. Oxygen rose high enough for the first wildfires, and Scotland's Pneumodesmus is among the oldest creatures known to have breathed air on land. By about 420 million years ago, millipedes shared the ground with centipedes and spider relatives, and the first ray-finned fish may have swum in the seas. Meanwhile the Iapetus Ocean closed entirely, and falling seas left salt basins from Michigan to West Virginia.
openers.devonian-period: The Devonian is popularly called the Age of Fishes, and with reason: jawed vertebrates, rare before, became common, and armored placoderms appeared in sudden diversity at its start. On land, the period's story is about plants. As they spread, carbon dioxide dropped steeply, and oxygen, only a fraction of today's level in the early Silurian, rose to near-modern levels. Beneath it all, the crust kept moving, from an island arc docking with Patagonia to huge alkaline magmas on Russia's Kola Peninsula.
openers.early-devonian-epoch: The Early Devonian rearranged both the map and the tree of life. The Caledonian mountains began to collapse, the Rheic Ocean began to close, and Asian blocks pulled away from Gondwana to open the Paleo-Tethys. Red sediments spread over a continent that would be called the Old Red Sandstone Continent. In the water, lobe-finned fishes and the first ammonoids appeared while jawless armored fishes peaked and began to fade. On land, Scotland's Rhynie chert froze an early ecosystem of plants, fungi and arthropods in stone.
openers.middle-devonian-epoch: In the Middle Devonian, Earth grew its first forests. Cladoxylopsid trees stood in the Eifelian, progymnosperms appeared, and the new woods drew carbon from the air and buried it. Reefs of stromatoporoid sponges reached their peak, and in a Polish lagoon something with toes left the oldest tetrapod tracks. But the seas were turning dangerous. The Kačák event raised sea level and spread anoxia, and the Taghanic event followed with another oxygen crisis.
openers.late-devonian-epoch: The Late Devonian was a time of giants, impacts and loss. In Western Australia, the Gogo Formation preserved soft tissues down to nerves and embryos, while deep-sea oxygen finally stabilized near modern levels. Meteorites struck from Russia's Kaluga to Sweden's Siljan Ring, the largest impact structure in Europe. Flood basalts erupted in Siberia, and mountains rose from the Canadian Arctic to the ancestral Sierra Nevada. Underneath it all, oxygen-starved seas buried organic matter, setting up some of the deadliest extinctions in Earth's history.
openers.carboniferous-period: The Carboniferous is the period of coal swamps, and some of its plants, such as the Cordaitales, grew right in them. In fresh water, giant lobe-finned fishes were the top predators. In the rocks of Scotland, a rare bed preserved a conodont with its body intact. And far to the east, Siberia, independent since the early Paleozoic, collided with Kazakhstania and raised the Altai Mountains.
openers.mississippian-subperiod: The Mississippian opens just after the Hangenberg extinction, with survivors moving in. Sharks and ray-finned fish took over the seas, and crinoids grew so thick that whole limestones are made of them. Stem tetrapods had already split into the lines leading to amphibians and amniotes, though their fossils are strangely scarce in a span called Romer's gap. Warm shallow seas laid down limestone across Britain and Ireland, but glaciers were building in South America. Seawater itself was changing, as aragonite seas replaced calcite seas.
openers.pennsylvanian-subperiod: The Pennsylvanian was the age of coal. Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land, and oxygen climbed to 25–30%, above today's 21%, while carbon dioxide crashed to one of its lowest levels ever. Ice sheets spread from southern Africa and South America, and repeating rock cycles called cyclothems record the seas rising and falling with them. Arachnids, myriapods and flying insects radiated, cycads and conifers appeared, and by the end the equatorial belt was drying out.
openers.permian-period: In the Permian, almost every major landmass was gathered into one supercontinent, Pangaea. Its climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons that brought harsh dry seasons to the interior. In the south, mountain building folded Gondwana from South America to New Guinea, and Glossopteris seed plants spread across the land. Among the reptiles, the lineage leading to lizards split from its sister group.
openers.cisuralian-epoch: The Cisuralian, the first Permian epoch, opened in the grip of an ice age and ended in a warming world. Carbon dioxide hit a record low and then rose fourfold within a few million years. Pelycosaurs such as Dimetrodon were the dominant land animals, insects diversified dramatically, and the first beetles appeared. Meanwhile the map kept shifting: Kazakhstania struck Baltica, Patagonia completed its collision, and the Cimmerian blocks broke away from Gondwana.
openers.guadalupian-epoch: The Guadalupian, the Middle Permian, was a time of reefs and new predators. Reef building peaked, with reefs from the Delaware Basin to the Tethys. On land, therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large animals, and saber-toothed gorgonopsians evolved. The epoch ended in crisis, as the Emeishan flood basalts erupted in China and the Capitanian extinction struck.
openers.lopingian-epoch: The Lopingian, the last epoch of the Permian and of the Paleozoic, opened with one of the largest retreats of the sea in the Phanerozoic. Advanced therapsids ruled the land, from saber-toothed gorgonopsians to beaked dicynodonts, and the first archosauromorphs and gliding reptiles appeared. In Europe the Zechstein Sea spread and laid down black shale and thick salt, while the long Late Paleozoic icehouse finally ended. Then, in Siberia, basalt lava flooded a vast area, about 7 million km² of which remains today.
openers.triassic-period: One supercontinent, one monsoon and no ice: that is the Triassic world. Pangaea reached its greatest land area after Siberia and the China cratons joined it, and its megamonsoon blew at full strength. Oxygen-poor seas and a searing Early Triassic climate, fed by repeated Siberian Traps eruptions, slowed life's return from the Great Dying. Still, new players appeared almost at once: rhynchosaurs, early neopterygian fishes, and coelacanths in their greatest burst of diversity. Microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow seas while the survivors regrouped.
openers.early-triassic-epoch: The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, and life paid for it. Oxygen-poor waters lingered, the Siberian Traps erupted again and again, and recovery from the largest mass extinction took millions of years. On land, Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some faunas, while temnospondyl amphibians bounced back first. In the sea, microbial reefs spread, coelacanths diversified, and shell-crushing predators began the Mesozoic marine revolution. Across Europe, desert playas laid down the red Buntsandstein.
openers.middle-triassic-epoch: A third extinction since the Permian closed the Early Triassic, yet what followed was a rebound. Within 4–6 million years of the Great Dying, complex ecosystems full of specialized animals began to re-form, as fossils such as China's Luoping biota record. Archosaurs pushed the therapsids aside to rule the land, while placodonts, Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined the ichthyosaurs at sea. Stony corals, the first stem turtles and the oldest sure lepidosaur all appear. Underneath it all, Pangaea began to crack: rift valleys opened soon after the Siberian Traps fell silent, and the Tethys pushed west.
openers.late-triassic-epoch: The Late Triassic opens with a crisis at sea and a shock to the climate. Marine reptiles had just suffered their highest extinction rates, and then the Wrangellia flood basalts poured out over about 5 million years, jolting global climate for perhaps 1–2 million years. In the rains and rivers of that world, the first true dinosaurs appeared and quickly split into sauropodomorphs and meat-eating theropods. Rift basins in Argentina and Virginia buried them with fish, insects and reptiles, while a vast delta plain spread across the Boreal Ocean. Even the oldest probable moth scales turn up, swallowed by a plant-eater.
openers.jurassic-period: The Jurassic begins with the land drying out and the dinosaurs moving in. As Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried, the great Pangean megamonsoon began to fall apart, and the Farallon plate started sinking beneath western North America as Pangaea broke up. With their reptile rivals gone after the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs surged in diversity and abundance, and the first definitive ornithischians appeared. In the sea, ammonoids that had nearly vanished radiated into the ammonites proper, and plesiosaurs were already richly varied. Even the amphibians changed, as the first modern frogs and salamanders began to diversify.
openers.early-jurassic-epoch: In the wreckage of the end-Triassic extinction, the Early Jurassic rebuilt fast. British seafloor communities began recovering almost at once, despite repeated relapses into anoxia, and ammonites and neoselachian sharks radiated through the seas. On land, dinosaurs surged into the space left by vanished rivals, crocodylomorphs found new niches, and the first definitive ornithischians appeared. Plant life turned over too: conifers replaced the hot fernlands of China's Sichuan Basin, while Dicroidium lingered only in Antarctica. Even ocean chemistry shifted, from aragonite seas to calcite seas.
openers.middle-jurassic-epoch: The Middle Jurassic opens with the Toarcian heat fading into a long cool interval, from about 174 to 164 million years ago. Sea level climbed steadily from the Aalenian, and the shallow Sundance Sea spread across northwest North America, while long-isolated terranes docked on the continent's western edge. At sea, most old ichthyosaur lines vanished and new long-necked plesiosaurs appeared. On land, tetanuran theropods reached every continent and split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs, carnosaurs and the first unequivocal stegosaurs appeared, and dinosaurs left their tracks on Skye. Even familiar living things show up: the first true Ginkgo trees and the first octopuses.
openers.late-jurassic-epoch: By the Late Jurassic, the map and the menu had both changed. Africa separated from Antarctica around 160 million years ago, and in Asia the Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean shut in a scissor-like collision. Reefs of sponges and stony corals expanded across warm seas, teleost fishes began their great diversification, and the two living turtle lines had already parted. On land, the Morrison Formation and Tanzania's Tendaguru Beds buried some of the richest dinosaur faunas known, while the first ceratopsian, Yinlong, and the oldest known eutherian, the shrew-like Juramaia, appeared. Offshore, the Kimmeridge Clay gathered the reptiles and plankton that would one day become North Sea oil.
openers.cretaceous-period: The Cretaceous is named for chalk, and more of it formed now than in any other Phanerozoic period. The seas rose in earnest, standing roughly 250 meters above today's by the Cenomanian, and an inland sea, the Eromanga, covered much of Australia. Gondwana's breakup, begun in the Jurassic, sped up and was largely finished by the period's end. Strange box-shaped bivalves called rudists built the reefs of the Tethys, while new life appeared on every front: the first raptors, sea turtles, social ants and termites, and birds with short, fused tails. The period began 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years.
openers.early-cretaceous-epoch: The Early Cretaceous begins 143.1 million years ago, with impacts on either side of the boundary: one in central Australia, another on the floor of the Barents Sea. Europe began rifting away from North America, and Australia filled with the inland Eromanga Sea. In the lagoons of southern England's Purbeck Group, insects, early mammals and dinosaur footprints were buried in great variety. Large carcharodontosaurid predators spread across the world, the first raptors appeared, and birds diversified into many forms. Smaller newcomers mattered too: orb-weaver spiders, social ants and termites, and the oldest known sea turtles.
openers.late-cretaceous-epoch: The Late Cretaceous began in a hothouse and ended in catastrophe. For 34 million years a shallow sea split North America in two, while giant spinosaurids and carcharodontosaurids ruled the tidal flats of North Africa. In the oceans, marine reptiles perfected the art of crushing shells. On land and in the air, the ancestors of modern birds and the first true crocodilians appeared, both lineages that would outlast the dinosaurs. Meanwhile Zealandia began to tear away from Antarctica, part of a long breakup that would reshape the southern continents.
openers.paleogene-period: The Paleogene began in the wreckage of the K–Pg extinction and became the age when mammals took over. Pantodonts were among the first large mammals, and the oldest undisputed placental fossils come from its first years. Multituberculates, the most successful Mesozoic mammals, enjoyed one last peak. Even the rocks recorded the turmoil: early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon in the deep sea.
openers.paleocene-epoch: The Paleocene is the story of recovery. Colorado's Denver Formation records mammals diversifying right after the K–Pg extinction, and the first large mammals soon appeared. Great swamps laid down coal that still powers America, with the Fort Union Formation alone yielding 43% of its coal. Asteroids kept falling too: one struck off Guinea-Bissau near the boundary, another left the 24 km Boltysh crater in Ukraine. By the end of the epoch, a world of small survivors had given way to a warming planet full of new kinds of life.
openers.eocene-epoch: The Eocene opened in heat. Around its start, oxygen in the atmosphere more or less doubled, and the warmth of the PETM brought modern mammal groups into North America. Primates, songbirds, parrots and loons all appear early in the epoch. India crashed into Eurasia, and Greenland split from Europe. Soon came the EECO, the warmest sustained interval of the whole Cenozoic.
openers.oligocene-epoch: About 33.9 million years ago, ice began to build up on Antarctica, and Earth entered the ice age it is still in. The Oligocene is the story of that cooling and everything it touched. Tropical forests shrank toward the equator and grasslands spread around the world. The sea drained from the Obik Sea, joining Europe to Asia, and Asian mammals poured west in a turnover called the 'great break'. Meanwhile Africa pushed into Eurasia, the Alps rose, and the Andes became a major mountain chain.
openers.neogene-period: The Neogene opens in a world that was getting cooler, drier and more seasonal. Africa's plant diversity fell sharply at the start, and grasses kept spreading until they dominated much of the world while forests dwindled. Mountains rose on two continents: the Andes lifted fastest in this time, and sediment from the rising Himalaya built the vast Bengal Fan. In the sea, whales and dolphins reached their greatest diversity and kelp forests first appeared. On land, apes evolved and spread across the Old World.
openers.miocene-epoch: Apes first evolved in the early Miocene, then diversified and spread across the Old World. Around them the world was turning seasonal. Global cooling gave the East Asian Summer Monsoon its modern form, and grasses came to dominate much of the land. The crust was busy too: the Andes rose fastest in this epoch, and the Tian Shan and Altai mountains formed. The oceans gained new life, from kelp forests to the greatest variety of whales and dolphins Earth has known.
openers.late-miocene: About 11 million years ago the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended, and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began. The cold reshaped life on every continent. Europe's large mammal diversity fell, and South America's giant crocodilians and native predators faded as wetlands vanished. Off southwest Africa, the cold Benguela Upwelling began. Meanwhile the land kept changing: the modern Yangtze River took shape, and Andean calderas such as Aguas Calientes poured out vast ignimbrites.
openers.pliocene-epoch: The Pliocene opened with a flood. Atlantic water broke through at the Strait of Gibraltar and refilled the dried-out Mediterranean. Soon the sea first flooded the land bridge between Alaska and Siberia too. From about 5.3 to 2.7 million years ago, a warm interval interrupted the long-term cooling trend. Old groups such as the oreodonts and the cat-like nimravids died out, the great white shark evolved, and a marine extinction wiped out 36% of large marine species.
openers.quaternary-period: Around 2.58 million years ago, ice sheets began to spread across the Northern Hemisphere, and the Quaternary glaciation began. It is still going on. The start is marked by a flip in Earth's magnetic field, from normal to reversed polarity. In North America, glacials and interglacials began to alternate again and again. In Africa, the hominin family branched out, and early Homo appeared beside robust australopithecines.
openers.pleistocene-epoch: The Pleistocene is the age of ice, and it began about 2.58 million years ago as ice sheets spread across the Northern Hemisphere. Ice at both poles dried the globe. Old groups lost ground: outside the Americas, every trunked mammal except the elephants and Stegodon died out. New hunters arrived, among them the saber-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus. In East Africa, hominin fossils became extraordinarily diverse.
openers.gelasian-age: The Gelasian, the first age of the Pleistocene, opens with Earth's magnetic field flipping about 2.58 million years ago. Ice sheets spread across the north, and the last shallow sea link across Panama closed no later than 2.45 million years ago. An asteroid hit the deep ocean southwest of Chile. Rivers and lakes rearranged too: Ethiopian waters joined the Nile, and earth movements dammed the Murray River into vast Lake Bungunnia. In East Africa, robust australopithecines such as Paranthropus boisei lived beside early Homo.
openers.calabrian-age: Around 1.8 million years ago, people were already living in the hills of Georgia, far outside Africa, and their bones are the oldest human remains known beyond that continent. Within a few hundred thousand years, Homo erectus stood at Yuanmou in southern China, on Java and beside the Sea of Galilee. At home in Africa, the australopithecines that had walked there since about 4 million years ago died out, and charred bones deep in a South African cave hint that someone was handling fire. Wolves of the genus Canis spread across Eurasia, mammoths crossed into North America, and colossal floods tore across the Channeled Scablands. This chapter follows that restless stretch of the Calabrian Age, when both the planet and the human family were on the move.
openers.chibanian-age: The age we still live in, magnetically speaking, began when Earth's field last reversed, ending the Matuyama chron and opening the Brunhes. By then the ice ages had settled into a new rhythm, and the Mid-Pleistocene Transition was complete by about 700,000 years ago. Giants were changing too: gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, and the last clawed chalicotheres lived on only into this stretch of time. In California a VEI 7 eruption poured out about 600 km³ of rock, while lava flows dammed the Colorado River again and again. On the human side, hand axes reached Europe, small hominins lived on Flores, and the lines leading to Neanderthals and Denisovans parted about 640,000 years ago.
openers.late-pleistocene-age: The Late Pleistocene opened in warmth. The Last Interglacial followed the Penultimate Glacial Period, and an exceptionally intense humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than its later Holocene counterpart. Hippos waded as far north as northern England, and sea level probably stood 6 to 9 m above today's. Modern humans were on the move, leaving stone tools in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago and fossils in Israel's caves, while in Java the last Homo erectus lived beside the Solo River. This chapter follows that warm start into the long Last Glacial Period, and the people and animals that lived through it.
openers.holocene-epoch: About 11,700 years ago, the cold of the Younger Dryas broke, and with it the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene ended. The abrupt warming set the remaining ice sheets of North America and Europe melting fast, and the sea jumped about 60 m in the early Holocene. Mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands took over the vast mammoth steppe, and many of its giant animals died out. In the Fertile Crescent, people began growing crops and herding animals. This last stretch of the course is the world people built their history in.
openers.greenlandian-age: The Greenlandian is the opening age of the Holocene, a time of melting ice and rising water. It began when the Younger Dryas cold spell ended about 11,700 years ago, and the warming set the last northern ice sheets collapsing. Sea level jumped about 60 m between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, while a stronger African monsoon pushed rain far north into the Sahara. Megafauna kept dying out, and in the Fertile Crescent people began to farm and herd. At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers raised stone pillars near the time of the first permanent settlements.
openers.northgrippian-age: The Northgrippian opens with a shock: global temperatures dropped abruptly around 8,200 years ago, as Lake Agassiz drained almost completely. Off Norway, three submarine landslides moved about 3,500 km³ of debris, among the largest known. Then the warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP, as the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split and rising seas made Tasmania an island. William Ruddiman argues that early farmers clearing forest began raising greenhouse gases about this time. The age closes with eruptions such as Mount Mazama's, whose collapse left the caldera of Crater Lake.
openers.meghalayan-age: The youngest age of the Holocene begins with a drought: a severe one that began about 4,200 years ago and probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC. Around 4,000 years ago a major pan-tropical change dried East Africa, and the last dwarf woolly mammoths died on Wrangel Island. Great eruptions punctuate the age, from Vesuvius in the Avellino eruption to the catastrophic blast that devastated Thera. Island survivors, such as the Caribbean ground sloths, outlasted their mainland kin, while mainland thylacines vanished. The age runs on to the present day.
openers.phanerozoic-eon: The Phanerozoic is the eon of visible animal life, and it begins with a burrow. A rock section at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, marks its base, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows. From about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly and produced the first members of most modern animal phyla. Seas rose, continents collided, and the chemistry of the ocean swung between oxygen-rich and oxygen-starved. Everything that follows, from trilobites to the present, belongs to this one eon.
openers.paleozoic-era: The Paleozoic, the era of ancient life, opens at the same burrowed layer as the Phanerozoic itself. In its first period, sea level began a long, gradual rise, and shallow seas crept over the continents. Tiny mineral tubes, spicules and plates, often only millimetres long, record the first animals to build hard parts. Mountains rose on Gondwana's western margin while the Kalahari and Mawson cratons joined to complete its south. This era carries life from the first shelly seafloor to the eve of the dinosaurs.
openers.mesozoic-era: The Mesozoic opens on a wrecked world and a single giant landmass. Pangaea's land area had just peaked, and a megamonsoon of record strength swept across it, while even the poles lay free of ice. In the seas, shell-crushing and boring predators began an arms race that would reshape seafloor life for the whole era. On land, the plant-eater Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some faunas, and beaked rhynchosaurs joined a burst of new reptiles. Yet the Siberian Traps kept erupting, and the hottest stretch of the Phanerozoic held recovery back for millions of years.
openers.cenozoic-era: The Cenozoic opened on a world swept clean. With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, mammals rapidly grew in size and diversity, filling the emptied niches. Four bird lineages had survived, among them Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds. Meanwhile the Earth itself kept moving: Apulia began colliding with Europe, and the Laramide orogeny kept raising the Rocky Mountains. This is the era of mammals, and of the mountains and climates that shaped them.

reviews.eoarchean-era: The Eoarchean left Earth its first lasting rock. The Acasta Gneiss and the first cratons, built of granite blocks from crust that was melted and reworked again and again, began the long work of making continents. Oceans held enough water for Isua's pillow basalts, a magnetic field shielded the air, and carbon already cycled much as it does today. In that setting, simple photosynthesis that released no oxygen appeared, and graphite at Isua and Akilia may hold the first traces of life, though every such claim is still disputed.
reviews.paleoarchean-era: The Paleoarchean turned faint hints of life into a fossil record. Stromatolites at Dresser and Strelley Pool, microfossils at Barberton and in the Fig Tree and Moodies rocks, and mats on tidal flats and around hot springs show microbes thriving in water and perhaps on land. They lived under a nitrogen-rich air with almost no oxygen, on a planet still struck by huge asteroids, such as the one that left the S2 layer. Around them, cratons like Kaapvaal, Pilbara, Zimbabwe and Dharwar grew and stabilized, possibly joining as Vaalbara.
reviews.mesoarchean-era: The Mesoarchean is when the machinery of the modern Earth started to turn. Cyanobacteria began splitting water and releasing oxygen, enough for a brief rise around 2,980–2,960 million years ago, and the Pongola ice spread across a world otherwise kept warm by methane and carbon dioxide. Beneath them, continental crust grew fast, the first signs of modern-style subduction appeared in the Pilbara, and cratons such as the North Atlantic and Yilgarn assembled, perhaps into Ur. Rivers in the Witwatersrand Basin meanwhile gathered the gold that still makes it the world's richest field, while impact structures like Miralga and Maniitsoq remain fiercely argued over.
reviews.neoarchean-era: The Neoarchean finished the job of building continents. Cratons stabilized on deep roots, welded along belts like the Limpopo and the Superior's Algoman collisions, and may have gathered into Kenorland and Arctica. By the eon's end continental crust was about 40 km thick and had likely risen above the sea. Volcanism ran at full heat, from komatiite floods and the Blake River supervolcano to the Ventersdorp lavas and the Great Dyke. Life kept pace: stromatolite reefs spread, and as nickel dwindled and oxygen came in pulses, the stage was being set for a changed atmosphere.
reviews.siderian-period: The Siderian is the period when oxygen won. Cyanobacteria had been making it for ages, but only once surface iron, sulfur and methane were used up did it build up in the air, rusting the seas into banded iron formations and multiplying the planet's minerals. The new gas was toxic to anaerobic life, perhaps causing the first known mass extinction. By destroying methane, it also weakened the greenhouse and helped bring on the Huronian ice. Below, plumes and dike swarms began to tear a supercontinent apart.
reviews.rhyacian-period: The Rhyacian shows oxygen reshaping both rock and life. The huge Lomagundi-Jatuli carbon swing records a surge of oxygen and buried organic matter, red beds show iron rusting on land, and the Makganyene ice may have reached the tropics. Amid these changes, eukaryotes probably arose, though early claims, including Gabon's Francevillian disks, are disputed. On the move below, the Eburnean and Transamazonian collisions began assembling Columbia, while a Karelian lagoon stored the carbon that became shungite.
reviews.orosirian-period: The Orosirian is the period when Columbia came together. Collision after collision, from the Trans-Hudson and Penokean in North America to the Svecofennian in Scandinavia and the Glenburgh and Capricorn in Australia, stitched cratons into Laurentia, Baltica and a supercontinent that kept growing at its edges. Two giant impacts, Vredefort and Sudbury, struck its crust. In the oceans, banded iron formations largely vanished as the deep sea took up oxygen, while Gunflint microbes and the coiled Grypania show life adjusting to the new world.
reviews.statherian-period: The Statherian set the tone of the long, stable Boring Billion, yet it was full of firsts. Sand seas spread across the cratons, and the Yavapai and Mazatzal arcs added new crust to southern Laurentia. In Gabon, natural reactors ran on uranium for a time. Most important for later life, the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes appear in North China, a sign that life in a low-oxygen world was not purely microbial.
reviews.calymmian-period: The Calymmian ties the rise of algae to a planet in slow transition. Eukaryotes that captured cyanobacteria became the first algae, red algal mats grew in India, and Horodyskia and the Volyn microfossils show eukaryotes branching out, even into the deep biosphere. Brief pulses of oxygen may have helped them. On the continents Columbia began to fragment, the Belt Basin filled on Laurentia's edge, and great batholiths rose in what is now the southwestern United States.
reviews.ectasian-period: The Ectasian links one supercontinent's end to another's beginning. A superplume and great igneous provinces, from the 1,380-million-year-old event to the Mackenzie floods, split Columbia apart. Its fragments then collided again in the Kibaran, Grenville and Musgrave orogenies to build Rodinia, with Laurentia at its core. In the shallow seas stromatolites reached their peak, just before grazing life began to push them into a long decline.
reviews.stenian-period: The Stenian shows Rodinia's assembly and life's growing sophistication side by side. Collisions such as the Sveconorwegian thickened crust while the Midcontinent Rift tried and failed to split North America, its lavas now lying beneath Lake Superior. In lakes and seas, life grew more complex: Bangiomorpha left the oldest evidence of sex, Ourasphaira the earliest known fungus, and the Nonesuch and Lakhanda rocks preserved whole microbial communities. Sex in particular sped up evolution, setting up the eukaryote boom to come.
reviews.tonian-period: The Tonian ties a breaking supercontinent to a blossoming of life. As Rodinia rifted, oceans like the Pharusian opened and Gondwana began to assemble through the East African Orogeny. At the same time, a second rise in oxygen and falling sulfide in the seas let eukaryotes diversify, colonize fresh water and grow armor against new predators, while planktonic cyanobacteria spread offshore. The first possible animals, sponge-like fossils, appeared, and the breakup itself may have triggered the Cryogenian ice that followed.
reviews.cryogenian-period: The Cryogenian ties volcanoes to ice and ice to life. The Franklin province's fresh basalt drew down carbon dioxide, and glaciation began barely a million or so years later. The Sturtian ice lasted some 57 million years, a relatively warm interval followed, and then the Marinoan brought the last major snowball. Through it all, sponges survived, testate amoebae appeared, seaweeds grew in a short glacial pause, and red and green algae took over the plankton they would rule until the Permian extinction.
reviews.ediacaran-period: The Ediacaran opens on a limestone cap above the last snowball and closes with a mass extinction. In between, the Pan-African collisions built Gondwana, the Iapetus Ocean opened, and enough oxygen gathered to form an ozone layer. Life answered. The Avalon explosion produced large, soft-bodied fronds and tubes, the first trails crossed microbial mats, and Cloudina built some of the first mineral skeletons. Then, about 538.8 Ma, the Ediacaran biota and the shelled Cloudina vanished abruptly, and Cambrian animals spread into the empty niches.
reviews.terreneuvian-epoch: The Terreneuvian shows the Cambrian explosion getting started. A burrow trace, Treptichnus pedum, marks its base, and small shelly fossils record animals building hard parts in a rapid but orderly sequence. Pulses of oxygen spread into shallow seas and match the radiation of these shelly animals. Meanwhile seas rose over flat continents, Gondwana completed its assembly, and archaeocyath sponges built the first animal reefs. By its close, Sirius Passet in Greenland was preserving whole communities of soft-bodied animals.
reviews.cambrian-series-2-epoch: Series 2 is the Cambrian explosion at full stretch. Trilobites with calcite eyes, giant radiodont predators and the first vertebrates crowd the soft-bodied records of Chengjiang, the Emu Bay Shale and the Burgess Shale. Animals even began to walk onto tidal flats. Then the Kalkarindji flood basalts erupted over more than 2,100,000 km², and the Sinsk Event spread anoxic water across the shelves. The archaeocyath reefs collapsed in the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, though mobile trilobites recovered fast.
reviews.miaolingian-epoch: The Miaolingian is a story of loss and recovery. It begins with the first major trilobite extinction, as Kalkarindji volcanism peaked, and the survivors grew larger tails and thicker cuticles. Anoxic deep water rose again in the Drumian and hampered reefs already in trouble, and the Dresbachian crisis struck around 502 Ma. Meanwhile conodonts appeared, Paradoxides spread worldwide, and the Paleo-Tethys began to open. By the late Cambrian, oxic waters spread and invertebrates moved into open water, starting the great Ordovician radiation.
reviews.furongian-epoch: The Furongian shows how closely Cambrian life tracked ocean oxygen. Spreading anoxia drove the end-Marjuman extinction, and the SPICE excursion that came with it recorded organic matter and pyrite being buried. The oxygen rise that followed helped photosynthetic plankton radiate. Two more extinctions, in the Jiangshanian and at the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, cut trilobites and brachiopods again. Through it all, the first cephalopods and brittle stars appeared, and new mountain belts began to rise along the Iapetus and western South America.
reviews.ordovician-period: The Ordovician turned a Cambrian sea into a Paleozoic one. Marine life radiated until diversity had risen severalfold, with nautiloids at their peak and suspension feeders and swimmers filling the water. Meanwhile the Iapetus Ocean narrowed, letting seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents. By the end of the period, the template for the rest of the Paleozoic seas was set.
reviews.early-ordovician-epoch: The Early Ordovician laid the foundations of the great radiation. Seas rose over the continents, and in those warm shallows new trilobites, echinoderms, brachiopods, sponges and corals appeared, with the first crinoids, eurypterids and horseshoe crabs. Plankton multiplied, feeding both seafloor filter feeders and swimmers. The climate was a super-greenhouse, yet animals thrived. Avalonia broke away and opened the Rheic Ocean, and the Taconic mountains began feeding nutrients to the sea.
reviews.middle-ordovician-epoch: The Middle Ordovician links cooling, plants and oxygen. As the climate shifted toward icehouse, biodiversity rose in step. The first land plants began burying organic carbon, drawing down CO2 and helping atmospheric oxygen rise. Impacts from a shattered asteroid struck at about a hundred times today's rate, and one crater at Decorah filled with exceptional fossils. By about 460 million years ago, glaciers were spreading on Gondwana, beginning the long Early Paleozoic Ice Age.
reviews.late-ordovician-epoch: The Late Ordovician shows a full world undone by ice. Continents collided, terranes drifted, and arthropods began moving onto land as extinction rates crept up through the Katian. Then a sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary spread ice over Gondwana, and sea level fell sharply. The first pulse of extinction came with the cold, and the second with spreading anoxia as the ice retreated. It was the first of the Big Five mass extinctions, yet diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.
reviews.silurian-period: The Silurian is a turnover story. Ancient groups that had survived since the Cambrian or Ordovician, among them asaphid trilobites, nektaspids, eocrinoids and paracrinoids, made their last appearance. In their place, jawed fish diversified while jawless fish declined. Stromatoporoid sponges branched into most of their orders, and nematophytes stood tall on land. Through it all, Armorica drifted north and the Rheic Ocean reached its greatest width.
reviews.llandovery-epoch: The Llandovery is the recovery after the end-Ordovician extinctions. As sea level rose again, surviving groups rebounded, and Lazarus taxa returned from refuges. Reefs spread, land plants covered much of the land, and the first vascular plants, Cooksonia, appeared by the epoch's end. Jawed fish emerged in China, from acanthodian-grade forms to the first bony fish. Meanwhile the Taconic orogeny ended and the Scandian collision of Baltica and Laurentia began.
reviews.wenlock-epoch: The Wenlock tied extinctions to swings in climate and carbon. The Ireviken event, the Lundgreni crisis and the Mulde event each struck, linked to cooling, anoxia or falling sea level. Each left a carbon isotope excursion in the rocks. At the same time, land life was transforming the planet: vascular plants and fungi spread, oxygen began rising toward modern levels, and falling CO2 cooled the climate.
reviews.ludlow-epoch: The Ludlow shows life pushing onto land while the sea endured a crisis. Baragwanathia and the first millipedes were early pioneers ashore. In the Ludfordian, growing ice drained the seas from the shelves, exposing land that plants and microbial mats quickly colonized. The same sea-level low accompanied the Lau event, which hit conodonts hardest and may have ended the palaeoscolecid worms. Sea scorpions rode out the trouble and went on to peak in the Pridoli, as the first sac fungi appeared.
reviews.pridoli-epoch: In the Pridoli, life on land reached a new threshold. Oxygen crossed the level needed for fire, and air-breathing arthropods such as Pneumodesmus, then centipedes and arachnids, built the first simple food webs ashore. In the sea, the Šilalė event cut the conodonts back, ascocerid nautiloids vanished, and the first ray-finned fish appeared. All the while, the Iapetus Ocean closed into Laurussia, and falling seas left thick salt deposits as the new mountains wore away.
reviews.devonian-period: The Devonian's big themes connect. Plants spreading over the land drew down carbon dioxide and buried organic carbon, letting oxygen climb toward modern levels. That richer air may have favored vertebrates that could breathe it. Meanwhile, the seas filled with jawed fishes, led by the armored placoderms, and the crust stayed busy, with the Chaitenia arc docking in Patagonia and Kola's magmas erupting at about the time of a later extinction.
reviews.early-devonian-epoch: The Early Devonian was a time of separation and assembly. Laurussia was completed while the Caledonian mountains collapsed, the Rheic Ocean began to close and the Paleo-Tethys opened behind departing Asian blocks. In the water, jawed fishes rose as jawless ones faded: lobe-fins split into coelacanths and rhipidistians, tetrapodomorphs and lungfish appeared, and cartilaginous fishes followed. On land, rooted plants made the first stable soils, and fossil sites such as the Rhynie chert record arthropods, fungi, and perhaps the first insect living among them.
reviews.middle-devonian-epoch: The Middle Devonian's stories meet in the forests. Cladoxylopsid trees and progymnosperms built the first woods, which buried carbon and may explain a cooling of around 5 °C. On land, wetlands with richer food webs followed, and the Catskill Delta preserved the fishes and plants of a world where vertebrates edged ashore, perhaps as early as the Zachełmie tracks. In the sea, stromatoporoid reefs flourished, but the Kačák and Taghanic events showed how quickly warmth and lost oxygen could undo them.
reviews.late-devonian-epoch: The Late Devonian links the rise of trees to the fall of the seas. Archaeopteris forests bound soils, made rivers meander, drew down carbon dioxide and fed nutrients into the oceans, where blooms stripped away oxygen. Those anoxic seas preserved organic matter that became oil, and they helped drive the Kellwasser and Hangenberg extinctions, which ended the reefs, the placoderms and most jawless fishes. Impacts and flood basalts struck too, though most seem mistimed to be the main cause. Through it all, seeds appeared, and limbed tetrapods such as Acanthostega survived bottlenecks that favored forms less tied to water.
reviews.carboniferous-period: The period's opening entries sketch its themes. Cordaitales grew in the coal swamps that give the Carboniferous its name, while lobe-finned fish such as Rhizodus hunted its rivers. Fossil beds like Granton preserved rare soft-bodied animals. And Siberia's collision with Kazakhstania made it effectively part of Pangaea, the supercontinent the period was assembling.
reviews.mississippian-subperiod: The Mississippian joined the world together and then chilled it. Gondwana, Laurussia and Siberia came together as Pangaea, raising the Variscan, Ouachita and Alleghanian mountains and splitting the oceans into isolated regions where marine life boomed. As the main ice age took hold, sea level fell, the Serpukhovian extinction struck tropical species, and deltas spread the Millstone Grit. On land, tetrapods left Romer's gap behind: temnospondyls flourished, reptiliomorphs appeared, and amniotes, with eggs that survive on dry land, arose while insects took to the air.
reviews.pennsylvanian-subperiod: The Pennsylvanian's coal forests, air and ice were tied together. The forests buried carbon as peat, lifting oxygen to its highest level and helping drive carbon dioxide so low that ice sheets spread across Gondwana, while sea level rose and fell in cyclothems. Giant arthropods such as Meganeura and Arthropleura thrived in that air until a cooler, drier climate collapsed the rainforests. The collapse favored amniotes, which had split into synapsids and sauropsids, and seed plants such as conifers, while the Urals rose and Pangaea was sutured.
reviews.permian-period: The Permian's big picture is one continent and one harsh climate. Pangaea, stretching from pole to equator, created the megamonsoon that swung its interior between drought and rain. In the south, the Gondwanide mountains rose and Glossopteris forests spread, building coal as the ice waned. Among the animals, quiet splits such as that of the lizard lineage set up the reptile world to come.
reviews.cisuralian-epoch: The Cisuralian turned an icehouse into a greenhouse. After carbon dioxide hit its record low, it rose again as drowned coal swamps stopped burying carbon, and the Artinskian warming melted most of the southern ice. Pangaea gained its last pieces as Kazakhstania met Baltica and the Urals rose, while volcanic provinces from Skagerrak to Panjal and Choiyoi erupted. On land, pelycosaurs ruled and deserts such as the Coconino dunes spread, while insects and beetles diversified and the first therapsids split off.
reviews.guadalupian-epoch: The Guadalupian's peaks and its ending are linked. Reefs reached their height, from the Capitan Reef of Texas outward, and therapsids such as dinocephalians took over the land after Olson's Extinction. Then sea level fell, the climate cooled, and the Emeishan Traps erupted, together driving the Capitanian extinction. Its losses opened the way for gorgonopsians as top predators and for ceratitid ammonoids, while the first cynodonts appeared soon after.
reviews.lopingian-epoch: The Lopingian ends in a single chain of cause and effect. The Siberian Traps heated coal and salt-rich rocks, releasing gases that more than doubled carbon dioxide, drove temperatures to as much as 35 °C and acidified the seas. Oceans lost their oxygen and filled with hydrogen sulfide, and the carbon isotope record bears the volcanic signature. The result was the Great Dying, which ended the trilobites, the Paleozoic corals, the gorgonopsians, the Glossopteris forests and countless insects. Impact ideas are largely rejected; the archosauromorphs and cynodonts that survived would inherit the world.
reviews.triassic-period: The Triassic was shaped by sheer size. Pangaea's land area peaked once Siberia and the China cratons joined, and that vast landmass drove a megamonsoon that brought rain to the once-dry Colorado Plateau. The greenhouse climate left even the poles without ice. Space rocks struck this world too, among them the impact that left North Dakota's buried Red Wing Creek structure, once wrongly tied to three other craters as a single event.
reviews.early-triassic-epoch: Every story in the Early Triassic runs back to the Siberian Traps. Their repeated pulses kept the climate the hottest of the Phanerozoic, starved the seas of oxygen and triggered fresh crises such as the Smithian–Spathian extinction. Recovery was slow and uneven: microbial reefs and Lystrosaurus herds filled the gaps first, and faunas looked much alike worldwide. Yet the same years produced the first frogs, ichthyosaurs, sauropterygians and dinosauromorph footprints. By the Latest Olenekian Cooling, as temperatures fell about 6 °C, the stage was ready for the Middle Triassic rebound.
reviews.middle-triassic-epoch: The Middle Triassic is the story of a world rebuilding. Some 4–6 million years after the extinction, carbon-isotope swings calmed and complex food webs returned, from coral-building seas to Chinese lakes with six or more trophic levels. Marine reptiles crowded the expanding Tethys, preserved in lagoons such as Monte San Giorgio, while archosaurs took over the land and the first flies, stem turtles and lepidosaurs appeared. At the same time the crust was moving: rifts opened along the future Atlantic, and Cimmerian blocks drifted north to close the Paleo-Tethys. A long cooling from 242 Ma held until the Wrangellia eruptions broke it.
reviews.late-triassic-epoch: The Late Triassic began with a climate shock and ended with a catastrophe. The Wrangellia eruptions brought the Carnian rains, and in that wet spell dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and new plankton diversified while ammonoids and crinoids suffered. Through the Norian, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, the first true turtles and mammaliaforms spread, even as crurotarsans still held more niches and impacts such as Manicouagan struck. Then the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted in brief, violent pulses, and the End-Triassic Thermal Event, acidified oceans and anoxia followed. The resulting mass extinction removed the crurotarsans and many other groups, leaving the land to the dinosaurs.
reviews.jurassic-period: Two quiet trends frame the Jurassic. As the continents drifted apart, the Pangean megamonsoon that had driven Triassic weather kept weakening, and Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried out. Among the animals, the old temnospondyls faded to a single surviving group, the brachyopoids. In their place the lissamphibians began to diversify, giving rise to the first modern frogs and salamanders.
reviews.early-jurassic-epoch: The Early Jurassic turned on two forces: a supercontinent splitting and a volcanic province erupting. As Pangaea rifted into Laurasia and Gondwana, new seaways such as the Viking Corridor and the Central American Seaway opened, the Central Atlantic began to form, and the Andes and the Pacific plate were born. On land, dinosaurs took over, sauropods became the leading plant-eaters, and the first ornithischians and crabs appeared, while the seas filled with ammonites, plesiosaurs and modern sharks. Then, about 183 million years ago, the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions warmed the climate by 4–8 °C, stripped oxygen from the oceans and drove the Toarcian extinction. The Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden preserves that stagnant sea in exquisite detail.
reviews.middle-jurassic-epoch: The Middle Jurassic was a time of branching. Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs, mammals forked into the lines leading to monotremes and therians, and lizards, snakes, salamanders and multituberculates all enter the record. Behind that radiation lay a changing planet: seas rising from the Aalenian, a cool interval with possible brief ice ages, a new Gulf of Mexico and a widening Atlantic Gateway. At sea, ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaurs and cryptoclidid plesiosaurs replaced older lines, preserved in deposits such as the Oxford Clay. By the close, the Kimmeridgian Warm Interval was bringing heat and rain, and China's Yanliao Biota was recording it all under layers of ash.
reviews.late-jurassic-epoch: The Late Jurassic was a world of giants on new continents. As new ocean floor split East from West Gondwana, the Arctic began to open and Cimmeria docked against Laurasia, western North America rose in the Nevadan orogeny and its floodplains filled with the Morrison sauropods. Stegosaurs peaked, the first ceratopsians and eutherian mammals appeared, and in Solnhofen's still lagoons Archaeopteryx left its feathered skeleton. A cool interval set in about 150 million years ago, the Morokweng asteroid struck, and Tamu Massif erupted on the Pacific floor. The period ended not with a mass extinction but with a turnover, driven mostly by falling and rising seas.
reviews.cretaceous-period: Four big stories frame the Cretaceous. Gondwana finished breaking apart into the southern continents, birthing the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans and isolating dinosaur faunas on separate landmasses. Small, fast-recycled ocean plates made the basins shallower, so seas rose until a third of today's land lay underwater. In those warm, shallow seas, coccolithophores laid down more chalk than in any other period, the white cliffs of Dover among it. And on Tethyan shelves, rudist bivalves crowded out stony corals as the main reef builders, until they collapsed before the period's end.
reviews.early-cretaceous-epoch: The Early Cretaceous was shaped from below. Flood basalts and hotspots, from Paraná–Etendeka to Kerguelen and Ontong Java, helped tear Gondwana apart, opened the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans, and pumped out the carbon behind the Weissert warming and the Selli anoxic event. Climate swung between cold snaps with glacial dropstones and the start of the Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse. Through it all, life on land changed for good: flowering plants appeared and began to take over, pollinating insects coevolved with them, and grasses, ants and termites arrived. Fossil sites from Jehol and Las Hoyas to Crato and Burmese amber caught feathered dinosaurs, early birds and the first marsupial and placental relatives in the act.
reviews.late-cretaceous-epoch: The Late Cretaceous was a hothouse world that slowly cooled, then ended in a single violent moment. Seas rose high enough to split North America and Africa, while marine reptiles, mosasaurs and giant pterosaurs ruled sea and sky. Continents kept breaking apart: Zealandia, India and the North Atlantic all began their drift. Then the Chicxulub asteroid struck, and about 76% of species vanished, among them every non-avian dinosaur, pterosaur and ammonite. Birds, crocodilians and mammals, all lineages that had appeared during the epoch, came through to inherit the world.
reviews.paleocene-epoch: In a single epoch, the Paleocene turned a devastated planet into a thriving one. Mammals and birds spread into every niche the dinosaurs had left, from pantodonts and creodonts to the first penguins and primate forerunners. Plates kept moving: India met Asia, Greenland broke free, and the North Atlantic Igneous Province poured out lava from Canada to Britain. Climate swung through hyperthermals and brief cool spells, until a long warming ended in the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. That carbon spike closed the epoch and opened the Eocene hothouse.
reviews.eocene-epoch: The Eocene ran from the warmest stretch of the Cenozoic to the first great ice sheets on Antarctica. In its hothouse, palms grew in Alaska, and modern mammals, horses, bats and the first whales spread across the world. Then the climate turned around 49 million years ago, helped by the Azolla fern and by new ocean gateways around Antarctica. As carbon dioxide fell and ice grew, the epoch ended in the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, which took Basilosaurus and nearly all archaic whales. The icehouse world that followed is the one that leads to the ice ages.
reviews.oligocene-epoch: Ice on Antarctica set the tone for the whole Oligocene. Falling carbon dioxide froze the poles, and the growing ice dropped sea level about 75 metres, which closed the Turgai Strait and let Asian mammals overrun Europe in the Grande Coupure. Opening gateways south of Australia and South America let a current circle Antarctica, while grasses spread and favored larger mammals such as Paraceratherium. Meanwhile the crust broke and buckled: Arabia began to pull away from Africa, the East African Rift began to form, and the San Andreas Fault began to grow.
reviews.miocene-epoch: The Miocene was a long slide from warmth into cold, with one great warm spell in the middle. Rising mountains drove much of it: the Andes and Tibet climbed, their rain shadows and monsoons dried the land, and grasses spread until grazing horses outnumbered browsers. A land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia closed the Tethys and let apes, elephants and many other animals cross. Flood basalts on the Columbia Plateau came with the Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum, and a sharp cooling step afterward grew the East Antarctic Ice Sheet to roughly its present size. In the shrinking Paratethys and the newly joined Americas, the same story played out: changing seaways set the fate of the life within them.
reviews.late-miocene: The Late Miocene was a world getting colder and drier. Cooling dried the air worldwide, and C4 grasses spread so widely that herbivores without high-crowned teeth went extinct. Seaways closed and basins dried: the Caspian became landlocked, the Paratethys shrank to a megalake, and the Mediterranean itself dried out in the Messinian salinity crisis. Through it all, in Africa, the human and chimpanzee lines parted, and early hominins such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin appeared.
reviews.pliocene-epoch: The Pliocene began warm, with carbon dioxide close to today's level and sea level about 25 m higher at its peak. Then geography turned the dial. The Isthmus of Panama joined the Americas, setting off the Great American Interchange and pushing heat and moisture north, and by 2.7 million years ago ice was spreading across the Northern Hemisphere. Savannas spread across East Africa as the climate dried. On them walked a growing cast of hominins, from Ardi and Lucy to the first Homo, who left footprints at Laetoli and the first stone tools at Lomekwi.
reviews.gelasian-age: Ice set the terms of the Gelasian. Ice at both poles dried the globe, grasslands spread, and loess piled up on China's plateau. In that drier Africa, hominins branched out, from Paranthropus with its heavy molars to Homo habilis, Homo erectus and the Oldowan and Acheulean toolkits. With the Americas now joined, South America's native predators faded and northern animals poured in. And Homo erectus walked out of Africa, reaching Dmanisi and settling southern Europe and Asia.
reviews.calabrian-age: The Calabrian opened with people at Dmanisi, the oldest human remains outside Africa, and within a few hundred thousand years Homo erectus had reached China, Java and the Levant. Behind them the older hominin lines thinned out: the australopithecines died out about 1.7 million years ago and Paranthropus about 1.2 million years ago. Fire runs through the chapter as a thread, from disputed charred bones at Wonderwerk Cave to cooked fish at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov. Meanwhile the climate itself changed gear in the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, as ice-age cycles stretched from about 41,000 to 100,000 years. Supereruptions in New Zealand and New Mexico, impacts in Ghana and Australasia, and flips of the magnetic field kept marking the rock as the age went by.
reviews.chibanian-age: The Chibanian began with Earth's last magnetic flip and ended in the meltwater of Termination II. In between, the ice ages beat to the new 100,000-year rhythm, swinging from giant glaciations like MIS 12 and MIS 6 to the long, warm MIS 11, and those swings broke Britain from France in two megafloods. Animals adjusted: woolly mammoths replaced steppe mammoths, bison crossed into North America, and the mammoth steppe spread with each cold spell. The human family branched too: Neanderthals and Denisovans parted from each other, while Homo sapiens appeared at Jebel Irhoud about 315,000 years ago. Fire became a daily tool, spears and Levallois cores showed planning, and burials at Krapina hinted at a concern for the dead.
reviews.late-pleistocene-age: The Late Pleistocene began in the warmth of the Eemian, when seas stood 6 to 9 m higher and hippos reached England, and ended with the sudden warming that closed the Younger Dryas. In between, the Last Glacial Period built ice up to 3 km thick, dropped sea level about 125 m and opened land bridges from Beringia to Tasmania. Modern humans used those bridges: one expansion out of Africa about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago carried people to Australia, Europe, Siberia and finally the Americas, mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans on the way. As they arrived, megafauna vanished, 88% of species in Australia and every mammal over 1,000 kg in the Americas, though how much people and climate each contributed is still debated. When the ice finally melted, meltwater pulses, giant lakes and floods reshaped coasts and rivers.
reviews.greenlandian-age: The Greenlandian is a single chain of cause and effect running from ice to water. The Younger Dryas ended, the northern ice sheets melted fast, and meltwater raised the sea about 60 m, drowning Doggerland and the Bering land bridge. Forests and wetlands replaced the mammoth steppe, and its giants dwindled, from the last mainland woolly mammoths to Smilodon and the American mastodon, though how far hunters were to blame is still argued. In the same warmer, wetter world, people first domesticated sheep, goats, cattle, pigs and cereals in the Fertile Crescent, and farming then rose independently from New Guinea to Mesoamerica.
reviews.northgrippian-age: The Northgrippian opened with the 8.2-kiloyear cooling, probably set off when lakes Agassiz and Ojibway flooded into the North Atlantic. Warmth returned and peaked in the Holocene Climatic Optimum, while the Laurentide Ice Sheet finally collapsed and the last land bridges to Tasmania and New Guinea drowned. As sea-level rise slowed, deltas such as the Mississippi's began to build, and farming spread into Europe. Then the long warming trend ended: neoglacial cooling began and the green Sahara dried into desert. Volcanoes such as Mazama, Kikai and Cerro Blanco, and impacts from Morasko to Henbury, marked the age's surface.
reviews.meghalayan-age: The Meghalayan began with the 4.2-kiloyear drought and has ended, so far, in a world reshaped by people. For most of it, nature set the pace: monsoons weakened, the central Sahara became a lasting desert, and eruptions from Thera to Samalas and Tambora brought volcanic winters that helped shape the Little Ice Age. People steadily added to the pressure, hunting moa, dodos and Steller's sea cow to extinction. From the Industrial Revolution on, greenhouse gases climbed, carbon dioxide passed 400 ppm at Mauna Loa, and warming, rising seas, acidifying oceans and bleaching reefs became the age's defining signals. Through it all, great earthquakes and eruptions kept reminding people of the planet's own power.

closing:
Earth began as wreckage. About 4.57 billion years ago, a collapsing cloud of hydrogen gave birth to the Sun, and the leftover disc of dust clumped into planets. Earth was largely built within 10 to 20 million years. Then a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia slammed into it, and the debris thrown into orbit gathered into the Moon. Iron sank to the center to form the core, and its churning metal raised the magnetic field that still shields the surface. The oldest intact rock that survives from that hellish first chapter, the Acasta Gneiss of northern Canada, is 4.03 billion years old.

Life appeared early and worked quietly. By about 3.48 billion years ago, microbial mats were building layered mounds called stromatolites in what is now Western Australia. Around 3.2 billion years ago, some microbes began releasing oxygen as waste, although scientists still argue over exactly when. For ages the oceans' dissolved iron soaked that oxygen up and rusted into iron ore. Then, between about 2.46 and 2.06 billion years ago, oxygen finally built up in the air, an irreversible change called the Great Oxidation Event. Somewhere in this deep past, perhaps near 3 billion years ago, the crust broke into moving plates, though the timing is still debated.

The next stretch looks slow but changed everything. Cells with a nucleus, the eukaryotes, appeared by about 2 billion years ago, and the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction comes from a red alga 1.05 billion years old. Continents gathered into supercontinents, Columbia and then Rodinia, and broke apart again. Between 717 and 635 million years ago, glaciers reached sea level near the equator. Whether Earth froze into a full snowball or kept a slushy band of open water is still disputed. After the thaw came the Ediacaran biota, large soft-bodied creatures that are the oldest known complex multicellular life.

Animals then took over the oceans, and plants and animals took over the land.
