From 538.8 million years ago, the Cambrian explosion produced the first representatives of most modern animal phyla within about 20 to 25 million years. Animals grew skeletons and began burrowing into the seafloor. The first land plants left spores about 470 million years ago. Forests rose by about 390 million years ago, and limbed vertebrates were walking by 365 million years ago. Around 335 million years ago, the continents locked together into Pangaea, a supercontinent that lasted about 160 million years.

Catastrophe pruned this world again and again. The worst came 252 million years ago, when the Siberian Traps poured out lava and gas, warming the planet and souring the seas. About 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species vanished. Dinosaurs rose from the survivors around 233 million years ago and ruled the land for most of the next 167 million years. Their reign ended 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about 10 kilometers wide struck off the Yucatán Peninsula. About 76% of species disappeared, including every dinosaur except the birds.

Mammals inherited the emptied world, and the planet slowly cooled. About 56 million years ago, thousands of billions of tonnes of carbon flooded the air and oceans, and global temperatures jumped about 5 to 8 °C. India rammed into Asia, and the Himalayas began to rise. About 33.9 million years ago, falling carbon dioxide let ice build up on Antarctica, opening the icehouse world that continues today. Grasslands spread, the human and chimpanzee lineages split about 8 million years ago, and Panama joined the Americas. By 2.58 million years ago, ice sheets were spreading across the Northern Hemisphere.

People are newcomers to this story. Homo erectus appeared in Africa about 2 million years ago. The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 315,000 years old. Modern humans left Africa between 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, and the Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago. The last ice age peaked between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Then, 11,700 years ago, Greenland warmed by about 8 °C within 40 years, the Holocene began, and farming soon took root in the Fertile Crescent.

Now one species has become a geologic force. Carbon dioxide stayed near 280 parts per million for 10,000 years before the mid-18th century, and it has since risen 54%. The global average temperature climbed from 14 °C in 1951–1980 to 15 °C in 2013–2017. Lake mud in Ontario holds a plutonium spike from 1952 hydrogen-bomb tests. In 2024, stratigraphers voted against naming a formal Anthropocene epoch, but the debate over the term goes on. Earth's history has been written by collisions, volcanoes, ice and microbes, and its newest layer is being written by humans.

entries.title: A dying star seeds the Sun's birth cloud

facts.text: A supernova shock wave in a dense part of the Milky Way seeded the region with heavy elements later built into Earth.
Calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions, which formed 2 million years before chondrules, are a key signature of this supernova.
Its shock wave may have triggered the solar nebula's collapse and set it rotating.

entries.text: Some of the atoms in Earth were forged in a star that exploded before the Sun existed. A supernova, the blast of a dying star, sent a shock wave through a dense part of the Milky Way and seeded it with heavy elements. That same shock wave may have triggered the collapse of the solar nebula, the gas cloud that became the Solar System, and set it spinning. Its signature survives in calcium–aluminum-rich inclusions, specks that formed 2 million years before chondrules.

entries.title: The Sun ignites and the Solar System begins
entries.article: Formation and evolution of the Solar System

facts.text: The Sun formed from the rapid collapse of a hydrogen molecular cloud, about 25,000 light years from the center of the Milky Way.
The spinning cloud flattened into a protoplanetary disc, the raw material of Earth, around the young T Tauri Sun.
Calcium–aluminium-rich inclusions, the first solids to condense from the hot disc, date to 4,567.30 ± 0.16 Ma; this age defines the Solar System's start and the Hadean's.
The young Sun's solar wind cleared out most disc material not yet gathered into larger bodies; by 10 million years the disc's gas was gone.
The Sun has grown about 30% brighter since it formed.

entries.text: Every date in Earth's history is counted from a handful of tiny white specks. About 25,000 light years from the center of the Milky Way, a hydrogen cloud collapsed rapidly and gave birth to the Sun. The spinning cloud flattened into a protoplanetary disk, a pancake of gas and dust circling the young T Tauri Sun, and it held the raw material of Earth. The first solids to condense from that hot disk were calcium–aluminum-rich inclusions. They date to 4,567.30 ± 0.16 million years ago, and that age defines the start of the Solar System and of the Hadean Eon. The young Sun did not wait long to tidy up. Its solar wind blew away most of the disk material not yet gathered into larger bodies, and by 10 million years the gas was gone. The star at the center was not yet the Sun we know. It has grown about 30% brighter since it formed, a slow change that shapes the puzzle of {{ref:hade-007}}.

entries.title: The iron catastrophe gives Earth its core

facts.text: In a geologically brief, postulated event, the iron catastrophe, dense iron and nickel sank to the centre of the young Earth to form its core.
Radioactive heating and leftover accretion heat melted the planet enough for metal to move; the sinking metal released energy in a runaway process.
Timing is uncertain: hafnium–tungsten models give 30–100 million years after the first solids, depending on giant-impact mixing; other sources say 10 or about 500 million years in.
It separated a metallic core, where siderophile metals gathered, from a primitive mantle, giving Earth its layered structure of core, mantle and crust.
The spinning molten metal set up Earth's magnetic field, which still shields the atmosphere and life from the solar wind.

entries.text: Earth's magnetic shield was born when a planet's worth of metal fell inward. Radioactive heating and heat left from accretion melted the young Earth enough for metal to move. Dense iron and nickel then sank to the center, and the sinking itself released energy, driving a runaway process called the iron catastrophe. It was geologically brief, though still a postulated event. The result was Earth's layered structure: a metallic core, where siderophile, or iron-loving, metals gathered, beneath a primitive mantle and, later, a crust. The spinning molten metal set up the magnetic field that still shields the atmosphere and life from the solar wind. When it happened is uncertain. Hafnium–tungsten models give 30–100 million years after the first solids; other sources say 10 or about 500 million years in.

entries.title: Did plates already move in the Hadean?

facts.text: Radiogenic heat and water still in the mantle lowered its viscosity, so Hadean mantle convection was vigorous.
Whether this convection drove plate tectonics or stayed trapped under a rigid lid is still debated.
Hadean oceans are thought to have triggered plate tectonics; one view has it starting vigorously, then slowing in the Archean.
Removal of the CO2-rich early atmosphere, helped by subduction of carbonate, is cited as evidence for Hadean plate tectonics.
Zircon evidence comes almost entirely from one Australian locality, and some geologists think those zircons formed in impacts.

entries.title: Earth assembles from colliding debris

facts.text: In runaway accretion, dust and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies, building Earth.
The proto-Earth formed at the cool outer edge of the habitable zone and grew through a series of giant impacts.
Accretion was largely complete within 10–20 million years, though one estimate allows 70–100 million and 2023 evidence suggests only about three million.
Accretion began soon after the first solids formed; Earth's age, 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years, marks the final stages of accretion and differentiation.
Shortly after it formed, Earth spun fast: a day lasted only about six hours.

entries.text: A day on the newborn Earth lasted only about six hours. The planet had just been built by collision. In runaway accretion, dust and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies, and the bigger a body grew, the faster it swept up more. The proto-Earth took shape at the cool outer edge of the habitable zone, the band around a star where liquid water can exist. It grew through a series of giant impacts. The work was fast. Accretion began soon after the first solids formed in {{ref:hade-002}} and was largely complete within 10–20 million years. One estimate allows 70–100 million years, while 2023 evidence suggests only about three million. Earth's official age, 4.54 ± 0.05 billion years, marks the final stages of accretion and differentiation, the sorting of the planet into layers. The fast spin was a leftover of all those collisions, and it would not last.

entries.title: A magma ocean covers the young Earth

facts.text: A magma ocean about 200 km deep covered Earth, melted by the Moon-forming and other impacts and by heat from forming the core.
Earth probably had a series of magma oceans from giant impacts; the last, from the Moon-forming impact, may have reached 2,000 km deep.
Siderophile elements in the mantle record magma-ocean depths of about 1,000 km during accretion.
The initial magma ocean solidified within about 5 million years, leaving hot volatiles that formed a heavy CO2 atmosphere.
Evidence is weaker than for the Moon, because Earth's crust is recycled and its mantle mixed.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree: the Magma ocean page cites chemical evidence, but the Giant-impact hypothesis page says there is no evidence Earth ever had one.
entries.text: For a time, Earth had no ground at all. Giant impacts and the heat of forming the core melted its outer layers into a magma ocean, a global sea of molten rock about 200 km deep. There were probably several such oceans. The last, raised by {{ref:hade-008}}, may have reached 2,000 km down, and siderophile elements in the mantle record depths of about 1,000 km during accretion. The first magma ocean solidified within about 5 million years. Hot volatiles it left behind formed a heavy carbon dioxide atmosphere. The evidence is weaker than on the Moon, because Earth recycles its crust and mixes its mantle. Sources also disagree: one cites chemical traces, another finds no evidence Earth ever had one.

entries.title: Why the early Earth did not freeze

facts.text: The young Sun gave only about 70% of today's output, so early Earth should have frozen, yet it seems to have had liquid water and life.
Models find that at 4.5 Ga, under a 30% dimmer Sun, at least 0.1 bar of CO2 was needed to stay above freezing; 10 bar is a plausible upper limit.
Greenhouse gases are thought to have kept the oceans from freezing; the carbonate–silicate cycle lets CO2 build up when cold slows weathering.
The Sun became a main-sequence star about 4.5 Ga and has brightened since; it now shines 1.4 times as bright as 4.6 Ga.
How much CO2 there was is still debated; other proposed answers include a lower surface albedo and mass loss from the young Sun.

entries.contested_note: How early Earth stayed warm under the dim Sun is an unsolved problem, and the amount of CO2 is still debated.
entries.text: By rights, the young Earth should have been a snowball. The young Sun gave only about 70% of today's output, yet Earth seems to have had liquid water and life. How it stayed warm is an unsolved problem. The favored answer is a greenhouse. Models find that 4.5 billion years ago, under a 30% dimmer Sun, staying above freezing took at least 0.1 bar of carbon dioxide. A plausible upper limit is 10 bar. A natural thermostat may have helped: in the carbonate–silicate cycle, cold slows the weathering of rock, so carbon dioxide builds up. How much there really was is still debated, and other proposals include a darker, less reflective surface and mass loss from the young Sun. The Sun has brightened ever since and now shines 1.4 times as bright as 4.6 billion years ago.

entries.title: Theia strikes and the Moon is born

facts.text: A Mars-sized protoplanet, Theia, struck the proto-Earth about 20–100 million years after the Solar System formed.
Debris thrown into orbit lingered as rings for a few million years, then gathered into the Moon.
The impact probably vaporized much of Earth's crust and upper mantle, wrapping the planet in rock vapor and disrupting any earlier water.
It is the favored explanation of the Moon's origin among astronomers; lunar rocks date the Moon to 4.53 ± 0.01 billion years.
The Moon's pull steadied Earth's wobbling axis of rotation, making climate more regular.

entries.text: The Moon is the wreckage of a planetary collision. In the explanation most astronomers favor, a Mars-sized protoplanet called Theia struck the proto-Earth about 20–100 million years after the Solar System formed. The blow probably vaporized much of Earth's crust and upper mantle. The planet was wrapped in rock vapor, and any water already present was disrupted. Debris thrown into orbit lingered as rings for a few million years, then gathered into the Moon. Lunar rocks date it to 4.53 ± 0.01 billion years. The impact also reshaped Earth for good. It fed the last and deepest of the {{ref:hade-006}} episodes, and it stripped away the planet's first atmosphere. Over the long run, the Moon's pull steadied Earth's wobbling axis of rotation. That steadiness made the climate more regular, a quiet gift to everything that would later live here.

entries.title: The Moon grows a pale crust

facts.text: About 100 million years after the Moon formed, its first crust, made of anorthosite, separated out from the magma below.
This ferroan anorthosite is read as plagioclase crystals that floated up through the lunar magma ocean, which was at first 200–300 km thick.
Anorthosite makes the pale lunar highlands, about 80% of the Moon's surface; ferroan anorthosites are dated to about 4.4 Ga.

entries.text: The bright patches on the Moon are its oldest skin. About 100 million years after the Moon formed, light plagioclase crystals floated up through its magma ocean, which was at first 200–300 km thick. They built the first crust, made of anorthosite, a pale rock dominated by that mineral. Ferroan anorthosites date to about 4.4 billion years ago, and anorthosite still forms the lunar highlands, about 80% of the Moon's surface.

entries.title: Earth's first oceans condense

facts.text: Zircon crystals show that liquid water and an atmosphere existed by 4.404 ± 0.008 Ga, very soon after Earth formed.
As the crust and surface cooled, water vapor condensed into a superocean covering nearly the whole planet.
The oceans stayed liquid despite the heat because the air pressure was about 27 atmospheres.
The water most likely came from mantle outgassing; isotopes make comets an unlikely main source.
Earth may have been mostly a water world between 4.4 and 4.3 Ga; dissolved CO2 probably made the seas slightly acidic, about pH 5.5.

entries.text: Earth had oceans almost as soon as it had a surface. Zircon crystals show that liquid water and an atmosphere existed by 4.404 ± 0.008 billion years ago, very soon after the planet formed. As the crust and surface cooled, water vapor condensed into a superocean that covered nearly the whole planet. Earth may have been mostly a water world between 4.4 and 4.3 billion years ago. The seas were hot, yet they stayed liquid, because the air pressed down at about 27 atmospheres and high pressure keeps water from boiling. Where did the water come from? Most likely from the mantle itself, released by outgassing. Isotopes, versions of an element that differ slightly in weight, make comets an unlikely main source. The water was not the clear sea of today. Dissolved carbon dioxide probably made it slightly acidic, about pH 5.5. Still, these were the oceans where life would later begin.

entries.title: A Jack Hills zircon, the oldest mineral on Earth

facts.text: The oldest dated mineral on Earth is a zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, 4.404 ± 0.008 Ga old.
It lies in a metamorphosed conglomerate of the Narryer Gneiss terrane; most zircons there are only 3.6–3.8 Ga old.
The 4.404 Ga grain is a slight outlier; the oldest consistently dated zircons are closer to 4.35 Ga.
Hadean zircons crystallized at fairly low temperatures from evolved melts and carry heavy oxygen, hinting at crust-forming processes like today's.
Hadean zircon is rare worldwide because plate tectonics recycled the crust that held it.

They are rare worldwide because plate tectonics recycled the crust that held them.

entries.title: A second, carbon dioxide atmosphere

facts.text: Early Hadean Earth first had a very thick, hydride-rich atmosphere like the solar nebula; the Moon-forming impact stripped this primary atmosphere away.
The cooling magma ocean released carbon dioxide and water, giving a heavy CO2 atmosphere at about 230 °C and over 27 atmospheres.
Outgassing from the crust had built this secondary atmosphere by 4,404 Ma at the latest, a minimum age.
Comets and carbonaceous chondrites added water and possibly organic molecules.
Volcanic outgassing and impacts later turned it into the nitrogen- and CO2-rich, weakly reducing atmosphere of the Paleoarchean.

entries.text: Earth lost its first sky in a single blow. Early Hadean Earth had a very thick atmosphere rich in hydrides, hydrogen compounds like those of the solar nebula, and the Moon-forming impact stripped it away. A second atmosphere rose from below. The cooling magma ocean released carbon dioxide and water, building a heavy CO2 atmosphere at about 230 °C and more than 27 atmospheres of pressure. Outgassing from the crust had built it by 4,404 million years ago at the latest. Comets and carbonaceous chondrites added water and possibly organic molecules. Over time, volcanic outgassing and impacts turned this air into the nitrogen- and CO2-rich, weakly reducing atmosphere of the Paleoarchean.

entries.title: Earth's first solid crust

facts.text: Zircons formed 4.4 Ga show the crust solidified about 100 million years after Earth formed; one source puts a stable crust in place by 4,433 Ma.
The first crust, formed as Earth's molten outer layer cooled, was probably mafic; partial melting of it made the first, more felsic continental crust.
The earliest crust probably formed like the Moon's first crust, from similar materials separating out of the magma.
Hafnium isotopes in zircons fit crust forming from 4.5 Ga onward, possibly an early reservoir like continental crust.
Only mineral grains survive from the Hadean crust; the oldest whole rock formations at the surface are Archean.

entries.text: Only crumbs survive of Earth's first crust. Zircons formed 4.4 billion years ago show that the crust solidified about 100 million years after the planet formed. One source puts a stable crust in place by 4,433 million years ago. It formed as the molten outer layer cooled, probably much like the Moon's first crust, from similar materials separating out of the magma. It was probably mafic, dark rock rich in iron and magnesium. Partial melting of it then made the first, more felsic continental crust, paler and richer in silica. Hafnium isotopes in zircons fit crust forming from 4.5 billion years ago onward. Yet only mineral grains remain; the oldest whole rock formations at the surface are Archean.

entries.title: A cool early Earth, and a paradox

facts.text: The cool early Earth hypothesis holds that temperatures were cold enough to freeze water between about 4.4 and 4.0 Ga.
The source calls this somewhat of a paradox, since zircons show liquid water by 4.404 Ga.
The Precambrian page allows a possible cool period within the bombardment-dominated Hadean.

Another view allows a possible cool period within a Hadean otherwise dominated by bombardment. The question remains open.

entries.title: The last impact that boiled the oceans

facts.text: Impacts declined; the last one big enough to vaporize the oceans struck about 4.3 Ga, and life probably emerged after it.
Later Hadean impacts were thousands to millions of years apart, but life stayed vulnerable to large ones.
Before about 4.3–4.2 Ga, Earth was very hostile to life.

entries.text: Before about 4.3–4.2 billion years ago, Earth was very hostile to life. Impacts were the reason. They declined over time, and the last one big enough to vaporize the oceans struck about 4.3 billion years ago. Life probably emerged only after it. Later Hadean impacts came thousands to millions of years apart, but any young life stayed vulnerable to the largest of them.

entries.title: Possible microfossils in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt

facts.text: Possible fossil microorganisms occur in hydrothermal-vent deposits from an ancient seabed in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq Belt, dated 3.77 to 4.28 Ga.
If 4.28 Ga old, they would be the oldest record of life, suggesting it emerged almost at once, in geological terms, after the oceans formed.
Silica-rich waters, chemical gardens, hydrothermal fluids and volcanic ejecta can mimic such shapes, so the traces may not be biological.

entries.title: LUCA, the ancestor of all life

facts.text: A 2024 molecular-clock study put LUCA, ancestor of all living things, at about 4.2 Ga (range 4.33–4.09 Ga): a genetic estimate, not a fossil.
That implies only about 100–200 million years between life's origin and LUCA, as the first habitable environments likely formed around 4.3–4.4 Ga.
A 2018 molecular-clock study concluded LUCA predated the Late Heavy Bombardment, making it over 3.9 Ga.
Other estimates run from 4.52–4.48 Ga (2018) to 4.2–3.6 Ga (2022) and 3.8–3.5 Ga (2000-era); most agree it existed by 3.5 Ga.

verification.title: The nature of the last universal common ancestor and its impact on the early Earth system

entries.text: Every living thing, from bacteria to blue whales, shares one ancestor: LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. A 2024 study put it at about 4.2 billion years ago, within a range of 4.33–4.09 billion. Most agree LUCA existed by 3.5 billion years ago.

entries.title: How much continent did the Hadean have?

facts.text: Models disagree on how much continental crust the Hadean had; in some, a global ocean covered Earth.
Models by Korenaga and colleagues have continental crust reaching today's volume between 4.2 and 4.0 Ga.
Dhuime and colleagues instead estimate only 25% of today's continental area by the end of the Hadean.
Continents may have appeared in the mid-Hadean, then vanished beneath a thick ocean by the eon's end.
Small proto-continents are generally thought to have existed before 4,280 Ma.

entries.title: How and where life may have begun

facts.text: Abundant Hadean geothermal settings, possibly including hot springs on volcanic land, may have let RNA form and copy itself, a possible route to life.
Evidence suggests the first RNA molecules formed before 4.17 Ga.

Life may have begun as far back as 4.4 Ga in hydrothermal vents, shielded from impacts and ultraviolet light; a deep-vent origin would allow 4.0–4.2 Ga.
The geologic record puts life's emergence most likely between 4.32 and 3.48 Ga; some sources call Hadean evidence of life controversial.

entries.title: The Late Heavy Bombardment, real or imagined

facts.text: Crater counts suggest intense impacts from about 4.1 to 3.8 Ga, cratering the Moon and, by inference, Earth, Mercury, Venus and Mars.
The main evidence is a clustering of Apollo impact-melt ages between about 3.8 and 4.1 Ga, from samples mostly near the Imbrium Basin.
Once widely accepted, it is now debated: critics see the cluster as debris of one large impact, and some evidence favors bombardment from 4.2 to 3.5 Ga.
It may have been caused by Neptune migrating outward through orbital resonances between Jupiter and Saturn.
Life either arose afterward or, more likely, survived it; hydrothermal heat may even have helped life begin.

entries.title: The first cratons, cores of the continents

facts.text: The first complete continental masses, or cratons, built of granite blocks, appeared on Earth around 3,800 Ma.
Cratons are old, stable parts of continental lithosphere with deep roots; most formed in the Archean.
Felsic magmas rose on the eastern edge of the Antarctic craton as the first great continental mass began to gather.
Antarctic zircons of 3.9–3.0 Ga suggest recycling within the crust was key to building the first cratons.
About 39% of modern continental crust formed in the Archean.

entries.text: Every continent today is built around an ancient, stubborn core. These cores are cratons: old, stable parts of the continental lithosphere, the rigid outer shell, with deep roots. The first complete continental masses of this kind, built of granite blocks, appeared around 3,800 million years ago, and most cratons formed in the Archean. One of the first great continental masses began to gather on the eastern edge of the Antarctic craton, where felsic magmas rose. Antarctic zircons of 3.9–3.0 billion years suggest that recycling within the crust, melting old rock into lighter new rock, was key to building them. The work was substantial: about 39% of modern continental crust formed in the Archean.

entries.title: The oldest banded iron formations

facts.text: The oldest known banded iron formations, at Isua in Greenland's greenstone belt, date from about 3,800–3,700 Ma.
Iron isotopes in them point to extremely low oxygen and to iron oxidized by anoxygenic photosynthesis.
Algoma-type iron formations formed mainly in the Archean; deposition later peaked near the eon's end.

Their iron isotopes point to extremely low oxygen and to iron oxidized by {{ref:arch-013}}. Iron formations of this Algoma type formed mainly in the Archean, and deposition later peaked near the eon's end.

entries.title: Greenland's Isua Greenstone Belt

facts.text: Volcanic and sedimentary sequences about 3,800 and 3,700 Ma old built the Isua belt, the largest exposure of Eoarchean supracrustal rock on Earth.
Isua pillow basalt, formed in an underwater eruption, shows that liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago.
Whether the belt formed by plate tectonics or by heat-pipe or plume volcanism is contentious, part of the wider debate on early tectonics.

entries.title: South China's Yangtze Block takes shape

facts.text: The Yangtze Block, the northwestern part of the South China Craton, is thought to have formed around 3.8–3.2 Ga.
3.8 Ga detrital zircons preserve remnants of this ancient crust.
Its Kongling Complex holds China's oldest rocks, with zircon ages of 3.3–2.9 Ga.

entries.title: The Pilbara Craton, a pristine Archean survivor

facts.text: Western Australia's Pilbara Craton holds crust up to 3.8 billion years old, intruded by granite domes and greenstone belts of about 3.5–3.2 Ga.
With the Kaapvaal Craton it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts left on Earth.
Detrital zircons of 3.8–3.6 Ga show crust was already eroding 300 million years before its oldest surviving rocks.
The craton stabilized around 3,600 Ma, as continents possibly gathered into Vaalbara.
By 2.97 Ga the West Pilbara Terrane had collided with and joined the East Pilbara Terrane.

entries.title: Photosynthesis without oxygen

facts.text: Anaerobic microbes, including chemotrophs and photosynthesisers, appear from about 3.7 Ga.
This simpler photosynthesis arose not long after life began and released no oxygen, using donors such as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur or iron instead of water.
Bacteria using it made ATP from a proton gradient, a mechanism used by nearly all later organisms.
Geochemical evidence suggests it emerged 3.3–3.5 Ga; fossils thought to be filamentous photosynthesisers date to 3.4 Ga.
The first photosynthesisers may have arisen at acidic hydrothermal vents, using their faint geothermal light and hydrogen sulfide rather than water.

entries.text: The first sun-powered life gave off no oxygen at all. Anaerobic microbes, which live without oxygen, appear from about 3.7 billion years ago, among them chemotrophs that fed on chemicals and early photosynthesizers. Their simpler, anoxygenic photosynthesis used hydrogen sulfide, sulfur or iron in place of water, so it released no oxygen. These bacteria made ATP, the cell's energy currency, from a proton gradient across a membrane, a mechanism nearly all later organisms still use. The first of them may have lived at acidic hydrothermal vents, using faint geothermal light. Geochemical evidence suggests this photosynthesis emerged 3.3–3.5 billion years ago, and fossils thought to be filamentous photosynthesizers date to 3.4 billion.

entries.title: Earth's magnetic field switches on

facts.text: Evidence from Greenland, published in 2024, shows Earth had a magnetic field by 3,700 million years ago.
Earlier paleomagnetic work on Australian lava and South African conglomerate showed a field since at least about 3,450 Ma.
Earth, like most planets, makes its field through the motion of electrically conducting fluids.
By 3.5 Ga the field, driven by currents in the molten outer core, helped stop the solar wind stripping away the atmosphere.

entries.title: Disputed traces of life at Isua

facts.text: About 3.7 Ga metasedimentary rocks at Isua, Greenland, hold graphite whose carbon isotopes suggest biological fractionation.
It is the earliest evidence of life from a rock unit rather than a single mineral grain.
In 2016 a team reported dome-shaped stromatolites 1–4 cm high, 220 million years older than those of the Dresser Formation.
The layers sit on volcanic rock dated 3.709 Ga and beneath beds dated 3.695 Ga.
The stromatolites are disputed: a 2018 study, joined by one original proponent, put the shapes down to rock deformation.

entries.title: The Kaapvaal Craton of South Africa

facts.text: South Africa's Kaapvaal Craton formed and stabilised between 3.7 and 2.6 Ga as large granite batholiths thickened its crust.
Its oldest parts are tonalitic gneisses of about 3.6–3.7 Ga, joined by granite-greenstone terranes of 3.0–3.5 Ga.
With the Pilbara Craton it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts known.
Its granite is exposed in the core of the Vredefort impact structure.
From 3.0 to 2.7 Ga, continent–arc collision built basins filled with thick volcanic and sedimentary sequences.

entries.title: The Wyoming Craton begins

facts.text: The Wyoming Craton began as a 100,000 km² Archean craton with gneisses of 3.6–3.0 Ga.
Late Archean magmatism and plate movements modified it, and by the end of the eon its three subprovinces had joined.
Its rocks reach 3.5 Ga, with detrital zircons up to 4.0 Ga.

entries.title: Vaalbara, a first supercontinent?

facts.text: The Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents, as far back as about 3.6 Ga.
The two cratons show strikingly similar rock sequences from 3.5 to 2.7 Ga, and share 3.5–3.2 Ga impact spherule layers.
Paleomagnetic data hint they were linked even at 3.87 Ga, but a Paleoarchean proto-Vaalbara cannot be proven.
By 2.78–2.77 Ga the cratons lay 30° of latitude apart, so Vaalbara had broken up by about 2.8 Ga, though these reconstructions are ambiguous.
Some scientists dispute Vaalbara, explaining the shared features as global processes, or date its assembly to the Mesoarchean or Neoarchean.

entries.contested_note: Whether and when Vaalbara existed is debated, and it competes with the largely incompatible Ur hypothesis.

entries.title: India's Dharwar Craton forms

facts.text: India's Dharwar Craton, the oldest part of the Indian peninsula, formed between 3.6 and 2.5 Ga.
Its three blocks joined between 2560 and 2500 Ma, closing all of its subduction zones.
Around 3350 Ma, ridge push drove oceanic crust down into the mantle, and slab melting produced its TTG crust.

verification.title: Formation of Archean (3600–2500 Ma) continental crust in the Dharwar Craton, southern India

entries.text: The oldest part of the Indian peninsula was built by ocean floor sinking and melting. India's Dharwar Craton formed between 3.6 and 2.5 billion years ago. Around 3350 million years ago, ridge push drove oceanic crust down into the mantle. The melting slab produced its TTG crust of tonalite, trondhjemite and granodiorite, light granite-like rocks. Its three blocks joined between 2560 and 2500 million years ago, closing all of its subduction zones, where one plate dives beneath another.

entries.title: The Barberton Greenstone Belt

facts.text: Lavas and sediments of the Barberton belt in South Africa and Eswatini were laid down between 3.5 and 3.2 Ga.
The area grew in two episodes of terrane accretion, about 3.5 and 3.2 Ga, matching pulses of TTG magmatism.
Its Makhonjwa Mountains are among the oldest in Africa, and its rocks hold some of the oldest traces of life.

entries.title: Spherule layers record giant impacts

facts.text: Eight spherule layers (S1–S8) in the Barberton belt, about 3.5–3.2 Ga, record at least four and perhaps eight or more impacts.
Spherules of 3.5 Ga in South Africa and Western Australia are the oldest known products of impacts on Earth.
A 2024 review counts 36 layers from 3.47–3.22 Ga and 2.63–2.49 Ga, a 'tail' of the Late Heavy Bombardment.
The record from 3.2 Ga includes impacts by objects up to 100 km wide.

entries.text: Thin beds of glassy beads are all that remain of asteroids that hit the early Earth. These spherules are droplets of rock melted and thrown out by an impact, then rained back down. Spherules 3.5 billion years old in South Africa and Western Australia are the oldest known products of impacts on Earth. In the Barberton belt, eight spherule layers, named S1 to S8 and about 3.5–3.2 billion years old, record at least four and perhaps eight or more impacts. A 2024 review counts 36 layers, from 3.47–3.22 billion and 2.63–2.49 billion years ago, and reads them as a tail of the Late Heavy Bombardment. The objects were not small: the record from 3.2 billion years includes impacts by bodies up to 100 km wide.

entries.title: Dresser stromatolites, the earliest undisputed life

facts.text: Stromatolites in the Dresser Formation of the Pilbara Craton, deposited about 3483–3479 Ma, are the earliest direct evidence of life.
Microbially induced sedimentary structures of the same age record microbial mats, the earliest life with good fossil evidence.
Its North Pole chert also holds microfossils, mat fabrics and carbon and sulfur biosignatures that suggest heat-loving microbes.
The stromatolites grew mostly in a shallow lagoon or flooded caldera where seawater mixed with hydrothermal fluids; some formed near hot springs on land.
The earliest undisputed evidence of life dates from at least 3.5 Ga, from the stromatolite record.

entries.text: In the red hills of Western Australia's Pilbara lies the oldest life no one seriously disputes. Stromatolites in the Dresser Formation, deposited about 3483–3479 million years ago, are the earliest direct evidence of life. Stromatolites are layered mounds built as microbial mats trap sediment, layer upon layer. The evidence runs deeper than the mounds. Microbially induced sedimentary structures of the same age record microbial mats, the earliest life with good fossil evidence. The formation's North Pole chert, a glassy silica rock, holds microfossils, mat fabrics, and carbon and sulfur signatures that suggest heat-loving microbes. The setting was hot and wet. The stromatolites grew mostly in a shallow lagoon or flooded caldera, a collapsed volcanic crater, where seawater mixed with hydrothermal fluids. Some formed near hot springs on land, a clue explored in {{ref:arch-023}}. Older claims, such as those at {{ref:arch-015}}, remain disputed. The stromatolite record gives the earliest undisputed evidence of life from at least 3.5 billion years ago.

entries.title: A nitrogen sky with almost no oxygen

facts.text: By about 3.4 Ga nitrogen was the main gas of a then-stable second atmosphere, which also held methane, carbon dioxide, water vapor and sulfur gases.
Volcanic outgassing, supplemented by gases from huge asteroids of the Late Heavy Bombardment, produced this Archean atmosphere.
It was anoxic and weakly reducing: oxygen stayed around or below 0.001% of today's level until about 2.4 Ga.
Sulfur-isotope signals rule out significant oxygen before about 2.45 Ga; river and delta grains of pyrite, siderite and uraninite older than 2.4 Ga also point to anoxia.
Any oxygen made by early photosynthesis was quickly used up oxidizing ferrous iron, sulfur and methane at the surface.

entries.title: Granite intrudes at the Johannesburg Dome

facts.text: Trondhjemitic and tonalitic granitic rocks intruded mafic–ultramafic greenstone in the central Kaapvaal Craton, forming South Africa's Johannesburg Dome.
U–Pb dating of single zircons gives 3340 ± 3 Ma, the oldest granitoid phase recognised there so far.
Later mafic dykes and granodiorites, some dated 3121 ± 5 Ma, support the view that the craton grew episodically by accretion.

entries.text: Johannesburg sits on a dome of very old granite. Tonalitic and trondhjemitic magma, both granite-like, intruded dark mafic–ultramafic greenstone in the central Kaapvaal Craton, forming South Africa's Johannesburg Dome. Uranium–lead dating of single zircons gives 3340 ± 3 million years, the oldest granitoid phase recognized there so far. Later mafic dikes and granodiorites, some dated 3121 ± 5 million years, support the view that the craton grew in episodes, piece by piece.

Uranium–lead dating of single zircons gives 3340 ± 3 million years, the oldest granitoid phase recognized there so far. Later mafic dikes and granodiorites, some dated 3121 ± 5 million years, support the view that the craton grew in episodes, piece by piece.

entries.title: The Zimbabwe Craton welds together

facts.text: The Zimbabwe Craton's Tokwe and Rhodesdale segments, with rocks as old as 3.46 Ga, stabilized about 3.3 Ga.
The craton formed by the suture of these two smaller crustal blocks.
With the Kaapvaal Craton and Limpopo Belt it rests on a buoyant mantle root about 250 km thick that yields diamonds.

entries.title: The S2 impact, a planet-shaking blow

facts.text: An asteroid about 37–58 km wide hit Earth around 3.26 Ga, leaving the S2 spherule layer in the Barberton Greenstone Belt.
Its crater may have been almost 480 km across, two and a half times the diameter of Chicxulub's.
It probably shook the whole planet with strong earthquakes and raised megatsunamis thousands of metres high.
It boiled the ocean surface, evaporating tens of metres of the global ocean.

entries.text: About 3.26 billion years ago, an asteroid about 37–58 km wide hit Earth. The only direct trace is the S2 spherule layer in the Barberton Greenstone Belt, but the scale of the blow is staggering. Its crater may have been almost 480 km across, two and a half times the diameter of Chicxulub's, the crater linked to the dinosaurs' end. The impact probably shook the whole planet with strong earthquakes. It raised megatsunamis thousands of meters high. Its heat boiled the surface of the sea, evaporating tens of meters of the global ocean. Any microbial mats in the shallows would have felt it.

entries.title: Microbial mats on Moodies tidal flats

facts.text: The Moodies Group, laid down about 3.22 Ga in South Africa and Eswatini, holds Earth's oldest well-preserved siliciclastic tidal deposits.
Microbial mats flourished on its tidal flats, and its microfossils are among the few accepted Archean examples.
It overlies the Fig Tree Formation in the Barberton Greenstone Belt of the Kaapvaal craton.

entries.title: Cyanobacteria learn to make oxygen

facts.text: Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesisers appears about 3.2 Ga, with local free oxygen around carbonate-platform stromatolites.
Cyanobacteria arose in fresh water or on land in the middle Archean; claims reach back to 3.5 Ga, and 2026 genetic work considers a 2.9–3 Ga origin established.
Cyanobacteria split water and released oxygen as waste, which first oxidized dissolved iron in the oceans to form iron ore.
Oxygen built up only slowly, poisoning many bacteria and eventually triggering the Great Oxygenation Event after the Archean.
Pilbara biomarkers of 2.7 Ga, once read as cyanobacteria and eukaryote steranes, were later shown to be contamination.

entries.text: Every breath you take traces back to a microbe that learned to split water. Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesizers appears about 3.2 billion years ago, with local free oxygen around stromatolites on carbonate platforms. The pioneers were cyanobacteria. They arose in fresh water or on land in the middle Archean. Some claims reach back to 3.5 billion years, and 2026 genetic work considers an origin 2.9–3 billion years ago established. Unlike {{ref:arch-013}}, they split water and released oxygen as waste. That oxygen did not fill the air at once. It first oxidized iron dissolved in the oceans, forming iron ore. It built up only slowly, poisoning many bacteria, and eventually triggered the Great Oxygenation Event after the Archean. Some evidence once seemed to settle the question early. Pilbara biomarkers of 2.7 billion years were read as signs of cyanobacteria and eukaryotes, but were later shown to be contamination. The timing remains debated.

entries.title: A hot world under a methane greenhouse

facts.text: Oxygen isotopes in Mesoarchean cherts suggest ocean temperatures of about 55–85 °C, though weathering studies suggest averages below 50 °C.
High levels of methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere may explain the warmth; the climate was at least temperate.
Volcanoes supplied the carbon dioxide and early microbes the methane, which lasted longer in an atmosphere without oxygen.
Nitrogen levels were probably similar to today's, so nitrogen played little part in warming the planet.
Methane broken apart by sunlight may also have made an organic haze, which would have had a cooling, anti-greenhouse effect.

entries.title: Ur, a contested early supercontinent

facts.text: Ur is a hypothetical supercontinent of rocks now in India, western Australia and southern Africa, formed around 3.1 Ga.
Its assembly is put at 3,200–2,600 Ma, covering 12–16% of today's continental crust.
The main argument is that cratons stable by about 3 Ga all sat in one region of Pangaea.
Rogers proposed Ur later grew into East Gondwana by accreting to East Antarctica.
A conflicting hypothesis joins western Australia and southern Africa as Vaalbara; most proposed Archean supercontinents are controversial.

entries.contested_note: Ur is hypothetical and controversial, and its reconstruction is largely incompatible with the rival Vaalbara hypothesis.

entries.title: The Saamian orogeny builds Fennoscandia's core

facts.text: The Saamian orogeny built an extensive area of tonalitic-trondhjemitic crust in Fennoscandia between 3.1 and 2.9 Ga.
Gneiss and greenstone belts of the Baltic Shield were laid down in the Kola Peninsula, Karelia and northeastern Finland around 3,100 Ma.
This Baltic Shield crust, over 3.1 Ga old, later formed the core of Kenorland.

entries.title: Miralga, an impact crater of disputed age

facts.text: Shatter cones near Marble Bar in the Pilbara reveal the Miralga, or North Pole Dome, impact structure; its crater may have exceeded 100 km.
A March 2025 study dated it to 3,470 ± 2 Ma, which would make it the oldest known impact structure by over a billion years.
A July 2025 study found shatter cones in rocks younger than 2.71 Ga, so the impact came after then and before 400 Ma.
A 2026 study dated impact-recrystallized zircon to 3.024 Ga and hydrothermal apatite to 3.019 Ga.
Spherules in its Antarctic Creek Member record a 3.5 Ga impact, but such spherules can travel far from their crater.

entries.contested_note: Its age is disputed: 3.47 Ga (March 2025), between 2.71 Ga and 400 Ma (July 2025), or about 3.02 Ga (2026).

entries.title: When did plate tectonics begin?

facts.text: A possible onset of plate tectonics is placed around 3 Ga, but its timing is still debated.
The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, including an oceanic arc at a Pilbara convergent margin about 3.12 Ga.
Minerals in ancient diamonds suggest the supercontinent cycle began roughly 3 Ga; diamonds from crustal eclogite became common after 3.0 Ga.
A hotter Paleoarchean mantle ruled out modern plate tectonics; some suggest a stagnant lid instead.
Other estimates range from the Hadean, over 4 Ga, to 2.2 Ga, or 800 Ma for fully modern-style tectonics.

entries.text: The ground beneath your feet moves a few centimeters a year, but when did it start moving? A possible onset of plate tectonics is placed around 3 billion years ago, yet its timing is still debated. The Mesoarchean holds the first evidence of modern-style subduction, where one plate dives beneath another. It includes an oceanic arc, a chain of volcanoes over a sinking plate, at a Pilbara convergent margin about 3.12 billion years ago. Diamonds add more clues. Minerals trapped in them suggest the supercontinent cycle, the repeated gathering and breakup of continents, began roughly 3 billion years ago. Diamonds from crustal eclogite became common after 3.0 billion. Earlier, the picture differs. A hotter Paleoarchean mantle ruled out modern plate tectonics, and some suggest a stagnant lid, a single unbroken shell, instead. Other estimates range from the Hadean, over 4 billion years ago, to 2.2 billion years, or just 800 million years for fully modern-style tectonics. The debate links back to {{ref:hade-004}}.

entries.title: Continental crust grows fast

facts.text: Continental crust grew relatively fast on the shields between 3.0 and 2.5 Ga, with widespread mantle melting and crustal growth in the Neoarchean.
Before 3.7 Ga continents held under 10% of today's crust, and there is little evidence of continental crust before 3.5 Ga.
Roughly 20–25% of today's continental crust existed by 3.0 Ga; after rapid crustal evolution it reached about 60% by 2.6 Ga.
The remaining fifth of the continental crust formed only during the last 2.5 billion years.
TTG rocks, major components of Archean cratons, formed by partial melting of water-rich mafic rock at high pressure; whether subduction drove this is debated.

entries.text: Before 3.7 billion years ago, continents held under 10% of today's continental crust. Then they grew quickly. There is little evidence of continental crust before 3.5 billion years ago, but roughly 20–25% of today's crust existed by 3.0 billion. After rapid crustal evolution, it reached about 60% by 2.6 billion years ago, with widespread mantle melting on the shields between 3.0 and 2.5 billion. Much of the new crust was TTG rock, formed when water-rich mafic rock partly melted at high pressure. Whether subduction drove that melting is debated. The remaining fifth of the continental crust formed only during the last 2.5 billion years.

entries.title: The Pongola glaciation, Earth's first known ice age

facts.text: The Pongola glaciation, from about 2.985 to 2.837 Ga, is the oldest known glaciation on Earth.
Its traces are diamictites of the Pongola Supergroup's Mozaan Formation in KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini.
It interrupted a Mesoarchean climate that was warm or temperate, kept mild by high methane and carbon dioxide.
Ice reached a palaeolatitude of 48 degrees; whether it extended toward the tropics is uncertain.
Sulfur-isotope changes suggest it may be tied to an early, short-lived oxygenation of the atmosphere.

entries.text: In a warm Archean world, ice suddenly appears in the rocks of southern Africa. The Pongola glaciation, from about 2.985 to 2.837 billion years ago, is the oldest known glaciation on Earth. Its traces are diamictites, jumbled mixtures of boulders and mud dropped by glaciers, in the Mozaan Formation of the Pongola Supergroup. They crop out in KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini. The cold was an interruption. The Mesoarchean climate was otherwise warm or temperate, kept mild by high methane and carbon dioxide, as in {{ref:arch-033}}. Ice reached a palaeolatitude, an ancient latitude, of 48 degrees. Whether it pushed further toward the tropics is uncertain. What cooled the planet? No one knows for sure. Sulfur-isotope changes suggest a link to an early, short-lived oxygenation of the atmosphere, described in {{ref:arch-042}}. If so, the first ice age on record was tied to the first stirrings of oxygen.

entries.title: Oxygen's first brief rise

facts.text: A transient episode of higher oxygen occurred around 2,980–2,960 Ma, in an atmosphere that otherwise had almost no free oxygen.
Oases of relatively high oxygen existed in some nearshore shallow seas by the Mesoarchean.
Sulfur isotopes link the coeval Pongola glaciation to an early, short-lived oxygenation.

Sulfur isotopes link this episode to the Pongola glaciation of the same age.

entries.title: The Witwatersrand Basin gathers its gold

facts.text: From about 2.97 to 2.71 Ga, rivers and a sea laid 5–7 km of mostly sedimentary rock in the Witwatersrand Basin on the Kaapvaal craton.
As uplift pushed the sea back, braided river deltas on a wide coastal plain concentrated heavy minerals: gold, pyrite and uraninite.
The basin holds the world's largest known gold reserves: over 40,000 tonnes mined, about 22% of all gold above ground.

entries.text: More gold has come out of one South African basin than anywhere else on Earth: over 40,000 tonnes mined, about 22% of all gold above ground. entries.title: The North Atlantic Craton assembles

facts.text: The North Atlantic Craton, now in West Greenland, Labrador and northwest Scotland, grew as terranes collided in a series of orogenies.
The Akia, Isukasia and Kapisilik terranes collided about 2950 Ma; more terranes merged 2850–2700 Ma and around Nuuk 2650–2580 Ma.
Regional magmatism, tectonism and metamorphism reworked and stabilized the craton in the Mesoarchean to Neoarchean.

entries.title: The Yilgarn Craton and its gold

facts.text: Western Australia's Yilgarn Craton was assembled between about 2.94 and 2.63 Ga from many terranes of older crust, mostly formed 3.2–2.8 Ga.

Most of its gold was deposited 2650–2630 Ma, after an earlier gold event at 2660–2655 Ma during crustal extension.

entries.title: The Abitibi greenstone belt

facts.text: The Abitibi greenstone belt of Ontario and Quebec, one of the world's largest Archean greenstone belts, formed 2,800–2,600 Ma.
Mostly volcanic, it is a stack of thrusted subterranes like those of paired arc–back-arc systems, with intrusions of 2,675–2,700 Ma throughout.
It contains the huge 2,707–2,696 Ma Blake River Megacaldera Complex.

entries.title: The Fortescue and Hamersley basins fill

facts.text: A thick pile of sedimentary and volcanic rock filled the Fortescue, Hamersley and Turee Creek basins on the Pilbara from about 2.78 to 2.42 Ga.
U–Pb dating puts the base of the Mount Bruce Supergroup at 2768 ± 16 Ma.
The Hamersley Basin on the Pilbara's southern margin was the last stable marine and river setting between the Yilgarn and Pilbara before rifting.

entries.title: The Slave Craton gains its deep root

facts.text: The Slave Craton's main stabilization came about 2.75 Ga, marked by abundant peridotite in its mantle root.
Kaapvaal shows a similar growth peak, suggesting much of Earth's continental lithospheric mantle formed in the Neoarchean.
Diamonds from craton roots are often over 3 billion years old; the Slave's oldest, 3.5–3.3 Ga, imply an early thick root.

entries.title: Tumbiana lakes and their puzzling microfossils

facts.text: Western Australia's Tumbiana Formation, about 2727–2715 Ma, was laid down in the oldest known carbonate-rich lake system.
Its limestones hold stromatolites such as Alcheringa narrina and organic-walled microfossils, adding to the few accepted Archean microfossils.
The microfossils' size and protrusions resemble eukaryotic microbes, but such features are not unique to eukaryotes and their affinity remains obscure.

entries.title: Kenorland, a possible supercontinent

facts.text: Kenorland, a hypothetical supercontinent, formed about 2.72 Ga through the accretion of Neoarchean cratons and new continental crust.
Its core, the Baltic or Fennoscandian Shield, traces back over 3.1 Ga, and Arctica formed part of it.
It broke up sometime after 2.45–2.1 Ga into proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn and Kalahari.
Alternatively the cratons formed separate supercratons, Superia and Sclavia; the Slave collided with Sclavia by 2.6 Ga, and Superia's final assembly came at 2520 Ma.
Kenorland's final assembly was finished by 2,600–2,550 Ma, with the Superior and Wyoming provinces side by side.

entries.title: Ventersdorp lavas bury the gold fields

facts.text: Massive outpourings of lava, the Ventersdorp lavas, erupted about 2.715 Ga and abruptly ended deposition of the Witwatersrand's gold-rich Central Rand Group.
Their cause is speculative: one source links them to the Kaapvaal craton's collision with the Zimbabwe Craton, another places them in a phase of rifting.
The lavas and the overlying Transvaal Supergroup were later warped into rings by the Vredefort impact.

entries.title: The Blake River supervolcano

facts.text: The Blake River Megacaldera Complex of Ontario and Quebec, the first known Precambrian supervolcano, began forming about 2,707 Ma.
Its first caldera, Misema, is 80 km long and 40 km wide, built from at least two coalescing mafic shield volcanoes.
Later phases built the New Senator Caldera (2704–2701 Ma) and the Noranda Caldera (2696 Ma), with 7–9 km of erupted rock.

entries.title: Komatiite floods and a mantle overturn

facts.text: A major eruption of komatiite lava, possibly global, occurred around 2,705 Ma and may mark an overturn of the mantle.
Komatiite magma forms when 30–40% of mantle rock melts at very high pressure, leaving a residue like Archean lithospheric mantle.
Komatiite lavas, erupting at up to about 1600 °C, formed almost only in the Archean, when the mantle may have been 100–250 °C hotter.

entries.title: Another pulse of oxygen

facts.text: Another pulse of oxygenation came about 2,700 Ma; some consider it a possible start of the Great Oxygenation Event.
Skewed sulfur isotopes in pyrites show a small rise in atmospheric oxygen around this time.
Cyanobacteria had appeared by at least 2.7 Ga, and an oxygen-containing atmosphere began to develop in the late Archean.
Most scholars still place the start of the Great Oxygenation Event in the Paleoproterozoic, about 2,400 Ma.

entries.title: Fossil raindrops weigh the ancient air

facts.text: Fossil raindrop imprints in 2,700 Ma volcanic ash of South Africa's Ventersdorp Supergroup show air less than twice as dense as today's, likely similar or thinner.
Gas bubbles in Archean lava that solidified at sea level about 2,700 Ma point to an air pressure of only 0.23 ± 0.23 bar.

entries.title: The Algoman orogeny builds the Superior Craton

facts.text: The Algoman, or Kenoran, orogeny built mountains in the late Archean through repeated continental collisions, compression and subduction.
Terranes now in the Canadian Shield collided about 2,700–2,500 Ma, adding land along a belt from South Dakota to Sudbury, Ontario.
The Superior Craton, the largest Archean craton, was stitched together from terranes in a run of orogenies between 2720 and 2680 Ma.
Subduction drove the docking; dates of about 2,700 Ma near Rainy Lake, Ontario, favour a moving-plate model for the boundary.
The orogeny closed the Archean about 2,500 Ma; by then the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick.

entries.title: Banded iron formations reach their peak

facts.text: Massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents.

entries.title: Kenorland breaks apart

facts.text: Magma-plume rifting began between 2.48 and 2.45 Ga in a supercontinent that had sat at low latitudes.
The drawn-out breakup left mafic dikes, rift basins and rifted margins on many continents through the Siderian and Rhyacian.
Final breakup produced large swarms of mafic dikes and sills across the North American provinces 2.2–2.1 Ga.
Its fragments became proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn craton and Kalahari; the breakup is associated with the Paleoproterozoic glacial epoch.
In the alternative view, the Sclavia supercraton broke up during a global pulse of mantle-plume magmatism around 2.33–2.1 Ga.

entries.title: The Great Oxidation Event

facts.text: Free oxygen first built up in the air and shallow seas, turning a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, an irreversible change.
Cyanobacteria, the first known oxygen producers, are generally credited; oxygen won out once surface reductants such as ferrous iron, sulfur and methane were used up.
Oxygen rose from almost none to as much as 10% of the modern level by the end of the event.
Between 2410 and 2320 Ma the oxygen partial pressure rose from about two millionths of a bar to at least two thousandths.
Sulfur isotope anomalies typical of an oxygen-free sky vanish after 2.4–2.3 Ga, and rust-red beds appear in soils by 2.3 Ga.

entries.text: Once, there was no oxygen in the air to breathe. Then, early in the Proterozoic, free oxygen built up in the atmosphere and shallow seas for the first time. It turned a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change was irreversible. Every breathing animal since depends on it. Cyanobacteria, the first known oxygen producers, are generally credited. They had been releasing oxygen for a long time, as in {{ref:arch-034}}. But oxygen won out only once surface reductants, chemicals that grab oxygen such as ferrous iron, sulfur and methane, were used up. The rise was steep. Between 2410 and 2320 million years ago, the oxygen partial pressure climbed from about two millionths of a bar to at least two thousandths. By the end of the event, oxygen had risen from almost none to as much as 10% of the modern level. The rocks record the switch. Sulfur isotope anomalies typical of an oxygen-free sky vanish after 2.4–2.3 billion years ago, and rust-red beds appear in soils by 2.3 billion.

It may have been the worst ever, but early life is too poorly known to compare it with the Big Five.
It is the only well-documented extinction before the Phanerozoic, since earlier life was microbial or soft-bodied.

entries.title: The Huronian glaciation

facts.text: A series of glacial periods, also called the Makganyene glaciation, named for diamictite-bearing rocks of the Huronian Supergroup near Lake Huron.
Rising oxygen cut atmospheric methane from 300 to 4 ppmv, weakening the greenhouse; average global temperatures fell below 0 °C.
The Siderian page dates three pulses: about 2440–2420 Ma (Duitschland), 2380–2360 Ma (Makganyene) and 2340–2310 Ma (Gowganda/Rietfontein).
Glacial deposits occur on six cratons, including Wyoming, Kaapvaal and Karelia-Kola, and correlate with Western Australian beds.
It is the earliest well-established ice age, with land-based ice; only the Pongola glaciation is older.

entries.text: Oxygen, the gas of life, may have plunged the planet into its first great ice age. Rising oxygen cut atmospheric methane from 300 to 4 ppmv, parts per million by volume, weakening the greenhouse that had kept Earth warm. Average global temperatures fell below 0 °C. The result was a series of glacial periods, also called the Makganyene glaciation. It is named for diamictite-bearing rocks of the Huronian Supergroup near Lake Huron; diamictite is a jumble of boulders and mud dropped by ice. The Siderian record dates three pulses: about 2440–2420 million years ago (Duitschland), 2380–2360 million (Makganyene) and 2340–2310 million (Gowganda or Rietfontein). The ice was widespread. Glacial deposits occur on six cratons, including Wyoming, Kaapvaal and Karelia-Kola, and correlate with beds in Western Australia. This is the earliest well-established ice age, with ice on land. Only {{ref:arch-041}} is older.

entries.title: The Eburnean orogeny shapes West Africa

It built the Eglab and Man shields of the West African Craton and structured its Birimian domain.

entries.text: West Africa's ancient heart was assembled in one long episode of mountain building. The Eburnean orogeny was a series of tectonic, metamorphic and plutonic events, the last meaning magma intruded and cooled underground. It built the Eglab and Man shields of the West African Craton and structured its Birimian domain. Together with the Transamazonian orogeny, it welded South American and West African cratons, an early step toward Columbia. Around 2070 million years ago, an upwelling of the asthenosphere, the soft layer beneath the plates, released a large volume of magma after the mountains had formed.

entries.title: The first eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus

facts.text: Eukaryotes are thought to have arisen in the Rhyacian when an Asgard archaeon took in an alphaproteobacterium; sexual reproduction probably appeared then too.

entries.text: Every plant, animal and fungus descends from a single act of swallowing. Eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, are thought to have arisen in the Rhyacian when an Asgard archaeon, a single-celled microbe, took in an alphaproteobacterium. The swallowed bacterium stayed on inside its host. Sexual reproduction probably appeared then too. The earliest known eukaryotic acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, date from between 2150 and 1950 million years ago. Yet when eukaryotes first appeared is debated. Claimed eukaryote records from 2.1 billion years ago are considered questionable. Another view puts the earliest evidence at 1.85 billion years, from symbiogenesis, the merging of archaea and proteobacteria under the new stress of oxygen. The oldest unambiguous eukaryote remains, from China, are 1.8–1.6 billion years old. Whatever the exact date, the rise of oxygen in {{ref:prot-006}} probably set the scene.

entries.title: Columbia, a supercontinent assembles

facts.text: Global-scale collisions gathered almost all of Earth's continental blocks into the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna.
Its proto-cratons became the cores of Laurentia, Baltica, the Ukrainian Shield, Amazonia and Australia, possibly with Siberia, North China and Kalaharia.
The collisions included the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies.
Zircons record an extensive high mountain range, the Nuna Supermountains, at 2.0–1.8 Ga.
Modern plate tectonics may have emerged by at least 2.2 Ga with Columbia's formation.

entries.text: Almost every piece of continent on Earth was once gathered into one. Global-scale collisions gathered almost all continental blocks into the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna. Its proto-cratons became the cores of Laurentia, Baltica, the Ukrainian Shield, Amazonia and Australia, possibly with Siberia, North China and Kalaharia. The collisions that joined them have their own names: the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies. Each was a long-running crash of crust that left a mountain belt behind. The mountains were huge. Zircons record an extensive high range, the Nuna Supermountains, between 2.0 and 1.8 billion years ago. Eroding peaks of that scale would have fed sediment and nutrients to the seas. Columbia may also mark a change in how the planet works. Modern plate tectonics may have emerged by at least 2.2 billion years ago, with Columbia's formation, linking back to the debate in {{ref:arch-039}}.

entries.title: Shungite, Earth's oldest petroleum

facts.text: Organic-rich muds settled in a brackish lagoon in Russian Karelia during active rifting; volcanic nutrients may have raised biological productivity.
The sequence is dated by a 1980 ± 27 Ma gabbro intrusion and underlying dolomites of 2090 ± 70 Ma; the deposit holds over 250 gigatonnes of carbon.
Metamorphism turned these oil source rocks into shungite; its veins and layers are migrated petroleum, now bitumen, of confirmed biological origin.

entries.title: The Vredefort impact, Earth's largest crater

facts.text: An asteroid struck the Kaapvaal craton in today's South Africa; first put at 10–15 km wide, it was estimated at 20–25 km in 2022.
It left the largest verified impact structure on Earth; the original crater was 170–300 km across, possibly larger than Chicxulub.
Erosion of 7–11 km has removed the crater; the Vredefort Dome's 70 km ring of hills is its rebounded central uplift.
It was one of two of the largest known impacts of the Orosirian.
By dropping the Witwatersrand rocks down, the strike preserved rich gold deposits that would otherwise have been eroded away.

entries.text: The largest verified impact structure on Earth lies just south of Johannesburg. About 2.02 billion years ago, an asteroid struck the Kaapvaal craton in today's South Africa. It was first put at 10–15 km wide; in 2022 it was estimated at 20–25 km. The original crater was 170–300 km across, possibly larger than Chicxulub. Little of it survives as a hole. Erosion of 7–11 km has removed the crater itself. What remains is the Vredefort Dome, a 70 km ring of hills that is the crater's rebounded central uplift, where deep rock sprang back up after the blow. It was one of two of the largest known impacts of the Orosirian. It also left a gift. By dropping the Witwatersrand rocks down, the strike preserved rich gold deposits, laid down in {{ref:arch-043}}, that would otherwise have been eroded away.

entries.text: Western Australia's two great cratons were joined in a single collision. entries.title: The Trans-Hudson orogeny forges North America

facts.text: The largest Paleoproterozoic orogenic belt in the world, it formed the Canadian Shield and the North American craton, Laurentia.
It sutured the Hearne-Rae, Superior and Wyoming cratons into North America's cratonic core.
Old cratonic blocks, island arcs and ocean deposits were folded, thrust, metamorphosed and intruded by hundreds of huge granite bodies.
It was the culminating event of Laurentia's assembly from six or seven Archean fragments, following the Wopmay orogeny.
Final closure of the Manikewan Ocean around 1.83 Ga merged the Hearne, Superior and Sask cratons; metamorphism peaked about 1.82–1.8 Ga.

entries.text: The core of North America was welded together along a single great seam. Following the Wopmay orogeny, it was the culminating event of Laurentia's assembly from six or seven Archean fragments.

entries.title: The Circum-Superior large igneous province

facts.text: Widespread mafic–ultramafic magmatism built the Circum-Superior Belt, a large igneous province, along the Superior craton's margin 1,884–1,870 Ma.
Its dikes, sills and lavas stretch over 3,400 km from Manitoba to Labrador and were emplaced in an extremely short geological time span.
It erupted while the Trans-Hudson, New Quebec and Penokean orogenies surrounded the Superior craton; in the Labrador Trough its 1,880 Ma magmatic event covered about 30,000 km².
Its origin is unclear: proposals include back-arc rifting, foredeep flexure, mantle plumes and microcontinent breakup; a 1,900 Ma global superplume is questioned.
It hosts major copper, nickel and platinum-group deposits, including Manitoba's Thompson nickel belt, and a rare Proterozoic komatiite belt.

facts.text: Black chert layers in banded iron formation on Lake Superior's north shore preserve microfossils of microbes like cyanobacteria.

entries.title: Banded iron formations disappear

facts.text: Banded iron formations largely vanish from the rock record worldwide after 1.85 Ga.
Their end is read as the oxygenation of the deep ocean, once the iron dissolved in seawater had been oxidized.
Before then the ocean was persistently iron-rich, with possible intervals of sulfidic euxinia.
The only extensive iron formations laid down later are tied to Cryogenian glacial deposits.
A 10 km asteroid struck water about 1,000 m deep 1.849 Ga, at the same time as a pause in iron-formation deposition.

entries.title: The Sudbury impact

facts.text: A chondritic bolide 10–15 km wide struck the Nuna supercontinent in what is now Ontario, Canada.
It left one of the oldest and largest known impact structures; debris would have been scattered across the globe.
The Sudbury Igneous Complex formed at the same time; its ores hold nickel, copper, platinum-group metals, gold and silver.
It has been proposed that the impact mixed the stratified ocean through tsunamis, vaporized seawater and runoff from wrecked continental margins.
It was one of the two largest known impacts of the Orosirian, near the end of the period.

entries.title: Columbia keeps growing at its edges

facts.text: After final assembly at c. 1.82 Ga, Columbia kept growing until 1.5 Ga through subduction-related magmatism and accretion at its margins.

Extensive magmatism about 1,750 Ma in Baltica, Sarmatia, Siberia, Laurentia and West Africa shows these cratons were linked.

entries.text: Deserts of shifting dunes are far older than any plant. Around 1.8 billion years ago, the oldest ergs, or sand seas, developed on several cratons. entries.title: The Boring Billion

facts.text: An informal span from about 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, also called Earth's Middle Ages, marked by tectonic stability, climatic stasis and slow biological evolution.
Bracketed by oxygenation events and global glaciations, it had very low oxygen and no glaciations, though a 1 Ga Scottish lake froze over in winter.
Its oceans may have been oxygen-poor, sulfidic and nutrient-starved, dominated by purple bacteria that used hydrogen sulfide instead of water: a so-called Canfield ocean.
The carbon isotope record shows no major excursions, and Mesoproterozoic global temperatures may have averaged about 19 °C, some 4 °C warmer than today.
It ended with the breakup of Rodinia in the Tonian, a second oxygenation event and the Cryogenian Snowball Earth.

entries.title: The first multicellular eukaryotes

facts.text: The Chuanlinggou Formation of the Yan Mountains, North China, preserves the first definitive multicellular eukaryotes: Qingshania, Tawuia and Changchengia.

Qingshania, dated elsewhere to 1.7 Ga, appears to consist of nearly identical cells.
Multicellular eukaryotes, likely descended from colonies of single cells, probably evolved about 2–1.4 Ga.
Such finds show that Mesoproterozoic life was not purely microbial, as once thought.

entries.text: Shatter cones and shocked quartz are the calling cards of an impact. Both turn up in Western Australia's Mid West, where a structure at least 30 km across marks an ancient strike. Its most cited age, about 1,630 million years, records a reheating of the granite. That reheating may date the impact, or only a regional tectonic event, so the impact's true age is uncertain.

entries.title: The Isan orogeny and Mount Isa's ores

facts.text: The Isan orogeny, a major mountain-building event, affected Queensland's Mount Isa Block about 1,600 Ma as large lead, silver, copper and zinc deposits were laid down.
Mount Isa's lower lead–zinc–silver ore and upper copper ore lie in the 1,000 m thick Lower Proterozoic Urquhart Shale, on one limb of a faulted fold.
The Mount Isa belt is one of the 1.8–1.5 Ga magmatic belts that grew along the North Australia Craton's margins.

entries.title: Eukaryotes capture cyanobacteria and become algae

facts.text: Around 1.6 Ga some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria as endosymbionts, gaining oxygenic photosynthesis through plastids.
These became the algae, which eventually overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers.
The Gaoyuzhuang Formation of North China, about 1,589 Ma, preserves some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia and Grandilingulata.
A diverse collection of fossil algae occurs in rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 Ga.

entries.text: Every green leaf on Earth contains the descendant of a captured microbe. Around 1.6 billion years ago, some eukaryotes took up cyanobacteria as endosymbionts, partners living inside their cells. They gained oxygen-making photosynthesis through plastids, the organelles descended from those captured cells. This was the second great act of swallowing, after the one in {{ref:prot-019}}. The new partnership produced the algae. Over time, they overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers, the organisms that make food at the base of the food web. The fossil record follows. North China's Gaoyuzhuang Formation, about 1,589 million years old, preserves some of the first algae, such as Tuanshanzia and Grandilingulata. A diverse collection of fossil algae occurs in rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 billion years. Red algae appear too, as in {{ref:prot-057}}.

entries.title: A brief Mesoproterozoic rise in oxygen

facts.text: Oxygen is proposed to have risen transiently to about 4% of present levels at times between 1.59 and 1.36 Ga.
Gaoyuzhuang rocks suggest a rise near 1.57 Ga; formations in Australia, Russia and North China show oxygenation near 1.4 Ga, though how global is unclear.
The seafloor was about 50–80% oxidized early in the Ectasian, declining afterwards.
Otherwise Boring Billion oxygen may have stayed below 0.1–1% of modern levels, stalling complex life.

verification.title: An expansive global oxygenation of Earth’s surface environments 1.4 billion years ago

entries.text: In the middle of the long, oxygen-starved Boring Billion, oxygen may have briefly spiked. It is proposed to have risen at times to about 4% of present levels between 1.59 and 1.36 billion years ago. Gaoyuzhuang rocks in North China suggest a rise near 1.57 billion years ago. Formations in Australia, Russia and North China show oxygenation near 1.4 billion, though how global it was is unclear. Early in the Ectasian, about 50–80% of the seafloor was oxidized, a share that later declined. Otherwise, oxygen may have stayed below 0.1–1% of modern levels, stalling complex life.

entries.title: The Volyn biota of Ukraine

facts.text: Exceptionally preserved microfossils formed in cavities of igneous rocks in what is now Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, about 1.5 Ga.
They include filaments of varied shapes and fungus-like organisms, possibly among the first fossils of the deep biosphere.

entries.title: Columbia breaks apart

facts.text: Columbia began to fragment about 1.5–1.35 Ga, with rifting along the margins of Laurentia, India, Baltica, Siberia, southern Africa and North China.
Widespread magmatism away from mountain belts formed anorthosite–mangerite–charnockite–granite suites in North America, Baltica, Amazonia and North China.
Atlantica split from Nena, and North China broke away along the Zhaertai–Bayan Obo rift, where mafic sills record the event.
Final breakup came about 1.3–1.2 Ga, marked by the 1.27 Ga Mackenzie and 1.24 Ga Sudbury dyke swarms in North America.
The fragments later reassembled into the supercontinent Rodinia.

Columbia began to fragment about 1.5–1.35 billion years ago, with rifting along the margins of Laurentia, India, Baltica, Siberia, southern Africa and North China. Final breakup came about 1.3–1.2 billion years ago, marked by the 1.27-billion-year-old Mackenzie and 1.24-billion-year-old Sudbury dike swarms in North America. The fragments later reassembled into {{ref:prot-071}}.

entries.title: Horodyskia, a string of beads

facts.text: Horodyskia, a string of beads joined by a fine thread, is one of the oldest known eukaryotes; its fossils span 1,480 to 550 Ma.
It may have been an early animal, but has also been read as a colonial foraminiferan.
It ranks among the first structurally complex eukaryotes.

entries.title: The Belt Basin fills

facts.text: Much of the Belt Supergroup was laid down about 1450–1400 Ma in a fault-bounded rift basin on the edge of Laurentia, within the supercontinent Columbia.
Mostly fine mud, silt and sand piled up more than 15 km thick over some 200,000 km², in a basin that was probably closed or lake-like.
Its rocks hold stromatolites and rich lead, zinc and silver ores, and they form the mountains of Glacier National Park.

Much of the mid-continent is underlain by the 1,450–1,350 Ma Granite-Rhyolite crustal province.

entries.title: The Kibaran orogeny in Africa

facts.text: A series of orogenic events in Africa ran from about 1,400 Ma until about 1,000 Ma, when Rodinia was assembled.
From 1.4 to 1.2 Ga it fused the Tanzanian and Congo cratons.
In a narrower sense, the name covers an event about 1,375 Ma that formed the Karagwe-Ankolean belt.

entries.title: A superplume splits Columbia

facts.text: A major large igneous province about 1,380 Ma links Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia, Congo and West Africa, formed as the Nuna supercontinent broke up.
Magmatism of the same age in Congo and Siberia shows the two continents stayed close for at least 120 million years.
Metamafic rocks of 1.37–1.35 Ga suggest a superplume affected three provinces, driving expansion and Columbia's breakup.

Metamafic rocks of 1.37–1.35 billion years suggest a superplume, a giant upwelling of hot mantle, drove Columbia's breakup.

entries.title: The Mackenzie Large Igneous Province

facts.text: A massive igneous event starting about 1,270 Ma built a province of 2.7 million km² across the Canadian Shield, from Arctic Nunavut to the Great Lakes.
It includes the Muskox layered intrusion, the Coppermine River flood basalts and the huge Mackenzie dike swarm.
Its volume was about 3 million km³, linked to the Mackenzie hotspot.
Its dykes mark the final breakup of the supercontinent Columbia.

entries.title: Rodinia assembles

facts.text: Fragments of the broken-up Columbia accreted and collided to form Rodinia, which assembled between 1.26 and 0.90 Ga.
Laurentia formed its core; it grew into the largest landmass yet, joining North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks.
A global superocean, Mirovia, surrounded it; the proto-Pacific Panthalassa later grew at its expense.
Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the 1.1–0.9 Ga Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies.
Its configuration and history are much less well understood than those of later supercontinents.

entries.text: The broken pieces of one supercontinent came back together as another. Fragments of Columbia, scattered by {{ref:prot-063}}, accreted and collided to form Rodinia, which assembled between 1.26 and 0.90 billion years ago. Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, sat at its center. Around it, Rodinia grew into the largest landmass yet, joining North American, East European, Amazonian, West African, Antarctic, Australian and Chinese blocks. Baltica and Amazonia collided with Laurentia in the Grenville, Sveconorwegian and Sunsás orogenies, between 1.1 and 0.9 billion years ago. A single global ocean, Mirovia, surrounded it. Later, the proto-Pacific Panthalassa grew at Mirovia's expense. For all its size, Rodinia remains shadowy. Its configuration and history are much less well understood than those of later supercontinents. Its later breakup, in {{ref:prot-108}}, would matter just as much as its assembly.
