entries.title: Stromatolites peak, then fall

facts.text: Stromatolites, mounds built by microbial colonies, reached their greatest abundance and diversity about 1.25 Ga.
Widespread cyanobacterial colonies and reefs then dominated the tidal zones of oceans and seas.
After about 1,250 Ma their abundance and diversity declined steeply, perhaps as predators began grazing on stromatolites and acritarchs.
The decline sped up around 1 Ga, at the end of the Stenian; grazing by more complex organisms is the most widely supported explanation.
By the start of the Cambrian they had fallen to 20% of their peak; Proterozoic stromatolites preserve cyanobacteria and possibly green algae.

The decline sped up around 1 billion years ago, at the end of the Stenian, and grazing by more complex organisms is the most widely supported explanation. By the start of the Cambrian they had fallen to 20% of their peak.

entries.title: The Grenville orogeny

facts.text: A long-lived mountain-building event, tied to the assembly of Rodinia, raised a belt from Labrador to Mexico and on to Scotland.
Laurentia collided with other blocks, notably Amazonia, beginning the construction of what are now the Appalachian Mountains.
Its main pulses were the Elzevirian (1240–1220 Ma), Ottawan (1090–1020 Ma) and Rigolet (1010–980 Ma).
Crust of this age is found worldwide; the same events are called Kibaran in Africa, Dalslandian in western Europe and Sunsás in Brazil.
From about 1190 to 980 Ma two continental blocks collided with Laurentia, folding mountains from Newfoundland to North Carolina.

entries.title: The Musgrave orogeny in central Australia

facts.text: Between 1.22 and 1.12 Ga three orogenic events shaped the Musgrave Province of central Australia, a 220,000 km² region formed via a magma plume.
The Musgravian orogeny about 1,200 Ma generated the voluminous Kulgera granites by melting the lower crust.

The province is one of the many belts of crust formed or reworked as Rodinia came together.

entries.title: The Grand Canyon Supergroup

facts.text: Nine formations of the Grand Canyon Supergroup were laid down in a sea between 1.2 billion and 740 million years ago, the Chuar Group in coastal and shallow seas.
Its oldest layer, averaging 1250 Ma, is the oldest in the canyon with fossils (stromatolites); the Cardenas Basalt, 1070 ± 70 Ma, tops the Unkar Group.
About 800 Ma the Grand Canyon orogeny tilted the supergroup 15° and broke it into fault blocks.

entries.title: The Sveconorwegian orogeny

facts.text: A mountain-building system was active from 1140 to 960 Ma in what is now southwestern Sweden and southern Norway.
Its most active phase, 1050–980 Ma, metamorphosed and thickened the crust; a collision between Amazonia and Baltica may have caused it.
It is grouped with the Grenvillian orogens that assembled Rodinia.

entries.title: The Midcontinent Rift, a split that failed

facts.text: About 1.1 Ga the core of North America began to split apart, opening a rift 2,000 km long through the middle of the continent.
The rift failed, leaving thick layers of igneous rock; it is the deepest failed rift on Earth.
Lava poured from cracks along the rift valley; its arms meet at Lake Superior, which fills the valley.
Its western arm runs through Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa and Nebraska; the eastern arm reaches central Michigan.
Magmatism of about the same age struck Africa, India and South America.

entries.text: The oldest evidence of sex comes from a tiny red seaweed in the Canadian Arctic. Bangiomorpha pubescens, a multicellular red alga from Somerset Island, closely resembles the living red alga Bangia. Its differentiated reproductive cells are the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction and of meiosis, the cell division that makes sex cells with half the usual set of genes. The boom described in {{ref:prot-087}} may owe something to this small alga.

entries.text: Even a billion years ago, microbes were eating each other. The Lakhanda Group of Russia's Uchur-Maya Depression preserves a community dominated by anaerobic bacteria, microbes that live without oxygen. The fossils also show evidence of food-web interactions, organisms feeding on other organisms. That makes the site a Lagerstätte, an unusually rich fossil bed, and an early glimpse of an ecosystem with links between its members.

entries.title: Ourasphaira, the earliest known fungus

facts.text: Ourasphaira giraldae, multicellular organic-walled microfossils with fungal affinity, is preserved in shale of the Grassy Bay Formation, Canadian Arctic.

Older fossils from 1.43 Ga have also been interpreted as multicellular fungi with differentiated cells.

entries.title: Eukaryotes diversify as acritarchs boom

facts.text: Eukaryotes, long inconspicuous, diversified rapidly around 1 Ga.
Acritarchs boomed in abundance, diversity, size and shape, growing more and longer spines, in their first large radiation.
The first dinoflagellates, some of which ate prey, may have been the first predators, pushing acritarchs into an arms race of defences.
After 1 Ga species durations dropped to about 100 million years, perhaps from increased grazing by early protists.

entries.title: Eukaryotes take over fresh water

facts.text: Abundant eukaryotic microfossils from Scotland's freshwater Torridon Group suggest eukaryotes dominated non-marine habitats by 1 Ga.
Nutrients from continental runoff probably favoured them near the continents.
By then eukaryotes, including multicellular forms, inhabited freshwater environments.
Phosphatic microfossils from Scotland's Diabaig Formation, 994 ± 48 Ma, are among the oldest known non-marine eukaryotes.
Molecular-clock evidence suggests photosynthetic, multicellular eukaryotes and fungi had moved onto land by 1000 Ma.

entries.title: Proterocladus, the first multicellular green alga

facts.text: Proterocladus antiquus, about 1 billion years old, is the first known preserved case of multicellularity in green algae.
Around 1 Ga the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae, though the line between a colony and a multicellular organism is blurred.

entries.title: The Rayner orogeny joins India and Antarctica

entries.title: Bitter Springs microfossils

Some fossils with ghostly internal structures, such as Glenobotrydion, have been read as green algae, among the earliest plants.
This style of preservation ended in the late Neoproterozoic, when silica-secreting organisms appeared.

entries.title: The first possible animals

facts.text: Sponge-like fossils in reefs about 890 Ma may be the oldest animals, but their identity is highly debated.
The first putative animal fossils date to the middle to late Tonian, c. 890–800 Ma; Otavia, about 800 Ma, has been described as a primitive sponge.
Molecular studies place the base of the animal family tree in the Tonian, though physical evidence for such early animals is lacking.
Sponges, a basal animal group, emerged in the Tonian and survived the later glaciations.

entries.title: The Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event

facts.text: Called the 'Second Great Oxidation Event', it raised oxygen in the air and oceans c. 850–540 Ma; marine rocks of 850–720 Ma record a large positive carbon-isotope excursion.
Oxygen rose from under 0.1% of present levels to over 13% during 900–815 Ma, and possibly to about 50% in the Cryogenian interglacial.
Oxygen rose above 1% of the atmosphere for the first time; air trapped in 813-million-year-old rock salt holds 10.9% oxygen.
It may have been one global event or a series of regional episodes, and the deep ocean stayed anoxic and iron-rich as late as 580 Ma.
The oxygen surge drove rapid evolution of multicellular life late in the era; some authors credit it with letting the oxygen-hungry Ediacaran biota spread.

entries.title: The Huainan worms

facts.text: Macroscopic, small worm-shaped organisms near Huainan City, Anhui, China, record a transitional stage in evolution, 840–740 Ma.
A similar biota about 1 billion years old was found on Russia's Timan Ridge.

entries.text: Some of the first creatures you could see without a microscope lived in what is now China. Near Huainan City, in Anhui, small worm-shaped organisms large enough to see with the naked eye record a transitional stage in evolution, 840–740 million years ago. A similar biota, about 1 billion years old, was found on Russia's Timan Ridge. Both hint that life was moving from microbes toward larger, more complex forms.

entries.title: The Adelaide Rift Complex opens

Its rift troughs and passive-margin basins kept developing until about 550 Ma.
Its rocks record Rodinia's breakup, two Snowball Earth glaciations, the Neoproterozoic oxygenation and the Ediacaran fauna.

entries.title: Cyanobacteria take to the open sea

facts.text: Marine planktonic cyanobacteria first appeared about 800 Ma, descended from seafloor and freshwater ancestors, and helped oxygenate the oceans.
Planktonic nitrogen fixers that evolved in the Cryogenian ended a long shortage of ammonium that had held back multicellular life.
Their spread is thought to have sped oxygenation and carbon dioxide removal, helping explain the severe Cryogenian glaciations.

entries.title: The Pharusian Ocean opens and closes

entries.title: The East African Orogeny begins Gondwana

facts.text: Gondwana began to form c. 800–650 Ma as India and Madagascar collided with East Africa in the East African Orogeny.
It was the main stage in joining East and West Gondwana along the Mozambique Belt, uniting Africa, India and Arabia.
The Arabian-Nubian Shield collided with eastern Africa in the Kenya–Tanzania region.
The Mozambique Ocean between Madagascar–India and the Congo–Tanzania craton began closing between 700 and 580 Ma.
In one model, arc accretion became a continental collision when Azania struck the Congo–Tanzania–Bangweulu Block around 640 Ma.

entries.title: Rodinia breaks apart

facts.text: Rifting began as early as 850–800 Ma, perhaps driven by a superplume; most agree the breakup proper began about 750 Ma, with eruptions on most continents.
Rodinia split into Proto-Laurasia, the Congo craton and Proto-Gondwana; new oceans such as the Adamastor and the proto-Pacific Panthalassa opened as Mirovia closed.
By 750 Ma Gondwana had rotated away, leaving Laurentia isolated near the equator; when the breakup ended c. 600 Ma, Baltica became isolated for some 200 million years.
Between 650 and 550 Ma the Iapetus Ocean opened and the Adamastor and Mozambique oceans closed, forming Gondwana.
The breakup may have triggered the Cryogenian Snowball Earth and the rapid evolution of life that followed.

facts.text: Magma flooded more than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland in about two million years, among Earth's largest magmatic episodes.
U-Pb dating puts its rapid emplacement at about 719.9 and 718.6 Ma.
With the Irkutsk province it marks the rifting of Siberia from Laurentia.
Weathering of its fresh basalt drew down carbon dioxide; glaciation began just 0.9–1.6 million years after its emplacement.

verification.title: Emplacement of the Franklin large igneous province and initiation of the Sturtian Snowball Earth

entries.text: More than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland vanished under magma in about two million years. The Franklin Large Igneous Province, a vast outpouring of basalt lava, ranks among the largest magmatic episodes in Earth's history. Uranium-lead dating puts its rapid emplacement at about 719.9 and 718.6 Ma. Together with the Irkutsk province in Siberia, it marks where Siberia rifted away from Laurentia. Its effect on climate was swift. As fresh basalt weathered, it drew carbon dioxide out of the air, and glaciation began just 0.9–1.6 million years after the lava cooled.

entries.title: The Sturtian: fifty-seven million years of ice

facts.text: A worldwide glaciation lasted from about 717 to 660 Ma, some 57 million years, the first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages.
The longest and most severe known glaciation after the Huronian, it may have been a Snowball Earth with ice at very low latitudes, or several regional glaciations.
Rodinia then lay near the equator, with glacial ice at or below sea level, evidence that the glaciation was global.
Its onset followed the Franklin large igneous province by 0.9–1.6 million years; basalt weathering and low ridge CO2 output after Rodinia's breakup may have caused the cold.
In the snowball episodes ice may have covered all but the highest mountains, with average temperatures about −50 °C.

entries.contested_note: Whether the ice reached the equator (Snowball) or left open water (Slushball) is still debated; the glaciation itself is not disputed.

entries.text: Ice at or below sea level, on a continent near the equator: that is the evidence that the Sturtian glaciation was global. It lasted from about 717 to 660 Ma, some 57 million years. It was the first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages and the longest and most severe known glaciation after the Huronian. The supercontinent Rodinia then straddled the equator, yet its glaciers reached the shore. The cold arrived only 0.9–1.6 million years after {{ref:prot-110}} erupted. One explanation joins the two: weathering of fresh basalt pulled carbon dioxide from the air, while Rodinia's breakup left mid-ocean ridges releasing little of it. In the snowball episodes, ice may have covered all but the highest mountains, with average temperatures near −50 °C. How far the ice reached is still debated. It may have been a Snowball Earth, with ice at very low latitudes. It may instead have been several regional glaciations, or a slushball with open water at the equator. That the glaciation happened is not in dispute.

entries.title: Snowball Earth: did the whole planet freeze

facts.text: The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that Earth's surface froze nearly completely, most commonly linked to the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations of the Cryogenian.
Glacial deposits formed at tropical latitudes, and glaciers reached sea level near the equator; such deposits are known from every continent.
Whether Earth was a full snowball or a slushball with an open equatorial band of water remains disputed.
Thick ice blocking sunlight would still have severely hindered primary production in shallow seas.
The cooling, and the rapid evolution that followed in the Ediacaran and Cambrian, are thought to have been triggered by Rodinia's breakup.

entries.contested_note: Glaciation itself is accepted, but whether ice covered the whole planet (Snowball) or left open tropical water (Slushball) is disputed.

entries.text: Glacial deposits laid down in the tropics turn up on every continent. Glaciers once reached sea level near the equator. From this comes the Snowball Earth hypothesis: that Earth's surface froze nearly completely, most often linked to the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations of the Cryogenian. Not everyone accepts the full freeze. The glaciation itself is accepted, but scientists still dispute whether ice covered the whole planet or left a slushball, with an open band of water around the equator. Either way, life struggled. Thick ice blocking sunlight would have severely hindered primary production, the growth of algae and other organisms that make food from light, in shallow seas. The trigger is thought to lie in Rodinia's breakup. The same breakup is linked to the rapid evolution of the Ediacaran and Cambrian. The frozen world sits right before the great burst of complex life.

entries.title: Shelled amoebae appear in the ice age

facts.text: Fossils of testate amoebae (Arcellinida), single-celled organisms with shells, first appear around 700 Ma in the Cryogenian.
Porter (2000) suggests red and green algae, stramenopiles, ciliates and dinoflagellates also evolved during this period.

entries.title: A warm pause between two snowballs

facts.text: Between the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations came a relatively warm interval with anoxic oceans and rising seas.
Global biodiversity during this interglacial was very low.
Oxygen may have reached about 50% of present levels, though chromium isotopes suggest oxygenation was slow and subdued, a lull in the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event.

entries.title: Island arcs crash into Gondwana's northern edge

facts.text: As Sturtian glaciers retreated, island arcs began colliding on the margin of future Gondwana, laying down the terranes of Avalonia, Armorica and Iberia.
An Andean-type volcanic arc formed about 650–600 Ma; a back-arc basin opened 590–560 Ma and closed 545–540 Ma.
The Avalonian belt collided with Gondwana around 650 Ma.

entries.title: Algae seize the ocean's plankton

facts.text: About 659–645 Ma, red and green algae replaced planktonic cyanobacteria as the main marine phytoplankton, a role they held until the Permian extinction.
Unicellular algae diversified rapidly, and their numbers rose by a factor of one hundred to one thousand.
Late in the Cryogenian, heterotrophic plankton appeared that fed on algae and prokaryotes, ending bacterial dominance of the oceans.

entries.text: Algae multiplied a hundred to a thousandfold. About 659–645 Ma, red and green algae replaced planktonic cyanobacteria as the main marine phytoplankton, the drifting organisms at the base of the ocean food web. Unicellular algae diversified rapidly, and they kept that role until the Permian extinction. The change rippled upward. Late in the Cryogenian, heterotrophic plankton appeared, drifting organisms that fed on algae and prokaryotes rather than making their own food. Bacteria had ruled the oceans for ages; now their dominance was over.

entries.title: Sponges survive the snowball

facts.text: Demosponges appear around 650 Ma, building skeletons of spicules from spongin protein and silica.
Some researchers argue the oldest sponge, and so animal, fossils are Cryogenian, but they may be proto-sponges or microbial precursors.
Sponges, which emerged in the Tonian, survived the Cryogenian glaciations.
The oldest sponge spicules, about 580 Ma from China's Doushantuo Formation and Mongolia, are also challenged.
Sponges recognisable as such, such as the non-mineralized Helicolocellus, appear in the latest Ediacaran.

entries.contested_note: The sponge identity of the Cryogenian fossils is uncertain; they may be proto-sponges or microbial structures.

entries.text: Sponges came through the Cryogenian glaciations alive. They had emerged in the Tonian, and demosponges appear around 650 Ma, building skeletons of spicules, tiny struts made of spongin protein and silica. The oldest fossils are another matter. Some researchers argue that the oldest sponge fossils, and so the oldest animal fossils, are Cryogenian. Others think they may be proto-sponges or microbial structures, and the question is unsettled. Even the oldest sponge spicules, about 580 Ma from China's Doushantuo Formation and Mongolia, are challenged. Sponges that are unmistakably sponges, such as the non-mineralized Helicolocellus, appear only in the latest Ediacaran.

entries.title: Songluo seaweeds in a break from the ice

facts.text: Large macroalgae fossils of the Songluo Biota grew in South China around 650 Ma, during a short break in the Marinoan glaciation.
It is the only known macrofossil biota from the Cryogenian, the first large carbonaceous fossils in rocks of that age.

entries.title: The Marinoan, the last great snowball

facts.text: The Marinoan, also called the Varanger or Elatina glaciation, was a worldwide glaciation late in the Cryogenian.
Its timing is poorly constrained; a 2025 study dates it to 639–635 Ma.
It is described as the most significant snowball Earth event, global in scope, recorded by diamictites in South Australia's Adelaide Geosyncline.
It ended through volcanic carbon dioxide and dissolving clathrates, perhaps hastened by methane from equatorial permafrost.
It was the last major snowball event; later ice ages covered less of the planet.

It was the last major snowball. Later ice ages covered less of the planet.

entries.title: Cap carbonates seal the last snowball

facts.text: The Ediacaran begins at a cap carbonate, the Nuccaleena Formation, directly above Elatina glacial deposits in South Australia's Flinders Ranges.
Neoproterozoic glacial deposits are commonly topped by a sharply overlying precipitated limestone or dolomite, metres to tens of metres thick.
A favoured explanation: after a snowball, carbon-dioxide-rich acid rain weathered rock, washing calcium into the sea to form carbonate layers.
Their glacial link is questioned: some are too thick for rapid deglaciation, and many glacial sequences lack them.
The boundary also marks the start of a distinctive pattern of carbon-isotope changes.

facts.text: At the start of the Ediacaran much of the long-stable acritarch plankton died out, replaced by larger, shorter-lived species.
From 635 to about 575 Ma, large ornamented Ediacaran microfossils, usually over 100 μm across, dominated.
They largely vanish before 560 Ma, about when the Ediacara biota arose; if animal resting stages, they fit frequent Ediacaran anoxia.

entries.title: Beardmore mountains rise in Antarctica

facts.text: The Beardmore orogeny built mountains in Antarctica from about 633 to 620 Ma.
It reflects Rodinia's final breakup, as its fragments began moving together again toward Pannotia.

entries.title: The Petermann orogeny raises the rocks of Uluru

facts.text: An intracontinental mountain-building event deformed central Australia's Musgrave basement and Amadeus Basin sediments between 630 and 520 Ma.
Its unusual east–west belt suggests India struck Western Australia from the northwest as Gondwana assembled.
It thrust up the rocks that now form Uluru, laid down around 550–530 Ma.

entries.title: Tidal layers record a 21.9-hour day

facts.text: Tidal rhythmites, layers of sand and silt laid down off estuaries with strong tides, preserve daily, monthly and seasonal cycles.
Their record fits a day of 21.9 ± 0.4 hours about 620 Ma, with about 400 days and 13.1 lunar months in a year.
Tides slow Earth's spin as the Moon recedes; its average recession since then, 2.17 cm a year, is about half today's rate.

entries.title: A mantle plume splits Laurentia from Baltica

facts.text: A mantle plume, the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province, forced Laurentia and Baltica apart, opening the Iapetus Ocean between them.
Rifting began with the Egersund dike swarm in Norway around 650 Ma; from 600 Ma the two continents rotated up to 180°.
The eastern Iapetus opened around 590 Ma, and its southern arm between Laurentia and South America about 550 Ma.
The ocean lasted from about 600 to 425 Ma in the Southern Hemisphere, bordered by Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and other continents.
The Tornquist Sea, between Avalonia and Baltica, probably formed at the same time.

entries.text: A plume of hot mantle rock, the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province, forced Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean between them. Rifting began with the Egersund dike swarm in Norway around 650 Ma. From 600 Ma the two continents rotated by up to 180°. The ocean opened in stages. Its eastern part opened around 590 Ma, and its southern arm, between Laurentia and South America, about 550 Ma. The Tornquist Sea, between Avalonia and Baltica, probably formed at the same time. Bordered by Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and other continents, the Iapetus lasted from about 600 to 425 Ma in the Southern Hemisphere.

entries.title: The ozone shield goes up

facts.text: By about 600 Ma enough oxygen had accumulated to form an ozone layer.
Before this, land-based life probably needed other chemicals to screen out ultraviolet radiation.
Atmospheric oxygen, between 1% and 18% of present levels at 800 Ma, began rising more significantly around 600 Ma.

entries.title: The Pan-African orogeny welds Gondwana together

facts.text: The Pan-African orogeny, a series of major mountain-building events, built the supercontinents Gondwana and Pannotia about 600 Ma.
It began around 635 Ma when the West African and Saharan cratons collided, closing the Pharusian Ocean.
By about 600 Ma most of western Gondwana had joined, while Australia and East Antarctica were still separate.
All African cratons were assembled by about 550 Ma.
Gondwana remained a landmass from about 600 Ma until Pangaea broke up in the Early Jurassic.

entries.title: Pannotia, a supercontinent that may never have been

facts.text: Pannotia, also called Greater Gondwana, is a proposed supercontinent that may have formed during the Pan-African orogeny.
It formed around 600 Ma and broke apart only some 50 million years later.
It broke up about 560 Ma as the Iapetus Ocean opened; Laurentia rifted from South America around 565 Ma.
A 2022 paper argues it never fully existed, having begun to break up before it was fully assembled.
Its breakup came with rising seas, dramatic changes in climate and ocean chemistry, and rapid animal diversification.

entries.title: The Acraman impact strikes South Australia

facts.text: A chondritic impactor struck what is now the Gawler Ranges of South Australia about 590 Ma; the age comes from its ejecta in nearby basins.
Estimates of the eroded crater's original size range from 35–40 km to 85–90 km; the larger implies 5.2 million megatons of TNT.
Its ejecta layer, with shocked minerals and an iridium anomaly, lies in Flinders Ranges rocks at least 300 km east.
A radiation of acritarch microorganisms begins just above the ejecta layer, and some authors suspect a link.

entries.title: Gaskiers, a short and sharp ice age

facts.text: Widespread glacial deposits formed over about 250,000 years, 579.88–579.63 Ma, the last major glacial event of the Proterozoic.
It was the shortest of at least three Neoproterozoic ice ages and, unlike the Sturtian and Marinoan, probably not a Snowball Earth.
Its deposits occur on eight paleocontinents, some at only 10–30° latitude.
It lies just below some of the oldest Ediacaran fossils, though a 9-million-year gap separates them.
A proposed scheme places the base of an Upper Ediacaran series at this glaciation.

entries.title: The Avalon explosion: big life arrives

facts.text: A proposed burst of animal evolution about 575 Ma, named for fossils on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, is thought to have produced the Ediacaran biota.
These large, mostly soft-bodied, often sessile tube- and frond-shaped organisms are the earliest known complex multicellular life.
Metazoan diversity rose quickly, including the first cnidarians and bilaterians, some 36 million years before the Cambrian explosion.
Their place in the tree of life is unclear; it is not even established that most were animals.
Most of these organisms died out in the end-Ediacaran extinction about 539 Ma.

entries.contested_note: The 2008 shape-diversity analysis that defined the Avalon explosion has been disputed; the Ediacaran biota itself is not.

entries.text: Some 36 million years before the Cambrian explosion, life got big. A proposed burst of evolution about 575 Ma, named for fossils on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, is thought to have produced the Ediacaran biota. These were large, mostly soft-bodied organisms, often fixed in place, shaped like tubes and fronds. They are the earliest known complex multicellular life. The diversity of metazoans, many-celled animals, rose quickly, and the first cnidarians and bilaterians joined them. Yet the newcomers are hard to classify. Their place in the tree of life is unclear, and it is not even established that most of them were animals. The explosion's definition is itself contested. A 2008 analysis of shape diversity gave the event its name, and that analysis has been disputed; the Ediacaran biota itself is not. Most of these organisms died out in the end-Ediacaran extinction about 539 Ma.

entries.title: The Shuram excursion, carbon's biggest swing

facts.text: The Shuram excursion is a shift in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 during the Ediacaran, first noticed in South Australia's Wonoka Formation.
Its timing is debated: it began around 573 Ma and ended around 562 or 551 Ma.
It is the largest negative carbon-13 excursion in Earth history, with a 50-million-year recovery, though diagenesis may exaggerate it.
Its cause is unknown; the oxygen-using Ediacaran biota radiated during it, exploiting a surplus of oxidants.
It may have helped spark the rise of animals that led to the Cambrian explosion.

entries.title: Charnia, the fossil that opened the Precambrian

facts.text: Charnia was a frond with leaf-like ridges branching alternately from a zig-zag midline, living on deep sea floors 570–550 Ma.

It is among the most iconic Ediacaran forms, yet among the hardest to place in the tree of life.

It holds one of the most diverse and best-preserved collections of Precambrian fossils.
It defines the deep-water Avalon assemblage, the oldest locality rich in Ediacaran fossils, some of which survive to the Cambrian's base.

entries.title: A failing magnetic field and a young inner core

facts.text: Rocks formed about 565 Ma record an unusually weak geomagnetic field with two distinct directions.
With frequent reversals then, this suggests the solid inner core was only beginning to form, an idea new Cambrian data appear to support.
A 2016 dynamo model predicted a weak field from 1.0 to 0.6 Ga and a strong dipole field after inner-core nucleation.

entries.contested_note: The inner core's age is unresolved, with estimates from 0.5 to 2 billion years; an Ediacaran start is one hypothesis.

entries.title: Cloudina builds the first animal skeletons

facts.text: Cloudinids, an early animal family, lived about 550 Ma and died out at the base of the Cambrian.
Cloudina, Namacalathus and a dozen other organisms built mineralized tubes in carbonate rocks 549–542 Ma.
They are among the earliest and most abundant small shelly fossils with mineralized skeletons.
Cloudina tubes often show predatory borings, so predation was at least present in the Ediacaran.
Rising oxygen lowered ocean acidity and raised seawater calcium around the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, possibly prompting skeleton-building.

entries.title: The Proto-Tethys Ocean opens

facts.text: The Proto-Tethys Ocean existed from the latest Ediacaran to the Carboniferous, about 550–330 Ma.
It lay between Baltica and Laurentia to the north and Gondwana to the south.
After the Cadomian events it formed the eastern part of an ocean system subducting beneath Gondwana's northern margin.

entries.title: A supermountain feeds the Cambrian explosion

facts.text: The East African Orogeny raised the Transgondwanan Supermountain, more than 8,000 km long and 1,000 km wide.
Its erosion built the Gondwana Super-fan, over 100 million km³ of sediment laid down over 260 million years.
The flood of sediment coincided with the Cambrian explosion and probably helped early animals diversify.
By the Ordovician the range had been worn down to a plain in modern Ethiopia.

entries.title: Nama: the thin last chapter of the Ediacaran

facts.text: The Nama assemblage, the last Ediacaran biotic interval (about 550–539 Ma), was depauperate, never regaining diversity lost as the White Sea biota gave way.
Namibia's Nama Group Lagerstätten preserve Rangea, erniettomorphs and eumetazoans from shallow seas shaped by tides, storms and deltas.
By the end of the Ediacaran, no more than a dozen of 92 possible modes of life were occupied.

entries.title: The Baykonurian, a late Ediacaran ice age

facts.text: The Baykonurian glaciation lasted from around 547 to 540 Ma, late in the Ediacaran.
Its deposits occur in Asia and Africa, and it apparently affected both hemispheres.
It has been proposed as a contributor to the Cambrian explosion.

entries.title: Trail-makers grow longer and sense farther

facts.text: Trace-makers grew steadily more elongate, with bodies over eight times longer than wide by the terminal Ediacaran.
Their trails formed tighter, more accurate loops, and their sensory range grew from millimetres or centimetres to decimetres around 540 Ma.
Some behavioural and sensory innovations of the Cambrian may therefore have begun in the terminal Ediacaran.

entries.title: The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen floods with magma

facts.text: The Southern Oklahoma Aulacogen formed between 525 and 550 Ma as Laurentia rifted; its other two arms became spreading zones of the young Iapetus Ocean.
Its flood basalts began or peaked around 540 Ma, covering about 40,000 km² with roughly 250,000 km³ of magma, and are linked to an end-Ediacaran event.
Magmatism came in two phases, first gabbroic and then rhyolitic.

entries.title: The end-Ediacaran extinction clears the stage

facts.text: The end-Ediacaran extinction, also called the Kotlin Crisis, is a mass extinction near the end of the Ediacaran, the last period of the Proterozoic.
Acritarch diversity fell sharply, and the soft-bodied Ediacaran biota and shelled Cloudina and Namacalathus disappeared.
Both groups vanish abruptly 538.8 ± 0.2 Ma, so their loss cannot simply reflect a closing preservational window.
A major negative carbon-isotope excursion marks the boundary; in Oman it coincides with the last Namacalathus and Cloudina.
Very few organisms crossed the boundary; Cambrian animals then radiated into the vacant niches.

entries.title: Fortune Head: where the Cambrian begins

facts.text: A rock section at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, is the formal base of the Cambrian, traced worldwide by the first Treptichnus pedum burrows.
Treptichnus pedum is a burrow trace fossil linked to early priapulid worms; finds a few metres below the boundary led to using its whole trace assemblage.
Modern radiometric dating puts the boundary at 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma; in 2022 the age was revised from 541 Ma.
The boundary opens the Paleozoic Era and the Phanerozoic Eon, and now lies below the first trilobites and small shelly fossils.
Several chemical markers show a drastic change in the environment around the start of the Cambrian.

entries.title: The Cambrian explosion

facts.text: Beginning about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly, producing the first representatives of most modern animal phyla.
The early Cambrian burst lasted about 20–25 million years; its high evolutionary rates had ended by 521 Ma, when trilobites appear.
Animals gained mineralised skeletons, more complex bodies and behaviour, and began burrowing, changing the sea floor and opening new ecosystems.
Molybdenum isotopes tie rising early Cambrian biodiversity to the spread of oxygenated bottom waters, supporting oxygen as a driver.
Its rate of diversification is unmatched among marine animals, though how explosive it really was is still debated.

entries.text: In about 20–25 million years, life went from a handful of body plans to nearly all of today's. Beginning about 538.8 Ma, complex life diversified suddenly and produced the first representatives of most modern animal phyla. This is the Cambrian explosion. Its rate of diversification is unmatched among marine animals, though how explosive it really was is still debated. Animals changed in every way at once. They gained mineralized skeletons, more complex bodies and more complex behavior. They began to burrow, churning the sea floor and opening new ecosystems below it. Oxygen may have lit the fuse. Molybdenum isotopes tie rising early Cambrian biodiversity to the spread of oxygenated bottom waters, which supports oxygen as a driver. The burst did not last forever. Its high evolutionary rates had ended by 521 Ma, when {{ref:camb-028}}.

entries.title: Small shelly fossils: the first hard parts

facts.text: Small shelly fossils, mineralized tubes, spicules and plates often only millimetres long, form a nearly continuous record from the latest Ediacaran to the end of the Early Cambrian.
Graham Budd's scheme runs from a Tube world (550–536 Ma) to a Sclerite world of halkieriids, tommotiids and hyoliths ending about 525 Ma.
Their fairly continuous record shows phyla appearing in a rapid but orderly sequence rather than a sudden jumble.
Signs of selective predator attacks on them suggest predation helped drive new species.
Most were thought wiped out in the end-Botomian extinction, but their apparent disappearance may partly reflect the loss of phosphate preservation.

entries.title: The Cambrian sea rises over the continents

facts.text: A marine transgression began at the start of the Cambrian, and sea level rose gradually through the period.
It was the second-greatest sustained sea-level rise of the Phanerozoic, as the climate grew warmer.
Shallow seas spread across flat eroded surfaces such as the sub-Cambrian peneplain and the Great Unconformity, burying them under marine sediments.
Seas spread over Baltica and much of Antarctica, and marine invertebrates flourished in the shallow waters.
In North America this Sauk transgression began in earnest only in the middle Cambrian.

entries.title: The Pampean orogeny builds Gondwana's western edge

facts.text: The Pampean orogeny built mountains on the western margin of Gondwana during the Cambrian, between about 535 and 520 Ma.
It partly involved an exotic terrane accreted to Gondwana's proto-Pacific margin, long before the Andes formed.
A magmatic belt of its igneous rocks formed from 525 to 515 Ma.

entries.title: First footprints on land

facts.text: The first known footprints on land date to about 530 Ma, though the evidence that arthropods were on land so early is unconfirmed.
Early Cambrian trace fossils suggest mollusc-like animals could spend at least 15 minutes on land.
Tracks from the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary, about 490 Ma, are read as large amphibious arthropods, perhaps euthycarcinoids, crossing coastal dunes.

entries.title: Kuunga–Damara collisions complete Gondwana

facts.text: Around 530 Ma the Kalahari and Mawson cratons joined in the Kuunga–Damara orogeny, completing southern Gondwana.
Deformation and metamorphism in the Damara orogeny peaked between 530 and 500 Ma.
Collisions in East Antarctica's Lützow-Holm and Prydz belts climaxed at 530 Ma.
A narrow ocean separated Amazonia from Gondwana until about 530 Ma; the last stages of assembly overlapped with the Cambrian explosion.
West Gondwana was stitched together along the Transbrasiliano lineament in the mid-Cambrian, as Amazonia collided with the São Francisco–Congo and Río de la Plata blocks.

entries.title: Oxygen pulses breathe life into Cambrian seas

facts.text: In Stages 2 and 3, linked carbon and sulphur isotope excursions record heavy burial of organic carbon and pyrite in productive but anoxic seafloor waters.
Oxygen-rich waters then spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas, extending the habitable seafloor.
These oxygen pulses match the radiation of small shelly fossils and the Cambrian arthropod radiation isotope excursion (CARE).
Oxygenation cut burial rates and anoxia returned; the cycle repeated several times in the early Cambrian.
Rising seawater 87Sr/86Sr shows stronger continental weathering, which fed nutrients to the oceans.

entries.text: The early Cambrian ocean breathed in and out. In Stages 2 and 3, linked carbon and sulphur isotope excursions record heavy burial of organic carbon and pyrite in productive seafloor waters short of oxygen. Burial locked away material that would otherwise use up oxygen. Oxygen-rich waters then spread from the deep ocean into shallow seas, extending the habitable seafloor. Each pulse undid itself. Oxygenation cut burial rates, and anoxia returned; the cycle repeated several times. The pulses match the radiation of small shelly fossils and the Cambrian arthropod radiation isotope excursion, or CARE. Meanwhile, rising strontium ratios in seawater show stronger continental weathering, which fed nutrients to the oceans.

Meanwhile, rising strontium ratios in seawater show stronger continental weathering, which fed nutrients to the oceans.

entries.title: Archaeocyaths build the first animal reefs

facts.text: Archaeocyaths, sessile cup-shaped sponges with porous calcareous skeletons, are first known from East Siberia at the start of the Tommotian, 525 Ma.
With cyanobacteria, they built the early Cambrian reefs in warm tropical seas, the oldest known large-scale structures made by animals.
They diversified rapidly in Stage 3, then declined sharply in Stage 4.

entries.title: Sirius Passet: a Cambrian window in Greenland

It is one of the Cambrian's major Lagerstätten, with the Burgess Shale and Maotianshan Shales.

entries.title: Trilobites arrive with calcite eyes

facts.text: Trilobite body fossils first appear around 521 Ma, as trilobites evolved mineralised calcite exoskeletons.
Their first appearance is the proposed base of Cambrian Series 2 and Stage 3, and the top of the Terreneuvian.
Trace fossils such as Rusophycus and Cruziana, claimed as trilobite tracks, appear from about 537 Ma.
They quickly diversified into the typical Cambrian orders, Redlichiida, Ptychopariida, Agnostida and Corynexochida, becoming the most diverse early Cambrian animals.
Even the earliest trilobites had complex compound eyes with calcite lenses.

entries.title: The Ross orogeny lifts the Transantarctic Mountains

facts.text: From about 520 to 450 Ma, Cambrian sediments in the Transantarctic Mountains were uplifted, folded, metamorphosed and intruded by granite batholiths.
After early Cambrian rifting, Antarctica deformed and the Transantarctic Mountains rose in the mid-Cambrian.

entries.title: Chengjiang: the Cambrian explosion in full color

facts.text: The Maotianshan Shales of Chengjiang, Yunnan, preserve an extremely diverse early Cambrian fauna with soft tissues, deposited no earlier than 518 Ma.
They hold the oldest diverse animal assemblage of the Phanerozoic, the best record of the Cambrian explosion.
Chengjiang has all the animal groups of the Burgess Shale but is about ten million years older, implying earlier or faster diversification.
Its chordates include Haikouella, Yunnanozoon and early fish such as Haikouichthys; its arthropods also occur elsewhere, suggesting a global range.
About one in eight of its animals are problematic forms of uncertain affinity.

entries.title: The first fish swim in Chengjiang

facts.text: The earliest known vertebrates belong to China's Chengjiang biota, about 518 Ma; fish are thought to have begun evolving around 530 Ma.
Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia had fins, vertebrate muscles and gills; Haikouichthys had distinct vertebrae.
Chordates, including tunicates and vertebrates, diversified in the Cambrian as mid-sized suspension feeders in open water or near the bottom.
Metaspriggina, from the younger Burgess Shale about 505 Ma, had an elongate body, prominent eyes and gills.
Despite their later abundance, early vertebrates remain rare in the Cambrian record.

entries.title: The first crustaceans

Most major crustacean groups, branchiopods, maxillopods and malacostracans, appear before the end of the Cambrian.

entries.title: The Sinsk Event: the first Phanerozoic mass extinction

facts.text: The Sinsk Event, about 513.5 Ma, began the end-Botomian crisis of Stages 4 and 5; it was the Phanerozoic's first mass extinction, removing over 60% of animal species.
A major transgression brought anoxic deep water onto the shelves, spreading black shales; the nearly synchronous Kalkarindji eruptions probably drove warming and deoxygenation.
It devastated reef faunas, above all the reef-dominating archaeocyath sponges, along with halkieriids and much of the small shelly fauna.
Many stem groups of sponges, cnidarians, brachiopods and molluscs died out; mobile animals such as trilobites recovered fast, but diversity stayed low into the early Ordovician.
Deep-water communities, such as the later Huayuan biota, may have come through largely intact in refugia.

entries.text: Over 60% of animal species disappeared. The Sinsk Event, about 513.5 Ma, began the end-Botomian crisis of Stages 4 and 5, the first mass extinction of the Phanerozoic. Mobile animals such as trilobites recovered fast, but diversity stayed low into the early Ordovician. Deep-water communities, such as the later Huayuan biota, may have come through largely intact in refuges.

entries.title: Kalkarindji floods Australia with basalt

facts.text: Around 511 Ma, flood basalts of the Kalkarindji large igneous province began erupting in what is now Australia.
They covered over 2,100,000 km², making it one of the largest and the earliest large igneous province of the Phanerozoic.
Eruptions in Stage 4 and the early Miaolingian released carbon dioxide, methane and sulphur dioxide, driving rapid climate change and warmer seas.
These changes show up as three large, rapid carbon isotope excursions.
The timing suggests the eruptions helped cause the early to middle Cambrian mass extinction.

entries.title: The Burgess Shale

facts.text: The Burgess Shale of British Columbia, about 508–505 Ma, preserves soft-bodied animals as thin dark carbon films.
One of the best-known Cambrian Lagerstätten, it preserves a key record of the Cambrian explosion.
Its biota includes strange arthropods like Opabinia, and Anomalocaris, the first great apex predator.
Metaspriggina, an early vertebrate with prominent eyes and gills, and medusa-stage jellyfish such as Burgessomedusa also occur there.

entries.text: Thin dark films of carbon on British Columbia slate turned out to be animals no one had imagined. The Burgess Shale, about 508–505 Ma, preserves soft-bodied creatures that elsewhere would have rotted away. It is one of the best-known Lagerstätten, or sites of exceptional preservation, of the Cambrian, and a key record of the Cambrian explosion. Its cast is strange. Opabinia is one of several odd arthropods there. Anomalocaris was the first great apex predator. Metaspriggina, an early vertebrate with prominent eyes and gills, swam among them, and medusa-stage jellyfish such as Burgessomedusa drifted overhead. The site is younger than {{ref:camb-033}}, yet it was the Burgess Shale that first revealed how varied Cambrian life had been.

entries.title: Trilobites suffer their first great extinction

entries.title: DICE: deep anoxic water rises again

facts.text: The Drumian carbon isotope excursion (DICE) marks the start of the Drumian age, about 504.5 Ma.
It was caused by anoxic deep waters rising into shallower settings as they transgressed.
DICE hampered the recovery of reef ecosystems already hit by the early-middle Cambrian mass extinctions.

entries.text: Around 504.5 Ma, deep water short of oxygen rose into shallower seas as the sea advanced over the land. That rise caused the Drumian carbon isotope excursion, or DICE, which marks the start of the Drumian age. It came at a bad time. Reef ecosystems were still recovering from the early to middle Cambrian mass extinctions, and DICE held that recovery back.

entries.title: Orsten: microscopic animals of the seafloor

facts.text: Sweden's Kinnekulle Orsten and Alum Shale reveal the oldest well-documented seafloor meiofauna, including microscopic arthropods such as free-living pentastomids.

entries.text: Some of the most revealing Cambrian fossils are too small to see without a microscope. Sweden's Kinnekulle Orsten and Alum Shale reveal the oldest well-documented meiofauna, the tiny animals that live among seafloor grains. Among them are microscopic arthropods such as free-living pentastomids. These sites show that the Cambrian sea floor teemed with life at a scale larger fossils miss.

Oxic waters expanded into deep and shelf seas in the latest Cambrian, as burrows deepened and body plans grew more complex.

entries.title: The end-Marjuman extinction strips the shallows

facts.text: Beginning in the mid-Guzhangian, an extinction cut species diversity by 45%; it ended early in the Furongian, perhaps mid-Paibian, about 3 million years later.
In South China it came in two phases: a slight decline over about 1.8 million years, then a sharper one over 1.2 million years.
Gradual ocean deoxygenation from the Guzhangian into the Jiangshanian, with the linked SPICE event, likely caused it; spreading anoxia killed off marjumiid and damesellid trilobites.
Shallow-water polymerid trilobites were replaced by deep-water olenimorph trilobites.
The onset of the SPICE excursion matches the extinction's second wave; diversity recovered at the very start of the Jiangshanian.

entries.title: SPICE: a carbon spike in a suffocating sea

facts.text: The Steptoean positive carbon isotope excursion (SPICE) was a global event between about 497 and 494 Ma, starting near the Guzhangian–Paibian boundary.
Erosion of Gondwana's mountains pushed seawater 87Sr/86Sr to a peak, and spreading seafloor anoxia boosted burial of organic matter and pyrite.
Sea-level changes, cooling of surface water, anoxia and trilobite and brachiopod extinctions are all associated with it.
Its end matches the End-Steptoean biomere extinction.
The oxygen rise that followed opened niches for photosynthetic plankton and helped drive their radiation.

entries.text: Mountains wearing away on Gondwana drove seawater strontium ratios to a peak. At the same time, anoxia spreading across the seafloor boosted the burial of organic matter and pyrite. The result was the Steptoean positive carbon isotope excursion, or SPICE, a global event between about 497 and 494 Ma that began near the Guzhangian–Paibian boundary. It came with sea-level changes, cooling of surface water, anoxia, and extinctions of trilobites and brachiopods. Its end matches the End-Steptoean biomere extinction. Then came a turn. The rise in oxygen that followed opened niches for photosynthetic plankton and helped drive their radiation.

entries.title: The Famatinian orogeny raises western South America

facts.text: The Famatinian orogeny ran from the Late Cambrian to at least the Late Devonian, with mountain building peaking about 490–460 Ma.
Plutonic rocks south of Chile's Salar de Atacama formed with it in the Cambrian and Ordovician.
A chain of volcanoes, the Famatinian magmatic arc, formed in what is now western South America.
The orogeny peaked when the Cuyania terrane collided with Pampia in the Ordovician.
From 480 to 435 Ma, rocks of the Cordillera Oriental were deformed as the arc developed.

entries.title: The Caledonian orogeny begins to close the Iapetus

facts.text: The Caledonian orogeny spans mountain-building events from the Ordovician to the Early Devonian, roughly 490–390 Ma.
Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia collided, raising mountains now in northern Britain and Ireland, Scandinavia, Svalbard, East Greenland and north-central Europe.
Its onset has also been dated to about 500 Ma, in the Late Cambrian.
The Iapetus Ocean, widest in the Late Cambrian–Early Ordovician, began closing by subduction between 500 and 488 Ma.
In the Late Cambrian the Iapetus mid-ocean ridge subducted beneath Gondwana, opening large back-arc basins.

entries.title: The Cambrian–Ordovician extinction

facts.text: An extinction at the Cambrian–Ordovician boundary ended the Cambrian; another radiation followed that established the dominant Paleozoic animals.
It eliminated many brachiopods and conodonts and severely reduced the number of trilobite species.
Almost all Redlichiida and most Late Cambrian trilobite stocks died out, and agnostid diversity fell sharply.
Volcanism, especially from large igneous provinces, has been speculated as the cause of the crisis.
Some researchers argue the apparent extinction is an artifact of a gap in the rock record.

entries.title: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event

facts.text: Marine animal life radiated through the Ordovician, replacing the Cambrian fauna with one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers.
Global diversity rose severalfold as the phyla filled out with many new classes and lower taxa.
The rise was neither global nor instantaneous; different groups diversified at different times from the Late Cambrian to the Middle Ordovician.
Proposed drivers include rising ocean oxygen, nutrients eroded from the Taconic mountains, global cooling and a meteorite shower.
It set the marine ecological template for the rest of the Paleozoic.

entries.text: Global marine diversity rose severalfold in the Ordovician. Through the period, marine animal life radiated and replaced the Cambrian fauna with one rich in suspension feeders and swimmers. The animal phyla filled out with many new classes and smaller groups. This was the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event, or GOBE. It was not one sudden burst. Different groups diversified at different times, from the Late Cambrian to the Middle Ordovician, and not everywhere at once. What drove it is still argued. Proposed causes include rising ocean oxygen, nutrients eroded from the Taconic mountains, global cooling and a meteorite shower. Whatever the mix, the outcome was lasting. The GOBE set the ecological template of the seas for the rest of the Paleozoic.

entries.title: The Iapetus Ocean narrows

facts.text: The Iapetus Ocean between Gondwana, Laurentia and Baltica was over 4,000 km wide at the start of the Ordovician.
Baltica drifted toward Laurentia while island arcs and microcontinents such as Ganderia were added to Laurentia and Avalonia.
As the ocean narrowed, seafloor brachiopods and trilobites spread between continents, while ostracods and fishes stayed isolated.
Several sources say Laurentia, Baltica and Avalonia had joined by the end of the Ordovician, forming Euramerica (Laurussia).

entries.title: Rising seas drown the continents

facts.text: Sea level rose more or less continuously through the Early Ordovician, levelling off around mid-period.
Shallow seas covered much of North America, Europe and Gondwana.

North America's Transcontinental Arch went under water, not to reappear until the Devonian.

entries.title: The Ordovician plankton revolution

facts.text: Several invertebrate lineages colonized open waters, starting new food chains from the end of the Cambrian into the early Ordovician.
The first phase of the GOBE, tied to planktonic communities, ended in the late Early Ordovician.
Chitinozoans radiated explosively across the Tremadocian and later became key markers for dating rocks.
Acritarchs, mostly marine algae, peaked in diversity and disparity in the Middle Ordovician.
More plankton allowed suspension feeders on the seafloor and swimmers in the water column to multiply.

entries.title: The Taconic orogeny raises the first Appalachians

facts.text: Volcanic island arcs collided with Laurentia, raising a great mountain chain from eastern Canada down the east of today's United States.
A change in plate motions in the middle Ordovician set the stage for this first Paleozoic mountain building in North America.
The orogeny affected most of New England.
Erosion of the new mountains fed iron and phosphorus to the oceans, a proposed driver of the GOBE.
Weathering of the rising Appalachians and Caledonides drew down CO2 in the Late Ordovician.

entries.text: A great mountain chain once ran from eastern Canada down the east of today's United States. It rose when volcanic island arcs collided with Laurentia in the Taconic orogeny, the first Paleozoic mountain building in North America. A change in plate motions in the middle Ordovician prepared the collision, and the orogeny affected most of New England. The mountains reached far beyond themselves. Their erosion fed iron and phosphorus to the oceans, a proposed driver of the GOBE. Later, the weathering of the rising Appalachians and Caledonides drew down CO2 in the Late Ordovician.

entries.title: From greenhouse to icehouse

facts.text: Oxygen isotopes in conodonts show the climate began shifting from greenhouse to icehouse at the end of the Early Ordovician.
A sharp Floian rise in carbon isotope ratios may mark cooling through organic carbon burial, proposed to have kick-started the GOBE.
By the end of the Middle Ordovician, low-latitude sea surfaces had cooled to today's equatorial temperatures.
Graptolite ranges suggest Earth was in a mild icehouse state by about 460 million years ago.
Biodiversity rose in step with cooling during the GOBE.

entries.text: By the end of the Middle Ordovician, low-latitude sea surfaces had cooled to today's equatorial temperatures. Biodiversity climbed in step with cooling during the GOBE. Graptolite ranges suggest Earth was in a mild icehouse state by about 460 million years ago.

entries.title: The Decorah impact in Iowa

facts.text: A meteor about 200 m wide struck what is now Decorah, Iowa, around 470 million years ago.
The possible crater, about 5.6 km across and now buried under the Winneshiek Shale, formed with energy equal to 1,000 megatons of TNT.
It may be part of the Ordovician meteor event.

entries.title: The first land plants leave their spores

facts.text: Cryptospores, the spores of the first land plants, appear about 470 million years ago and dominate plant fossil assemblages for some 60 million years.
Land plants evolved from green algae; the earliest were bryophytes, similar to mosses and liverworts.
Baltica was an early cradle of land plants, with a diverse flora by the Darriwilian.
By burying organic carbon, they began drawing down CO2 and transforming land environments and the global climate.
Without deep roots, they did little to break rock into soil.

entries.text: The first land plants are known by their spores. Cryptospores appear about 470 million years ago and dominate plant fossil assemblages for some 60 million years. The plants that made them evolved from green algae. The earliest were bryophytes, similar to mosses and liverworts. Baltica was an early cradle. By the Darriwilian it already held a diverse flora. Small as they were, these plants changed the planet. By burying organic carbon, they began drawing down CO2 and transforming both land environments and the global climate. There were limits to what they could do. Without deep roots, they did little to break rock into soil, a job left to the larger plants that came later.

entries.title: Clearwater East: one crater, not a twin

facts.text: An impact in Quebec, Canada, formed the 26 km Clearwater East crater; argon-argon dating of its impact melt gives about 460-470 Ma.
Its neighbour Clearwater West formed much later, in the Early Permian; their different meteorite signatures show adjacent craters need not be twins.
Its central peak, hidden under lake water and sediment, was confirmed by bathymetric surveys and core drilling.

entries.text: Two craters sit side by side in Quebec, but they are not twins. The 26 km Clearwater East crater formed about 460–470 Ma, by argon-argon dating of its impact melt. Clearwater East's central peak lies hidden under lake water and sediment; depth surveys and core drilling confirmed it.

entries.title: The Paleozoic Oxidation Event begins

facts.text: Atmospheric oxygen rose between 470 and 400 Ma, the Paleozoic Oxidation Event.
The first land plants, spreading from about 470 to 445 Ma, trapped organic carbon in sediments and reduced the oxygen sink.
Oxygen later reached and exceeded today's level of about 21% in the early Carboniferous.

entries.text: Between 470 and 400 Ma, oxygen in the air rose in what is called the Paleozoic Oxidation Event. The first land plants, spreading from about 470 to 445 Ma, helped drive it. They trapped organic carbon in sediments, where it could no longer react with oxygen, so less oxygen was used up. The rise kept going. Oxygen later reached and exceeded today's level of about 21% in the early Carboniferous.

entries.title: The Ordovician meteor shower

facts.text: The break-up of the L-chondrite parent body in space sent fragments into Earth-crossing orbits.
About 100 times as many meteorites struck Earth each year as today, and the raised rate lasted for millions of years.
Shock ages in many L-chondrite meteorites that still fall today, and helium-3 in seafloor sediments, support the event.
Craters such as Ames (16 km, Oklahoma), Rock Elm (6 km, Wisconsin) and Slate Islands, and possibly Decorah and Granby, may belong to this shower.
It was once suggested to have sparked the GOBE, but other evidence puts it about 600,000 years after the Darriwilian diversity burst.

entries.title: The Early Paleozoic Ice Age

facts.text: A long ice age, also called the Andean-Saharan glaciation, lasted from about 460 to 420 million years ago.
Glaciers were probably present in Gondwana by the Sandbian, with several short glaciations then and in the Katian.
Ice centred on the Sahara in the Ordovician and shifted to South America in the Silurian; it is known from Arabia, West Africa and the Andes.
Gondwana's position over the South Pole may have allowed ice to form despite high CO2 levels.
Sea level rose and fell as ice caps grew and melted.

entries.text: Ice spread over Gondwana while carbon dioxide was still high. A long ice age, also called the Andean-Saharan glaciation, lasted from about 460 to 420 million years ago. Glaciers were probably present by the Sandbian, with several short glaciations then and in the Katian. In the Ordovician the ice centered on the Sahara; in the Silurian it shifted to South America. It is known from Arabia, West Africa and the Andes. Geography may explain it. Gondwana sat over the South Pole, which may have let ice form despite the high CO2. As ice caps grew and melted, sea level rose and fell.

entries.title: The Hunic terranes split from Gondwana

facts.text: Back-arc spreading split the Hunic terranes from Gondwana in the late Ordovician, opening the Paleo-Tethys Ocean.
The terranes began moving north toward Euramerica.

entries.text: Behind a line of volcanoes, the crust stretched and tore. This back-arc spreading split the Hunic terranes, a group of crustal blocks, away from Gondwana in the late Ordovician. entries.title: The Kazakh terranes gather into Kazakhstania

facts.text: The Kazakh terranes, an equatorial archipelago of island arcs and microcontinents, merged as part of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt.
Accretion of crust to paleo-Kazakhstan was complete by the end of the Ordovician and Silurian.
Another account places the amalgamation of these Central Asian terranes into Kazakhstania in the late Silurian.

Chitinozoan microfossils date the impact to about 458 million years ago.

entries.title: Deicke and Millbrig: ash falls bigger than Toba

facts.text: Huge eruptions during the Taconic orogeny, probably from a volcanic arc, left ash now preserved as the Deicke and Millbrig bentonites on Laurentia.
The Millbrig ash fall, about 454 Ma, was the largest in the last 590 million years.
Each eruption's ash layer was larger in volume than that of the Toba eruption.

Each eruption's ash layer was larger in volume than that of the Toba eruption.

entries.title: Extinction rates rise in the Katian

facts.text: Extinction rates rose significantly in the early or middle Katian, several million years before the Hirnantian glaciation.
This early phase of extinction is linked to large igneous province activity, possibly the Alborz LIP of northern Iran, and to the Boda event.
Bryozoan losses were drawn out: their extinction rates were higher in the early and late Katian, and origination rates dropped sharply in the late Katian.

entries.title: Arthropods walk onto land

facts.text: The oldest clear evidence of animals on land is of arthropods around 450 Ma.

They may have thrived on the food supply provided by early land plants.
Late Ordovician trace fossils a little over 445 Ma probably record land invertebrates.

entries.title: Avalonia collides with Baltica

facts.text: Eastern Avalonia collided with Baltica at about 30°S, closing the Tornquist Sea.
The collision formed the north-western Trans-European Suture Zone and coincided with the Shelveian orogeny of western England and Wales.
It stopped the Rheic Ocean widening south of Avalonia, with huge magmatism in Avalonia and a gigantic ash fall in Baltica.
Avalonian magmatism peaked between 457 and 449 Ma.

entries.title: The Alice Springs Orogeny tilts Uluru

facts.text: Long-lived intraplate mountain building, with north-south shortening of under 100 km, began in central Australia about 450 Ma and ended about 300 Ma.
Beginning in the Late Ordovician, its folding of central Australian basins had raised the MacDonnell Ranges by the Carboniferous.
It may have tilted the sandstone layers of Uluru to near vertical.

A 2023 paper proposed that its impact winter triggered the Hirnantian glaciation and extinction; the idea remains untested.

entries.title: HICE: a carbon marker for the Hirnantian

facts.text: A positive carbon isotope excursion, the HICE, ran through the Hirnantian alongside the short but large glaciation.
Its cause is still debated, but it is a key marker for defining the Ordovician–Silurian boundary worldwide.
Its exact age is uncertain because the Hirnantian is short and dating errors are comparatively large.

entries.title: The Hirnantian glaciation at its peak

facts.text: A sudden cooling at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary rapidly expanded glaciers, one of the most severe glaciations of the Phanerozoic.
Ice caps covered Gondwana over the South Pole, in today's Africa and South America; the cold was probably harsher than the Last Glacial Maximum.
Oxygen isotope ratios jumped by an extraordinary 2–4‰ at the start of the Hirnantian, and CO2 dropped sharply.
Sea level fell sharply, from about 220 m above today's to about 141 m.
The ice retreated abruptly at the end of the Hirnantian, and Earth returned to a much warmer climate in the Rhuddanian.

entries.title: The Hirnantian ocean loses its oxygen

facts.text: As the glaciers retreated, black shales spread from isolated basins to all latitudes and depths, marking a global anoxic event.
Repeated spells of anoxia mark the Ordovician–Silurian boundary.
Anoxia is the most common suspect for the extinction's second pulse; sudden volcanism may have supplied sulphur dioxide that favoured euxinia.
The Hirnantian–Rhuddanian anoxia may be one of the longest-lasting anoxic events in geologic time; its cause is uncertain.

facts.text: A thin shale bed in Oneida County, New York, preserves trilobites such as Triarthrus eatoni with soft tissues replaced by pyrite.

entries.title: The first jawed fish

facts.text: The first jawed vertebrates, which arose from among the ostracoderms, may have appeared in the Late Ordovician, about 445 Ma.
Late Ordovician scale microfossils, possibly from acanthodians ('spiny sharks'), are the earliest evidence of jawed fish.
Jawed fish became common in the Devonian, the 'Age of Fishes'.

entries.title: The Late Ordovician mass extinction

facts.text: The first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions struck in two pulses: at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary and in the later Hirnantian.
Estimates run from about 60% of marine genera to 85% of marine species lost; only the end-Permian extinction was larger.
The first pulse is tied to the sudden Hirnantian glaciation; the second to warming and spreading anoxia as the ice retreated.
Trilobites lost about 70% of genera and 50% of families; many brachiopods, bryozoans and corals also vanished.
Despite its severity it changed ecosystem structure little, and diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.

entries.text: Only one extinction in Earth's history was larger. The Late Ordovician mass extinction, the first of the 'Big Five', removed by various estimates from about 60% of marine genera to 85% of marine species. Only the end-Permian extinction surpassed it. It came in two pulses. The first, at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary, is tied to the sudden Hirnantian glaciation. The second, later in the Hirnantian, came with warming and spreading anoxia as the ice retreated. Trilobites lost about 70% of their genera and 50% of their families. Many brachiopods, bryozoans and corals also vanished. Yet for all its severity, it changed the structure of ecosystems little, and diversity recovered quickly in the Silurian.

entries.title: Armorica drifts away from Gondwana

facts.text: The Armorican Terrane Assemblage split away from Gondwana in the Silurian and drifted toward Laurussia through the Devonian.
Its complete separation, across the young Paleo-Tethys, is thought to have come toward the end of the Silurian.
Armorica later collided with Laurussia in the Variscan orogeny, late in the Carboniferous.

entries.title: Armored jawless fish reach their peak

facts.text: By the Late Silurian the armoured jawless fish (ostracoderms) reached the high point of their evolution.
Anaspids appear in the early Silurian; osteostracans, probably arising in Euramerica, appear in the Llandovery or Wenlock.
Thelodont scales were widespread worldwide; the tadpole-like archipelepidiforms, basal thelodonts, lived from the late Telychian to the Sheinwoodian.
Heterostracans of the order Traquairaspidiformes appear in the Late Silurian.
The Silurian rise of jawed fish coincided with a sharp decline of jawless fish such as conodonts and ostracoderms.

entries.title: Jawed fish diversify

facts.text: A major Silurian milestone was the diversification of jawed fish: placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish.
Cartilaginous and bony fish, the jawed groups still alive today, appeared by the late Silurian.
Fish diversified greatly in the Silurian and Devonian, though with fewer new body plans than in the Cambrian explosion.
Lobe-finned fish (Sarcopterygii) emerged in the Silurian and early Devonian, all still aquatic.
By about 419 Ma jawed fish had split into placoderms, bony fish and the spiny-shark/cartilaginous-fish clade; the placoderm Entelognathus already had a bony jaw skeleton.

entries.title: Dob's Linn: where the Silurian begins

facts.text: Dob's Linn, a small valley in southern Scotland, holds the reference section (GSSP) for the Ordovician–Silurian boundary and the base of the Llandovery.
The boundary is set where the graptolites Parakidograptus acuminatus and Akidograptus ascensus first appear in the Birkhill Shale.
The base of the Silurian follows the end-Ordovician extinctions, which wiped out up to 60% of marine genera.

entries.title: Life rebounds after the end-Ordovician extinction

facts.text: As melting ice raised sea level and re-flooded continental shelves, biodiversity rebounded within the surviving orders.
Early Silurian communities were simpler and broader-niched, but faunas became among the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic.
Many 'Lazarus taxa' missing from the latest Ordovician reappeared, so small populations had survived in refuges.
Atrypid brachiopods and trilobites began recovering in the Rhuddanian; pentamerid brachiopods not until the Aeronian.
Sponges dominated South China's oxygen-poor seafloors in the earliest Rhuddanian; bryozoans and echinoderms soon recovered too.

Atrypid brachiopods and trilobites began recovering in the Rhuddanian, while pentamerid brachiopods waited until the Aeronian. Bryozoans and echinoderms soon recovered too.

As melting ice raised sea level and re-flooded the continental shelves, biodiversity rebounded within the surviving orders. Early Silurian communities were simpler and broader in their habits, but faunas became among the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic. Sponges dominated South China's oxygen-poor seafloors in the earliest Rhuddanian. Atrypid brachiopods and trilobites began recovering in the Rhuddanian, while pentamerid brachiopods waited until the Aeronian. Bryozoans and echinoderms soon recovered too.

entries.title: The first placoderms, armored jawed fish

facts.text: The first identifiable placoderms, armoured jawed fish, appear in the late Llandovery.
The vertebrate jaw probably evolved in the Silurian and appeared in placoderms, which diversified further in the Devonian.
Their Silurian record is fragmentary, probably because they lived where fossils rarely formed; the antiarch Silurolepis from Ludlow rocks of Yunnan is a rare near-complete find.

entries.title: Land plants spread across the continents

facts.text: Mercury isotope excursions show land plants had spread across much of Earth's land surface by the Early Silurian.
Plants were already moving onto land in the Llandovery; Eohostimella, probably a land plant, is known from rocks about 440–430 Ma.
Spores and plant microfossils of this age have been found in China and Pennsylvania.
Silurian land floras were broadly similar across the globe, with little regional difference.

entries.title: Silurian reefs spread to high latitudes

facts.text: Widespread reef building began in the Llandovery and continued into the Devonian.
Barrier reefs covered much more seafloor than reefs do today and grew even at high latitudes; tabulate corals formed prominent mounds.
Coral photosymbiosis may have begun in the Llandovery; photosymbiotic corals appear by the Middle Silurian.
Hederelloids flourished, some living in symbiosis with the rugose coral Entelophyllum.

entries.title: The Taconic orogeny comes to an end

facts.text: The Taconic orogeny, which built mountains across New England, ended about 440 Ma.
Subduction stopped and the Iapetus Terrane was accreted onto eastern North America.
As the mountains eroded in the Silurian and Devonian, sediment spread over the Appalachians and the North American midcontinent.

entries.title: Silurian glaciers shift to South America

facts.text: Milder glaciations followed the Hirnantian ice age through the Silurian, the last in the Late Silurian.
The centre of glaciation moved from the Sahara to South America; ice is recorded in Arabia, West Africa, the Amazon and the Andes.
Glacial phases struck in the early and latest Aeronian, late Telychian to mid-Sheinwoodian, Homerian and Ludfordian.
Silurian ice caps were smaller than the Late Ordovician ones, and glaciers almost vanished by mid-Silurian.
A lack of tillites in the middle to late Silurian makes glaciation a problematic explanation for its climate swings.

entries.title: The oldest unambiguous jawed fish

facts.text: Qianodus and Fanjingshania, from Aeronian rocks in Guizhou, China, about 439 Ma, are the oldest unambiguous remains of jawed vertebrates.
Both are acanthodian-grade stem chondrichthyans, early relatives of cartilaginous fish; possibly older Ordovician records exist.
Acanthodians, the 'spiny sharks', arose about 50 million years before the first true sharks.
Unambiguous jawed-vertebrate fossils, mostly primitive acanthodians, appear by the early Silurian and become abundant by the Devonian.

A fish of this age, Shenacanthus, had placoderm-like armour plates on its chest.

entries.title: The first bony fish

facts.text: The oldest known bony-fish fossils, about 436 million years old, have teeth arranged midway between those of sharks and true bony fish.
These early bony fish still had mostly cartilaginous skeletons; their novelty was foregut pouches that later became swim bladders and lungs.
Bony fish appeared in the Silurian and became common and diverse in the Devonian.
One of their branches, the lobe-finned fish, later gave rise to all land vertebrates.
Guiyu oneiros, about 425 Ma from Yunnan, China, is one of the earliest articulated bony fish, mixing placoderm-like traits with those of ray- and lobe-finned fish.

entries.title: The Scandian collision of Baltica and Laurentia

facts.text: In the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny, Baltica and Laurentia collided from about 435 to 410 Ma.
Avalonia, Baltica and Laurentia drifted together near the equator, starting to form Euramerica.
Mountains rose from New York State through Greenland and Britain to Norway as the collision folded long-accumulated coastal sediments.
Thrusting built Scotland's Moine Thrust Belt (435–420 Ma), and Caledonian nappes stacked up in Scandinavia.
Baltica's margin was buried about 120 km deep around 429 Ma, forming micro-diamonds; trilobite faunas from both sides mixed as the ocean narrowed.

entries.title: Cooksonia, the first vascular plant

facts.text: Cooksonia, the oldest known vascular plants (tracheophytes), appear in the Wenlock, in the middle of the Silurian.
Cooksonia remained an important part of the flora until the end of the Early Devonian, spanning 433 to 393 Ma.
A Cooksonia species from about 432 Ma, C. barrandei, is known from its spore-bearing stage (sporophyte).
Most Cooksonia-bearing rocks are marine; the plants probably grew along rivers and streams.
Slightly later, more complex Gondwanan plants like Baragwanathia suggest vascular plants have a longer history, perhaps reaching into the early Silurian.

entries.title: The Ireviken extinction event

facts.text: The Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, struck at the Llandovery–Wenlock boundary and lasted about 200,000 years.
At Ireviken, Gotland, over half of trilobite species died out; worldwide, 80% of conodont species vanished.
It began in the deep ocean and spread to shelf seas: graptolites, conodonts and trilobites suffered most, while shallow reefs were barely touched.
It is linked to global cooling and was followed by a positive carbon isotope excursion (a separate entry).
Its eight extinction steps appear to track orbital (Milankovitch) cycles; sediments of the event show metal enrichment.

entries.title: Carbon spikes after the Ireviken event

facts.text: After the first Ireviken extinctions, δ13C rose from +1.4‰ to +4.5‰ and δ18O from −5.6‰ to −5.0‰.

The Silurian had more isotope excursions, a sign of climate swings, than any other period.

entries.title: The Lundgreni event

facts.text: The Lundgreni event, or Mid-Homerian Biotic Crisis, was an extinction in the middle Homerian, recorded in Iberia, Bohemia and Poland.
It hit graptolites, benthic animals and microphytoplankton hardest; graptolite richness hit a global low and cyrtograptids died out.
Eutrophication and anoxia are blamed; a double-peaked positive carbon isotope excursion began with it.

entries.title: The first scorpions

facts.text: Scorpions date back to the Silurian, about 430 Ma; the oldest known, Dolichophonus loudonensis, lived in what is now Scotland.

entries.title: Oxygen climbs to modern levels

facts.text: A stepwise mid-Paleozoic rise of oxygen to and above modern levels ran from about 428 to 359 Ma, alongside the spread of vascular plants.
Oxygen stood near 13% of today's level in the early Silurian but approached modern levels in the Devonian.
Land plants' higher photosynthetic yield likely drove it; burying organic carbon in rocks also cut the oxygen sink.
Falling CO2, as carbon was trapped in rocks, also cooled the climate.

entries.title: The Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution

facts.text: From 428 to 359 Ma land plants, especially vascular plants, and fungi rapidly colonised and diversified on dry land; the critical phase was the Late Silurian–Early Devonian.
Vascular plants arose from simpler land plants, dikaryan and glomeromycotan fungi spread, and myriapods, arachnids and hexapods became fully terrestrial.
Plant diversity rose on a scale compared with the Cambrian explosion of animals, notably in tall, woody vascular plants that later formed canopies.
Volcanic islands of the Rheic Ocean were hotspots of plant evolution, and the new vegetation reshaped the water cycle and global climate.
It changed ocean nutrients and sediment cycling worldwide, likely feeding plankton blooms tied to the Late Devonian extinction.

entries.title: The Mulde extinction event

facts.text: The Mulde event, an anoxic event, was the second of three relatively minor Silurian mass extinctions.
It coincided with a global drop in sea level and was closely followed by an isotope excursion.
Carbon isotopes suggest a sustained drop in CO2 at the time of the extinction.
Its onset matches the Fröjel Formation of Gotland; apparent conodont losses may reflect changed sediments rather than real extinction.
