entries.title: Baragwanathia, a clubmoss ahead of its time

facts.text: Lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving lineages of vascular plants, date back to the Silurian, about 425 Ma.
Baragwanathia, a clubmoss with branching stems and needle-like leaves 10–20 cm long, was advanced for its age; it is known from Australia, Canada and China.
Middle Silurian plants were mostly under 10 cm tall.
The lycophyte order Drepanophycales ranges from the Late Silurian to the Late Devonian, about 430–360 Ma.

entries.title: Kerrera's millipedes, among the first animals ashore

facts.text: Kampecaris obanensis and Archidesmus from Kerrera, Scotland, about 425 Ma, are the definitive oldest millipedes.
Millipedes are among the oldest known land animals and among the first animals to colonise land.
Air-breathing arthropods from Kerrera (425 Ma) and Ludlow (420 Ma) are older than the zircon age of Pneumodesmus.

entries.text: On the small Scottish island of Kerrera, rocks about 425 million years old hold the oldest definite millipedes. Two species, Kampecaris obanensis and Archidesmus, settle the question that older, vaguer fossils leave open. Millipedes are among the oldest known land animals, and among the first animals of any kind to colonize land. Kerrera is not alone. Air-breathing arthropods from Ludlow, in England, date to about 420 million years ago. Both sites are older than the zircon age of Pneumodesmus, another early land walker met in {{ref:silu-061}}, whose own date is disputed. These small creatures were pioneers, but quiet ones. Land animals made little impact on Earth as a whole until they diversified in the Devonian, when soils, forests and food webs on land became far richer.

entries.title: Palaeoscolecid worms make their final appearance

facts.text: Palaeoscolecids, worms known since the late Early Cambrian, last appear in the Ludfordian.
The Lau event may have finished them off.

entries.title: Ice returns and the sea drains off the shelves

facts.text: The last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian and is associated with the Lau event.
Ice growth in the middle Ludfordian caused a major marine regression, exposing vast new land.
Plants and cyanobacterial mats quickly colonised the new land, furthering plant diversification.

entries.text: The last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian. In the middle of the age, growing ice locked away seawater. The oceans pulled back in a major regression, a retreat of the sea from the coasts. Vast new land lay exposed. Life moved in fast: plants and mats of cyanobacteria, the photosynthesizing microbes, quickly colonized the bare ground, pushing plant diversification further. The same cold snap is tied to {{ref:silu-054}}, the extinction that followed.

entries.title: The Lau event, the Silurian's last extinction

facts.text: The Lau event, last of three Silurian extinctions, began at the start of the late Ludfordian; it is named after Lau parish on Gotland.
It struck conodonts hardest; graptolites suffered in the Kozlowskii event just after, which may have been coeval.
It coincided with a glacially driven global sea-level low, and most major groups saw higher extinction rates.
Rated 6.2 in severity, it permanently altered communities; stromatolites and microbial mats spread, as after the end-Ordovician and end-Permian extinctions.
It may have finished off the palaeoscolecid worms.

entries.text: Conodonts, tiny eel-like animals with teeth, took the hardest blow in the last of three Silurian extinctions. It began at the start of the late Ludfordian and is named after Lau parish on the island of Gotland. Graptolites, colonial floating animals, suffered in the Kozlowskii event just after, which may have been the same crisis. The timing points to a cause. The event coincided with a glacially driven global sea-level low, part of {{ref:silu-051}}, and most major groups saw higher extinction rates. Rated 6.2 in severity, it permanently altered marine communities. In the gap, stromatolites and microbial mats spread, the same pattern seen after the end-Ordovician and end-Permian extinctions. It may also have ended the palaeoscolecid worms.

entries.title: Sea scorpions at the height of their reign

facts.text: Eurypterids (sea scorpions) were major parts of Silurian marine faunas, peaking in diversity in the Pridoli, 423 to 419.2 Ma.
Most eurypterid groups are first recorded in Silurian rocks; eurypterines make up 90% of eurypterids in most beds.
Large pterygotids with rudder-like tails and big pincers appeared in the Late Silurian; Acutiramus reached about 2 m.
Eurypterus, the most abundant eurypterid, lived from about 432 Ma to the end of the Pridoli; Pennsylvania's Tonoloway Formation holds a mass assemblage.

entries.text: Acutiramus, a Late Silurian sea scorpion, reached about 2 m long. Sea scorpions, or eurypterids, were major parts of Silurian marine faunas, and most of their groups are first recorded in Silurian rocks. Their diversity peaked in the Pridoli, 423 to 419.2 million years ago. One group, the eurypterines, make up 90% of the eurypterids in most beds. Large pterygotids, with rudder-like tails and big pincers, also appeared in the Late Silurian. The most abundant of all was Eurypterus, which lived from about 432 million years ago to the end of the Pridoli. Pennsylvania's Tonoloway Formation holds a mass assemblage of them.

facts.text: The earliest known ascomycete fungi date from 423 to 419 Ma, in the Silurian.
Dikaryan fungi, the group including ascomycetes, began expanding and diversifying in the Silurian.

entries.title: Charcoal marks the first wildfires

facts.text: Oxygen first rose high enough for wildfires in the Pridoli, when the first charcoal appears in the fossil record.
Silurian charcoal shows oxygen had crossed about 15%, enough to sustain fire for the first time.

events.date_text: during the Pridoli, 423–420 million years ago (422.7–419.6 Ma)

entries.date_display: during the Pridoli, 423–420 million years ago (422.7–419.6 Ma)
entries.text: Fire needs fuel and it needs oxygen. By the Pridoli, both were finally present. The first charcoal in the fossil record appears in this epoch, showing that atmospheric oxygen had risen high enough to sustain wildfires. Silurian charcoal suggests oxygen had crossed about 15% of the air, the threshold for burning. From here on, fire becomes a recurring force in the history of land plants.

entries.title: The Šilalė event strikes the conodonts

facts.text: The Šilalė event, early in the Pridoli, was a conodont extinction marked by a negative carbon isotope excursion.
The isotope low is traced from Lithuanian cores to the Appalachian Basin of North America.
Conodonts declined while brachiopods grew in diversity and abundance; it coincided with the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year orbital eccentricity cycle.

The crisis coincided with the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year cycle in the shape of Earth's orbit.

entries.title: Pneumodesmus, the oldest known air breather

facts.text: Pneumodesmus newmani, a millipede-like myriapod from Scotland, is among the first myriapods and the oldest creatures known to have lived on land.
Openings in its cuticle are read as spiracles, making it the earliest known arthropod with a tracheal system for breathing air.
Its age is disputed: a 2023 study argued for the late Wenlock, about 430 Ma, but zircon dates and a 2025 study favour the Pridoli–Lochkovian, about 414 Ma.
Millipedes, first appearing in the Silurian, are among the oldest known land animals.

entries.text: Small holes in a fossil's skin made it famous. Pneumodesmus newmani, a millipede-like myriapod from Scotland, has openings in its cuticle read as spiracles, the breathing pores of a tracheal system. That makes it the earliest known arthropod built to breathe air, and among the oldest creatures known to have lived on land. Its age, though, is disputed. It was once put at about 428 million years old, in the Wenlock. A 2023 study defended the Wenlock age, about 430 million years ago. Zircon dates and a 2025 study instead favor the Pridoli to Lochkovian, about 414 million years ago. Either way, it belongs with the millipedes, which first appear in the Silurian as among the oldest known land animals.

entries.title: Arachnids and centipedes join the millipedes

facts.text: By the Pridoli, about 420 Ma, millipedes were joined on land by centipedes and trigonotarbid arachnids.
Timelines list the earliest trigonotarbid arachnids and land scorpions at about 420 Ma.
Predators among them imply simple food webs that included plant- or detritus-eating prey.
Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods all became fully terrestrial during the Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution.

entries.text: Millipedes did not have the land to themselves for long. By the Pridoli, about 420 million years ago, centipedes and trigonotarbid arachnids, extinct spider relatives, had joined them. Timelines list the earliest trigonotarbids and land scorpions at about the same date. Some of the newcomers were predators, so there must have been prey, which ate plants or detritus, the dead remains of living things. Simple food webs had formed on land. Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods all became fully terrestrial during the Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution.

entries.title: Andreolepis, perhaps the first ray-finned fish

facts.text: The earliest known ray-finned fish may be Andreolepis hedei, about 420 Ma, found in Russia, Sweden and Estonia.
Timelines list the earliest ray-finned fish at about 420 Ma.
Ray-finned fish now make up the vast majority of living fish; their crown group arose much later, near the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary.

entries.text: Almost every fish alive today, from tuna to goldfish, is a ray-finned fish, with fins held up by thin bony rods. The earliest known member of the group may be Andreolepis hedei, about 420 million years old, found in Russia, Sweden and Estonia. Timelines put the first ray-finned fish at about the same date. The group took a long time to hit its stride. Its crown group, the lineage that includes all living members, arose much later, near the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary.

entries.title: The Iapetus closes and Laurussia is born

facts.text: By the end of the Silurian, about 420 Ma, the Iapetus Ocean had closed entirely, leaving the Iapetus Suture.
Avalonia and Baltica fused with Laurentia in the Caledonian orogeny, forming Laurussia, later the northern part of Pangaea.
Laurentia–Avalonia convergence and Iapetus subduction had ceased by about 420 Ma.
Laurussia's southern margin took shape in this collision; peak metamorphism in Scandinavia's thrust sheets came about 420 Ma.

entries.text: An entire ocean disappeared by the end of the Silurian. The Iapetus Ocean had closed completely by about 420 million years ago, leaving a seam called the Iapetus Suture. Avalonia and Baltica fused with Laurentia in the Caledonian orogeny, a mountain-building collision, and formed Laurussia. That continent would later become the northern part of Pangaea. Convergence between Laurentia and Avalonia, and subduction of the Iapetus seafloor, had ceased by about 420 million years ago. The collision shaped Laurussia's southern margin, and rocks in Scandinavia's thrust sheets reached peak metamorphism, their deepest heating and squeezing, at about the same time.

entries.title: Seas fall and salt fills the Salina basin

facts.text: At the end of the Silurian, sea level dropped again, leaving evaporite basins from Michigan to West Virginia; the new mountains eroded rapidly.
A warm, arid late Silurian climate in a shallow inland basin laid down Salina Group evaporites 120–800 m thick.
Sea level had risen through the first half of the Silurian and fell through the rest.

At the period's end it dropped again, leaving evaporite basins, where seawater dried into salt, from Michigan to West Virginia. A warm, arid climate over a shallow inland basin laid down the Salina Group evaporites, 120–800 m thick. Meanwhile the new mountains eroded rapidly.

entries.title: Jawed fishes take over in the Age of Fishes

facts.text: Jawed vertebrates, which appeared in the late Ordovician, became common in the Devonian, popularly called the 'Age of Fishes'.
Fish variety rose greatly, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks.
By about 419 Ma jawed fishes had split into placoderms, bony fishes, and a clade of spiny sharks and early cartilaginous fish.
Cartilaginous and bony fishes both diversified and played a large role in Devonian seas.
Lobe-finned fishes such as coelacanths and lungfish were the most diverse bony fishes of the period.

entries.text: The Devonian earned its popular name, the Age of Fishes, honestly. Jawed vertebrates had appeared in the late Ordovician, but only now did they become common. Fish variety rose greatly, especially among ostracoderms, placoderms, lobe-finned fishes and early sharks. The family tree had already branched. By about 419 million years ago jawed fishes had split into three lines. They were the armored placoderms, the bony fishes, and a clade of spiny sharks and early cartilaginous fish. Both cartilaginous and bony fishes diversified through the period and played a large role in Devonian seas. Among the bony fishes, the lobe-finned forms, such as coelacanths and lungfish, were the most diverse. That detail matters, because the lobe-fins are the group from which four-limbed animals would later come.

Patagonia's margin turned convergent in the Devonian, leading to collision that began in the mid-Carboniferous.

entries.title: Kola's alkaline volcanoes

facts.text: Devonian magmatism on Russia's Kola Peninsula built alkaline-ultramafic complexes, carbonatites, kimberlite pipes and the large nepheline syenite massifs of Khibiny and Lovozero.
Its rocks total an estimated 15,000 ± 2,700 cubic km, from small melt fractions of garnet peridotite beneath lithosphere about 200 km thick.
This Kola large igneous province erupted about when the Viluy and Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets provinces did, and is a suggested trigger of the Hangenberg extinction.

entries.title: Roots pull carbon dioxide from the sky

facts.text: Carbon dioxide levels dropped steeply through the Devonian as land plants spread.
Spreading plant roots increased silicate weathering, as shown by carbonates formed in soils.
The long-term fall in CO2 and rise in oxygen led on to the late Paleozoic icehouse.
Anoxic events grew longer in the Devonian; the growing plant biota probably buffered CO2.

events.date_text: during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)

entries.date_display: during the Devonian, 420–359 million years ago (419.6–358.9 Ma)
entries.text: Plants changed the air simply by putting down roots. As land plants spread through the Devonian, carbon dioxide levels dropped steeply. Roots broke up rock and increased silicate weathering, a chemical reaction that locks carbon dioxide away; carbonates formed in ancient soils record it. The growing plant cover probably also buffered carbon dioxide while anoxic events in the oceans grew longer. The long-term fall in carbon dioxide, together with rising oxygen, led on to the late Paleozoic icehouse.

entries.title: Oxygen climbs toward modern levels

facts.text: Atmospheric oxygen, about 13% of today's level in the early Silurian, rose to near-modern levels during the Devonian.
The oxygen increase from 470 to 400 Ma, the Paleozoic Oxidation Event, is explained by early plants trapping organic carbon in sediments.
In the early Devonian oxygen was still relatively low, possibly about half of modern values.
Land plants spreading over the continents buried more organic carbon, which likely allowed the higher oxygen levels.
Rising oxygen may have favoured vertebrates able to breathe air, helping push tetrapods onto land.

entries.title: Placoderms, the armored rulers of Devonian waters

facts.text: Placoderms, armoured jawed fishes, appear with seemingly sudden diversity at the very start of the Devonian.
They went on to dominate almost all known aquatic ecosystems, in fresh and salt water alike.
Petalichthyid placoderms peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian and lived worldwide.
Entelognathus, a 419-million-year-old placoderm, had a bony mouth skeleton like a bony fish's.
Placoderm giants such as Dunkleosteus grew up to seven metres long.

entries.title: The Caledonian mountains begin to collapse

facts.text: After Baltica's margin was subducted and overthrust by nappes, the Caledonian orogen began to collapse in the Early Devonian.
Burial of the Baltican margin peaked about 410 Ma, recorded in Norway's Western Gneiss Region; those rocks were exhumed about 400-385 Ma.
The collapse brought extension and subsidence and lasted a long time in Scandinavia.

entries.date_display: during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)
entries.text: Mountains can fall under their own weight. After Baltica's margin was subducted and overridden by nappes, huge sheets of rock, the Caledonian mountain belt began to collapse in the Early Devonian. Burial peaked about 410 million years ago, recorded in Norway's Western Gneiss Region, and those rocks were brought back up about 400–385 million years ago. The collapse stretched and lowered the crust, and in Scandinavia it lasted a long time.

entries.title: Jawless armored fishes peak, then fade

facts.text: Armoured jawless 'ostracoderms' peaked in diversity in the Early Devonian and then declined; thelodonts did the same.
Cephalaspis, an iconic osteostracan and the most advanced jawless fish, appeared about 415 Ma.
By the Middle Devonian jawed fishes were thriving while ostracoderms dwindled, never to recover.

entries.title: The last of the radiodonts

facts.text: Radiodonts, the group of Cambrian predators that includes Anomalocaris, make their last appearance in the Early Devonian.
A late survivor was Schinderhannes bartelsi from Germany.

entries.title: Asian blocks drift away and open the Paleo-Tethys

facts.text: North and South China, with Tarim, rifted from Gondwana's northern margin, opening the Paleo-Tethys Ocean behind them.
South China and Annamia (Southeast Asia) also rifted from Gondwana; they later collided in the Carboniferous.
The blocks stayed close enough to Gondwana that their Devonian fossils resemble Australian species more than north Asian ones.
From about 440 Ma, the Paleo-Tethys Ocean lay between the Hunic terranes and Gondwana.
South China and Indochina split from Gondwana in the Silurian and moved north, shrinking the Proto-Tethys and opening the Paleo-Tethys behind them.

entries.text: Pieces of future Asia were once part of Gondwana. North and South China, along with Tarim, rifted from Gondwana's northern margin, and a new ocean, the Paleo-Tethys, opened behind them. South China and Indochina had split away in the Silurian and moved north, shrinking the older Proto-Tethys ahead of them. South China and Annamia, today's Southeast Asia, later collided in the Carboniferous. The blocks did not go far at first. Their Devonian fossils resemble Australian species more than north Asian ones.

entries.title: The Rheic Ocean begins to close

facts.text: The Rheic Ocean between Laurussia and Gondwana, wide at the start of the Devonian, began to close in the Early Devonian.
Gondwana moved toward Euramerica as Rheic oceanic crust was subducted.
Franconia and Saxothuringia struck Laurussia near the end of the Early Devonian, pinching out the eastern Rheic Ocean.
Closure finished in the Mississippian, when Gondwana and Laurentia collided to form Pangaea.

entries.date_display: during the Early Devonian, 420–393 million years ago (419.6–393.5 Ma)
entries.text: At the start of the Devonian, a wide ocean, the Rheic, separated Laurussia from Gondwana. In the Early Devonian it began to shrink. Gondwana moved toward Euramerica as the Rheic seafloor was subducted, pulled down beneath the plates. Near the end of the Early Devonian, two small blocks, Franconia and Saxothuringia, struck Laurussia and pinched out the eastern part of the ocean. The closure would not finish until the Mississippian, when Gondwana and Laurentia collided to form Pangaea.

entries.title: The Old Red Sandstone builds a red continent

facts.text: Old Red Sandstone sediments began accumulating around 419 Ma across Britain, Ireland, Norway, northeastern North America, Greenland and Svalbard.
These mostly Devonian rocks were laid down in varied environments from the late Silurian into the earliest Carboniferous.
In Scotland, uplifted Silurian rocks eroded into fresh water, probably large river deltas, between 408 and 370 Ma.
Its abundant red beds gave Laurussia the name Old Red Sandstone Continent.
Around 370 Ma, at Siccar Point in Scotland, rainy-season rivers near the equator laid iron-rich sands that winds reworked into dunes.

entries.title: Lobe-finned fishes appear and divide

facts.text: The first lobe-finned fishes, about 418 Ma, closely resembled spiny sharks.
In the Early Devonian (416-397 Ma) they split into two main lineages, the coelacanths and the rhipidistians.
While placoderms dominated the seas, some lobe-finned fishes moved into fresh water (416-385 Ma).
Coelacanths had their heyday in the Late Devonian and Carboniferous (385-299 Ma).

entries.text: The first lobe-finned fishes, about 418 million years ago, looked a lot like spiny sharks. Little hinted at what they would become. While placoderms dominated the seas, some lobe-fins moved into fresh water, between 416 and 385 million years ago. The coelacanths had their heyday later, in the Late Devonian and Carboniferous, from 385 to 299 million years ago.

entries.title: Arthropods settle coasts and floodplains

facts.text: By about 415 Ma numerous arthropods lived on coasts and alluvial plains, and some were eating plants.
Early rooted plants made the first stable soils, home to mites, scorpions, trigonotarbids and myriapods.
Land animals had a major impact on Earth only once they diversified in the Devonian.

entries.text: By about 415 million years ago, numerous arthropods lived along coasts and on alluvial plains, the flat land beside rivers, and some were eating plants. Early rooted plants had built the first stable soils. Mites, scorpions, trigonotarbids and myriapods made homes in them. Land animals began to have a major impact on Earth only once they diversified in the Devonian.

entries.title: The first true nautilids

facts.text: The earliest nautilids (order Nautilida) appear around 410 Ma.
Rutocerina, the earliest true nautilid, had shells like those of oncocerid nautiloids, its likely ancestors.
Nautilid genera rose to about 22 by the Middle Devonian, while other nautiloids declined.

entries.text: The order of the living chambered nautilus has roots around 410 million years ago. Rutocerina, the earliest true nautilid, had a shell like those of the oncocerid nautiloids, its likely ancestors. Nautilids then flourished as their cousins declined: by the Middle Devonian there were about 22 genera, while other nautiloids dwindled.

entries.title: Rhynie chert, an ecosystem frozen in stone

facts.text: Silica-rich water from volcanic hot springs petrified plants, fungi, lichens and animals in place, almost instantly, in Scotland's Rhynie chert.
Formed about 410 Ma in the Pragian, it is one of the first known fully terrestrial ecosystems, from an early stage of land colonization.
Its animals include euthycarcinoids, branchiopods, arachnids and hexapods; Rhyniognatha, possibly the oldest insect, is known from its mandibles.
Fungi among its rootless, leafless plants suggest fungi played a large role in plants' move onto land.
Nematophytes, enigmatic land organisms known since the Silurian, last appear here.

entries.text: Hot springs in Scotland turned a whole community to stone. Silica-rich water from volcanic springs petrified plants, fungi, lichens and animals in place, almost instantly. The result is the Rhynie chert, formed about 410 million years ago in the Pragian. It is one of the first known fully terrestrial ecosystems, caught at an early stage of land colonization. Its animals include euthycarcinoids, branchiopods, arachnids and hexapods, and Rhyniognatha, possibly the oldest insect, is known from its jaws. The plants were rootless and leafless, and fungi living among them suggest fungi played a large role in plants' move onto land. The chert also holds the last nematophytes, enigmatic land organisms known since the Silurian.

entries.title: Trimerophytes and the start of the leafy plants

facts.text: Early members of the euphyllophytes, the clade of trimerophytes, ferns, progymnosperms and seed plants, are known from Early Devonian fossils.
Trimerophytes are a class of early vascular plants known only from the Devonian.
Timeline of life puts the earliest trimerophytes and lycophytes at 410 Ma.

entries.text: Ferns, seed plants and most of the green world belong to one great clade, the euphyllophytes. Its early members are known from Early Devonian fossils. Among them were the trimerophytes, a class of early vascular plants known only from the Devonian. Timeline of life puts the earliest trimerophytes and lycophytes at 410 million years ago.

entries.title: Ammonoids coil into existence

facts.text: The earliest ammonoids appeared in the Emsian stage of the Early Devonian, around 410-408 Ma.
They arose from straight-shelled bactritid 'nautiloids', with transitional fossils showing the shell coiling step by step.
Bactritids also first appear in the Early Devonian; their radiation with ammonoids may reflect falling oxygen in deeper water.
Ammonoids later became abundant in the Mesozoic and vanished around the end-Cretaceous extinction.
Agoniatitids radiated in the Emsian, and a new order, the Goniatitida, arose before 391.9 Ma, giving rise to later ammonoid orders.

entries.text: Ammonoids, with their tightly coiled shells, began as straight shells. The earliest appeared in the Emsian, around 410–408 million years ago, descended from straight-shelled bactritid nautiloids. Transitional fossils show the shell coiling step by step. Bactritids also first appear in the Early Devonian, and their radiation alongside the ammonoids may reflect falling oxygen in deeper water. One early group, the agoniatitids, radiated in the Emsian, and a new order, the Goniatitida, arose before 391.9 million years ago and gave rise to later ammonoid orders. The line would become abundant in the Mesozoic and vanish around the end-Cretaceous extinction.

entries.title: Tungsenia and the fish ancestors of tetrapods

facts.text: The oldest known tetrapodomorph, Tungsenia from China, dates to about 409 Ma.
Tetrapods have their roots in these early Devonian tetrapodomorph fishes.
Kenichthys, a small Chinese lobe-fin of about 395 Ma, shows the internal nostril (choana) caught mid-evolution.
Its relatives became the most numerous bony fishes of Devonian and Carboniferous waterways.

entries.text: Every four-limbed animal traces its roots to a group of Devonian fishes, the tetrapodomorphs. The oldest known member, Tungsenia from China, dates to about 409 million years ago. A little later, about 395 million years ago, a small Chinese lobe-fin called Kenichthys shows the internal nostril, or choana, caught midway through its evolution. This group did well for itself. Its relatives became the most numerous bony fishes of Devonian and Carboniferous rivers and streams.

entries.title: Jaekelopterus, the largest arthropod ever

facts.text: A giant claw of the sea scorpion Jaekelopterus rhenaniae from Germany's Klerf Formation shows the largest arthropod ever known.
An Emsian chelicera from the Klerf Formation would have been about 45.5 cm long when complete.
Even so, eurypterines lost over half their diversity within 10 million years in the Early Devonian.

entries.text: A single claw from Germany's Klerf Formation reveals the largest arthropod ever known. It belonged to the sea scorpion Jaekelopterus rhenaniae. Complete, this pincer would have been about 45.5 cm long. Size did not save the group. Eurypterines lost over half their diversity within 10 million years in the Early Devonian.

entries.title: Pyrite-coated fossils of the Hunsrück Slate

facts.text: The Hunsrück Slate of Germany, latest Pragian to early Emsian, is one of few marine Devonian Lagerstätten with soft-tissue preservation.
Many of its fossils are coated with a pyrite layer.
Its fauna includes the trilobite Chotecops and the puzzling placoderm Stensioella.

entries.title: Rhyniognatha and the first insects

facts.text: The oldest proposed insect fossil, Rhyniognatha hirsti, is about 400 million years old and known only from mandibles.
Its identity as an insect has been contested.
Early Devonian rocks of about 400 Ma preserve only a few kinds of flightless insects.
The first possible insect fossils appear around 416 Ma.

entries.title: Laurussia completed

facts.text: Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and smaller terranes, colliding in the Caledonian orogeny, formed Laurussia (Euramerica) by about 400 Ma.
In Scotland's northwest Highlands, part of the Iapetus Ocean closed as Laurentia met Baltica about 400 Ma.
The continent lay in the dry belt along the Tropic of Capricorn, then drifted north and rotated counterclockwise.
The collision raised a string of mountain ranges along its southeastern coast.
Low Early Devonian seas split its seafloor fauna into provinces, which were united by the Middle Devonian.

Laurussia lay in the dry belt along the Tropic of Capricorn, then drifted north and turned counterclockwise. Low seas in the Early Devonian split its seafloor animals into separate provinces, which were united again by the Middle Devonian.

entries.title: Lungfish and the dipnoan renaissance

facts.text: Lungfish appeared about 400 Ma and evolved rapidly through the Devonian, the 'dipnoan renaissance'.
By the Middle Devonian (397-385 Ma) they had evolved proto-lungs and proto-limbs for spells outside water.

entries.title: Sharks and their kin arrive

facts.text: Cartilaginous fishes (sharks, rays and chimaeras) had appeared by about 395 Ma, in the Middle Devonian, evolving from acanthodians.
The oldest unambiguous cartilaginous-fish fossils are Middle Devonian, though shark-like scales go back to the Ordovician.
They became diverse and important in Devonian seas.

entries.text: Shark-like scales go back to the Ordovician, but the oldest unambiguous fossils of cartilaginous fishes are Middle Devonian. By about 395 million years ago these fishes, the sharks, rays and chimaeras, had appeared, evolving from acanthodians, the spiny sharks. Their skeletons are made of cartilage rather than bone. They quickly became diverse and important in Devonian seas.

entries.title: Cladoxylopsid trees grow the first forests

facts.text: In the Eifelian, cladoxylopsid trees formed the first forests in Earth history.
Trees over eight metres tall appeared by the Middle Devonian; the earliest known fossil forest is Eifelian.
Shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms also spread.
By the late Givetian, cladoxylalean ferns, lycopsids and progymnosperms had all evolved tree-like forms.
Plant heights rose from about 30 cm at the start of the Devonian to 30 m by its end.

entries.text: At the start of the Devonian, plants stood about 30 cm tall. By its end, the tallest reached 30 m. Somewhere in between, Earth grew its first forests. The pioneers were cladoxylopsid trees, which formed the first forests in Earth history during the Eifelian. Trees over eight meters tall had appeared by the Middle Devonian, and the earliest known fossil forest dates from the Eifelian. Cladoxylopsids were not alone. Lower, shrub-like forests of lycophytes, horsetails, ferns and progymnosperms spread too. The leap to height happened more than once. By the late Givetian, three separate groups had evolved tree-like forms: the cladoxylalean ferns, the lycopsids and the progymnosperms. Height is a race for light, and several lineages joined it at once. The consequences went far beyond the forest floor, because so much new plant matter changed the air, the soils and the rivers, as {{ref:devo-038}} and {{ref:devo-072}} show.

entries.title: Sponge and coral reefs flourish

facts.text: Stromatoporoid sponges recovered strongly in the Early and Middle Devonian, peaking in diversity in the Eifelian.
Devonian reefs were either microbial or built by stromatoporoids with tabulate and rugose corals.
A barrier reef in Australia's Kimberley region once stretched 350 km along a Devonian continent.
Reefs also lined Laurussia's southeast coast, now southern England and Belgium.
Microbes built reefs in warm periods; corals and stromatoporoids dominated in cooler times.

entries.text: A Devonian barrier reef in Australia's Kimberley region once stretched 350 km along a continent's edge. Reefs like it were built either by microbes or by stromatoporoids, layered sponges, together with tabulate and rugose corals. entries.title: Forests cool the Middle Devonian

facts.text: Newly evolved forests drew carbon from the air and buried it in sediments.
This may be reflected in a Middle Devonian cooling of around 5 °C.

facts.text: Progymnosperms first appear in the Middle Devonian; the group lasts into the Lopingian (late Permian).

entries.title: The Variscan mountains begin to rise

facts.text: Variscan mountain building began in the Middle Devonian and continued into the early Permian.
Armorican terranes drifting north closed the Rheic Ocean ahead of them and began colliding with southeastern Laurussia.
From about 390 Ma, Rheic ocean floor subducted beneath the Mid-German highs south of Laurussia.
It deformed crust from Iberia and Ireland to France, Germany and the Czech Republic.
By the end of the Devonian, all the Armorican terranes were joined to Laurussia.

entries.text: A mountain belt that would deform crust from Iberia and Ireland to France, Germany and the Czech Republic started to grow in the Middle Devonian. This was the Variscan orogeny, and it continued into the early Permian. Its engine was a set of Armorican terranes, small blocks of crust drifting north. They closed the Rheic Ocean ahead of them and began colliding with southeastern Laurussia. From about 390 million years ago, Rheic seafloor subducted beneath the Mid-German highs south of Laurussia. By the end of the Devonian, all the Armorican terranes were joined to Laurussia.

entries.title: The Catskill Delta spreads west

facts.text: Rivers and marshes built the Catskill Delta, carrying sediment eroded from the Acadian Mountains westward into the inland Kaskaskia Sea.
Its red-sandstone clastic wedge, up to 3,000 m thick in Pennsylvania and New York, records large-scale deposition on land during the Acadian orogeny.
It preserves many early tetrapodomorph fishes and land plants, important evidence for how vertebrates moved onto land.

entries.text: A wedge of red sandstone up to 3,000 m thick lies under Pennsylvania and New York. It records large-scale deposition on land during the Acadian orogeny. It also preserves many early tetrapodomorph fishes and land plants, key evidence for how vertebrates moved onto land.

entries.title: Zachełmie, the oldest tetrapod tracks

facts.text: Tracks at Zachełmie, Poland, from the Eifelian, are the oldest evidence of tetrapods; some prints show digits.
They predate the oldest tetrapod body fossils by about 18 million years.
Made in shallow lagoons on a marine carbonate platform, they support an intertidal origin for land vertebrates.
If genuine, they make Tiktaalik-like elpistostegids late-surviving relics; the next oldest tracks, about 385 Ma, are from Valentia Island, Ireland.
Some researchers read the traces instead as fish feeding traces (Piscichnus).

entries.title: The Kačák event darkens the seas

facts.text: Near the end of the Eifelian, the Kačák event, lasting perhaps 200,000 to 700,000 years, brought a global sea-level rise and anoxia that laid down black shales.
High insolation probably warmed the oceans, raising sea level by thermal expansion and strengthening monsoons that filled Scotland's Achanarras lake, the Orcadian Basin's deepest.
Open-ocean animals were hit hardest: agoniatitid ammonoids suffered heavy losses as tornoceratids diversified, and conodonts and dacryconarids turned over.
Warming decimated the cool-water Malvinoxhosan Realm off Gondwana, while invading cosmopolitan species replaced the Eastern Americas Realm fauna of southwest Laurussia.
Estimates put its loss at about 24% to 32% of marine genera, milder than the Late Devonian extinctions that followed.

entries.title: The Taghanic event suffocates the shallows

facts.text: The Taghanic event was a Givetian extinction caused by hypoxia from an anoxic event that depleted ocean oxygen.
It sharply cut trilobite diversity, especially in shallow water, and killed off the trilobite order Lichida.
One study ranks this Givetian crisis as the eighth most ecologically severe mass extinction.
Another passage puts it at the Givetian/Frasnian boundary and credits it with wiping out about half of coral genera.

entries.text: Trilobites lost an entire order, the Lichida, in the Givetian. One study ranks it as the eighth most ecologically severe mass extinction. Another account places it at the Givetian/Frasnian boundary and credits it with wiping out about half of coral genera.

entries.title: Wetlands and the first modern land ecosystems

facts.text: Modern-style land ecosystems appeared only in the Late Devonian, about 385 to 359 Ma.
Land plants stabilized freshwater habitats, letting the first wetlands develop with increasingly complex food webs.
These wetlands later gave way to coal forests in the Early Carboniferous.

entries.title: The Late Devonian warms again

facts.text: The Late Devonian warmed back to Early Devonian levels, shown by more continental weathering and plant distribution, without a matching CO2 rise.
Arid climates became less widespread and temperate climates more common.

entries.title: Dead seas make Devonian oil

facts.text: Widespread ocean anoxia during the Late Devonian extinctions halted decay, so organic matter was preserved in seafloor sediments.
With oil-holding porous reef rocks, this made Devonian rocks an important source of oil, especially in Canada and the United States.
The Late Devonian to Early Mississippian Bakken shales, laid down partly in euxinic waters, underlie about 520,000 km2 of the Williston Basin and are a prolific oil source rock.

entries.text: The Williston Basin's Bakken shales cover about 520,000 km2 and are a prolific source of oil. They began with suffocated seas. Some Bakken layers formed in euxinic waters, without oxygen and full of hydrogen sulfide. Paired with porous reef rocks that hold oil, this made Devonian rocks an important oil source, especially in Canada and the United States.

entries.title: The Viluy Traps flood Siberia with basalt

facts.text: Rifting and deep mantle plumes fed the Viluy (Vilyuy) Traps, Siberian flood basalts that first erupted in the Late Devonian.
They formed along a Devonian triple-junction rift system at the edge of the Siberian Platform.
The main eruptions ran from about 381 to 366 Ma (±5 Myr), with a secondary pulse toward the end-Devonian.
Dating finds two volcanic phases, the first matching the Kellwasser event's age.
Long thought a major cause of the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, its main eruptions seem to predate it.

entries.contested_note: Its role in the Late Devonian extinction is debated.

entries.title: The Antler orogeny starts the western mountains

facts.text: Subduction of Panthalassic ocean floor along Laurussia's western margin drove the Antler orogeny in the ancestral Sierra Nevada region.
It began a series of western North American orogenies that culminated in the Laramide.
Its start is debated: most sources say Late Devonian, but its own article says it began after the Devonian.

entries.title: Gogo's fossils and the oldest live birth

facts.text: Western Australia's Gogo Formation, about 380 Ma (Frasnian), preserves soft tissues in 3D, down to nerves and embryos with umbilical cords.
Over fifty fish species have been described from it, along with arthropods.
The 380-million-year-old placoderms Materpiscis, Incisoscutum and Austroptyctodus are the oldest known examples of live birth.
Gogonasus, one of the earliest tetrapodomorphs, dates from 380 Ma.

Over fifty fish species have been described from Gogo, along with arthropods. Among them is Gogonasus, one of the earliest tetrapodomorphs.

entries.title: The buried Kaluga crater

facts.text: An impact in what is now Kaluga Oblast, Russia, left a crater 15 km across, dated to 380 ± 5 Ma in the Late Devonian.
The crater now lies buried under about 800 m of sediment and is not exposed at the surface.

entries.title: The Alamo impact hits a Nevada sea

facts.text: One or more hypervelocity objects slammed into shallow seas in what is now southeastern Nevada, 377-378 Ma.
Among the best-exposed and most accurately dated impacts, it came about 5.9 Myr before the Frasnian-Famennian extinctions and probably did not affect them.
Its age roughly matches the earliest Antler orogeny deposits, and it may have dislodged huge slide blocks.

facts.text: A meteorite struck what is now Dalarna, central Sweden, leaving the Siljan Ring, about 52 km across and the largest impact structure in Europe.

entries.title: The Acadian orogeny raises the Atlantic seaboard

facts.text: The Acadian orogeny built mountains along North America's Atlantic seaboard for about 50 million years from roughly 375 Ma, into the early Mississippian.
Avalonian terranes accreted to Laurentia's eastern margin, most likely starting late in the Early Devonian.
Volcanoes and uplift in New England shed sediment into an inland sea, and the Catskill Delta filled the Acadian foreland basin.
In the British Isles, Acadian transpression of 404-394 Ma joined the landmasses into the islands as they are now.
Collisions with Avalonian crust broken from Gondwana closed the southern Iapetus Ocean and raised a high mountain belt between 375 and 359 Ma.

entries.text: For about 50 million years from roughly 375 million years ago, mountains grew along North America's Atlantic seaboard. This was the Acadian orogeny, which lasted into the early Mississippian. Its cause was the accretion of Avalonian terranes to Laurentia's eastern margin, most likely starting late in the Early Devonian. Collisions with this crust, broken from Gondwana, closed the southern Iapetus Ocean and raised a high mountain belt between 375 and 359 million years ago. In New England, volcanoes and uplift shed sediment into an inland sea, and {{ref:devo-035}} filled the basin at the mountains' foot. Across the ocean, Acadian squeezing of 404–394 million years ago joined the British Isles into their present shape.

entries.title: Tiktaalik, a fish halfway to land

facts.text: Tiktaalik, a lobe-finned fish with many tetrapod-like features, lived about 375 Ma; it was found in Frasnian rocks of Nunavut, Canada.
It bridges fishes such as Panderichthys, about 380 Ma, and early tetrapods such as Acanthostega.
Its group, the elpistostegalians, disappeared at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary.
If the older Zachełmie tracks are tetrapod, Tiktaalik's group was an evolutionary dead end.

entries.title: The Kellwasser event, a Big Five extinction

facts.text: The Kellwasser event, named for Germany's Kellwassertal, struck at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary and is one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions.
The Late Devonian crisis came in pulses from the mid-Givetian to the end-Famennian and killed about 70% of species.
Marine life was hit hardest, especially shallow warm-water reef-builders: stromatoporoid sponges and rugose and tabulate corals.
Most remaining jawless fishes died, placoderms lost much diversity, all Frasnian tetrapods vanished, and only two trilobite orders survived.
Suggested causes include anoxia spread by rising seas, global cooling and nutrient runoff from tree roots; volcanism is debated and the causes remain uncertain.

entries.text: About 70% of species died in the Late Devonian crisis. Its sharpest blow, the Kellwasser event, is named for Germany's Kellwassertal valley and struck at the Frasnian-Famennian boundary. It ranks among the Big Five mass extinctions. The crisis came in pulses, from the mid-Givetian to the end of the Famennian. Marine life suffered most, and the warm shallow reefs worst of all. Their builders, stromatoporoid sponges and rugose and tabulate corals, were devastated, ending the great reefs of {{ref:devo-041}}. Most remaining jawless fishes died. Placoderms lost much of their diversity. All Frasnian tetrapods vanished, and only two trilobite orders survived. Why it happened is still uncertain. Suggested causes include anoxia spread by rising seas, global cooling, and nutrient runoff from the roots of new forests, which fed blooms in the sea. Volcanism is debated. The likeliest story may be several causes working together, but researchers have not settled it.

entries.title: Magma floods the Dnieper-Donets rift

facts.text: A mantle plume drove magmatism in the Dnieper-Donets rift of the East European Platform, starting in the late Frasnian and peaking in the Famennian.
Rifting was also most active in the Famennian.
This Pripyat-Dnieper-Donets igneous province has been linked to the Frasnian-Famennian extinction.

entries.title: The first seeds

facts.text: Seed plants first appear in the Famennian, the last Devonian stage, as a sister group to archaeopteridaleans or to progymnosperms.
A 385-million-year-old seed-plant precursor from Belgium predates the earliest seed plants by about 20 million years.
Seed plants had diversified substantially by the Famennian; the earliest seed ferns are Late Devonian lyginopterids.
Seeds sped plants' spread on land and let them exploit uplands away from river edges.
Pollen first appears in the Late Devonian, still indistinguishable from spores.

entries.title: Hyneria, a giant hunter in murky rivers

facts.text: Hyneria, a large predatory lobe-finned fish of the tristichopterid group, lived in fresh water during the Famennian.
H. lindae reached about 2.5-3 metres, possibly 3.5 metres, and used large sensory canals to find prey in murky water.
It was the largest and most common lobe-finned fish of Pennsylvania's Red Hill Shale; a second species, up to 2.7 m long, comes from Waterloo Farm.

entries.title: Archaeopteris forests change the world

facts.text: Archaeopteris forests spread rapidly in the Late Devonian, even colonizing Gondwana's coasts.
Archaeopterid trees reached 30 m, and giant Archaeopteris dominated a fairly uniform, low-diversity Famennian flora.
Trees drew down CO2, cooling the climate toward the later ice age, part of the 'Late Devonian wood crisis'.
Their deepening roots raised weathering and nutrient runoff, feeding algal blooms that caused anoxia in deeper waters.
Their order, Archaeopteridales, ranges through the Middle and Late Devonian.

entries.text: Archaeopterid trees grew up to 30 m tall, and in the Late Devonian their forests spread rapidly, even onto Gondwana's coasts. Giant Archaeopteris dominated a fairly uniform, low-diversity Famennian flora. Its order, the Archaeopteridales, ranges through the Middle and Late Devonian. These forests had global effects, part of what is called the Late Devonian wood crisis. Trees drew down carbon dioxide, cooling the climate toward the coming ice age. Their deepening roots raised weathering and washed nutrients into the sea, feeding algal blooms that stripped oxygen from deeper waters.

entries.title: Acanthostega and Ichthyostega grow legs

facts.text: Limbed vertebrates such as Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, known from fossils about 365 million years old, were among the earliest able to walk.
Acanthostega had legs, lungs and gills, but its limbs were too weak to carry it on land.
Fins with bones and joints became the two pairs of walking legs of the first tetrapods in the Famennian.
The oldest Late Devonian tetrapod fossils come from Greenland; by the period's end tetrapods lived worldwide, even in high-latitude Gondwana.
Late Devonian extinctions bottlenecked stem-tetrapods twice and selected against the most aquatic forms.

entries.text: Acanthostega had legs, lungs and gills, yet its limbs were too weak to carry it on land. That paradox sums up the first tetrapods. Limbed vertebrates such as Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, known from fossils about 365 million years old, were among the earliest able to walk. Their legs came from fins. In the Famennian, fins with bones and joints became the two pairs of walking legs of the first tetrapods. The oldest Late Devonian tetrapod fossils come from Greenland, but by the end of the period tetrapods lived worldwide, even in high-latitude Gondwana. The road was not smooth. The Late Devonian extinctions bottlenecked the stem-tetrapods twice, and each time they selected against the most aquatic forms. The survivors were the ones least tied to water, a filter that helped shape the land animals to come.

entries.title: Flynn Creek, a well-kept crater

facts.text: About 360 Ma, an impactor perhaps 90-190 m wide blasted a shallow crater 3.8 km across and 150 m deep in what is now Tennessee.

Within a few million years shales of the Late Devonian Chattanooga Sea buried it, making it one of the best-preserved ancient impact structures.

entries.title: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age begins

facts.text: The Late Paleozoic Ice Age began in the Late Devonian and lasted into the Late Permian, about 360 to 255 Ma, with large land ice sheets.
Its first glacial episodes came in the late Famennian and Tournaisian; the shift from greenhouse to icehouse was stepwise.
Late Devonian glacial deposits occur in Brazil's Solimoes, Amazonas and Paranaiba basins and in Bolivia, near the South Pole.
Plants' burial of carbon, with the uplift of Gondwana, tipped Earth from greenhouse into an icehouse lasting through the Carboniferous and Permian.

entries.title: Waterloo Farm, a fossil coast near the pole

facts.text: Waterloo Farm near Makhanda, South Africa, is an approximately 360-million-year-old Famennian fossil site in the Witpoort Formation.
It is the only record of a near-polar coastal ecosystem, overturning assumptions about high latitudes in the latest Devonian.
It is the most important Late Devonian fossil site of southern Gondwana.

facts.text: All placoderms died out in the end-Devonian Hangenberg event; no species is confirmed in the Carboniferous.

entries.title: The Hangenberg event ends the Devonian

facts.text: The Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, closed the Famennian; Polish ash beds bracket its black shale at 358.97 ± 0.11 and 358.89 ± 0.20 Ma.
It killed the last placoderms and stromatoporoid reef sponges, left Proetida the only trilobite order, and nearly exterminated the ammonoids.
Severe cooling and glaciation at the end of the Famennian, the dawn of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, may have driven it.
Other suggested causes include anoxia from high plankton productivity, Kola and Timan-Pechora volcanism, ozone loss hinted by malformed spores, and a nearby supernova.
Most marine and freshwater groups died out or shrank to a few lineages; one estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though plants were spared.

entries.text: Two ash beds in Poland pin down a catastrophe. They bracket a black shale at 358.97 ± 0.11 and 358.89 ± 0.20 million years ago. That shale records the Hangenberg event, or end-Devonian extinction, which closed the Famennian. The toll was heavy. It killed the last placoderms and the stromatoporoid reef sponges. It left Proetida as the only trilobite order and nearly wiped out the ammonoids. Most marine and freshwater groups died out or shrank to a few lineages. One estimate ranks it the fourth-deadliest extinction, though land plants were spared. The likely trigger was cold. Severe cooling and glaciation at the end of the Famennian marked the start of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age and may have driven the losses. Other proposed causes pile up: anoxia from high plankton productivity, volcanism in Kola and Timan-Pechora, ozone loss hinted at by malformed spores, and even a nearby supernova. None is settled, and several may have acted together.

entries.title: Siberia joins the growing supercontinent

facts.text: Siberia, an independent continent since the early Paleozoic, collided with Kazakhstania, raising the Altai Mountains.
Closure of the Turkestan Ocean brought northern Tarim against Kazakhstania from the mid-Carboniferous to the start of the Permian.
With Kazakhstania joined to Laurussia, Siberia was effectively part of Pangaea by 310 Ma, though strike-slip motion went on into the Permian.

entries.title: La Serre marks the start of the Carboniferous

facts.text: The base of the Carboniferous is fixed at the La Serre section in Montagne Noire, southern France.
It is marked by the first appearance of the conodont Siphonodella sulcata, descended from S. praesulcata.
Later study found S. sulcata below the boundary, weakening the marker.

entries.title: Crown tetrapods split and walk ashore

facts.text: By the very start of the Carboniferous, stem tetrapods had split into two crown lines: one leading to modern amphibians, the other to amniotes.
The earliest confirmed land-dwelling tetrapods come from early Carboniferous deposits, some 20 million years after the first Devonian forms.
Lineages with extra digits died out, fixing hands and feet at no more than five digits.
Surviving tetrapods radiated on dry land and became the dominant land animals of the Carboniferous and Permian.

entries.title: Romer's gap, a hole in the tetrapod record

facts.text: Tetrapod fossils are strikingly scarce from the Tournaisian into the early Visean, a span known as Romer's gap.
Land vertebrates were recovering from the Hangenberg extinction, and ichthyostegalian forms gave way to temnospondyls and reptiliomorphs.
Finds at Blue Beach, Nova Scotia, and in Scotland now show stem tetrapods and amphibians diversifying rapidly.

entries.title: Tropical seas build the Carboniferous Limestone

facts.text: Warm, shallow tropical seas teeming with life laid down limestone widely across Britain and Ireland, in basins separated by landmasses such as the Wales-London-Brabant Massif.
The rock is built from the shells and hard parts of sea creatures such as corals, brachiopods and crinoids, set in carbonate mud.
Carbonates dominated the early Carboniferous across the British Isles and Western Europe; later uplifted, the limestone forms karst country such as the Mendips and Yorkshire Dales.

entries.title: Crinoids at their peak

facts.text: Camerate crinoids peaked in diversity in the Mississippian; Agaricocrinus, about 345 Ma, was part of this echinoderm radiation.
Crinoids were so numerous that some Lower Carboniferous limestones near Clitheroe, England, consist almost entirely of their remains.
Their diversity fell from the Middle Mississippian as shell-crushing fish and sharks multiplied.

entries.title: Sharks and ray-finned fish inherit the seas

facts.text: After the end-Devonian Hangenberg extinction, sharks and their kin and ray-finned fish took over in diversity and abundance.
Few Devonian species of either group survived, so both had also suffered losses; no placoderm is confirmed in the Carboniferous.
Cartilaginous fish, especially holocephalans such as the stethacanthids, went through a major radiation.
Helicoprionids, eugeneodonts with a single circular tooth whorl in the lower jaw, first appeared.
The first large sharks, ratfishes and hagfish appear around 350 Ma.

entries.title: The Early Tournaisian Warm Interval

facts.text: After a brief glaciation at the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary, the climate warmed in the Early Tournaisian Warm Interval, 358–353 Ma.
Global average temperature was about 22 °C, with tropics near 30 °C and polar regions about 1.5 °C.

entries.title: Early Mississippian glaciations

facts.text: By about 350 Ma, glacial strata were building up in sub-Andean basins of Bolivia, Argentina and Paraguay.
A mid-Tournaisian glaciation left species-poor frigid tundra in western Argentina.
These short, minor glaciations preceded the main ice age, part of a stepwise shift from greenhouse to icehouse.

entries.title: Temnospondyls begin the Age of Amphibians

facts.text: The earliest temnospondyl traces are Tournaisian footprints, about 350 Ma; the first body fossils, such as Balanerpeton, are Visean, around 330 Ma.
Temnospondyls, often seen as primitive amphibians, flourished worldwide through the Carboniferous, Permian and Triassic.
All their clades except the stereospondylomorphs, from edopoids to dissorophoids, appeared during the Carboniferous.
Their rise as dominant land vertebrates earned the Carboniferous the name 'Age of Amphibians'.

entries.title: Lepidodendron, the scale tree

facts.text: Lepidodendron, a massive tree lycophyte, first appeared near the Tournaisian–Visean boundary.
Lepidodendron and Sigillaria went on to dominate the coal swamps, with horsetails and seed ferns between them.
Their order, the Lepidodendrales, ranges from the Carboniferous to the Late Permian.

facts.text: Seawater's magnesium-to-calcium ratio rose from the early Carboniferous; by the Middle Mississippian, aragonite seas had replaced calcite seas.
Aragonite reef builders, including algae and sponges, appeared in the Pennsylvanian.

entries.title: Insects take to the air

facts.text: The oldest known winged insects appear in the mid-Mississippian; flight may have evolved even earlier, in the Late Devonian.
Winged insects (pterygotes) went through a major radiation across the Carboniferous, 358 to 299 million years ago.
Sap-sucking palaeodictyopteroids dominated, and cockroach relatives (Blattoptera) became the most successful insects by the Pennsylvanian.
In the Pennsylvanian, Neoptera appeared and Miomoptera show the earliest evidence of complete metamorphosis.

entries.text: When did animals first take wing? The oldest known winged insects appear in the mid-Mississippian, though flight may have evolved even earlier, in the Late Devonian. Once airborne, they spread fast. Winged insects, the pterygotes, went through a major radiation across the Carboniferous, 358 to 299 million years ago. Sap-sucking palaeodictyopteroids dominated at first, and cockroach relatives, the Blattoptera, became the most successful insects by the Pennsylvanian. Two more innovations came in the Pennsylvanian. The Neoptera appeared. And the Miomoptera show the earliest evidence of complete metamorphosis, a life cycle with a separate larva, pupa and adult. Flight and metamorphosis together set up the insects for the success that followed.

entries.title: A long boom in marine life

facts.text: A long radiation of marine life, the Carboniferous–Earliest Permian Biodiversification Event, began in the Visean with the main phase of the ice age.
Fusulinid foraminifera and brachiopods led it; fusulinids diversified extremely fast, peaked in the Visean and later grew giant, some hosting photosynthetic algae.
Closure of the Rheic Ocean, falling sea level and Pangaea's assembly split the oceans into isolated regions, which may have driven it.
Bryozoans, renewed by the Hangenberg extinction, also peaked in the Visean, while cephalopods and swimming conodonts declined.

Fusulinids diversified extremely fast and peaked in the Visean, and so did bryozoans, renewed after the Hangenberg extinction. Cephalopods and swimming conodonts declined. The likely driver was geography. Closure of the Rheic Ocean, falling sea level and Pangaea's assembly split the oceans into isolated regions, where species could evolve apart.

entries.title: East Kirkton's early land animals

facts.text: The East Kirkton quarry in Scotland preserves land and freshwater animals; its richest layer dates to about 341 Ma, in the Visean.
It yielded dozens of early tetrapods, including the temnospondyl Balanerpeton and the proto-amniote Westlothiana ('Lizzie'), plus scorpions and eurypterids.
Its mostly land-dwelling fauna reflects a wider Carboniferous shift away from amphibious life.

entries.title: The Variscan collision at full strength

facts.text: Gondwana and peri-Gondwanan terranes collided obliquely with Laurussia, with metamorphism, igneous activity and large-scale deformation; full collision came around 340 Ma.
Northwest Africa met southeastern Euramerica, raising the southern Appalachians and the Meseta and Mauritanide mountains.
Europe's Variscan orogeny and North America's Alleghanian orogeny were parts of one continental collision.
Its main (Sudetic) compressional phase ran from about 330 to 320 Ma, when Hercynian granites intruded central Europe.
Together with the Alleghanian, it raised the Central Pangean Mountains, complete by about 295 Ma at their greatest height.

entries.title: Pangaea comes together

facts.text: Gondwana, Euramerica (Laurussia) and Siberia came together as the supercontinent Pangaea around 335 million years ago.
Plate motions sped up as Pangaea assembled, and the Rheic Ocean between Gondwana and Laurussia closed.
Blocks kept joining and rifting away into the early Mesozoic; Pangaea lasted about 160 million years, until its breakup began around 175 Ma.
Glacial deposits of this age, scattered from South America to Australia, later helped prove continental drift and the existence of Pangaea.

entries.text: Around 335 million years ago, the world's continents became one. Gondwana, Euramerica (Laurussia) and Siberia came together as the supercontinent Pangaea. The assembly was not gentle. Plate motions sped up as the pieces converged, and the Rheic Ocean between Gondwana and Laurussia closed. Pangaea was never truly finished, either: blocks kept joining and rifting away into the early Mesozoic. All told, it lasted about 160 million years, until its breakup began around 175 million years ago. The supercontinent left its own proof. Glacial deposits of this age lie scattered from South America to Australia, on lands now oceans apart. Ice could not have spread across such distant places unless they were once joined, and those deposits later helped prove continental drift and the existence of Pangaea. The same collisions raised mountain belts such as {{ref:carb-024}} and set up the climates and ice ages of the following periods.

entries.title: The ice age tightens its grip

facts.text: The main phase of the ice age began between 335 and 330 Ma, in the late Visean, as the climate cooled and CO2 fell.
Its onset brought a global fall in sea level and unconformities lasting millions of years.
Ice spread from up to 30 centres across Gondwana; around 330 Ma an ice sheet kilometres thick covered much of Africa over the South Pole.
Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells; the most intense phase came late in the Pennsylvanian.
Its glacial deposits reach 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m in Brazil's Itararé Group.

entries.text: Around 330 million years ago, an ice sheet kilometers thick covered much of Africa over the South Pole. It belonged to the main phase of the Late Paleozoic Ice Age. That phase began between 335 and 330 million years ago, in the late Visean, as the climate cooled and carbon dioxide fell. The onset reshaped coastlines everywhere. Sea level fell worldwide, leaving unconformities, gaps in the rock record lasting millions of years. Ice spread from up to 30 centers across Gondwana. Glacial periods millions of years long alternated with warmer spells, and the most intense phase came late in the Pennsylvanian. The ice left thick evidence. Its deposits reach 1,000 m thick in southern Africa's Dwyka Formation and 1,400 m in Brazil's Itararé Group. Those piles of scraped and dumped rock record ice that came and went for tens of millions of years.

entries.title: The Ouachita orogeny

facts.text: In the mid-Carboniferous, the South American part of Gondwana struck Laurussia's southern margin obliquely in the Ouachita orogeny, beginning in the Late Mississippian.
The uplifted Ouachita Mountains created foreland basins such as the Delaware Basin and fed rivers through the Pennsylvanian and Permian.

entries.title: The Serpukhovian extinction

facts.text: The largest extinction of the Carboniferous struck in the early Serpukhovian, removing about 31% of marine genera.
A major glaciation at the Visean–Serpukhovian boundary cooled the seas, and the extinction picked off species adapted to narrow, tropical temperature ranges.
Diverse Mississippian crinoid and rugose-coral communities gave way to species-poor, cosmopolitan ones; trilobites declined sharply while ammonoids peaked.
Driven more by low speciation than high extinction, its long-term ecological impact may have exceeded the end-Ordovician extinction's.
It ties with the Hangenberg event as the seventh-worst post-Cambrian mass extinction, though it may have been weaker in North America.

entries.title: The Millstone Grit spreads over northern England

facts.text: With Britain near the equator, rivers from northern uplands and the Wales-Brabant High carried sand and mud into the Pennine Basin.
When sea level fell as southern ice caps grew, deltas advanced across the region, leaving the thick sandstones of the Millstone Grit.
Lying beneath the Coal Measures, these gritstones now form the edges and moors of the Pennines and the Peak District.

entries.title: Amniotes and the egg that left the water

facts.text: One tetrapod lineage evolved membranes around the embryo, so its eggs could survive on dry land: the amniotes.
Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 Ma, with Paleothyris among the earliest, 330–320 Ma; the Carboniferous article puts their first appearance in the late Carboniferous.
Clawed Tournaisian footprints from Australia's Snowy Plains Formation have been claimed as amniote tracks, which would push their origin to the start of the period or earlier.
Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes took over.

entries.contested_note: When amniotes arose is disputed: 2025 footprint finds suggest the earliest Carboniferous or Devonian, against earlier views of a mid-to-late Carboniferous origin.

entries.text: An egg that dries out is a dead egg. One tetrapod lineage solved that problem. It evolved membranes around the embryo, so its eggs could survive on dry land, and these animals are the amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals. When they arose is disputed. Timelines place the first amniotes around 330 million years ago, with Paleothyris among the earliest, 330–320 million years ago. Another account puts their first appearance in the late Carboniferous. Clawed footprints from the Tournaisian of Australia's Snowy Plains Formation have been claimed as amniote tracks. If so, amniotes go back to the start of the period or earlier. Researchers have not settled the question. What is clearer is how they took over. Amphibians ruled until the mid-Carboniferous, when climate change cut their diversity and amniotes rose in their place.

entries.title: The Alleghanian orogeny builds the Appalachians

facts.text: Africa, then part of Gondwana, collided with North America, part of Euramerica, in at least five deformation events.
The collision built the Appalachian and Allegheny Mountains, a wide, high chain along today's eastern seaboard.
It began about 325 Ma and lasted some 65 million years, into the Permian.
The collision helped form Pangaea; sediment from the rising mountains filled basins such as the Black Warrior Basin.
When West Africa struck in the Late Pennsylvanian, compression turned northwest and the same grinding raised the Little Atlas range around 300 Ma.

entries.title: The first great glacial maximum

facts.text: The first major glacial period of the ice age, Serpukhovian to Moscovian, spread ice sheets from cores in southern Africa and South America.
In the Bashkirian a global fall in sea level marked the ice age's first major glacial maximum.
At the Mississippian–Pennsylvanian boundary, a positive oxygen-isotope excursion matched sea-level falls and widespread glacial deposits across southern Gondwana.
The low sea level left an unconformity that separates the Mississippian from the Pennsylvanian in North America.
Closure of the ocean gateway between the Rheic and Tethys in the early Bashkirian changed ocean circulation and added to the cooling.

entries.title: Oxygen reaches its all-time high

facts.text: All models show oxygen rising from 15–20% at the start of the Carboniferous to highs of 25–30%, above today's 21%.
Pyrite records suggest about 15% early in the period, over 25% in the Pennsylvanian, then a drop below 20% toward its end.
Charcoal from wildfires grows more common from the Late Devonian into the Carboniferous, another sign of rising oxygen.
Coal-forest photosynthesis buried carbon as peat and released oxygen into the air.

entries.text: Today the air is 21% oxygen. In the Pennsylvanian it reached 25 to 30%. All models agree on the rise, from 15–20% at the start of the Carboniferous to those highs. Pyrite, an iron sulfide mineral, gives a more detailed record. It suggests about 15% early in the period, over 25% in the Pennsylvanian, then a drop below 20% toward its end. Charcoal tells the same story. Remains of wildfires grow more common from the Late Devonian into the Carboniferous, because fire burns more readily in richer air. The source of the extra oxygen was the coal forests. Their photosynthesis released oxygen into the air, and their buried peat kept the carbon from taking it back by decay, as {{ref:carb-044}} describes. Whether the oxygen-rich air let arthropods and other animals grow large is still debated.

entries.title: Carbon dioxide falls to an all-time low

facts.text: Atmospheric carbon dioxide crashed to one of its lowest levels ever in the Pennsylvanian and early Permian, falling below 300 ppm.
Burial of organic matter, widespread ocean anoxia and weathering of the rising Central Pangean Mountains drew it down, cooling the climate and triggering glaciation.
Fast-growing coal forests also locked away carbon; a very late Carboniferous forest resurgence cooled the globe and brought polar ice back to Gondwana.
Near the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, erosion of mafic mountain rocks pushed CO2 as low as 175 ppm, and it stayed under 400 ppm for 10 million years.
From a record low about 298 million years ago, CO2 rose fourfold by 294 million years ago.

entries.title: Mountains bring monsoon rains

facts.text: The Central Pangean Mountains set up a perennial monsoon over today's Europe and eastern North America, keeping them swampy while the Colorado Plateau stayed dry.

The first signs of moisture moving toward the poles appeared in the late Carboniferous.

entries.title: Coal forests cover the tropics

facts.text: Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land in the late Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian), lasting into the Permian.
Towering lycopsid rainforests dominated equatorial Euramerica, the high point of Paleozoic land plants; peat mires also ringed the North and South China cratons.
Their buried peat became coal: about 90% of all coal beds formed in the Carboniferous and Permian, just 2% of Earth's history.
Why coal formation peaked is debated: a lag before lignin-digesting fungi evolved, or a unique mix of equatorial lands, high productivity and sinking wet basins.
Glacial sea-level falls exposed wide shelves where peat mires grew; rising interglacial seas then buried them.

entries.text: About 90% of all coal beds formed in the Carboniferous and Permian, just 2% of Earth's history. The source was a world of swamps. Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land in the Pennsylvanian and lasted into the Permian. Towering lycopsid rainforests dominated equatorial Euramerica, the high point of Paleozoic land plants, and peat mires also ringed the North and South China cratons. When the trees died, they piled up as peat, and the buried peat became coal. The ice age helped. Glacial falls in sea level exposed wide shelves where peat mires grew, and rising seas in warmer spells then buried them. Why coal formation peaked so sharply is debated. One idea is a lag before fungi evolved that could digest lignin, the tough material in wood. The other is a unique mix of equatorial lands, high plant productivity and sinking wet basins.

entries.title: Cyclothems, stripes of a swinging sea

facts.text: In the Pennsylvanian, repeating sediment cycles called cyclothems formed in shallow seas across tropical Laurussia and the China cratons.
Each records a sea-level fall and rise over about 100,000 years, as Gondwana's ice sheets advanced and retreated on a Milankovitch cycle.
The swings reached up to 120 m, with slow falls and rapid rises because ice sheets grow slowly but melt quickly.

entries.title: Equatorial Pangaea dries out

facts.text: Pangaea's equatorial belt grew drier toward the end of the Carboniferous, beginning a dry trend that lasted into the Triassic.
Across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, falling CO2 and low-latitude aridity brought a permanent shift to seasonally dry woodland.
Weaker continental weathering in the drier climate lowered the seawater strontium-isotope ratio toward the period's end.
After about 318 Ma, seasonality swung often between humid and arid; a cycle of aridification began in the late Moscovian, with abrupt faunal changes.
Late Pennsylvanian soils record drier, better-drained, more stable landscapes as the regional climate turned drier.

entries.title: Conifers and cycads appear

facts.text: Cycads, the Callistophytales seed ferns and the Voltziales conifers appeared in the late Carboniferous; ginkgophytes also arose in the period.
Early walchian conifers such as Walchia favoured higher, drier ground, where gymnosperms grew in the Pennsylvanian.
The oldest probable cycad leaves, such as Crossozamia from South Korea and China, date to around 300 Ma.

entries.title: Arthropods grow to giant sizes

facts.text: Arachnids, myriapods and especially flying insects underwent a major radiation in the late Carboniferous.
The millipede-like Arthropleura, up to 2.6 m long, was the largest land invertebrate of all time.
The griffinfly Meganeura, with a wingspan of about 75 cm, was the largest flying insect ever and dominated the skies around 305 Ma.
Giant insects, millipedes and scorpions thrived while tetrapods stayed small, until the rainforest collapse.
The gigantism may reflect high oxygen levels, though how oxygen shaped body size is debated.

entries.title: The Oslo Rift tears open

facts.text: Around today's Oslo, the main phase of graben formation began in the late Carboniferous, as tectonic forces tore the crust apart in the last phase of the Variscan orogeny.

entries.title: The Ural Mountains begin to rise

facts.text: The Uralian orogeny, which raised the Ural Mountains, began in the Late Carboniferous, about 323 Ma, and went on through the Permian.
Kazakhstania began colliding with Laurussia as the Ural Ocean closed in the Bashkirian.
Siberia, Kazakhstania and Baltica collided to form Laurasia, the basis of most of present-day Eurasia.
Deformation continued into the Permian, with granites intruding the region; around 300 Ma the Urals were uplifted as Pangaea was finally sutured.
The Magnitogorsk island arc in the Ural Ocean collided with Baltica's passive margin from the Late Devonian to early Carboniferous.

entries.title: Synapsids and sauropsids part ways

facts.text: Amniotes split into two lines: synapsids, the mammal lineage, and sauropsids, the line of reptiles and birds.
Timelines place the first sauropsids around 320 Ma and the first synapsids around 318 Ma; the earliest fossils of both date to about 313 Ma.
Synapsid pelycosaurs appeared in the Late Carboniferous and went on to dominate land for some 40 million years.
By the end of the period amniotes had diversified into pelycosaur families, protorothyridids, captorhinids, saurians and araeoscelids.

entries.title: Ice fills the young Karoo Basin

Their tillites, diamictites and striated pavements, the Dwyka Group, begin the Karoo Supergroup and reach about 800 m thick in the south.

entries.title: The Carboniferous rainforest collapse

facts.text: A cooler, drier climate fragmented and then collapsed the coal-forest rainforests; tree lycopsids and other wetland groups were lost in the Kasimovian glacial interval.
Lycopsid forests gave way to tree-fern forests: a complex replacement, not the loss of all rainforest.
Scale trees largely vanished from North America and Europe but persisted in Cathaysia, where coal forests revived at the very end of the period.
Amphibians and amniotes were both hit; the collapse may have let amniotes overtake amphibians, and seed plants overtake ferns and lycophytes.
A minor marine and land extinction, it left vast deserts across the continental interior.

entries.text: The great coal forests did not die out all at once; they broke into pieces. A cooler, drier climate first fragmented the rainforests and then collapsed them. Tree lycopsids and other wetland groups were lost in the Kasimovian glacial interval, as {{ref:carb-067}} describes. It was a replacement more than an ending. Lycopsid forests gave way to tree-fern forests, a complex change, not the loss of all rainforest. Scale trees largely vanished from North America and Europe but persisted in Cathaysia, where coal forests even revived at the very end of the period. Animals felt it too. Amphibians and amniotes were both hit, and the collapse may have let amniotes overtake amphibians, and seed plants overtake ferns and lycophytes. It was a minor extinction on land and at sea. But it left vast deserts across the continental interior, the landscape of the Permian to come.

facts.text: The first diapsid reptiles, such as Petrolacosaurus, appear around 305 Ma.
By the end of the Carboniferous, amniotes included saurians and araeoscelids among several new groups.

entries.title: The ice age peaks

facts.text: An exceptionally intense cooling struck around 300 Ma, when a very large part of Gondwana lay under glacial conditions.
A second major glacial period began in the late Gzhelian, with ice sheets spreading from cores in Australia and India into the early Permian.
The ice age peaked across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary; in the glacial maximum, 299–293 Ma, global average temperature was about 13 °C.
Brazil's Paraná Basin had its last glaciation in the early Gzhelian.

entries.title: Glossopteris forests rule the south

facts.text: Glossopteridales, an extinct order of seed plants, are known from the Permian of Gondwana.
Once Gondwana had fused with Pangaea, glossopterid trees, chiefly Glossopteris, dominated large parts of the south.
As glaciation waned in the Middle Permian, the Glossopteris flora flourished and huge coal deposits formed, as in southern Brazil and Uruguay.
These forests collapsed in the end-Permian mass extinction.

entries.title: The Gondwanide orogeny folds the south

facts.text: Mountain building in the Permian deformed southern Gondwana, in what are now southern South America, South Africa, Antarctica, Australia and New Guinea.
Its folds survive in Argentina's Sierra de la Ventana and South Africa's Cape Fold Belt.
Uplift linked to it split Brazil's Paraná Basin in two.
In South Africa, folding continued into a new phase from about 260 Ma, after the ice sheets had melted and a great lake, the Karoo Sea, spread.
