entries.title: Pangaea complete

facts.text: During the Permian almost every major landmass was gathered into the supercontinent Pangaea; only parts of East Asia, such as Cathaysia, lay apart.
Gondwana's collision with the northern continents completed the bulk of Pangaea, leaving the Appalachian–Ouachita mountains near its centre.
The consolidated supercontinent stretched from the equator to both polar regions.
Kazakhstania struck Baltica in the Cisuralian and Siberia joined in the late Permian; North China, South China and Indochina fused with Pangaea by the period's end.
Pangaea was complete roughly 20 million years before the end-Permian extinction.

entries.text: In the Permian, almost every major landmass on Earth was part of a single continent. The supercontinent Pangaea stretched from the equator to both polar regions. Only parts of East Asia, such as Cathaysia, lay apart. Gondwana's collision with the northern continents had completed most of it, leaving the Appalachian and Ouachita mountains near its center. The last pieces arrived during the Permian itself. Kazakhstania struck Baltica in the Cisuralian. Siberia joined in the late Permian, and North China, South China and Indochina fused with Pangaea by the period's end. The supercontinent did not have long to enjoy its completion. Pangaea was complete roughly 20 million years before the end-Permian extinction. Its shape set the climate of the age: a single vast landmass spanning the globe, with an interior far from the sea, as {{ref:perm-014}} describes.

entries.title: The Pangean megamonsoon

facts.text: Permian climate was extremely seasonal, ruled by megamonsoons that brought high aridity and harsh seasons to Pangaea's interior.
Monsoon circulation shows in Permian rocks; Early Permian wind directions record a summer wet season.
As the continents drifted north and spread more evenly across the equator, the megamonsoon intensified.
Dryness alternating with seasonal rain became the normal climate across much of the continent.

entries.title: Insects diversify into modern orders

facts.text: Insects diversified dramatically in the Early Permian, and most living insect orders arose during the period.
Insects with complete metamorphosis radiated, and scorpionflies, true dragonflies and barklice first appeared.
Older dominant groups, the palaeodictyopterans and giant griffinflies, declined; the palaeodictyopteran decline from the mid-Permian is linked to a change in flora.
Insects and plants were already locked in an arms race of feeding damage and plant defences.

entries.title: Cimmeria rifts away and the Neo-Tethys opens

facts.text: Rifting along northern Gondwana broke off the Cimmerian blocks, including Sibumasu (Shan–Thai), Qiantang and Lhasa, in the Early Permian.
The Neo-Tethys Ocean opened behind them as they drifted toward Laurasia, closing the Paleo-Tethys ahead.
A rift in what is now the Himalayan region grew into the Neo-Tethys, an ocean that would dominate much of the Mesozoic.

entries.title: Synapsids rule the land

facts.text: Pelycosaurs, early synapsids, peaked in the Cisuralian and were the dominant land animals for some 40 million years.
Synapsids, the group that later gave rise to mammals, thrived and diversified greatly, quickly growing large.
Early Permian faunas of North America and Europe were led by plant-eating edaphosaurids and meat-eating sphenacodontids, alongside diadectids and amphibians.
Pelycosaurs and their descendants, the therapsids, are the commonest land vertebrates in the best-known Permian fossil beds.
A few pelycosaurs lingered: the youngest known, from South Africa, is about 260 million years old.

entries.title: Carbon dioxide quadruples after a record low

facts.text: Atmospheric CO2 hit a record low about 298 Ma, then rose abruptly fourfold by 294 Ma.
Cooling had limited plant growth and rising oxygen fed more fires; both returned CO2 to the air, reaching about 300 ppm in the Permian.
Rising seas drowned the coal swamps that had buried carbon, so more CO2 stayed in the atmosphere and warmed the planet.
By the Cisuralian, oxygen and carbon dioxide had returned to more normal levels.

entries.title: The Skagerrak large igneous province

facts.text: A large igneous province centred on today's Skagerrak strait erupted at 297 ± 4 Ma.
It covered at least 0.5 million km², including the Oslo and Skagerrak grabens, south-western Sweden, Scotland, northern England and the central North Sea.
It is the oldest of a series of provinces tied to the African superplume, followed by Bachu, Emeishan, the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic.
It is tied to the Moscovian and Kasimovian stages of the rainforest collapse, about 310–296 Ma, together with Siberia's Barguzin-Vitim province.

entries.title: The Central Pangean Mountains at their height

facts.text: The range rose where Euramerica collided with northern Gondwana in the Variscan and Alleghanian orogenies, which began about 340 Ma and ended about 295 Ma.
At its highest, in the early Permian, it rivalled today's Himalayas; its western part, the Appalachians, was uplifted then.
Lying along the equator, it cast a rain shadow that turned northern coal swamps into seasonally dry land and later aided Europe's Zechstein salt deposits.
Weathering cut the peaks to about half their height by the Late Permian; its debris spread sandstone and conglomerate across Europe.
Remnants include the Appalachian and Ouachita Mountains, the Atlas and the Bohemian Massif.

entries.title: The Panjal Traps erupt

facts.text: The Panjal Traps, a large igneous province, erupted in what is now northwestern India; zircons give a uranium-lead age of 289 ± 2 Ma.
Their lavas, up to 2,500 m thick in Ladakh and Kashmir, may once have covered over 200,000 square km, comparable to the Emeishan Traps.
They are tied to the opening of the Neo-Tethys Ocean, which carried the Cimmerian blocks away from Gondwana's northeastern margin.
Lava chemistry shifts from enriched continental types to depleted ocean-floor types; the eruptions took place at about 33 degrees south.
Once linked to the Capitanian or end-Permian extinctions, they are far older; the Siberian Traps are the better candidate for those.

entries.title: The Artinskian warming melts the ice

facts.text: When the Permian began, the Late Paleozoic Ice Age was at its peak.
By 287 Ma temperatures had risen and the south polar ice cap retreated in the Artinskian Warming Event; glaciers clung on in eastern Australia's uplands.
Ice sheets shrank from the late Sakmarian on, a deglaciation sometimes treated as the end of the ice age proper.
Around 285.1 Ma orbital cycles stopped driving glacial growth and began driving marine anoxia and aridity, the turning point from icehouse to greenhouse.
As the glaciers receded, sea levels rose and the continental interiors dried out.

entries.title: The Clearwater West crater

Its neighbour Clearwater East is about 460-470 Ma old; different magnetic and meteorite signatures show that adjacent craters need not be twins.
It is a complex crater whose central peak formed when the crater walls collapsed and the floor rebounded.

entries.title: The Choiyoi volcanic province

facts.text: Subduction-related volcanism along Gondwana's western margin built the Choiyoi province, in today's Argentina and Chile, from about 286 to 247 Ma.
Its lavas, breccias and rhyolitic ignimbrites cover at least 200,000 and probably 500,000 square km, reaching 2-4 km thick.
During the Permian the arc magmatism migrated 350 km inland, reaching San Rafael about 280 Ma.
In Patagonia, Late Permian slab break-off melted the crust, an episode preserved in the Choiyoi volcanic province.
It has been suggested as an additional cause of the end-Permian extinction.

entries.text: Volcanic rock covers at least 200,000, and probably 500,000, square km of today's Argentina and Chile, 2–4 km thick. Weathering of large igneous provinces emplaced in the Kungurian drew down carbon dioxide and brought on the P3 glaciation.

facts.text: About 275 Ma the Grand Canyon region dried out and quartz sand dunes spread across a growing desert, forming the Coconino Sandstone.

Wind piled its quartz sand into large cross-bedded dunes, famous for trackways of scorpion-like arthropods and early tetrapods.

entries.title: Reefs peak and the Capitan Reef rises

facts.text: Reef building peaked in the Guadalupian, with reefs abundant from the Delaware Basin and Zechstein Basin to the Tethys and cool Panthalassa shelves.
Texas's Capitan Reef, the best-known example, was built mainly by calcareous sponges and encrusting algae rather than corals.
Brachiopods were key ecosystem engineers in Permian reef complexes.
Later, tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel; rising heat and salinity killed the reef, and brines laid down the Castile Formation evaporites.
The Capitan Formation, a giant fossil reef curving around the Delaware Basin that may have risen 61-91 m above the seafloor, is called the world's best-preserved Paleozoic reef complex.

entries.title: Therapsids take over from the pelycosaurs

facts.text: Therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large land animals in the Guadalupian, a role they kept into the Early Triassic.
The takeover came as the world grew drier; a poor fossil record across 'Olson's Gap' hides how it unfolded.
Giant dinocephalians, both plant- and meat-eaters, dominated Middle Permian faunas of South Africa and Russia.
Therocephalians arose and took over the sabre-toothed predator niche.
Coastal swamp corridors along East Pangaea let animals migrate between what are now South Africa and Russia.

entries.text: As the Permian world grew drier, the land changed hands. Therapsids replaced pelycosaurs as the dominant large land animals in the Guadalupian, and they kept that role into the Early Triassic. How the takeover unfolded is hidden. A poor fossil record across Olson's Gap leaves the transition mostly unseen. What follows it is clear. Giant dinocephalians, both plant-eaters and meat-eaters, dominated Middle Permian faunas of South Africa and Russia. Therocephalians arose and took over the role of saber-toothed predator. Those two regions share animals for a reason. Coastal swamp corridors along East Pangaea let animals migrate between what are now South Africa and Russia. The therapsids would go on to produce {{ref:perm-060}}, the line that eventually led to mammals.

entries.title: Sea level falls to a Paleozoic low

facts.text: Sea level stood several tens of metres above today's through the Early Permian.
A sharp fall began in the Roadian, reaching the lowest level of the whole Paleozoic, near today's, in the Wuchiapingian.
This Permian regression may be tied to the formation of Pangaea.
Falling seas, rising carbon dioxide and a worsening climate marked the Lopingian, ending in the end-Permian extinction.

entries.title: Olson's Extinction

facts.text: A proposed extinction around 273 Ma, in the late Cisuralian or early Guadalupian, long before the end-Permian crisis.
Most pelycosaur lineages vanished: edaphosaurids and ophiacodontids died out near the Kungurian–Roadian boundary while caseids and therapsids diversified.
Temnospondyl amphibians declined sharply afterwards, and extinction rates in fish rose.
Extreme environments in Kansas, combining heat and acidic waters, coincide with it, pointing to climate change as a possible cause.
A review of Kungurian and Roadian beds found the faunal turnover real, not a shift in where fossils were sampled.

entries.contested_note: Some authors argue the extinction is an artefact of poor sampling or gradual change, and the timing of 'Olson's Gap' is contested.

entries.title: Saber-toothed gorgonopsians appear

facts.text: Sabre-toothed gorgonopsians first evolved about 270 Ma and lasted until about 252 Ma.
The oldest identifiable one, Phorcys, dates to about the Wordian–Capitanian boundary, but finds show the group was diversifying by the early Wordian.
Small at first, with 10–15 cm skulls, they grew to bear-like sizes; Inostrancevia reached 3.5 m and about 300 kg.
Once the Capitanian extinction removed the dinocephalians, gorgonopsians became apex predators.

entries.title: The Hunter–Bowen orogeny

facts.text: Arc accretion in the Permian and Triassic affected about 2,500 km of eastern Australia's continental margin.
Major contraction came about 270–260 Ma and around 253 Ma, with a later phase about 235–230 Ma; a megafold had formed earlier, around 290 Ma.
Pangaea's counterclockwise rotation drove transpression along the subduction zone of the eastern Australian margin.

entries.title: The Capitanian mass extinction

facts.text: It began around 262 Ma and peaked around 259 Ma, closing the Capitanian stage and the Guadalupian (Middle Permian) epoch.
About 33–35% of marine genera and 60–63% of marine species died out; ammonoids, corals, reef algae, foraminifera, bryozoans and brachiopods suffered most.
On land the dinocephalians and the last varanopids vanished, and anomodont diversity halved.
It is linked to the Emeishan eruptions, which drove two ocean anoxic events and acidification, and to a sea-level fall that killed reefs.
Its severity is debated: some rank it fifth worst ecologically, while others find only low-latitude northern taxa hit, or a regional South China crisis.

entries.title: The Emeishan Traps erupt

facts.text: Eruptions of this flood-basalt province in south-western China began 265 Ma or earlier, peaked between 262 and 261 Ma, and ended about 259 Ma.
The basalts cover more than 250,000 km², up to 5.5 km thick, with an estimated volume of about 300,000 km³.
The eruptions had global ecological impact and are tied to the Capitanian mass extinction, though they were dwarfed by the later Siberian Traps.
Around 260 Ma the Emeishan Thermal Excursion interrupted a mid-Capitanian cool period; afterwards weathering of the basalts drew down CO2 and cooled the early Wuchiapingian.
Coronene enrichment at the Guadalupian–Lopingian boundary, without an iridium anomaly, points to massive volcanism rather than an impact.

entries.title: The first cynodonts

facts.text: Cynodonts, the therapsid group ancestral to mammals, first appeared in the Late Permian, about 260 Ma, and spread worldwide.

entries.title: The sea retreats and the reefs fail

facts.text: The Guadalupian–Lopingian boundary, dated by ash beds to 259.857 ± 0.084 Ma, coincided with one of the Phanerozoic's most prominent marine regressions.
Evaporites and land deposits lie over marine carbonates across the boundary, and a vast unconformity marks it in strata worldwide.
Falling seas and regional salinity swings ended the golden age of reef building in the 'end-Guadalupian reef crisis'.
Closure of the Sino-Mongolian Seaway has been proposed as a driver of biodiversity loss in the Paleo-Tethys.
Global diversity, rebuilt by disaster taxa late in the Guadalupian, dropped again in the Wuchiapingian.

entries.title: Dicynodonts and pareiasaurs flourish

facts.text: Late Permian lands were dominated by advanced therapsids, sabre-toothed gorgonopsians and beaked plant-eating dicynodonts, alongside large herbivorous pareiasaurs.
Dicynodonts flourished after the Capitanian extinction and became among the most successful therapsids, surviving almost to the end of the Triassic.
South Africa's Beaufort Group was then a semi-arid cold steppe, crossed by seasonal rivers draining into the Karoo Sea.

entries.title: The first archosauromorphs

facts.text: Archosauromorphs, the reptiles that later produced pseudosuchians, dinosaurs and pterosaurs, first appeared and diversified in the Late Permian.
The first archosauriforms appeared in the latest Permian.
A molecular estimate puts the split of turtles from the line of birds and crocodilians at about 255 Ma.
A marine clade of ichthyosauromorphs, sauropterygians and thalattosaurs may have originated from archosauromorphs in the Late Permian.
Archosauromorphs exploded in diversity after the end-Permian extinction.

entries.title: Rifting begins along the future Atlantic

Extension that began in the late Permian spread across Laurussia from central Europe to eastern Canada, opening north–south rift valleys.
Pangaea's breakup can loosely be traced back to about 252 Ma.

entries.title: The Kupferschiefer, a copper-bearing black shale

facts.text: About 257 Ma, anoxic water in the enclosed Zechstein basin laid down the Kupferschiefer, a black shale and marl at the base of the Zechstein Group.
Though usually only 30-60 cm thick, it spreads over 600,000 square km across six countries and holds up to 30% organic matter.
Mineral-rich groundwater later formed sulfide ores in it, one of the world's most important copper deposits, mined since at least 1199 AD.

entries.title: The Zechstein Sea lays down thick salt

facts.text: A marine transgression, probably tied to deglaciation, created the Zechstein Sea, a hypersaline inland sea over today's North Sea, lowland Britain, Germany and Poland.
In the rain shadow of the Central Pangean Mountains near the equator, at least five evaporation cycles piled up salt, anhydrite and dolomite about 1,000 m thick.
The sea's eventual disappearance was part of the marine regression that preceded and accompanied the end-Permian extinction.

entries.title: The longest icehouse ends

facts.text: The Late Paleozoic icehouse, under way since the Late Devonian, finally ended around 255 Ma.
It was the most extensive and longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic.
A last regional glaciation, P4, lasted in Australia from the middle Capitanian to the late Wuchiapingian.
The final alpine glaciers melted in what is now eastern Australia around 255 Ma, in the late Wuchiapingian.
By one account, the last greenhouse period began in the late Permian as this ice age ended.

entries.text: The final alpine glaciers melted in what is now eastern Australia around 255 million years ago. With them ended the Late Paleozoic icehouse, under way since the Late Devonian. It was the most extensive and longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic. The ending was slow. The great southern ice sheets had shrunk long before, in the Artinskian warming, but cold returned in spells. A last regional glaciation, P4, lasted in Australia from the middle Capitanian to the late Wuchiapingian. Only then did the ice go for good. By one account, the most recent greenhouse period began in the late Permian as this ice age ended. The timing matters. The world entered the end-Permian crisis already warm and ice-free, and {{ref:perm-082}} would push it much further.

entries.title: Salt fills the Delaware Basin

facts.text: As tectonics restricted the Hovey Channel, the deep Delaware Basin of Texas and New Mexico was cut off from the sea and its brines grew ever saltier.
Up to 91 m of finely laminated gypsum and anhydrite, the Castile Formation, settled in water over 500 m deep, followed by thick halite of the Salado.
By the end of the Ochoan the basin had filled to the top of the Capitan Reef and was mostly dry land.

entries.title: The Siberian Traps flood a continent

facts.text: Basalt lava flooded a vast area of Siberia; about 7 million km2 of basalt, some 4 million km3, remains today.
It was one of the largest volcanic events of the last 500 million years, erupting for roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary.
Magma heated the coal- and evaporite-rich rocks of the Tungus basin, which can release large amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases.
Its CO2, SO2, halogens and metals drove warming, ocean anoxia and acidification, ozone loss, acid rain and repeated mercury poisoning.
Zircon dating ties the eruptions to the extinction, and the traps are believed to be its primary cause.

entries.text: About 7 million km² of basalt still covers Siberia today, some 4 million km³ of rock. It is what remains of the Siberian Traps, one of the largest volcanic events of the last 500 million years. The eruptions went on for roughly two million years across the Permian–Triassic boundary. The lava alone was not the main danger. Magma heated the coal- and evaporite-rich rocks of the Tungus basin, which can release large amounts of toxic and greenhouse gases. Carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, halogens and metals poured out. They drove warming, ocean anoxia and acidification, ozone loss, acid rain and repeated mercury poisoning. Zircon dating ties the eruptions to the end-Permian extinction, and the traps are believed to be its primary cause. Each of the killing mechanisms that follow, from {{ref:perm-082}} to {{ref:perm-086}}, leads back here.

entries.title: The Glossopteris flora collapses

facts.text: Glossopteris trees dominated much of southern Gondwana through the Permian, until these ecosystems collapsed in the end-Permian extinction.
In Australia the flora collapsed around 370,000 years before the boundary; in western Gondwana probably a few hundred thousand years before.
Just above the boundary, an Australia-wide conifer flora largely replaced it.
The glossopterid order arose at the start of the Permian; most or all of its members died out in the extinction, 251.9 million years ago.

entries.title: A carbon signature of catastrophe

facts.text: A large, abrupt global fall in δ13C coincides with the extinction and helps locate the boundary in rocks that cannot be dated radiometrically.
The negative excursion measured 4–7% and lasted about 500,000 years, though alteration of the rocks makes its exact size hard to pin down.
Carbonate rocks worldwide record a swift drop of about 1% in the 13C/12C ratio.
Methane from clathrates was once favoured as the light-carbon source, but isotopes point mainly to volcanic CO2 and thermogenic methane from the Siberian Traps.
A burst of methane-producing microbes may explain part of the swings; on land, Norwegian floras turned over before the big negative shift.

entries.text: Carbon atoms record the extinction even where rocks cannot be dated by radioactivity. A large, abrupt global fall in δ13C, the share of heavy carbon, coincides with the extinction and helps locate the boundary. Carbonate rocks worldwide record a swift drop of about 1% in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12. The excursion measured 4–7% and lasted about 500,000 years, though altered rocks blur its exact size. Methane from frozen seabed clathrates was once the favored source of the light carbon. Isotopes now point mainly to volcanic carbon dioxide and methane cooked out of rocks by the Siberian Traps. Methane-producing microbes may explain some of the swings.

entries.title: The end-Permian hothouse

facts.text: The Siberian Traps released more than 5 teratonnes of CO2, more than doubling the atmosphere's carbon dioxide.
CO2 rose from around 400 to 2,500 ppm as some 3,900–12,000 gigatonnes of carbon entered the ocean-atmosphere system.
Average surface temperature jumped from about 18 °C to as much as 35 °C; tropical seas off Iran topped 35 °C.
This rapid greenhouse release caused the extinction and began an extreme hothouse lasting several million years into the Triassic.

entries.title: The Great Dying

facts.text: Earth's most severe known extinction, it removed about 57% of families, 62% of genera, 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrate species.
The main marine pulse took 60,000–100,000 years; U–Pb dating of Meishan ash beds places it between 251.941 and 251.880 Ma.
The consensus cause is the Siberian Traps eruptions, whose CO2 and SO2 brought global warming, sulfurous oxygen-starved seas and acidified oceans.
Shell-building marine animals suffered most; on land it was the largest insect mass extinction and equally catastrophic for plants.
It ended the Paleozoic Era; recovery was slow, with land ecosystems needing some 30 million years to rebuild.

Recovery was slow: land ecosystems needed some 30 million years to rebuild.

entries.title: Acid seas and acid rain

facts.text: Rising CO2 acidified the oceans, by up to 0.7 pH units, matching the selective loss of heavily calcified animals.
Acidification was worst at mid-latitudes; with anoxia, a marine transgression devastated shallow shelf communities.
On land, acid rain lowered soil pH and sped soil erosion, washing land-derived organic matter into the sea.

entries.text: The oceans grew more acidic by up to 0.7 pH units as carbon dioxide rose. That matches the pattern of loss, which fell hardest on heavily calcified animals. Acidification was worst at mid-latitudes, and together with anoxia a rising sea devastated shallow shelf communities. On land, acid rain lowered soil pH and sped erosion, washing organic matter from the land into the sea.

entries.title: Seas without oxygen

facts.text: Oxygen-starved and hydrogen-sulfide-rich (euxinic) waters spread through the oceans from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic.
Across most of the Tethys and Panthalassa, anoxia appears at the extinction itself, though at some sites it began earlier.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria thrived and filled the sea with hydrogen sulfide, even in the sunlit shallows.
Hydrogen sulfide escaping from the sea may have poisoned life on land and in the water.
The extinction, triggered by runaway Siberian Traps CO2, was marked by ocean deoxygenation; ocean overturn has also been proposed.

entries.title: Sea level swings at the boundary

facts.text: Global sea level is reported to have fallen 250 m during the Permian–Triassic extinction.
A drastic regression shrank shallow shelf habitats, hastening the final decline of trilobites.
Other work ties the main warming to a marine transgression, which with anoxia ravaged shallow shelf life.

Other work tells a different story, tying the main warming to a rise in sea level, which with anoxia ravaged shallow shelf life.

entries.title: The last spiny sharks

facts.text: The acanthodians or 'spiny sharks', an early class of jawed fishes, became extinct in the Permian–Triassic extinction.
Their diversity had been low but stable through the Carboniferous and slipped further in the Permian.

entries.title: The last fusulinids

facts.text: Fusulinid foraminifera, large single-celled shell-builders, went extinct in the Permian–Triassic extinction.
The Capitanian crisis had already cut them to dwarf forms, and they were nearly gone before the final blow.
Lagenid forams survived, probably thanks to wider environmental tolerance and range.

entries.title: The last gorgonopsians

facts.text: Sabre-toothed gorgonopsians, the Late Permian's top land predators, died out in the extinction's final phase.
They began to disappear from Africa and Eastern Europe just before the extinction.
Biarmosuchians also vanished, while dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts shrank to a handful of species each.

entries.title: The last griffinflies

facts.text: Several Paleozoic insect groups, including the giant griffinflies (protodonates) and palaeodictyopteroids, were extinct by the end of the Permian.
Of the Paleozoic insect groups, only three are known after the extinction, the largest known mass extinction of insects.

entries.title: The last progymnosperms

facts.text: The Noeggerathiales, the last surviving progymnosperms, persisted until the end of the Permian.
Progymnosperms were woody, spore-bearing plants thought to have given rise to the seed plants.

entries.title: The Paleozoic corals vanish

facts.text: Rugose and tabulate corals, the reef-building corals of the Paleozoic, died out in the Permian–Triassic extinction.
About 96% of coral and other anthozoan genera were lost.

entries.text: About 96% of coral and other anthozoan genera were lost in the Permian–Triassic extinction. Their loss left the seas without the reef builders that had served them through the Paleozoic.

entries.title: The last lycopsid swamps

facts.text: Carboniferous-style lycopod and horsetail swamps survived to the end of the Permian only in Cathaysia, equatorial islands that became South China.
By then tree lycopsids were rare, marginal plants there, no longer the main coal formers.

entries.title: The last trilobites

facts.text: Trilobites, which had thrived since the Cambrian, vanished at the end of the Permian after nearly 300 million years.
The Proetida, the only order left after the Devonian, lasted to the end; by the Changhsingian a handful of genera remained, by one count just two.
Falling sea level shrank their shallow-shelf habitats, so their final decline came shortly before the main extinction.

entries.title: Pangaea dries out

facts.text: Near the end of the Permian, Pangaea grew drier as the supercontinent coalesced.
Terminal Permian volcanism and global warming sharply worsened this aridity.
In the Kuznetsk Basin of Siberia, drying killed humid-adapted Cordaites forests a few hundred thousand years before the boundary.

entries.title: The impact idea, largely rejected

facts.text: Suggestions that an asteroid impact triggered the extinction are now largely rejected.
Candidate craters include the 250 km Bedout structure off northwest Australia and a hypothesized 480 km Wilkes Land crater in Antarctica.
Reported clues include shocked quartz, fullerenes with extraterrestrial gases and meteorite fragments, but iridium is not anomalous and many boundary sites lack impact evidence.

entries.contested_note: An impact trigger is largely rejected; the proposed craters are all contentious and their ages and origins still debated.

entries.title: The last sea scorpions

facts.text: Eurypterids, the 'sea scorpions', dwindled in numbers and diversity through the Permian.
When they died out is contentious: either early in the Middle Permian or in the Permian–Triassic extinction, 251.9 million years ago.
A terminal-Permian cuticle fragment from Australia, once called the youngest eurypterid, may instead be a scorpion.

entries.title: Pangaea's megamonsoon blows at full strength

facts.text: The Pangean megamonsoon reached its greatest strength in the Triassic, when Pangaea's land area peaked after Siberia and the China cratons joined.
Its circulation may have reversed part of the easterly global winds, sending westerlies onto the west coast.
Shifting winds brought moisture to the previously dry Colorado Plateau.
A greenhouse climate left the continents ice-free, even at the poles.

entries.text: When nearly all the land on Earth sits in one block, the weather follows. The Pangean megamonsoon, a vast seasonal swing of wind and rain, reached its greatest strength in the Triassic. It peaked when Pangaea's land area was largest, after Siberia and the China cratons, ancient continental cores, had joined it. Its circulation may have reversed part of the global easterly winds, sending westerlies onto the west coast. Those shifting winds carried moisture to the previously dry Colorado Plateau. Meanwhile a greenhouse climate kept every continent free of ice, even at the poles.

entries.title: A buried crater scars North Dakota

facts.text: An impact in what is now McKenzie County, North Dakota, left the Red Wing Creek structure, about 9 km across and now buried some 2,000 m deep.
Thick Jurassic rocks fill the disturbed structure, suggesting a Triassic impact; its age is estimated at 200 ± 25 million years.
It was once grouped with Manicouagan, Saint Martin and Rochechouart as one multiple impact, but those craters proved to be millions of years apart.

entries.title: Shell-crushers launch the Mesozoic marine revolution

facts.text: The Mesozoic marine revolution, a rise in shell-crushing and boring predators and seafloor bulldozing, began with the Mesozoic.
Increasingly capable predators stressed fixed-in-place sea life, shifting the balance as some prey adapted faster than others.
Stalked crinoids were easy prey for shell-crushing predators from the Triassic on.

conflicts.note: Timeline of life gives 250 Ma for the start

entries.text: On the Mesozoic seafloor, sitting still became dangerous. With the new era began the Mesozoic marine revolution, an arms race marked by more shell-crushing and boring predators and more animals bulldozing the seafloor. As predators grew steadily more capable, they stressed animals fixed in place. The balance shifted, because some prey adapted faster than others. Stalked crinoids, sea lilies anchored to the bottom, made easy targets for the shell-crushers from the Triassic on.

entries.title: Beaked rhynchosaurs appear in the aftermath

facts.text: Beaked herbivorous rhynchosaurs appeared in the Induan, shortly after the extinction, within a major diversification of reptiles.
Basal forms such as Noteosuchus come from the earliest Triassic of South Africa's Eastern Cape.
They became most abundant and worldwide in the Carnian, then died out early in the Norian.

Their peak came much later, in the Carnian, when they were abundant worldwide, and they died out early in the Norian.

entries.title: Stifling, acidic seas stall the ocean's recovery

facts.text: Oxygen-poor waters persisted through the Early Triassic, which may explain the slow recovery of marine life, especially on the seafloor.
Biomarkers of green sulfur bacteria show hydrogen sulphide reaching sunlit shallow water from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic.
Persistently high carbon dioxide in air and sea hampered the recovery of shell-building organisms.
Alternating oxygen-rich and oxygen-free seafloor conditions may explain carbon-isotope swings of the time.

entries.text: Poison gas drifted into sunlit shallows. Chemical fossils of green sulfur bacteria, microbes that need both light and hydrogen sulfide, show the gas reaching shallow water from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic. Oxygen-poor water lingered through the whole epoch, which may explain why sea life, especially on the seafloor, recovered so slowly. Persistently high carbon dioxide in air and sea also hampered shell builders. Seafloors flipping between oxygen-rich and oxygen-free states may explain the carbon-isotope swings of the time, shifts in the balance of heavy and light carbon.

entries.title: Desert playas lay down the red Buntsandstein

facts.text: Across the Germanic Basin, from England to Poland, arid continental playas laid down the Buntsandstein, red sandstones and conglomerates with little clay.
With the later Muschelkalk and Keuper it forms the three-part Germanic Trias; it holds small reptiles, plants and Chirotherium tracks.
A major late Anisian rise in global sea level flooded the basin with a tropical sea, ending Buntsandstein deposition and starting the Muschelkalk.

Coelacanths, lobe-finned fishes, had their greatest burst of diversity in the Early Triassic, just after the Great Dying. Lungfishes reached their peak variety during the Triassic. Today only three lungfish genera survive.

entries.title: Pangaea bakes in the Phanerozoic's fiercest heat

facts.text: The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, during and just after the Siberian Traps' huge greenhouse-gas release.
Pangaea's interior was mostly hot and arid, with widespread deserts, while the poles stayed temperate.
Equatorial temperatures may have jumped 8–10 °C at the start of the Triassic, to averages of 32–35 °C.
The climate swung repeatedly: a thermal maximum at the boundary, a brief Dienerian cooling (251–249 Ma), then a Latest Smithian Thermal Maximum (about 249–248 Ma).
Extreme heat may have left land between about 30°N and 40°S without tetrapods from the Induan until the early Spathian.

entries.title: Lystrosaurus spreads to every corner of Pangaea

facts.text: The pig-sized plant-eating dicynodont Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some earliest Triassic land vertebrate faunas.
It was the most common land vertebrate and spread to every corner of Pangaea after the extinction.
Herding, tolerance of extreme, variable climates, very fast growth and early sexual maturity probably explain its success.
Trackways from South Africa's Karoo Basin show dicynodonts were abundant right after the crisis.
Its usual label as a post-extinction disaster taxon has been questioned by some recent evidence.

entries.title: Microbes build reefs in the extinction's wake

facts.text: Microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow, mostly low-latitude seas in the earliest Triassic, in both oxygen-poor and oxygenated water.
Microbe–animal reefs, built partly by keratinous sponges, dominated many surviving communities and steadied damaged ecosystems.
Microbial mats left wrinkle structures at sea and on land; their later disappearance signals returning burrowers and recovering ecosystems.

entries.title: The Siberian Traps erupt again and again

facts.text: Carbon-isotope swings and mercury spikes suggest massive Siberian Traps activity recurred several times in the Early Triassic.
These pulses caused further extinctions and may have kept the climate hot; the eruptions persisted into the Early Triassic.
Later Traps activity is linked to the Smithian–Spathian, Olenekian–Anisian and Anisian crises.
A methane release cannot explain the repeated large carbon-isotope shifts.

entries.text: The great eruptions that ended the Permian did not stop when the Triassic began. entries.title: Life crawls back from the worst extinction ever

facts.text: Life took millions of years to recover from the largest mass extinction, slowed by its severity and the harsh Early Triassic climate.
Successive extinction waves and prolonged environmental stress held recovery back; Early Triassic faunas were poor in species and much alike worldwide.
Seafloor communities stayed low in diversity until the end of the Early Triassic, about 4 million years after the extinction.
On land, ecosystems took about 30 million years to recover; episodes of acidity stunted them well into the Triassic.
Marine recovery then accelerated explosively in the Anisian, as crowded niches sharpened competition.

entries.text: On land, full recovery took about 30 million years. That is how deep the wound of the largest mass extinction ran, and how harsh the Early Triassic climate was. Successive extinction waves and prolonged environmental stress held recovery back again and again. Early Triassic faunas were poor in species and much alike worldwide, the same few survivors turning up everywhere. The sea healed faster, but not quickly. Seafloor communities stayed low in diversity until the end of the Early Triassic, about 4 million years after the extinction. On land, episodes of acidity stunted ecosystems well into the Triassic. Then, in the Anisian, marine recovery accelerated explosively. Crowded niches sharpened competition, and life began to diversify on every front.

entries.title: Temnospondyl amphibians bounce back first

facts.text: Temnospondyls recovered first and peaked in diversity in the early Triassic; most major stereospondyl groups, such as capitosaurs and trematosaurs, appeared then.
Tupilakosaurids thrived as disaster taxa in the Induan; temnospondyls shrank then, but regained pre-extinction sizes in the Olenekian.
Temnospondyls then declined through the Middle and Late Triassic; only brachyopoids and trematosauroids survived beyond it.

entries.text: Big amphibians were the quickest to recover. entries.title: Moenkopi tidal flats redden the American Southwest

facts.text: Rivers, tidal flats and brief marine incursions laid down the Moenkopi's red sandstones and siltstones across the American Southwest, up to about 550 m thick.
Its fossils point to a warm tropical climate, perhaps with monsoonal wet–dry seasons.
Its Early Triassic bivalves, 27 species in 18 genera, cast doubt on the idea that bivalves recovered only in the Middle Triassic.

entries.title: Seas creep up from a Permian–Triassic low

facts.text: Sea level hit its lowest at the Permian–Triassic boundary and stayed low through the Triassic compared with other periods.
Starting near today's level, it rose to about 10–20 m above present during the Early and Middle Triassic.
The rise sped up in the Ladinian, peaking at up to 50 m above today's level in the Carnian.

entries.title: Guiyang fossils capture an entire marine food web

facts.text: The Guiyang biota, an exceptionally preserved late Induan assemblage from China's Daye Formation, dates to about 250.8 Ma.
It holds every trophic level of a marine ecosystem, from primary consumers to apex predators.

facts.text: A new Dicroidium flora took hold around the Induan–Olenekian boundary and peaked in diversity in the Anisian.
Trees of the fern-leaved seed fern Dicroidium dominated large parts of Gondwana during the Triassic.

entries.title: Triadobatrachus, the oldest known frog, appears

facts.text: Triadobatrachus massinoti, the earliest known frog, dates from about 250 Ma.
The first lissamphibians, or modern amphibians, appeared in the Triassic; frog forerunners were present by the Early Triassic.
Stem salamanders and caecilians also arose, but lissamphibians became common only in the Jurassic as temnospondyls waned.

entries.title: Ichthyosaurs carry reptiles back to the sea

facts.text: Ichthyosaurs evolved from land reptiles that returned to the sea, much as the ancestors of whales and dolphins later did.
Ichthyosaurs first appeared around 250 Ma, just two million years after the end-Permian extinction, among the first marine reptiles.
The oldest ichthyopterygian remains come from the Olenekian of Spitsbergen; early forms lined northern Pangaea's coasts, from Japan and China to Canada.
Ichthyosaurs in the narrow sense arose near the Early–Middle Triassic boundary, about 245 Ma; by the Middle Triassic some were very large.
Ichthyosaurs lasted until about 94 Ma, in the Late Cretaceous.

entries.title: Mountain building strikes western North America

facts.text: The Sonoma orogeny hit western North America around the Permian–Triassic transition, after the Late Devonian Antler orogeny.
It is linked to the Sonomia island arc or microcontinent accreting onto the continent's western margin.
Some geologists dispute whether converging plates produced it.

entries.title: Colliding blocks piece together East Asia

facts.text: Annamia, Sibumasu, Qiangtang and Lhasa collided with South China and each other between about 250 and 230 Ma, raising the Indosinian orogeny.
This southern Asian continent then collided, about 240–220 Ma, with North China, Tarim and other blocks along the Central China orogen.
North and South China's collision closed the Qinling ocean; deep subduction destroyed part of the North China craton's root.
Final closure of the Paleoasian Ocean, c. 240–230 Ma, joined Tarim and North China to Kazakhstan and Siberia, forming the Central Asian orogenic belt.
These East Asian blocks gave Pangaea its greatest land area, as climate changed sharply and the megamonsoon developed; any link is still being studied.

These additions gave Pangaea its greatest land area as climate changed sharply and the megamonsoon developed, though any link is still being studied.

entries.title: A second blow: the Smithian–Spathian extinction

facts.text: A second extinction after the end-Permian one, the Smithian–Spathian boundary event, struck during the Olenekian.
It was one of the grim episodes that returned through the Early Triassic and delayed life's recovery.
The late Smithian crisis was a widespread ocean anoxic event; the Smithian ended with a thermal maximum around 249–248 Ma.
Renewed Siberian Traps volcanism and ocean anoxia have been linked to it.
Idaho's Paris biota is the first diverse fossil assemblage known after the event.

Renewed Siberian Traps volcanism has been linked to it, and the Smithian closed with a thermal maximum around 249–248 million years ago. entries.title: Idaho's Paris biota marks a fresh start

facts.text: The Paris biota of Idaho is an exceptionally diverse marine assemblage from the earliest Spathian, about 249 Ma.
It is the first diverse assemblage after the Smithian–Spathian extinction, about 3 million years after the end-Permian one.
Its animals lived in a shallow, near-equatorial sea on Pangaea's west coast; beds with its ammonoids are dated to 248.853 ± 0.086 Ma.

entries.title: Flipper-limbed sauropterygians take to the water

facts.text: Sauropterygians, flipper-limbed marine reptiles, evolved from land ancestors soon after the end-Permian extinction.
The earliest appeared about 248–247 Ma, in the Spathian, and were already notably diverse.
Hupehsuchians, ichthyopterygians and sauropterygians were among the first marine reptiles, entering the scene in the Olenekian.
They flourished through the Triassic; all but the plesiosaurs died out at the period's end.

entries.title: A sharp cooling ends the Early Triassic heat

facts.text: During the Latest Olenekian Cooling, from 248 to 247 Ma, temperatures fell by about 6 °C.
The Middle Triassic stayed cooler than the Early Triassic, with temperatures falling through most of the Anisian.
Cooler Anisian oceans let animal-built reefs become common again.

entries.title: A third extinction closes the Early Triassic

facts.text: A third post-Permian extinction event struck at the Olenekian–Anisian boundary, ending the Early Triassic.
Siberian Traps activity has been linked to it, and to later Middle–Late Anisian and Anisian–Ladinian crises.

entries.title: Pangaea starts to tear along the future Atlantic

facts.text: Shortly after the Siberian Traps eruptions ended, around 247 Ma, rift valleys began to form; Fundy and Argana basin rift sediments date to 247 Ma.
Extension began in the northern Central Atlantic in the Anisian and the southern part in the Carnian; by 230 Ma new rift valleys had formed and filled.
From about 227 to 202 Ma, deep half-graben basins between New Jersey and Morocco held large rift lakes, red beds and shales, the Newark Supergroup.
Rifting spread to Newfoundland and Iberia, the eastern Mediterranean, and southwestern Gondwana and Patagonia, opening basins such as the Lusitanian and Cuyo.
Three-armed grabens joined into the future Mid-Atlantic Ridge, but Pangaea had not yet separated; Laurasia parted from Gondwana between 215 and 175 Ma.

entries.title: The first stony corals, tomorrow's reef builders

facts.text: The first scleractinian (stony) corals appeared in the late Anisian.
Scleractinians are the basis of all Mesozoic and modern reefs.
They diversified rapidly during the Carnian pluvial episode, linked to symbiotic dinoflagellates (zooxanthellae) settling in their tissues.
They did not become the dominant reef builders until the end of the Triassic.
Reefs built by modern-type scleractinian corals first became relatively common in the Carnian.

entries.title: Archosaurs push the mammal relatives aside

facts.text: Archosaurs, at first rarer than therapsids, began displacing them in the mid-Triassic and were the dominant land vertebrates by the Middle Triassic.
From the early Triassic they took most medium to large land carnivore niches; over 35 million years they came to include crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs.
Pseudosuchians were ecologically dominant, from plant-eating aetosaurs to big 'rauisuchian' predators; land faunas were shared with dinosauromorphs.
Large cynodonts such as traversodontids still held some big herbivore and predator niches.

entries.title: Placodonts, nothosaurs and kin crowd Triassic seas

facts.text: Placodonts, thalattosaurs, Tanystropheus and other marine reptiles joined ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians in the Middle Triassic.
Pachypleurosaurs and nothosaurs were common, especially around the Tethys; Atopodentatus is the earliest known plant-eating marine reptile.
Some nothosaurs reached 5–7 m long, and some ichthyopterygians attained very large body masses.
Almost every known clade of Triassic marine reptile has been found in South China.

entries.title: Seas and lakes rebuild complex food webs

facts.text: Complex, diverse ecosystems with specialised animals began to re-form in the Middle Triassic, 4–6 million years after the extinction.
Carbon-isotope swings abruptly stabilised in the middle Triassic, soon followed by the recovery of shelled sea life.
Marine reptiles, ray-finned fishes, ammonoids, bivalves and gastropods all reached higher diversity again; crinoids regained ecological dominance.
By the early Ladinian, Chinese lake coprolites show freshwater food webs with six or more trophic levels; phytoplankton, corals and crustaceans had recovered.
Full recovery took about 30 million years; global marine diversity regained pre-extinction levels only in the Middle Jurassic.

Carbon-isotope swings abruptly calmed, and the recovery of shelled sea life soon followed. Even so, full recovery took about 30 million years. Global marine diversity regained its old level only in the Middle Jurassic.

entries.title: The Tethys pushes west and floods central Europe

Rising seas flooded central Europe as the shallow Muschelkalk Sea, which reached the North Pyrenean Zone.
Rifting that formed the Meliata Ocean basin began in the Anisian.

entries.title: Cimmerian blocks drift north and close the Paleo-Tethys

facts.text: The Cimmerian orogeny began about 240–200 Ma as Cimmerian blocks collided with Kazakhstania and North and South China.
Drifting north, the Cimmerian blocks closed the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them and opened the Neo-Tethys behind.
The Paleo-Tethys, open for about 400 million years, had shrunk to a narrow seaway by the Late Triassic, its closure raising the orogeny.
Its western arm stayed open until about 205 Ma, when Iranian blocks hit Eurasia's Turan platform; the belt ran from Anatolia east to the Indosinian orogen.
The Qiangtang terrane of northern Tibet joined Asia in the Late Triassic.

entries.text: An ocean that had lasted about 400 million years was squeezed shut. A string of continental fragments, the Cimmerian blocks, drifted north, closing the Paleo-Tethys ahead of them and opening the Neo-Tethys behind. By the Late Triassic the old ocean had shrunk to a narrow seaway. Its closure raised the Cimmerian orogeny, which began about 240–200 million years ago as the blocks collided with Kazakhstania and North and South China. The Qiangtang terrane of northern Tibet joined Asia in the Late Triassic. The western arm stayed open until about 205 million years ago, when Iranian blocks hit Eurasia's Turan platform. The finished belt ran from Anatolia east to the Indosinian orogen.

entries.title: A giant delta plain fills the Boreal Ocean

facts.text: A vast river delta plain spread across northern Pangaea's Triassic Boreal Ocean, today's Barents Sea, from 237 to 227 Ma.
Rapid sedimentation after the extinction had built a shallow basin; Induan silts span 1,000 km of the Greater Barents Sea Basin.
Deposition slowed in the Olenekian–Anisian, revived in the Ladinian with deltas advancing over 500 km, and the plain had formed by 237 Ma.

entries.title: Wrangellia floods the land with basalt

facts.text: Wrangellia flood basalts poured onto land over about 5 million years, building a large igneous province now exposed in a 2,500 km belt.
The eruption around 234 Ma caused abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling.
Carbon and osmium isotopes tie it to the Carnian climate upheaval; seawater osmium shifted at the Ladinian–Carnian boundary.
The Wrangellia terrane was later added to western North America.

entries.title: The Carnian rains turn Pangaea's deserts green

facts.text: Around 234–232 Ma, for perhaps 1–2 million years, global climate shifted sharply, with major changes to life on land and in the sea.
Volcanism off North America, the Wrangellia large igneous province, set off abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling.
Pangaea's arid climate turned hotter and more humid; rainfall and runoff surged, turning the dry interior into lush alluvial forests.
Carbonate platforms shrank, and many marine invertebrates, especially ammonoids, bryozoans and crinoids, went extinct.
Early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and possibly mammaliaforms diversified during the event, and coccoliths and dinoflagellates joined the plankton.

entries.text: For perhaps 1–2 million years, it rained on Pangaea as never before. Around 234–232 million years ago, in the Carnian pluvial episode, global climate shifted sharply, changing life on land and in the sea. The trigger was volcanic. Eruptions off North America, the Wrangellia large igneous province, set off abrupt global warming that ended the Ladinian–Carnian cooling. Pangaea's arid climate turned hotter and more humid. Rainfall and runoff surged, and the dry interior became lush forests along rivers. At sea, carbonate platforms, shallow limestone shelves, shrank, and many invertebrates died out, especially ammonoids, bryozoans and crinoids. Yet the same upheaval was a beginning. Early dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and possibly mammaliaforms, mammals and their closest kin, diversified during the event, and coccoliths and dinoflagellates joined the plankton.

entries.title: The first true dinosaurs appear

facts.text: The earliest true dinosaurs likely appeared in the Carnian, around the time of the Carnian pluvial episode, and diversified rapidly.
Brazil's Santa Maria Formation, radiometrically dated to 233.23 Ma, and Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation, 231–230 Ma, hold early dinosaurs such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor.
Nyasasaurus from Tanzania's Manda Formation hints that dinosaurs may date back to the Anisian, about 243 Ma.
They arose from avemetatarsalians, a minor part of Triassic ecosystems, and became dominant only in the Jurassic.
Whether the Carnian pluvial episode drove their rise is doubtful: avemetatarsalian diversity grew faster in the Ladinian and Norian.

entries.title: Ischigualasto's ash and mud bury early dinosaurs

facts.text: In a reactivated half-graben rift basin in northwestern Argentina, rivers from volcanic highlands laid down sandstones, mudstones and ash beds up to about 1 km thick.
Rainfall was strongly seasonal; one study traces a shift from warm, humid conditions to drier ones around 229.5 Ma, with partial recovery by 227.8 Ma.
Dense with fossils, it is a konzentrat-lagerstätte with some of the earliest unambiguous dinosaurs, such as Herrerasaurus and Eoraptor, amid abundant rhynchosaurs and cynodonts.

entries.title: Pterosaurs take to the Triassic skies

facts.text: Pterosaurs evolved about 228 Ma, a little after the first true dinosaurs.
Like dinosaurs, they arose from avemetatarsalians, which were a minor part of Triassic ecosystems.
Feathers may already have been present in the Early Triassic common ancestor of pterosaurs and dinosaurs.
Early long-tailed pterosaurs appeared in the Norian and quickly spread worldwide.
Norian lagoon deposits in northern Italy, such as the Calcare di Zorzino (c. 216.6–212 Ma), preserve pterosaurs and other reptiles.

entries.title: A disputed end-Carnian crisis drowns a delta

facts.text: Several plant-eating archosauromorph groups died out, and big herbivorous therapsids such as kannemeyeriid dicynodonts dwindled across Laurasia.
Repeated floods drowned the vast Triassic Boreal Ocean delta plain, shifting shorelines over 1,000 km and wiping out many of its organisms.
Coastal habitat loss hit semi-aquatic crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals, and a reef crisis struck South China.

entries.title: Plant-eating dinosaurs spread through the Norian

facts.text: Plant-eating sauropodomorphs diversified in the Norian and began to displace large herbivorous therapsids, perhaps coping better with growing aridity.
Plateosaurus, an early sauropodomorph, evolved around 214 Ma in Europe, Greenland and North America.
Most Triassic dinosaurs were small predators; Coelophysis, 1–2 m long, was one of the few common ones.
Crurotarsan archosaurs still filled more ecological niches than dinosaurs.

Even now, crurotarsan archosaurs, the crocodile line, still filled more ecological niches than dinosaurs did.

entries.title: The last rhynchosaurs vanish

facts.text: Hyperodapedontine rhynchosaurs, abundant beaked plant-eaters, died out in the early Norian.
Teyumbaita from Brazil is the only rhynchosaur known with confidence to have survived into the Norian.
Their exact extinction date is uncertain: they lasted at least into the early to middle Norian, though one suggestion places it in an end-Carnian extinction.

entries.title: A mid-Norian die-off strikes the seas

facts.text: A marine extinction in the middle of the Norian struck radiolarians, sponges, conodonts and Triassic ammonoids.

entries.title: Sea level sinks to a Rhaetian low

facts.text: After a Carnian high of up to 50 m above today's, sea level fell from the Norian onward.
It bottomed out about 50 m below present in the mid-Rhaetian, and low levels lasted into the earliest Jurassic.
With no evidence of Triassic ice sheets, glaciation is unlikely to explain these sea-level changes.
At the very end of the Triassic the sea flooded most of central and western Europe, turning it into an archipelago.
A sea-level drop seen in Europe and the Middle East at the extinction now seems regional rather than global.

entries.title: Mammaliaforms, the closest kin of mammals, appear

facts.text: Mammaliaforms, mammals plus their closest extinct kin, arose from advanced probainognathian cynodonts in the Late Triassic; some sources place their origin in the Carnian.
Unambiguous mammaliaforms such as morganucodonts and haramiyids appeared in the Norian across Europe and Greenland, as probainognathians became prominent.
The oldest claimed forms are doubtful: Tikitherium may be a misidentified Cenozoic shrew, and Adelobasileus is no older than 225 Ma.
Early mammaliaforms were small, mostly nocturnal, warm-blooded insectivores in the shadow of dinosaurs; old jaw bones were moving into the middle ear.
Cynodonts were the only therapsids to outlast the Triassic, and mammaliaforms diversified widely in the Jurassic.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on timing: some studies place mammal origins in the Carnian pluvial episode, others in the Norian or at the end of the Triassic.

entries.title: A cooler spell follows the Carnian heat

facts.text: A relatively cool spell, the Early Norian Cool Interval, lasted from about 227 to 217 Ma.
It followed the Mid-Carnian Warm Interval that the Carnian pluvial episode had ushered in.
At the Carnian–Norian boundary, a positive carbon-isotope excursion suggests more organic carbon was being buried.

Early stem teleosts such as Prohalecites lived in the western Tethys; teleosts now make up over 99% of living ray-finned fishes.

entries.title: Warmth returns, and Pangaea turns swampy

facts.text: Warmer conditions, the Mid-Norian Warm Interval, followed from about 217 to 209 Ma.
Around 214 Ma it was briefly interrupted by a cooling possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact.
Around 212 Ma, a peak in orbital eccentricity made much of Pangaea swampy and shrank its arid zones.

entries.title: An asteroid 5 km wide blasts out Manicouagan

facts.text: An asteroid about 5 km wide struck what is now Quebec, excavating a multiple-ring crater about 100 km across, among Earth's largest.
It was the second-largest impact of the Mesozoic, after Chicxulub.
Shocked-quartz ejecta from it is found as far away as England and Japan.
It may have caused a brief cooling, a mid-Norian marine extinction and the Adamanian–Revueltian turnover, but direct evidence is lacking.
Some 13 million years older than the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, it is no longer thought to have caused the end-Triassic extinction.

entries.title: A turnover reshapes Southwest faunas

facts.text: In the American Southwest, several land vertebrates vanished quickly around 215 Ma as others appeared, a turnover in the Chinle Formation.
Trilophosaurus, Desmatosuchus, dicynodonts and many phytosaurs disappeared locally; new aetosaurs and phytosaurs replaced them.
Pollen shifted to dry-adapted plants, suggesting rising aridity; the Manicouagan impact is one proposed cause.

A major Norian rifting episode, about 210 Ma, split Gondwana in two parts.

entries.title: A disputed die-off at the Norian–Rhaetian boundary

entries.title: The Central Atlantic magmatic province erupts

facts.text: As central Pangaea rifted, vast eruptions began: the first CAMP lavas date to 201.566 ± 0.031 Ma, the last to 201.36 ± 0.02 Ma.
CAMP is Earth's largest continental igneous province, about 11 million km² on four continents, with 2–6 million km³ of lava.
Lava came in four main pulses, each lasting no more than about 100 years, spread over some 600,000 years.
It ended the long rifting of the Central Atlantic; large magma bodies had built up about 100,000 years before the eruptions.
It is widely blamed for the Triassic–Jurassic extinction; the link became firmer in 2013.

entries.text: Lava covered about 11 million km² across four continents. As central Pangaea rifted, the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, or CAMP, built Earth's largest continental igneous province, with 2–6 million km³ of lava. The first lavas date to 201.566 ± 0.031 million years ago and the last to 201.36 ± 0.02 million years ago. The eruptions came in four main pulses. Each lasted no more than about 100 years, and together they were spread over some 600,000 years. Large bodies of magma had built up about 100,000 years before the eruptions began. CAMP ended the long rifting of the Central Atlantic. It is widely blamed for the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, a link that became firmer in 2013.

entries.title: Volcanic carbon drives an extreme end-Triassic warming

facts.text: An extreme warming, the End-Triassic Thermal Event, struck at the very end of the Triassic and drove the mass extinction.
Carbon dioxide bubbles in CAMP basalts show the volcanism helped trigger it.
CAMP pulses released carbon over mere centuries, inviting comparison with today's human-caused warming.
Longer-term warming and ocean acidification followed the eruptions, and a thermal spike marks the start of the Jurassic.

entries.title: The end-Triassic extinction hands the land to dinosaurs

facts.text: One of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions ended the Triassic 201.4 million years ago; about 46–72% of marine genera disappeared.
On land most archosaurs except crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs died out, with most therapsids and large amphibians; one estimate puts tetrapod losses at 42%.
Ammonites were nearly wiped out, conodonts vanished and reefs collapsed, completing the oceans' shift to the modern evolutionary fauna.
Floras turned over, with 17–73% of Rhaetian plants lost by various estimates, though some see restructuring rather than a plant mass extinction.
Driven by CAMP volcanism and the warming it caused, it removed the crurotarsans and let dinosaurs dominate the Jurassic.

entries.title: Oceans lose their oxygen and turn acidic

facts.text: Black shales and a sharp negative uranium-isotope shift show marine oxygen fell steeply during the extinction.
Anoxia reached the western and eastern Tethys and Panthalassa, and persisted into the Hettangian as land nutrients fed the seas.
Malformed nannoplankton and a worldwide pause in carbonate deposition point to severe ocean acidification.
Green sulphur bacteria, which photosynthesise with hydrogen sulphide, grew markedly across the boundary.
It is the best-established case of a marine mass extinction caused by acidification, selectively killing organisms with thick aragonite skeletons.

entries.text: Misshapen nannoplankton tell of seas turned corrosive. Black shales and a sharp negative uranium-isotope shift show that ocean oxygen fell steeply during the extinction. Green sulfur bacteria, which photosynthesize with hydrogen sulfide, grew markedly across the boundary. A worldwide pause in carbonate deposition adds to the evidence of severe acidification. This is the best-established case of acidification causing a marine mass extinction, selectively killing organisms with thick skeletons of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.

entries.title: Phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchians die out

facts.text: Phytosaurs and aetosaurs, common in Late Triassic faunas, were completely wiped out by the end-Triassic extinction.
Among pseudosuchians only small crocodylomorphs survived; herbivores like aetosaurs and carnivorous rauisuchids died out.
Timing is hard to pin down: the Rhaetian and Hettangian hold few large land animals, and some groups may have vanished earlier.

entries.title: Modern amphibians branch out: the first frogs and salamanders

facts.text: Lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, began to diversify in the Jurassic, including the first modern frogs and salamanders.
The stem-caecilian Eocaecilia is known from the Early Jurassic of Arizona; stem-frogs and albanerpetontids follow in the Middle Jurassic.
Of the once-diverse temnospondyls, only brachyopoids survived into the Jurassic.

entries.title: Pangaea's great monsoon starts to fail

facts.text: At the start of the Jurassic the Pangean megamonsoon began to fall apart as Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried out.
The monsoon kept weakening through the Jurassic as the continents drifted apart.

entries.title: Plesiosaurs crowd the earliest Jurassic seas

facts.text: A rich radiation of plesiosaurs is known from the Hettangian, implying the group had already diversified in the Late Triassic.
Most plesiosaurs in the Hettangian Blue Lias were short-necked rhomaleosaurids.
Large plesiosaurs joined sharks and other ichthyosaurs as predators of ichthyosaurs.
Plesiosaurs also invaded fresh water; small forms are known from Jurassic China and Australia.
By the Toarcian, about 180 million years ago, longer-necked plesiosaurids reached up to 10 metres.

entries.title: Conifers reclaim the fernlands of Sichuan

facts.text: In China's Sichuan Basin, hot, arid fernlands of the Triassic–Jurassic transition gave way to cheirolepid conifer floras in the Hettangian and Sinemurian.
Ferns and other plants with dissected leaves coped better with the crisis and spread across the boundary into the Jurassic.
The extinct conifer family Cheirolepidiaceae, known by its Classopollis pollen, was abundant through the Jurassic.

entries.title: Seafloor life recovers in fits and starts

facts.text: In Britain, seafloor communities began recovering almost at once after the extinction, despite repeated relapses into anoxia.
Oxygen depletion and nutrient runoff persisted into the Hettangian and may have delayed recovery.
In Argentina's Neuquén Basin, recovery ran from the late early Hettangian to a new balance of diversity by the late Hettangian.
The carbon cycle settled only in the Sinemurian, when brachiopods and dasycladacean algae rediversified.
Tropical reefs, which had collapsed, did not fully recover until much later in the Jurassic.

entries.title: Ammonites rebound from near-extinction

facts.text: Ammonoids, almost wiped out at the end of the Triassic, radiated into many new forms with complex sutures: the ammonites proper.
The orders Psiloceratina, Ammonitina, Lytoceratina, Haploceratina, Perisphinctina and Ancyloceratina all appeared during the Jurassic.
Jurassic ammonite faunas formed about 20 provinces in a northern Pan-Boreal and a southern Pan-Tethyan realm.
Serpenticone ammonites, coiled like snakes, are abundant in Europe's Jurassic rocks.

entries.title: Dinosaurs take over the land

facts.text: With rival reptile groups gone after the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs surged in diversity and abundance in the Early Jurassic.
Land faunas shifted from joint rule by dinosauromorphs and pseudosuchians to dominance by dinosaurs alone.
From the Early Jurassic, dinosaurs and pterosaurs were the commonest land reptiles; lizards and tuatara relatives filled the small-reptile roles.
Dinosaurs had spread to every continent by the Early Jurassic at the latest.
They stayed the dominant land vertebrates through the Jurassic and Cretaceous, until 66 million years ago.

entries.text: When the end-Triassic extinction cleared away their reptile rivals, dinosaurs did not just survive. They surged. In the Early Jurassic they grew rapidly in both diversity and abundance, and land faunas changed hands. Through the Triassic, dinosauromorphs and pseudosuchians, the crocodile line, had shared the land. Now dinosaurs ruled it alone. From the Early Jurassic on, dinosaurs and pterosaurs were the commonest land reptiles, while lizards and tuatara relatives filled the roles of small reptiles. By the Early Jurassic at the latest, dinosaurs had spread to every continent. Their reign was long. They stayed the dominant land vertebrates through the rest of the Jurassic and the whole Cretaceous, until 66 million years ago.

entries.title: Modern sharks and the first rays appear

facts.text: Neoselachians, the group of all living sharks and rays, radiated from the Early Jurassic.
Rays (batomorphs) first appear in the Early Jurassic; the oldest confirmed ray, Antiquaobatis, is from the Pliensbachian of Germany.

By the Late Jurassic they had largely replaced hybodonts, the Triassic's dominant sharks, in the sea.

entries.title: Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates fill the plankton

facts.text: Coccolithophores and dinoflagellates, both first seen in the Triassic, radiated in the Early to Middle Jurassic and became prominent phytoplankton.

The rise of calcareous plankton in the Middle Jurassic altered ocean chemistry; their seafloor deposits buffered against large CO2 emissions.

entries.title: Blue Lias layers keep time with Earth's orbit

facts.text: The Blue Lias, alternating limestone and shale beds, was laid down from the latest Triassic into the early Sinemurian.
Its rhythmic layers record short climate swings driven by orbital (Milankovitch) cycles.
It is rich in fossils; most of its Hettangian plesiosaurs are rhomaleosaurids.

entries.title: The Andes begin to rise

facts.text: The Andean orogeny, still ongoing and responsible for raising the Andes, began in the Early Jurassic, about 200 million years ago.
Subduction-related volcanism along western South America has continued since about 200 million years ago.
Its first phases brought extension, rifting, back-arc basins and the emplacement of large batholiths.
Early subduction built the La Negra volcanic arc in northern Chile.
The Atacama Fault is thought to have formed as the orogeny began.

entries.title: Conodonts vanish after more than 300 million years

facts.text: Conodonts, jawless fish whose tooth-like elements are key index fossils, finally died out at the start of the Jurassic, around 200 million years ago.
They had lasted more than 300 million years, since the Cambrian.
They vanished first in the Tethys and eastern Panthalassa; survivors lasted into the earliest Hettangian of Hungary and central Panthalassa.
By the end of the Triassic only a handful of conodont species remained.
A mid-Norian marine crisis, possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact, may have hastened their decline.

entries.title: The Navajo sand sea buries western North America

facts.text: In the Jurassic the Colorado Plateau grew ever drier until some 388,000 km² of western North America became a vast desert like the Sahara.
The Navajo Sandstone formed in an arid erg on western Pangaea, swept by winter monsoon winds; a 2019 radioisotopic study puts its start around 200–195 Ma.
Its dunes reached 670 m thick at Zion Canyon, where it now forms towering cliffs.

entries.title: Pangaea tears into Laurasia and Gondwana

facts.text: Pangaea, which held all the major landmasses, began to rift apart around 200 million years ago; the breakup ran to about 160 million years ago.
Through the Early Jurassic it split into Laurasia (Eurasia and North America) in the north and Gondwana in the south; it had fully broken up by the Middle Jurassic.
By about 200 Ma the Central Pangean Mountains had worn down to a few uplands; widespread magmatism, including the Karoo and Ferrar provinces, preceded the rupture.
The breakup opened the Tethys between the landmasses and greatly strengthened the water cycle; another source has the Tethys Seaway splitting Pangaea in two only in the Late Jurassic.
North and South America separated in the Late Jurassic; by about 150 Ma their divergence was making oceanic crust off Colombia's Pacific coast.

entries.title: A seaway opens between the Americas

facts.text: The Central American Seaway formed between about 200 and 154 million years ago, during the initial breakup of Pangaea.
North and South America, still joined when the Jurassic began, had rifted apart by the start of the Late Jurassic.
The seaway, also called the Hispanic Corridor, linked the North Atlantic and Tethys with eastern Panthalassa.
Fossil evidence suggests it was already open in the Early Jurassic; it closed only when the Isthmus of Panama formed.

entries.title: Vulcanodon and the first true sauropods

Even earlier, the four-legged Ledumahadi of South Africa reached about 12 tonnes, far above other early sauropodomorphs.
By the end of the Early Jurassic, possibly after a global warming event, sauropods had become the dominant large plant-eaters on land.

entries.title: A long cool spell chills the Early Jurassic

facts.text: The first part of the Jurassic was a cool interval lasting from about 199 to 183 million years ago.
Evidence suggests the late Pliensbachian was an icehouse, perhaps with Northern Hemisphere glaciation early and late in the stage.
Dropstones and glendonites in northeastern Siberia point to cold winters in the Early to Middle Jurassic.
It ended with a 4–8 °C warming spike in the early Toarcian.

entries.title: The Toarcian extinction wipes out most Tethyan corals

facts.text: The Toarcian extinction, about 183 million years ago, struck in two pulses: the Pliensbachian–Toarcian boundary event and the larger anoxic-event pulse.
It was catastrophic for corals: 90.9% of Tethyan coral species and 49% of genera were wiped out.
Ammonoids, already squeezed by the Gibbosus Event a million years earlier, suffered further losses.
On land, seed ferns and spore plants declined, possibly from mercury poisoning.
Megalosaurid dinosaurs diversified later in the Toarcian, perhaps filling niches emptied by the die-off.

entries.title: Karoo-Ferrar lavas flood southern Gondwana

facts.text: The Karoo and Ferrar provinces of southern Africa and Antarctica erupted about 183 million years ago, just before Gondwana's breakup.
With about 2.5 million cubic kilometres of magma, it is one of Earth's most extensive large igneous provinces.
As southern Africa passed over the Bouvet hotspot, basalt flooded the Clarens desert and covered nearly all of southern Africa.

entries.title: Holzmaden's Posidonia Shale preserves skin and blood cells

facts.text: The Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden, Germany, laid down about 183 million years ago during the anoxic event, holds superb complete fish and marine reptile skeletons.
Its stagnant-basin preservation became a benchmark for other fossil sites.
A 182.7-million-year-old ichthyosaur from it still contained collagen and blood cells; a plesiosaur kept traces of skin.

entries.title: Oxygen drains from the Toarcian oceans

facts.text: About 183 million years ago, early in the Toarcian, oxygen vanished from wide areas of the ocean; it is the only oceanic anoxic event documented from the Jurassic.
It was possibly the most extreme case of widespread ocean deoxygenation in the entire Phanerozoic.
Karoo-Ferrar CO2 warmed the climate, acidified the oceans and boosted weathering; the nutrient flood eutrophied the seas and drove anoxia.
The carbon release was large enough to disrupt the otherwise steady 9-million-year carbon cycle of the Jurassic.
Toarcian anoxia laid down organic-rich black shales, including oil shales mined commercially in China.

entries.text: About 183 million years ago, early in the Toarcian, oxygen vanished from wide areas of the ocean. This Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event is the only one documented from the Jurassic. It was possibly the most extreme case of widespread ocean deoxygenation in the whole Phanerozoic. The chain began with volcanoes. Carbon dioxide from the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions warmed the climate, acidified the oceans and sped up weathering on land. The flood of nutrients washed into the sea and eutrophied it, overfeeding plankton until the water lost its oxygen. The carbon release was large enough to disrupt the otherwise steady 9-million-year carbon cycle of the Jurassic. The stagnant seas laid down organic-rich black shales, including oil shales now mined commercially in China.

entries.title: A Toarcian heat spike pushes seas past 30 °C

facts.text: Global temperatures spiked by about 4–8 °C early in the Toarcian; the warm interval lasted until about 174 million years ago.
Sea surface temperatures likely topped 30 °C, and Pangaea's interior probably exceeded 40 °C.
The rapid warming intensified tropical storms worldwide, and a stronger water cycle made lakes expand.
A brief cold snap interrupted the warming just before the anoxic event.
Sea level rose gradually to a peak of about 75 metres above today's during the Toarcian.

entries.title: The Central Atlantic begins to open

facts.text: Rifting between North America and Africa came first, beginning in the Early Jurassic, with rift basins such as the Newark Basin from Mexico to Nova Scotia.
The central Atlantic ocean basin began opening about 180 million years ago as a narrow ocean between the northern and southern parts of Pangaea.
Seafloor spreading between North America and Africa–South America began the breakup of Pangaea.
The North Atlantic stayed narrow through the Jurassic; the South Atlantic did not open until the Cretaceous.
The oldest large-scale ocean crust still surviving, in the northwest Atlantic and west Pacific, is about 180–200 million years old.

entries.title: Gondwana starts to come apart

facts.text: Gondwana started to fragment around 180 million years ago, after the fast emplacement of the Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts.
Madagascar and Antarctica began rifting away from Africa, opening the western Indian Ocean.
The oldest magnetic anomalies show initial break-up in today's southern Weddell Sea about 180 to 160 million years ago.
Rifting at Falkland latitudes began about 190 million years ago, pushing Patagonia westward.
Fragmentation sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely complete by its end.

entries.title: Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs reshuffle their ranks

facts.text: Between the end of the Toarcian and the start of the Bajocian, most ichthyosaur lineages appear to have died out.
Ophthalmosaurids appeared in the early Bajocian and from then on made up almost all ichthyosaurs.
Among plesiosaurs, microcleidids died out and rhomaleosaurids nearly so, while cryptoclidids, the dominant later Jurassic group, appeared in the Bajocian.

facts.text: The earliest members of the genus Ginkgo, with ovule and pollen organs like the living species, appear in the Middle Jurassic of the Northern Hemisphere.
Ginkgoales were among the most important parts of Eurasian Jurassic floras.

entries.title: The first octopuses appear

facts.text: The earliest octopuses appeared in the Middle Jurassic, having split from the vampyromorphs in the Triassic to Early Jurassic.
Molecular evidence suggests the squid and octopus lineage split from the belemnoids in the Permian.
One timeline lists the oldest known octopus fossil at about 296 Ma.

entries.title: The Sundance Sea floods northwestern North America

facts.text: From the Middle Jurassic, the shallow Sundance Sea covered much of northwest North America in five successive marine transgressions.
Dinosaurs left tracks along its shores, as at Red Gulch in Wyoming.
It retreated for the last time late in the Jurassic, buried by Morrison Formation river sediments.
