entries.title: Long-isolated terranes dock with North America

facts.text: The Alexander and Wrangellia terranes, long isolated in Panthalassa, were accreted to western North America in the Middle Jurassic.
The Cache Creek Ocean probably closed at the same time, and the Stikinia terrane was also added during the Jurassic.

entries.title: Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs

facts.text: By the Middle Jurassic, tetanuran theropods had reached every continent and split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs.
Allosauroids were the first giant theropods, over 2 tonnes; Asfaltovenator of South America may be the oldest.
Coelurosaurs first appeared too, including early tyrannosauroids such as Proceratosaurus from the Bathonian of Britain.

entries.title: Seas rise toward a Late Jurassic high

facts.text: Sea level rose steadily from the Aalenian, apart from dips in the Bajocian and near the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary.
It peaked possibly 140 metres above today's at the Kimmeridgian–Tithonian boundary, probably because seafloor spreading sped up.
Sea level had fallen sharply in the Early Jurassic and stayed low through the Middle Jurassic before rising considerably toward the Late Jurassic, deepening seaways between continents.

facts.text: Carnosaurs first appeared in the Middle Jurassic around 174 Ma; their last definite family, the carcharodontosaurids, died out about 90 Ma.

entries.title: Dinosaur tracks and bones on the Isle of Skye

facts.text: Middle Jurassic rocks of Skye's Trotternish peninsula, about 174-166 million years old, preserve dinosaur footprints and bones.
Bones of large theropods, sauropods and thyreophorans have been found there, with footprints of all three at Staffin Bay, Duntulm and Brother's Point.

entries.title: Toarcian warmth gives way to a cool spell

facts.text: After the Toarcian Warm Interval ended around 174 Ma, the Middle Jurassic Cool Interval followed, lasting until about 164 Ma.
The cool interval may have been broken by brief icehouse episodes, including a possible short-lived ice age in the late Bajocian.
Europe turned noticeably more humid at the Aalenian–Bajocian boundary, then drier during the middle Bajocian.
The Callovian–Oxfordian boundary, at the close of the cool interval, saw especially marked global cooling, possibly even an ice age.

entries.title: Salamanders and newts emerge

facts.text: The first salamanders and newts appeared around 170 Ma.
Early crown-group salamanders such as Chunerpeton and Pangerpeton are known from the Middle–Late Jurassic Yanliao Biota of China.
By the end of the Jurassic salamanders had reached North America, as Iridotriton from the Morrison Formation shows.

entries.title: The young Atlantic becomes a seaway

facts.text: As Pangaea broke up between about 170 and 150 Ma, the young Atlantic Ocean began to form a seaway, the 'Atlantic Gateway'.
By the Late Jurassic a still-narrow Atlantic had just separated Europe from North America.
A rift spread from the spreading Central Atlantic along the continental margin of northwestern France toward Aquitaine.
The deep basins that later held the Paratethys formed in the Oxfordian as an extension of the Central Atlantic rift.

entries.title: A weak magnetic field leaves faint seafloor stripes

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field was weak from about 170 to 130 Ma, so the deep seafloor of that age carries faint magnetic anomalies.
These faint stripes, off eastern North America, northwest Africa and in the western Pacific, were once read as a 'Jurassic Quiet Zone' superchron, but rocks on land record reversals.
The oldest seafloor surviving today dates to about 170 Ma.

The oldest seafloor surviving today dates to about 170 million years ago.

entries.title: Iberia slides away from Europe

facts.text: From 170 to 120 Ma Iberia slid more than 200 km sideways past Europe as it rifted away from the Grand Banks.
In the Late Jurassic the Iberian microcontinent broke from the European plate, and the Valais Ocean opened between them.

entries.title: The Obolon' impact strikes Ukraine

facts.text: An impact in what is now Poltava Oblast, Ukraine, left the Obolon' crater, a confirmed buried structure about 20 km across.
One estimate puts its age at 169 ± 7 million years, in the Middle Jurassic.

entries.title: Lizards and snakes enter the fossil record

facts.text: The oldest unambiguous squamate fossils are Bathonian, from the Northern Hemisphere, when many modern groups, snakes included, first appear; a timeline dates the first lizards to about 168 Ma.
Crown squamates probably originated in the Early Jurassic: their last common ancestor is estimated at about 190 Ma, and one timeline puts the first squamates at about 199 Ma.
Squamates, the lizards and snakes, first diversified during the Jurassic and kept diversifying through the Cretaceous.
Snakes probably evolved from burrowing or aquatic lizards; their earliest fossils date to between 167 and 143 Ma.
By the Late Jurassic, early gecko relatives such as Eichstaettisaurus and the oldest accepted anguimorph, Dorsetisaurus, had appeared.

entries.title: Choristoderes, puzzling freshwater reptiles, appear

facts.text: The oldest unequivocal choristodere, the small lizard-like Cteniogenys, comes from Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) rocks in Britain, about 168–166 Ma.
Choristoderes were freshwater aquatic reptiles of uncertain affinity; the order lasted until the Miocene.
Coeruleodraco, from China's Late Jurassic, was a more advanced choristodere but still small and lizard-like.

Coeruleodraco, from China's Late Jurassic, was more advanced but still small and lizard-like. The order lasted until the Miocene.

entries.title: Multituberculates begin a 100-million-year run

facts.text: The earliest known multituberculates, such as Hahnotherium and Kermackodon, come from Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) rocks of England and Russia, about 168–166 Ma.
One of the most successful mammal orders, they survived and dominated for over 100 million years, longer than any other mammaliaform order, until the Oligocene.
In the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous, early multituberculates were abundant and widespread across Laurasia.

entries.title: The mammal family tree forks into modern branches

facts.text: Fossils about 167 Ma old, including Ambondro, Amphilestes, Amphitherium and teeth from Madagascar, show the monotreme and therian lines had split, dating the crown group's appearance.
Other sources put the crown group's origin, from earlier mammaliaforms, in the Early Jurassic, probably late in that epoch.
Mammaliaforms, among the few cynodont lineages to survive the end-Triassic extinction, diversified extensively in the Jurassic; the docodont Castorocauda shows they already had fur.
Jurassic mammals stayed small, mostly under 10 kilograms, but spread widely; about 150 Ma the chipmunk-sized Fruitafossor seems to have dug into social-insect nests, probably termites'.
Cladotherian mammals first appeared around 170 Ma, and in the Late Jurassic dryolestidans were among the most diverse mammal groups in North America and Europe.

conflicts.note: Mammal § Origins, Therapsida (6ba4d9f23189) and Middle Jurassic ('late Early Jurassic', d5760f53fbd0) place the origin in the Early Jurassic

entries.text: Teeth from Madagascar help date the birth of modern mammals. Those fossils, with Ambondro, Amphilestes and Amphitherium, about 167 million years old, show the monotreme and therian lines had already split. That split marks the crown group, the living mammals and their common ancestor. Other sources place its origin earlier, probably late in the Early Jurassic. Mammaliaforms diversified widely in the Jurassic, and the docodont Castorocauda shows they already had fur. Most stayed under 10 kilograms but spread widely. About 150 million years ago, the chipmunk-sized Fruitafossor seems to have dug into social-insect nests, probably termites'. Cladotherians appeared around 170 million years ago, and their dryolestidans became among the most diverse mammals of Late Jurassic North America and Europe.

facts.text: During the Callovian the Turgai Epicontinental Sea formed, a marine barrier between Europe and Asia.

entries.title: Liopleurodon's sea: the Oxford Clay

facts.text: The Oxford Clay, a marine mudstone of Callovian-Oxfordian age, settled over much of southeast England, from Dorset to Yorkshire.
Its sea held plesiosaurs such as Liopleurodon and Cryptoclidus, marine crocodiles, the ichthyosaur Ophthalmosaurus, belemnites and bivalves such as Gryphaea.
Its lower Peterborough Member is a fossil-rich organic mudstone, and at Christian Malford, Wiltshire, it preserves exceptionally detailed coleoid fossils.

entries.title: The Gulf of Mexico opens

facts.text: North America began separating from South America in the Early Jurassic, opening the gulf in a new rift beside what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.
Seafloor spreading in the Gulf of Mexico began about 165 Ma, in the Middle Jurassic.
The Maya Block was carried away from the Laurentian craton as the gulf opened and North America drifted northwest, away from Pangaea.
The Florida Platform, once part of Africa, stayed with North America and gathered carbonate, evaporite and siliciclastic sediments as the gulf opened.
How Middle America's crustal blocks moved after 170 Ma is still not widely agreed upon.

entries.title: Rocky Mountain building begins in western North America

facts.text: Between 165 and 155 Ma an exotic terrane, the Mezcalera promontory, began to be subducted, and Rocky Mountain orogenesis began.
A volcanic flare-up in the Sierra Nevada arc ran from 170 to 150 Ma.
Deformation in the southern Sevier fold-and-thrust belt began around 160 Ma.

entries.title: Layers of ash save China's Yanliao Biota

facts.text: The Yanliao Biota, fossil beds of northeastern China spanning about 165 to 150 Ma, includes the Tiaojishan and Haifanggou formations.
Alternating volcanic tuff and sediment preserved some of the world's best Jurassic fossils: dinosaurs, mammals, salamanders, insects, lizards and plants.
The Daohugou beds formed between 164 and 158 Ma; the Tiaojishan Formation spans from 165 Ma to between 156 and 153 Ma.
The Haifanggou Formation adds fossil arthropods, amphibians, pterosaurs and mammaliaforms.

entries.title: The Kimmeridgian Warm Interval brings heat and rain

facts.text: A warm phase, the Kimmeridgian Warm Interval, followed the Middle Jurassic cool spell and lasted from about 164 to 150 Ma.
Fossil wood suggests it was one of the wettest stretches of the Jurassic.
A widening Central Atlantic and western Indian Ocean supplied new moisture, softening seasonal swings in the Pangaean interior.
Very high carbon dioxide levels in the Late Jurassic drove high temperatures around the globe through the greenhouse effect.
Europe nonetheless grew steadily more arid over the Late Jurassic.

facts.text: Pterodactyloid pterosaurs first appeared around 163 Ma.
Pterosaur diversity peaked in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.

entries.title: Lhasa begins docking with Qiangtang

facts.text: The Lhasa terrane began colliding with the Qiangtang terrane about 163–145 Ma, joining it along the Bangong suture; the collision lasted into the early Late Cretaceous.
Lhasa was one of the terranes, with West Burma, that rifted from northern Gondwana in the Triassic and Jurassic and later collided with Asia.
The sutured Lhasa terrane now forms southern Tibet.

entries.title: The two living turtle lineages part ways

facts.text: The two living turtle groups, Pleurodira and Cryptodira, had diverged by the beginning of the Late Jurassic.
The oldest pleurodires, the Platychelyidae, and the oldest unambiguous cryptodire, Sinaspideretes from China, are Late Jurassic.
The Thalassochelydia, a diverse marine turtle lineage unrelated to modern sea turtles, lived in Late Jurassic Europe and South America.

entries.text: Every living turtle either tucks its neck sideways or pulls it straight back. The Thalassochelydia, a diverse marine turtle lineage unrelated to modern sea turtles, lived in Late Jurassic Europe and South America.

entries.title: Kimmeridge Clay: the mud that became North Sea oil

facts.text: Fossil-rich marine clay holding ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs built up from the Late Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous, from Dorset to Lincolnshire and the North Sea.
Algae and bacteria buried in Jurassic seafloor mud became North Sea oil and gas; the Kimmeridge Clay and its equivalents are the province's major source rock.
Elsewhere, the Jurassic Sargelu and Naokelekan formations source Iraq's oil, and the Middle-Late Jurassic Arabian Intrashelf Basin holds the world's largest oil reserves.

Elsewhere, Jurassic rocks fuel other oil fields: the Sargelu and Naokelekan formations source Iraq's oil, and the Middle–Late Jurassic Arabian Intrashelf Basin holds the world's largest oil reserves.

entries.title: The Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean snaps shut

facts.text: After closing gradually from west to east since the Late Triassic, the ocean shut in a rapid scissor-like collision of Siberia with the North China–Amuria and Erguna blocks.
The closure raised the Verkhoyansk–Kolyma mountain belt of Siberia.
Paleomagnetic data suggest its oceanic crust subducted beneath Mongolia's terranes in the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous.

entries.title: Reefs return, and crabs move in

facts.text: Reefs, which had declined at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, expanded greatly in the Late Jurassic, both sponge reefs and scleractinian coral reefs.
They resembled modern reefs but had more microbial carbonate and hypercalcified sponges, and weaker biological binding.
Crabs, rare until then, became abundant as they moved into reefs, whose crevices sheltered them from predators.

entries.title: Teleost fishes begin their great radiation

facts.text: Teleosts, now over 99% of living ray-finned fish, began a major diversification in the Late Jurassic.
Early members of modern teleost groups such as Elopomorpha and Osteoglossoidei appeared at this time.
The earliest known ellimmichthyiforms, and clupeomorphs as a whole, come from the Late Jurassic of Peru.
The oldest anatomically modern gars also appeared in the Late Jurassic.

entries.title: Tanzania's Tendaguru beds and the towering Giraffatitan

facts.text: The Tendaguru Beds of south-eastern Tanzania, a Lagerstätte known for large dinosaur bonebeds, are the richest Late Jurassic strata in Africa.
Its dinosaurs lived on semi-arid coastal plains in the subtropical south, alternating with shallow seas; the fauna resembles the Morrison Formation's and stayed stable through the Late Jurassic.
Finds include Giraffatitan, the tallest and heaviest dinosaur known from good skeletons, and over a thousand bones of the stegosaur Kentrosaurus.

entries.title: New ocean floor splits East and West Gondwana

facts.text: Around 160 Ma Africa separated from Antarctica; India followed in the Early Cretaceous.
East and West Gondwana parted, with new oceanic crust forming between them about 160–155 Ma.
Narrow ocean basins opened between Eastern Gondwana (Antarctica, Australia, India, Madagascar), Western Gondwana (Africa, Arabia, South America) and Laurasia.
East Antarctica moved south faster than Africa and South America, opening the Weddell, Riiser-Larsen, Mozambique and Somali basins; Weddell Sea spreading began about 147 Ma.
Australia and Antarctica began pulling apart in the Late Jurassic, and magmatism of the Australia–India breakup, 158–136 Ma, built the Wallaby Plateau.

entries.title: The Morrison floodplains teem with giant sauropods

facts.text: The Morrison Formation of western North America, mostly river and floodplain deposits, was laid down between about 156.3 and 146.8 Ma.
It accumulated as the Sundance Sea retreated before highlands rising to the west.
It holds one of the best-known sauropod faunas, 24 recognized species, among them Apatosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Barosaurus, Camarasaurus and Diplodocus.
Predators such as Allosaurus, Ceratosaurus and Torvosaurus left bite marks on bones at the Mygatt-Moore Quarry.
Morrison quarries about 150 Ma old are dense with dinosaurs; at Cleveland-Lloyd, the densest known Jurassic concentration, animals died around a drought-stricken pond.

entries.title: The Nevadan orogeny raises the ancestral Sierra Nevada

facts.text: The Nevadan orogeny built mountains along western North America's margin from about 155 to 145 Ma; mountain building continued in the Cretaceous Sevier and Laramide orogenies.
The first of several massive batholiths were emplaced in the northern Cordillera from the mid-Jurassic, marking the Nevadan orogeny.
It began as an Andean-type magmatic arc while the Farallon plate subducted beneath North America.
Arc magmatism and the accretion of oceanic arcs built the ancestral Sierra Nevada and Klamath Mountains.
Terranes such as the Tuolumne River and Slate Creek were added to the continent, and the Josephine Ophiolite formed about 155–150 Ma.

entries.title: Archaeopteryx and the first birds

facts.text: Archaeopteryx, long considered the earliest bird though the avian–non-avian boundary is unclear, lived around 150 Ma in southern Germany, then a warm tropical archipelago.
Birds evolved from small predatory coelurosaurian theropods of the clade Paraves; the first stem-group birds appeared in the Jurassic, several sources say the Late Jurassic.
The earliest avialans appear in the Middle to Late Jurassic, definitively represented by Archaeopteryx.
Its fossils already carry advanced flight feathers, so feathers must have begun evolving before the Late Jurassic.
With lizards, birds are among the living reptile groups that first appeared in the Jurassic.

entries.text: Its feathers were already built for flight. Archaeopteryx lived around 150 million years ago in southern Germany, then a warm tropical archipelago, and has long been considered the earliest bird. The line between birds and other dinosaurs is blurry, though, and drawing it is not simple. Birds evolved from small predatory coelurosaurian theropods of the clade Paraves. The first stem-group birds appeared in the Jurassic, several sources say the Late Jurassic. The earliest avialans, the bird branch, appear in the Middle to Late Jurassic, and Archaeopteryx represents them definitively. Its fossils carry advanced flight feathers, so feathers must have begun evolving before the Late Jurassic. Birds share a Jurassic debut with lizards, both among the living reptile groups that first appeared then.

entries.title: Solnhofen's lagoons preserve feathers and jellyfish

facts.text: The Solnhofen limestones of Bavaria, a Tithonian Konservat-Lagerstätte about 149–148 Ma old, preserve fine imprints of soft-bodied animals such as jellyfish.
The area was an archipelago at the edge of the Tethys, with salty lagoons whose oxygen-free bottom waters kept scavengers away.
Animals and plants washed into the lagoons were buried in soft carbonate mud, preserving dragonfly wings and stray feathers.
Over 600 species are known, including 29 kinds of pterosaur and the famous early bird Archaeopteryx.
Nearby sites of the same Solnhofen Archipelago, such as Ettling, preserve fish, horseshoe crabs, beetles, crustaceans and turtles.

entries.title: Tamu Massif, perhaps Earth's largest volcano, erupts

facts.text: Lava erupted at the Pacific-Farallon-Izanagi triple junction in the northwest Pacific, building the Shatsky Rise, Earth's third-largest oceanic plateau.
Its oldest and largest edifice, Tamu Massif, formed in one brief eruptive period of a few million years and then became extinct.
Tamu's basalt dome spans about 450 by 650 km, comparable to New Mexico, with slopes of at most one degree.
It is likely the largest volcano yet found on Earth, though gaps in seismic profiles leave open whether it is one volcano or several.
Its origin is debated: a mantle plume, decompression melting at a mid-ocean ridge, or a recycled mantle slab.

entries.title: Extinction or turnover? The Jurassic draws to a close

facts.text: The end-Jurassic was once counted among eight mass extinctions; it is now seen as a complex turnover, some groups rising and others declining.
The evidence is mainly European, and the turnover was probably driven by sea level, which fell in the late Tithonian and rose again at the boundary.
Reefs declined sharply at the close of the Jurassic, cutting decapod crustacean diversity.
Most life was not strongly affected; several ichthyosaur and pliosaur lineages crossed the boundary.
The boundary, 143.1 ± 0.6 Ma on the ICS chart, is the only period boundary still lacking a GSSP.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on whether the end-Jurassic was a minor mass extinction or a milder, mostly European faunal turnover.

entries.text: The end of the Jurassic was once counted among eight mass extinctions. Now it looks more like a complex turnover, with some groups rising and others declining, and sources disagree on whether it was a minor mass extinction at all. The evidence is mainly European. Most life was not strongly affected, and several ichthyosaur and pliosaur lineages crossed the boundary. The boundary itself, 143.1 ± 0.6 million years ago, is the only period boundary still lacking a GSSP, an agreed reference point in the rocks.

entries.title: Tiny algae build the chalk of Dover's cliffs

facts.text: More chalk formed in the Cretaceous than in any other Phanerozoic period, and the period is named for it.
Chalk is made of coccoliths, the tiny calcite plates of coccolithophore algae that thrived in Cretaceous seas.
Upper Cretaceous chalk forms the white cliffs of Dover and similar cliffs on the Normandy coast of France.
Coccolithophore and other calcareous nannoplankton diversity grew through the Mesozoic, peaking at about 150 species in the Late Cretaceous.

entries.title: Rising seas drown a third of the land

facts.text: Sea level rose in earnest from the early Cretaceous; by the Cenomanian it stood roughly 250 metres above today's.
At the peak of the Cretaceous transgression, one-third of Earth's present land area lay under the sea.
Other estimates put sea level about 300 metres higher than today, in a hot, humid world with no permanent ice.
Many small, fast-recycled ocean plates made ocean basins shallower, pushing sea levels up.
In North America this flooding, the Zuñi sequence, may have been driven by the Mid-Cretaceous Superplume, and receded late in the period.

entries.title: Gondwana shatters into the southern continents

facts.text: Gondwana had started to break up in the Jurassic, but its fragmentation sped up in the Cretaceous and was largely finished by the period's end.
Pangaea completed its breakup into the present continents, though they sat in quite different positions.
South America, Antarctica and Australia rifted away from Africa, while India and Madagascar stayed joined; the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans were born.
Gondwana's continental breakup began near Tasmania.
As Pangaea broke up, dinosaurs became strongly differentiated by landmass by the Early Cretaceous.

entries.text: The breakup began near Tasmania. Gondwana had started to fragment in the Jurassic, but in the Cretaceous the pace quickened, and by the period's end the job was largely done. entries.title: Strange bivalves called rudists build the Tethys reefs

facts.text: Rudists, box-, tube- or ring-shaped bivalves that arose in the Late Jurassic, became major reef builders of the Tethys in the Cretaceous.
Rudist reefs may have driven scleractinian corals out of many tropical shelves, including today's Caribbean and Mediterranean.
They had collapsed by the K–Pg extinction and vanished completely at the close of the Cretaceous.

entries.title: The Cretaceous begins without an agreed starting line

facts.text: The Cretaceous and its first stage, the Berriasian, begin 143.1 million years ago, give or take 600,000 years.
It is the only system boundary still lacking an agreed reference section (GSSP), so its base is formally undefined.
The first appearance of Calpionella alpina, a calpionellid, has been proposed as the marker defining the base of the Cretaceous.
Calpionellids were enigmatic planktonic protists with urn-shaped calcite shells, briefly abundant from the latest Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous.

entries.title: Purbeck's lagoons hold insects, mammals and footprints

facts.text: The Purbeck Group of southern England spans the latest Jurassic and earliest Cretaceous, and holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Cretaceous faunas.
Its beds formed in a semi-arid setting of freshwater lakes, brackish water, tidal flats and lagoons.
It is famous for fossil insects, with hundreds of species, plus reptiles, early mammals from its 'Mammal Bed', and dinosaur footprints.

entries.title: Early birds branch out, and enantiornithines take over

facts.text: Avialan birds diversified into a wide variety of forms; some had short, fused pygostyle tails by the Early Cretaceous.
The enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Cretaceous, until they died out with other dinosaur groups at the end of the Mesozoic.
The Jehol Biota holds a great diversity of birds, including the earliest advanced birds; Las Hoyas in Spain preserves many enantiornithines.
Archaic birds had appeared in the Jurassic; true toothless birds arose from toothed ancestors in the Cretaceous.

facts.text: An asteroid or comet struck central Australia about 142.5 million years ago, very close to the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.
The original crater rim, now eroded away, was about 22 km across; the 5-km ring left today is the eroded central uplift.
Abundant shatter cones are the strongest evidence of its impact origin.

entries.title: Europe pulls away from North America

facts.text: Europe rifted away from North America between 140 and 120 Ma, in a second major phase of North Atlantic breakup.
The opening seaway let cool water flow from the Boreal Ocean into the Tethys.
The Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift began forming about 140 Ma, a first stage of Greenland's separation.
The Bay of Biscay began opening around 126 Ma and was complete by 85 Ma, uplifting the Armorican Massif.
The new ocean did not follow the old Iapetus suture, stranding Laurentian rocks in north-west Europe and Avalonian rocks in Newfoundland.

facts.text: The Southeast African LIP formed 140–95 Ma at the triple junction where Gondwana split into Antarctica, South America and Africa.
The Mozambique Ridge formed 140–122 Ma, peaking about 120 Ma above the Africa–Antarctica spreading zone.
In a later pulse, 100–94 Ma, the Agulhas Plateau formed with the Northeast Georgia Rise and Maud Rise over the Bouvet hotspot.

entries.title: The Eastern Alps begin to stack up

facts.text: The Austroalpine nappes of the Eastern Alps were stacked in the first, Eo-Alpine, mountain-building phase, 140–84 Ma.
Africa began moving towards Europe again, and oceanic crust of the Piemont-Liguria Ocean was subducted beneath the Apulian plate.
The first continental collision, of the Adriatic subplate with Europe, came in the Late Cretaceous; the main Alpine mountain building followed in the Paleocene–Eocene.

facts.text: The Sevier orogeny raised mountains in western North America from 140 to 50 Ma.
It has been tied to North America's collision with a chain of island arcs about 125 Ma; in Utah the Willard thrust sheet moved around 120 Ma.
As its mountains rose in the west, the Western Interior Basin to the east widened.

entries.title: Cold spells bring ice to the Early Cretaceous

facts.text: The cooling of the latest Jurassic continued into the Berriasian, when snowfall was common at high latitudes.
Records suggest glacial periods in the Valanginian, Hauterivian and Aptian, though the Mesozoic was long thought to be ice-free.
Ice-rafted dropstones suggest Northern Hemisphere ice sheets may have reached as far south as Iberia in the Hauterivian and Aptian.
The early Barremian Hauptblatterton Thermal Event marked the final end of the Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval.
Deposits laid down directly by glaciers are known only from the Early Cretaceous of the Eromanga Basin in southern Australia.

facts.text: Titanosaurs, the last great sauropod group, lived from about 136 to 66 Ma and were the dominant herbivores of their time.
An early subadult from Paraíba, Brazil, is about 136 million years old.
They spread almost worldwide; titanosaur fossils are known from every continent, Antarctica included.
On the islands of Cretaceous Europe some, like Magyarosaurus, were likely island dwarfs.

entries.title: Paraná–Etendeka flood basalts pour out as Gondwana splits

facts.text: The Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province spans the Paraná Basin of South America and the split-off Etendeka traps of Namibia and Angola.
Its lavas covered about 1,000,000 km2 after eruption, with an original volume projected at over 2.3 million km3.
The flood basalts were tied to Gondwana's rifting and the opening of the South Atlantic, over the Tristan hotspot.
Its activity caused the middle Valanginian Weissert Thermal Excursion, a warming event.

entries.title: Jehol: volcanic ash buries feathered dinosaurs

facts.text: The Jehol Biota is the ecosystem of north-eastern China between 135 and 121 Ma, preserved in lake beds and volcanic ash of the Yixian and Jiufotang formations.
It holds feathered dinosaurs, including the first known feathered non-avian theropods, many birds, and the largest known Mesozoic mammals.
It also yields the earliest known flowering plants, alongside insects, fish, pterosaurs and amphibians, in huge numbers of individuals.
It has the earliest members of groups that later spread worldwide: neoceratopsians, therizinosaurs, tyrannosaurs and oviraptorids.
Radiometric dating in 2021 placed the Yixian between 125.755 and 124.122 million years ago, a span of about 1.6 million years.

entries.title: The Weissert Event: a sudden heat spike

facts.text: The Weissert Event was a hyperthermal, a rapid global warming in the middle of the otherwise mild Tithonian–early Barremian Cool Interval.
Carbon dioxide from the Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province is the leading suspected trigger, though its drawn-out eruption leads some to doubt it.
Its carbon-isotope excursion began about 134.5 Ma and its plateau lasted to about 132.4 Ma; estimates of its length run from 1.4 to 2.08 million years.
The warming brought oceanic anoxia but, unlike other anoxic events, no widespread black shales; nannoconid plankton bloomed as ocean productivity soared.
Its end brought sharp cooling, about 1–2 °C in southern France and up to 4 °C around the Boreal Ocean, perhaps even a brief ice age.

entries.title: The first flowering plants leave their pollen

facts.text: The earliest widely accepted evidence of flowering plants is single-grooved pollen from the late Valanginian, about 134 Ma, found in Israel and Italy.
Flowering plants appeared in the Early Cretaceous and began to diversify rapidly, a major change of the epoch.
Among the oldest flowering-plant macrofossils are Montsechia from Barremian Spain and Archaefructus (124.6 Ma) from China's Yixian Formation.
Pollen typical of eudicots first appears in the late Barremian, and the earliest monocots are known from the Aptian.
They radiated first in the tropics, then spread toward the poles thanks to the gentle temperature gradient.

entries.title: Australia begins its slow parting from Antarctica

facts.text: Separation between Australia and East Antarctica began about 132 Ma; they had begun rifting by 96 Ma, when seafloor spreading between them followed.
The Australian plate was born as it parted from Antarctica and Zealandia, a split finished in the Cenomanian.
By 96 Ma a shallow seaway had begun forming between them, leaving only a narrow link along the South Tasman Rise and Wilkes Land.
A narrow land connection between South America, Antarctica and Australia persisted until about 50 million years ago.
Full separation came much later; the general consensus places it by 60 million years ago.

entries.title: The South Atlantic begins to open

facts.text: The South Atlantic started to open about 130 Ma, as the Falkland Plateau, broken from southern Africa at 132 Ma, moved west.
South America began drifting west away from Africa, while Laurasia rotated clockwise and moved north.
Paraná–Etendeka magmatism drove further seafloor spreading c. 135–130 Ma, south of the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise.
The split also opened the West and Central African Rift System, including the Benue Trough, which began rifting at the start of the Cretaceous.
By the Aptian–Albian, Africa was cut off from the rest of Gondwana and Laurasia, staying an island continent through most of the Cenozoic.

entries.title: High Arctic magma helps open the Arctic Ocean

facts.text: HALIP magmatism lasted from 130 Ma to about 60 Ma; its first, tholeiitic phase ran to 80 Ma with dikes, sills and basalt flows.

It still covers over 1,000,000 km2, one of Earth's largest magmatic complexes, though much has eroded away.
Crustal stretching began in the Canadian Arctic Rift System 130 Ma, with widespread sills and dikes intruded 129–127 Ma.
The Iceland hotspot may have started as a plume under the Alpha Ridge c. 130–120 Ma.

entries.title: Earliest marsupial and placental relatives appear in China

facts.text: Sinodelphys, from 125-million-year-old shale in Liaoning, China, is the earliest known metatherian, the marsupial line; it had climbing feet.
Eomaia, a eutherian of the same age, shared features with marsupials that the placental line later lost.
Both already had an upright, non-sprawling limb posture.
Other therian mammals are unknown before the Early Cretaceous; the Jurassic Juramaia may itself be Early Cretaceous.
The finds suggest early mammals began to diversify from Asia.

entries.title: Flowers and pollinators remake life on land

facts.text: In the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution, from around 125 to 80 Ma, flowering plants diversified intensely alongside the pollinating insects that coevolved with them.
Animal-pollinated flowers set off a burst of coevolution: beetles were pollinating by the earliest Late Cretaceous, and moths and butterflies have coevolved with them since.
In the mid-Cretaceous, species diversity on land overtook that of the sea, reversing a pattern held for nearly all of Earth's history.
By 110–90 Ma they dominated forest trees and had displaced conifers, cycads and bennettitaleans by the period's end, though full ecological dominance came only in the early Cenozoic.
Their spread may have sped up weathering and nutrient flow into the oceans, a possible driver of the Mesozoic marine revolution.

facts.text: The Early Cretaceous saw seaways expand and sauropods, stegosaurs and other high-browsing groups decline.
The youngest definitive stegosaurs, including Mongolostegus from Mongolia and Yanbeilong from China, date to the Aptian–Albian.
Stegosaurians appear to have died out in the late Early or early Late Cretaceous; reported later finds have mostly proved misidentified.

entries.title: Earth's magnetic field stops flipping for 37 million years

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field kept normal polarity, with no reversals, for about 37 million years, from the Aptian through the Santonian.
On the calibrated time scale the superchron, chron C34n, began at 120.964 Ma and ended at 83.650 Ma.
Reversals had grown steadily rarer in the run-up to it.
It is one of two well-established superchrons, with the Permian Kiaman.
All Ontong Java Plateau lavas are normally magnetized, so presumably erupted after it began.

entries.title: The Selli Event chokes the oceans of oxygen

facts.text: The Selli Event, or OAE1a, was a global oceanic anoxic event at the start of the Aptian.
It was tied to large-igneous-province volcanism and killed marine life through warming, ocean acidification and oxygen loss.
Its carbon-isotope shift began within 22,000–47,000 years; the event lasted about 1.1–1.3 million years, and recovery over a million.
Carbon released by Barents Sea intrusions, perhaps 9,000 Gt, may have triggered it.
With OAE2 it was one of the two Cretaceous anoxic events that most changed ocean chemistry, leaving black shales worldwide.

entries.title: The Kerguelen hotspot piles up a giant plateau

facts.text: The Kerguelen hotspot's output peaked 120–95 Ma, building the Southern and Central Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge.
Kerguelen Plateau and Broken Ridge cover 2,300,000 km2; the province holds about 25 million km3 of lava.
Its earliest products include Australia's Bunbury Basalt (137–130.5 Ma) and India's Rajmahal and Sylhet Traps (118–115 Ma), linked to the eastern Indian Ocean's opening.
Growth of the Southern Kerguelen Plateau 118–119 Ma contributed to oceanic anoxic event 1.
The Kerguelen microcontinent may have carried dense conifer forest in the mid-Cretaceous.

entries.title: The Aptian–Albian Cold Snap chills the planet

facts.text: After the Barremian–Aptian Warm Interval, the Aptian–Albian Cold Snap began about 118 Ma.

Global mean surface temperature fell to about 20.7 °C, and glacial dropstones in western Tethys sediments hint at an ice age.

For plant history it is an important episode, deserving more weight than other minor events.

entries.title: Ontong Java: the greatest eruption in 200 million years

facts.text: The Ontong Java, Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus probably formed as one contiguous large igneous province in the south-west Pacific, by far Earth's largest.
When eruptions ended it covered 1% of Earth's surface with 80 million km3 of basalt, several times the Deccan Traps.
The 'Ontong Java event' was the largest volcanic event of the past 200 million years, erupting up to 22 km3 of magma a year for 3 million years.
The Ontong Java Plateau formed around 116 Ma, with a much smaller event around 90 Ma; renewed rifting about 116 Ma split Manihiki from Hikurangi.
Its eruptions were long thought to coincide with OAE1a, but basalt ages of 117–108 Ma and normal magnetization make that unlikely.

entries.title: Deinonychus: the sickle claw that remade dinosaur science

facts.text: Deinonychus, a dromaeosaurid up to 3.4 m long with a large sickle-shaped claw on each foot, lived in North America about 115–98 million years ago.

Its bird-like forelimbs led Ostrom to revive the idea that birds descend from dinosaurs, which is now almost universally accepted.

entries.title: Borealopelta, an armored dinosaur 'mummy' from Alberta

facts.text: Borealopelta, a 5.5 m nodosaurid ankylosaur, was buried in marine sands and shales of Alberta's Clearwater Formation about 110–112 million years ago.

Pigments suggest a reddish-brown, countershaded body; such camouflage implies even this large armoured animal faced predators.

entries.title: The Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse switches on

facts.text: Temperatures rose sharply after the cold snap ended around 111 Ma, opening the Mid-Cretaceous Hothouse, which lasted until the early Campanian.
A string of Albian hyperthermals followed: Leenhardt (~110 Ma), l'Arboudeyesse, Amadeus (~106 Ma), Event 6 (~102.5 Ma) and Breistroffer (~101 Ma).
Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera show gradual warming from the Albian to peak warmth in the Turonian.
Late Albian tropical seas averaged about 30 °C, while arid belts on land repeatedly pushed north.
In the Cloverly Formation, oxygen isotopes show cool conditions lingering after the cold snap until a late-Albian warming pulse ushered in the hothouse.

entries.title: South America and Africa finally let go

facts.text: Identical dinosaur footprints in Brazil and Cameroon around 120 Ma suggest a land link survived into the early Aptian.
North of the equator rifting began after 120.4 Ma and lasted until c. 100–96 Ma; the Benue Trough rifted c. 118 Ma.
By 110 Ma the Mid-Atlantic Ridge reached the Proto-Caribbean and South Atlantic, separating South America from Africa and completing the Atlantic's length.
Carcharodontosaurids of South America may have been split from African relatives by this breakup.
Around 100 Ma South Atlantic spreading sped up sharply, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge grew from 1,200 to 7,000 km, and Africa began moving north-east.

North of the equator, rifting began after 120.4 million years ago and lasted until about 100–96 million years ago; the Benue Trough rifted about 118 million years ago. By 110 million years ago, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge reached the Proto-Caribbean and South Atlantic, separating South America from Africa and completing the Atlantic's length. The breakup may have split South America's carcharodontosaurids from their African relatives. Around 100 million years ago, South Atlantic spreading sped up sharply. The ridge grew from 1,200 to 7,000 km, and Africa began moving north-east.

entries.title: Argentinosaurus and Patagotitan, the titanosaur giants

facts.text: Argentinosaurus, from Argentina's Huincul Formation, was among the largest land animals ever, about 30–35 m long and 65–80 tonnes.
A 2026 study placed the Huincul Formation in the Albian, about 106 million years ago; earlier work suggested a younger Cenomanian–Turonian age.
Its close relative Patagotitan, from Patagonia's Cerro Barcino Formation, comes from rocks dated to about 101.62 million years ago.
Patagotitan was first billed as the largest land animal, 37 m and 69 tonnes, but later estimates cut it to about 31 m and 50–60 tonnes.
Titanosaurs were the dominant sauropods of the Cretaceous and include some of the largest land animals known.

entries.title: Dinosaurs endure the polar night at Dinosaur Cove

facts.text: Dinosaur Cove's fossil beds, about 106 million years old, formed on a rift-valley floodplain as Australia began to separate from Antarctica, inside the Antarctic Circle.
Its 'polar dinosaurs' include small plant-eaters such as Leaellynasaura and Atlascopcosaurus; one fossil hints at adaptations to low light during the polar winter.
The poles were seasonally cold, but some dinosaurs lived in the polar forests year-round, under a climate much milder than today's.

entries.title: The granite of Half Dome and El Capitan forms

facts.text: As the Farallon Plate subducted beneath North America, rising magma built the plutons of the Sierra Nevada Batholith; most of its granite formed 105–85 million years ago.

Uplift and erosion later exposed the batholith as the granite peaks of the High Sierra, including Mount Whitney, Half Dome and El Capitan.

entries.title: Shell-crushers perfect the Mesozoic marine revolution

facts.text: Shell-crushing predation, the driver of the Mesozoic marine revolution, was perfected by marine reptiles and other predators in the Late Cretaceous.
Sea urchins radiated into predatory niches and are thought to have perfected coral grazing.
Faster weathering and nutrient flow from the angiosperm boom may have helped drive it.

entries.text: In Late Cretaceous seas, a shell was no longer a safe place to hide. entries.title: The Mississippi embayment, cradle of a great delta

facts.text: The Mississippi River Delta traces back about 100 Ma, when the Mississippi embayment formed in the Late Cretaceous.

entries.text: The Mississippi River Delta has a surprisingly deep history. It traces back about 100 million years, to the Late Cretaceous, when a broad low trough called the Mississippi embayment formed. That embayment, an arm of lowland open to the sea, gave the future river a path to the Gulf. Everything the delta became later was built on this ancient foundation.

entries.title: Modern birds take flight in the Cretaceous

facts.text: Modern birds probably arose around the Early–Late Cretaceous boundary, about 100 Ma, and diversified dramatically around the K–Pg extinction.
Most studies put their last common ancestor in the Cretaceous, from Early to latest; a 2015 study placed it at about 95 Ma and the fowl–Neoaves split at 85 Ma.
About 100 Ma the ancestors of all modern birds evolved a more open pelvis for larger eggs; around 95 Ma birds gained a better sense of smell.
A 2024 genomic study put the fowl–Neoaves split near 100.5 Ma, the palaeognath–neognath split around 130 Ma, and later bird orders in step with flowering plants.
Waterfowl (Anseriformes) and shorebirds (Charadriiformes) are the only modern bird orders with an established Late Cretaceous fossil record.

entries.text: Every duck, sparrow and ostrich alive today descends from birds that shared the world with dinosaurs. Modern birds, the Neornithes, probably arose around the boundary between the Early and Late Cretaceous, about 100 million years ago. Around then, their ancestors evolved a more open pelvis for laying larger eggs, and by about 95 million years ago they had a sharper sense of smell. A 2015 study placed their last common ancestor near 95 million years ago and the fowl–Neoaves split at 85. A 2024 genomic study pushed that split back to about 100.5 million years ago. The dating is contested, though: molecular clocks favor a Cretaceous radiation, while fossils point to a Paleogene one, a dispute called 'rocks versus clocks'. Only waterfowl and shorebirds have an established Late Cretaceous fossil record. The birds diversified dramatically around the K–Pg extinction.

entries.title: Zealandia tears away from West Antarctica

facts.text: A dramatic shift from arc to rift magmatism around 100 Ma began separating Zealandia from West Antarctica, a split completed about 84 Ma.
Zealandia includes New Zealand, the Campbell Plateau, Chatham Rise, Lord Howe Rise, Norfolk Ridge and New Caledonia.
The Hikurangi Plateau first subducted beneath New Zealand around 100 Ma, during its collision with Gondwana.
The West Antarctic Rift System began stretching in the Late Cretaceous, before Zealandia's Campbell Plateau broke away from Antarctica.

entries.title: The Western Interior Seaway cuts North America in two

facts.text: For 34 million years, from about 100 Ma to 66 Ma, the Western Interior Seaway joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean.
It began as an Arctic arm pushing south, the Mowry Sea, which later merged with a southern embayment to complete the seaway.
The seaway split North America into western and eastern landmasses, isolating their plants and animals.
Its bottom waters went through repeated anoxic spells, leaving organic-rich shales that are now a major oil source.
It narrowed late in the Cretaceous into an inland arm of the Gulf of Mexico and vanished in the early Cenozoic.

entries.title: The long-necked giants vanish from North America

facts.text: Sauropods vanish from western North America around 98 Ma, in the Cenomanian, starting a gap through most of the Late Cretaceous called the 'sauropod hiatus'.
Proposed causes: competition with ornithischians, habitat lost to the Western Interior Seaway, or sampling bias, though even revised dates leave a mid-Cenomanian to mid-Campanian gap.
It ended shortly before the Cretaceous closed, when Alamosaurus, probably a South American immigrant, arrived; in Europe, trackways and a tooth suggest sauropods persisted throughout.

entries.title: A shallow sea splits Africa in half

facts.text: Around 95–90 Ma a seaway linking the Mediterranean and the proto-Atlantic partly flooded the Tuareg Shield; a Cenomanian–Turonian transgression drowned the Kem Kem ecosystem.
Bivalves show a shallow sea split Africa in half in the Coniacian and Santonian, linking the Tethys to the South Atlantic.
The Benue Trough probably formed the main link to the Gulf of Guinea, via the Chad and Iullemmeden basins, where marine Late Cretaceous sediments lie.

entries.title: The Caribbean large igneous province floods the sea floor

facts.text: By 135–130 Ma Farallon plate subduction had begun along the proto-Caribbean; the Galápagos hotspot started building the province in the eastern Pacific about 95–90 Ma.
Argon–argon dating puts the main magmatism at 95–83 Ma and a second pulse at 81–69 Ma; a plume arriving about 86 Ma spread volcanism into north-west South America.
Volcanism spanned 139–69 Ma, mostly 95–88 Ma, building several oceanic plateaus and hotspot tracks in phases at 124–112, 94–83 (main) and 80–72 Ma.
It holds roughly 4.4 million cubic kilometres of volcanic rock, the Caribbean–Colombian oceanic plateau, whose crust now makes up most of the Caribbean plate.
Its main phase coincides with the Cenomanian–Turonian oceanic anoxic event, suggesting a causal link.

entries.title: The Cenomanian–Turonian extinction

facts.text: Recent work confirms real extinctions of vertebrates, invertebrates and microbes at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition, not just a preservation artifact.
Planktic foraminifera died out in five phases, and trace-fossil diversity plummeted as the event began.
It is one of the lesser extinctions linked to oceanic anoxia, mostly striking marine life.
Warming from the High Arctic and other large igneous provinces is thought to have driven it.

entries.text: For years some researchers wondered whether this extinction was real or just a trick of poor preservation. Recent work settles it: vertebrates, invertebrates and microbes truly died out at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition, about 93.9 million years ago. Planktic foraminifera, tiny shelled drifters of the open sea, vanished in five phases. The variety of burrows and tracks plummeted as the event began. It was one of the lesser extinctions tied to oceanic anoxia, when seawater runs out of oxygen, and it mostly struck marine life. Warming from the High Arctic and other large igneous provinces is thought to have driven it.

entries.title: OAE2: the last time the whole ocean suffocated

facts.text: OAE2 is considered the most recent truly global oceanic anoxic event.
Sulfidic, oxygen-free water spread into the sunlit surface ocean, and black shale such as the Livello Bonarelli at Gubbio was laid down.
Osmium isotopes and trace metals point to submarine volcanism from large igneous provinces as a likely trigger.
It left a positive carbon isotope excursion, one of the main carbon isotope events of the Mesozoic.
The interval had the highest carbon dioxide levels of the Cretaceous and was one of the Phanerozoic's hottest.

entries.text: About 93.9 million years ago, the world's oceans began to choke. The Cenomanian–Turonian oceanic anoxic event, OAE2, is considered the most recent truly global oceanic anoxic event. Sulfidic, oxygen-free water rose into the sunlit surface ocean. On the seafloor, black shale piled up, including the Livello Bonarelli at Gubbio in Italy. Osmium isotopes and trace metals point to undersea volcanism from large igneous provinces as a likely trigger. The event left a positive carbon isotope excursion, a shift in the ratio of carbon types that ranks among the Mesozoic's main carbon events. The interval had the highest carbon dioxide levels of the Cretaceous and was one of the hottest times of the Phanerozoic.

entries.title: The Cretaceous Thermal Maximum: a hothouse planet

facts.text: Warming began at the Cenomanian–Turonian transition and peaked about 90 million years ago, one of the Phanerozoic's hottest intervals.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose above 1,000 ppm, against a pre-industrial 280 ppm, with sea level at a highstand.
Tropical seas reached at least 30 °C, perhaps 33–42 °C, and the equator-to-pole temperature gradient was unusually gentle.
Crocodile-like champsosaurs lived in the Canadian Arctic, where mean annual temperatures exceeded 14 °C.
Warmth lasted to the Turonian–Coniacian boundary, broken by brief cool spells; claimed Turonian Antarctic ice is disputed.

entries.title: Ichthyosaurs, the fish-lizards, die out

facts.text: Ichthyosaurs, present since about 250 Ma, were more diverse in the Cretaceous than once thought, perhaps radiating as continental breakup lengthened the coastlines.
A first extinction pulse at the start of the Cenomanian wiped out two of their three remaining feeding guilds, leaving only unspecialised apex predators.
After the Cenomanian–Turonian anoxic event only Platypterygius hercynicus survived, and it disappeared about 93 million years ago.
Their extinction was a pair of abrupt events, not a long decline, probably tied to the environmental upheaval and climate change of the Cenomanian and Turonian.
Pliosaurs are also reported to have vanished in that anoxic event, and mosasaurs took over the ichthyosaurs' role as rulers of the oceans.

entries.title: The Andes switch from stretching to squeezing

facts.text: Around 90 Ma the Andean orogeny changed character: faster ocean spreading and stronger subduction turned western South America from extension to compression.
Subducting ocean lithosphere switched from south-east to north-east motion at about the same time.
Back-arc basins in central Chile and Mendoza were inverted, and uplift turned western Peru's marine basins continental, with erosion from the Late Cretaceous onward.

entries.text: Around 90 million years ago, western South America stopped pulling apart and began to be crushed. Faster ocean spreading and stronger subduction turned the margin from extension to compression, and the Andean orogeny changed character. At about the same time, the sinking ocean floor switched from south-east to north-east motion. Back-arc basins in central Chile and Mendoza were squeezed and inverted. Uplift turned western Peru's marine basins into dry land, and erosion took hold from the Late Cretaceous onward.

entries.title: The Niobrara Chalk and its flying reptiles

facts.text: The Niobrara Chalk built up 87–82 million years ago from the coccoliths of microorganisms in the Western Interior Seaway; it underlies much of the Great Plains.
Its Smoky Hill Chalk is famous for rich marine fossils, including plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, pterosaurs and primitive aquatic birds.
Pteranodon, a pterosaur with wingspans over 6 m, occurs in most of its layers; about 1,200 Pteranodon specimens are known.

entries.title: Maiasaura, the good mother lizard

facts.text: Maiasaura, a duck-billed dinosaur, lived in what is now Montana and Alberta about 86.3 to 70.6 million years ago.
It raised its young in colonies of closely packed earthen nests, about 7 m apart, each holding 30 to 40 eggs.
Hatchlings with weak legs and worn teeth show adults brought food to the nest, the first evidence of parental care in dinosaurs.

entries.text: The first proof that dinosaurs cared for their young came from a nesting ground in Montana. It nested in colonies of closely packed earthen mounds, about 7 m apart, each holding 30 to 40 eggs. Hatchlings had weak legs but worn teeth. They could not have walked off to feed, so adults must have brought food to the nest.

entries.title: The long Late Cretaceous cooling begins

facts.text: From the Santonian, near the end of the mid-Cretaceous hothouse, global climate began to cool, a trend continuing through the Campanian.
Oxygen isotopes in foraminifera show peak warmth in the Turonian, followed by gradual surface cooling to the end of the Maastrichtian.
Tropical sea surfaces cooled from about 35 °C in the early Campanian to about 28 °C in the Maastrichtian; turtles declined during a Campanian cooling event.
The Late Cretaceous stayed warmer than today, but its cooling trend, including a Campanian–Maastrichtian cool, dry phase, continued into the Cenozoic.
Whether continental ice sheets existed is unclear, given conflicting ocean-temperature estimates.

entries.title: Zealandia drifts off and the Tasman Sea opens

facts.text: The continent of Zealandia, stretching from New Caledonia to New Zealand's subantarctic islands, separated from Australia about 85 million years ago.
About 83 million years ago a rift entering eastern Tasmania split the Lord Howe Rise from the South Tasman Rise.
The Lord Howe Rise, a 3,000 km continental ribbon, drifted off as rifting opened the Tasman Sea and new crust formed in the deep Tasman Basin.

entries.title: The magnetic field's long calm ends

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field ended the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (C34n), a 37-million-year stretch with no polarity reversals.
Calibrated ages place the superchron from 120.964 Ma to the start of chron C33r at 83.650 Ma.
Since the superchron, the frequency of reversals has generally increased slowly.

entries.text: For 37 million years, Earth's compass never flipped. That long stretch without polarity reversals is called the Cretaceous Normal Superchron, or C34n. A polarity reversal is the moment when magnetic north and south swap places. Calibrated ages place the superchron from 120.964 million years ago to the start of chron C33r at 83.650 million years ago. When it ended, the field began reversing again. Since then, reversals have generally become slowly more frequent.

entries.title: India breaks free and races north

facts.text: India rifted from Madagascar about 83 Ma and drifted rapidly north toward Eurasia, reaching about 18 cm per year in the Paleocene.
The Indian plate's very rapid northward drift, covering about 6,000 km, began around 84 million years ago.
By about 83.5 million years ago seafloor was spreading between India and Antarctica, asymmetrically near the Kerguelen Plateau.
Late Cretaceous flood basalts up to 200 m thick spread over Madagascar.

entries.title: The Maastrichtian chill

facts.text: About 70.5 million years ago surface and bottom waters cooled sharply, and marine species richness rose by 43%.
Cooling peaked about 67.5 million years ago, with surface waters at 13 °C, as richness and productivity began to fall.
The Western Interior Seaway was coldest in the early Maastrichtian, about 16 °C, warming to about 22 °C later.
Carbon was increasingly stored in the deep sea from the mid-Maastrichtian, possibly through cooling and stronger deep circulation.
Ice sheets and sea ice appear to have briefly returned to Antarctica near the very end of the Maastrichtian.

entries.title: The Deccan Traps flood India with lava

facts.text: The Deccan Traps began erupting in western India 66.25 million years ago, fed largely by the Réunion hotspot; the bulk erupted 66–65 million years ago.
Eruptions came in three phases, two before the K–Pg boundary and one after, leaving about 1.5 million cubic kilometres of lava.
They warmed climate about 3 °C over the last 100,000 years of the Cretaceous, with a brief 5 °C cold snap 30,000 years before the boundary.
Plant fossils record a 250 ppm rise in carbon dioxide across the boundary, likely from Deccan activity.
Once proposed as a major extinction cause, they are now generally held to have played a minor role at most.

entries.title: The Chicxulub asteroid strikes

facts.text: An asteroid about 10 km wide struck just off the Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across.
Its date matches the K–Pg boundary; 2013 argon dating gave 66.043 ± 0.043 Ma, and impact glass matches boundary ash.
It spread an iridium-rich clay with shocked quartz and tektite glass worldwide, and megatsunamis swept the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean.
A lingering impact winter halted photosynthesis, and the oceans rapidly acidified.
It is widely accepted as the primary cause of the K–Pg extinction, the only mass extinction definitively tied to an impact.

entries.text: In a single moment, a rock about 10 km wide ended the age of dinosaurs. The asteroid struck just off the Yucatán Peninsula and left the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across. Megatsunamis swept the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean. Debris fell across the whole planet as a clay rich in iridium, a metal rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The clay also holds shocked quartz, grains crushed by enormous pressure, and tektites, droplets of melted glass. Then came an impact winter. Dust and soot lingered, sunlight faded, photosynthesis halted, and the oceans rapidly acidified. Argon dating in 2013 gave an age of 66.043 ± 0.043 million years, matching the K–Pg boundary, and impact glass matches the boundary ash. Chicxulub is widely accepted as the primary cause of {{ref:cret-148}}. It is the only mass extinction definitively tied to an impact.

entries.title: The Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction

facts.text: About 76% of species and 47% of genera vanished, including all non-avian dinosaurs, in the fifth and latest great mass extinction.
On land every animal over 25 kg died, along with all pterosaurs and many mammals, birds, lizards, insects and plants.
At sea it killed plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites and rudists, over 90% of coccolithophore species and about 60% of reef-coral genera.
It was rapid, perhaps under 10,000 years, and ocean productivity and circulation collapsed for at least tens of thousands of years.
All major mammal lineages and most turtles survived; mammals then expanded into the large-animal niches dinosaurs left.

entries.text: About three-quarters of all species on Earth disappeared in what may have been a geological instant. The K–Pg extinction wiped out about 76% of species and 47% of genera, including all non-avian dinosaurs. It was the fifth and latest of the great mass extinctions. On land, every animal heavier than 25 kg died, along with all pterosaurs and many mammals, birds, lizards, insects and plants. At sea it killed plesiosaurs, mosasaurs, ammonites and rudist clams. Over 90% of coccolithophore species, the chalk-making plankton, vanished, and about 60% of reef-coral genera. The killing was fast, perhaps under 10,000 years. Ocean productivity and circulation then collapsed for at least tens of thousands of years. Yet some survived. All major mammal lineages and most turtles came through. Mammals then spread into the large-animal niches that the dinosaurs left empty, a story picked up in {{ref:pale-007}}.

entries.title: The last ammonites

facts.text: Ammonoids, present since about 410 million years ago, vanished during or soon after the K–Pg extinction.
Their planktonic eggs and larvae were devastated; of all cephalopods, only nautiloids and coleoids survived.
A few ammonite genera, such as Baculites and Hoploscaphites, may have lingered briefly into the earliest Danian.

entries.title: The last belemnites

facts.text: Belemnites, already declining and confined to a few high-latitude regions, died out in the K–Pg extinction.
As with ammonites, their embryos probably could not survive ocean acidification; sea butterflies replaced their larvae in the food chain.

Sea butterflies, small swimming snails, took the place of their larvae in the food chain.

entries.title: The last pterosaurs

facts.text: Azhdarchid and nyctosaurid pterosaurs were present in the Maastrichtian and likely died out at the K–Pg boundary.
All pterosaurs perished in the K–Pg extinction.

entries.text: The first vertebrates to fly under their own power did not survive the asteroid. The skies passed entirely to the birds.

entries.title: A New Jersey bone bed from the day of disaster

facts.text: A bone bed in New Jersey's Hornerstown Formation, the Main Fossiliferous Layer, is one of the few sites recording mass death at the K–Pg boundary.
Iridium and shocked quartz in the layer suggest it formed from ecosystem collapse during the extinction.
The 66-million-year-old layer is rich in marine life from the shallow sea that covered southern New Jersey.

Iridium and shocked quartz in the layer suggest it formed as ecosystems collapsed during the extinction.

entries.title: The end of the non-avian dinosaurs

facts.text: Scientists agree that all non-avian dinosaurs, then an estimated 628 to 1,078 species, died out at the K–Pg boundary.
Found in Maastrichtian rocks on every continent, they are absent from Cenozoic rocks everywhere; birds are the only surviving dinosaur lineage.
Their large size, few small species and no known ability to burrow, swim or dive may have left them exposed.
Whether they were already declining is uncertain; 2025 dates on New Mexico beds show diverse faunas into the latest Maastrichtian.
Titanosaurs, the last long-necked sauropods, were still thriving when the extinction struck.

entries.title: Shiva, a disputed second crater

facts.text: The potential Shiva crater, 450–600 km across, would far exceed Chicxulub and has been dated to about 66 million years ago.
Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues proposed it formed at the K–Pg boundary and helped cause the extinction.

At 450–600 km across, it would far exceed Chicxulub, and it has been dated to about 66 million years ago. But Shiva is only a proposed impact structure, and it has not been confirmed.

entries.title: Rudist reefs and giant inoceramids vanish

facts.text: Reef-building rudist clams and giant inoceramid bivalves died out at the K–Pg boundary; most inoceramids had been declining well before.
Rudists were once thought to have died out half a million years early, but apparently fell to the K–Pg event itself.
Inoceramids, a bivalve family known from the Permian to the latest Cretaceous, included giants: Inoceramus shells exceeded 1 m, and one Greenland specimen reached 1.87 m.

entries.text: Some Cretaceous reefs were built not by corals but by clams. These reef-building rudists died out at the K–Pg boundary, along with the giant inoceramid bivalves. Most inoceramids, though, had been declining long before the end.

entries.title: Tanis, a snapshot of the impact's first hour

facts.text: At Tanis, North Dakota, seismic waves from the impact 3,000 km away raised 10–100 m seiche waves in the Western Interior Seaway within minutes.
The waves flung marine, freshwater and land animals and plants inland while microtektites from Yucatán rained down.
Its fossil fish suggest the impact struck in Northern Hemisphere spring.

entries.text: Within minutes of the impact, 3,000 km away, the ground in North Dakota began to shake. At Tanis, seismic waves raised seiche waves, sloshing surges in an enclosed sea, 10–100 m high in {{ref:cret-089}}. The waves flung marine, freshwater and land animals and plants inland. At the same time, microtektites, tiny glass beads blasted from Yucatán, rained down from the sky. Fossil fish from the site even suggest the impact struck in the Northern Hemisphere spring.

entries.title: Mammals inherit the Earth

facts.text: With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, mammals rapidly increased in size and diversity and filled the emptied niches.
The K–Pg extinction had wiped out every land animal heavier than about 25 kg, leaving many niches open at the start of the Paleocene.
Many crown placental groups arose, including the earliest afrotherians, xenarthrans, rodents, carnivorans and the primate forerunners called plesiadapiforms.
Most Paleocene mammals stayed small, under about 20 kg, until near the end of the epoch.
Mammals have been the dominant land animals ever since, a shift that eventually set the stage for humans.

image.caption: Momotarou2012, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

entries.text: When the dust settled after the asteroid, the world was suddenly empty of big animals. The K–Pg extinction had killed every land animal heavier than about 25 kg, leaving many niches open at the start of the Paleocene. Mammals moved in. With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, they rapidly increased in size and diversity and filled the vacant roles. Many crown placental groups arose, the branches that lead to living mammals. They included the earliest afrotherians, the African group that now includes elephants, and xenarthrans, the line of sloths and armadillos. Rodents and carnivorans appeared, along with plesiadapiforms, the forerunners of primates. Growth in size took time, though. Most Paleocene mammals stayed small, under about 20 kg, until near the end of the epoch. Still, the shift was permanent. Mammals have been the dominant land animals ever since, and that dominance eventually led to humans.

entries.title: Modern birds explode into new forms

facts.text: Four bird lineages survived the K–Pg extinction: the ostrich group, waterfowl, ground fowl and Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds.
Surviving modern birds diversified rapidly at the start of the Paleogene, filling niches left by extinct Mesozoic bird groups.
It was one of the fastest diversifications of any group; modern bird groups had likely split within about four million years.
Nearly all modern bird lineages except fowl and palaeognaths trace their origins to the Paleocene, according to DNA studies.
Paleocene bird fossils are scarce and mostly waterbirds; the earliest known tree-dwelling crown bird, the mousebird Tsidiiyazhi, dates to about 62 Ma.

entries.title: Nadir, a second impact off West Africa

facts.text: An asteroid at least 400 m wide struck the seafloor on the Guinea Plateau, off Guinea-Bissau, leaving a crater about 9.2 km across.
It formed at or near the K–Pg boundary, around the same time as Chicxulub; the age is uncertain by about a million years.
The impact would have raised tsunami waves up to 1 km high and released greenhouse gases from buried black shales.

entries.title: Pantodonts, the first big plant-eating mammals

facts.text: Pantodonts, herbivorous mammals, were among the first large mammals to evolve after the end of the Cretaceous.
The earliest pantodonts, such as dog-sized Bemalambda, appear in the early Paleocene Shanghuan Formation of China.
In North America they appear in the middle Paleocene and grew larger through the epoch; Barylambda was the largest Paleocene form.

entries.text: The first mammals to grow large after the extinction were plant-eaters called pantodonts. Barylambda was the largest Paleocene form, a sign of how quickly mammals were filling the spaces dinosaurs had left.

entries.title: Corral Bluffs, a window on the recovery

facts.text: Colorado's Denver Formation holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Paleocene mammal faunas, recording mammal diversification right after the K–Pg extinction.
Its rocks span the latest Cretaceous to the early Paleocene, before, during and after the boundary event.
Its Danian Corral Bluffs locality yields new species such as the alligator relative Mandrasuchus.

entries.title: The oldest undisputed placental mammals

facts.text: The oldest undisputed placental mammal fossils come from the early Paleocene, just after the non-avian dinosaurs died out.
The earliest known placental and marsupial mammals are recorded from the Paleocene, though most Paleocene mammals have uncertain relationships.
The first Paleocene land mammal age (Puercan) brought taeniodonts, early hoofed 'condylarths' and possible primate relatives such as Purgatorius.
Placentals, marsupials and monotremes all originated in the Cretaceous, before their fossils become common.

entries.title: Multituberculates peak, then fade

facts.text: Multituberculates, rodent-like mammals that were the most successful Mesozoic mammals, reached their peak diversity in the early Paleocene.
European and North American forms bounced back quickly after the K–Pg event, but Asian forms were devastated.
They declined from the middle Paleocene, probably outcompeted by placental mammals such as rodents and ungulates.

entries.title: The Alpine collision begins

facts.text: By the Paleocene the Piemont-Liguria Ocean had fully subducted under the Apulian plate, and Apulia began colliding with Europe.
This collision would go on to raise the Alps and the Apennines.
The Briançonnais microcontinent then arrived at the subduction zone.
Africa, Arabia and India had long been converging on Eurasia, but the major phases of Alpine mountain building began in the Paleocene to Eocene.
Alpine stresses uplifted the Sudetes and may have faulted rocks as far away as Öland in Sweden.

Powder River Basin coal began forming about 60 Ma as the land rose out of a shallow sea.
In Wyoming, thick coal beds built up as eroding highlands buried plant matter.

entries.title: The Laramide uplift keeps raising the Rockies

facts.text: The Laramide orogeny, which began in the Late Cretaceous, kept raising the Rocky Mountains through the Paleocene.
It deformed the crust deeply, from Canada to northern Mexico, in pulses separated by quiet phases.
The Denver Basin deepened between 66 and 45 million years ago as the uplift built the Colorado Rockies.
Together with the collapse of the continental borderland, it reversed the course of the California River.
By one account it ended at the end of the Paleocene; other sources place its end between 55 and 35 million years ago and call the timing disputed.

entries.title: Boltysh, an aftershock from space

facts.text: An impact in what is now Ukraine left the Boltysh crater, 24 km across.
Argon–argon dating in 2021 places it in the Danian, about 650,000 years after the Chicxulub impact.
That study suggested the impact may have disrupted recovery from the K–Pg extinction and could explain a fern spike.

entries.title: Dan-C2, the first hyperthermal

facts.text: Early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon, especially in the deep sea.

entries.title: The Latest Danian Event

Egypt's Qreiya 3 site, laid down in oxygen-poor seas after the event, holds over 500 articulated fish fossils.

entries.title: The Labrador Sea opens and Greenland breaks free

facts.text: Seafloor spreading pushed north from the Central Atlantic between North America and Greenland, opening the Labrador Sea around 62 Ma and Baffin Bay around 57 Ma.
The opening split the North Atlantic Craton, a block of ancient crust shared by Labrador and Greenland.
Spreading reached the northern Labrador Sea as Greenland slid past Ellesmere Island.
By 56 Ma Greenland had become a separate plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift.
By the early Eocene, about 54 Ma, spreading had moved into the northeast Atlantic between Greenland and Eurasia.

entries.title: The North Atlantic Igneous Province erupts

facts.text: A mantle plume, ancestor of today's Iceland hotspot, rose beneath Greenland around 65 Ma.
Its most active magmatism ran from about 60.5 to 54.5 Ma, in a pre-break-up phase (62–58 Ma) and a break-up phase (56–54 Ma).
It was the third-largest magmatic event of the last 150 million years, roughly 5 million cubic km of rock from Canada and Greenland to Britain.
It built flood basalts on Baffin Island and the last volcanic rocks of the British Isles, formed between 63 and 52 Ma.
Volcanism on Greenland's southeast margin coincided with the Latest Danian warming around 62.2 Ma.

entries.text: The fire that now feeds Iceland's volcanoes was lit beneath Greenland about 65 million years ago. A mantle plume, a column of hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth, rose there. It was the ancestor of today's Iceland hotspot. Its most active magmatism ran from about 60.5 to 54.5 million years ago. It came in two pulses: a pre-break-up phase from 62 to 58 million years ago and a break-up phase from 56 to 54 million years ago. The result was the third-largest magmatic event of the last 150 million years. It produced roughly 5 million cubic kilometers of rock, spread from Canada and Greenland to Britain. It built flood basalts on Baffin Island. It also made the last volcanic rocks of the British Isles, formed between 63 and 52 million years ago. Volcanism on Greenland's southeast margin coincided with {{ref:pale-025}} around 62.2 million years ago, and the province's break-up phase helped split Greenland from Europe.

entries.title: India meets Asia

facts.text: India, racing north since the Late Cretaceous, had begun its collision with Asia by the Paleocene.
One account dates the India–Eurasia collision to the middle Paleocene, about 60 Ma, starting the Himalayan orogeny.
Southern Tibet's Gangdese batholith reawakened around 65 Ma as India approached and stayed active for 20 million years.
Between about 60 and 50 Ma, the leading edge of Greater India struck the West Burma block.
The size of Greater India and the timing of collision are debated; models range from late Paleocene contact to collision in the middle Eocene.

entries.title: Titanoboa and the first rainforest

facts.text: Colombia's Cerrejón Formation, about 60–58 Ma, holds the earliest record of Neotropical rainforest, on a wet coastal plain near 5°N.
Titanoboa, which lived there, grew over 13 m long, the longest snake ever recorded; a 60-million-year-old Colombian turtle, Carbonemys, had a 1.7 m shell.
A snake that size implies mean annual temperatures of 30–34 °C, though leaf-based estimates run 6–8 °C cooler.
Its plants already belonged to modern rainforest families such as palms, legumes and aroids.
Low plant diversity and unspecialized insect damage show the forest was still recovering from the K–Pg extinction 7 million years later.

entries.title: Late Paleocene cooling and brief ice

The icing of Antarctica may have begun as early as the late Paleocene, between 60 and 45.5 Ma.
Other evidence finds no significant ice sheets or sea ice from the late Paleocene into the early Eocene.

entries.text: For a time, animals could walk from Britain to Greenland. A land bridge, now sunk beneath the Atlantic, appeared in the late Paleocene and linked the British Isles to Greenland, and so Europe to North America. This Thulean route was open around 57 and 55.8 million years ago. On the other side of the world, Beringia linked North America and Asia at 65.5 and 58 million years ago. The Thulean bridge disappeared in the early Eocene.

entries.title: The Mid-Paleocene Biotic Event

facts.text: Around 59 Ma, just before the Selandian–Thanetian boundary, temperatures spiked, probably from a mass release of deep-sea methane hydrate.
It and a second pulse 300,000 years later (MPBE-2) released about 83 and 132 billion tonnes of methane-derived carbon, suggesting 2–3 °C of warming.
At Itzurun, Spain, it shows as a dark 1 m layer poor in calcium carbonate.

Together they released about 83 and 132 billion tonnes of methane-derived carbon, suggesting 2–3 °C of warming. At Itzurun, Spain, the event shows as a dark 1 m layer poor in calcium carbonate.

entries.title: The long slide into the Eocene hothouse

facts.text: From the late Paleocene through the early Eocene, about 58 to 50 Ma, Earth warmed over the long term, punctuated by hyperthermals.
Surface temperatures rose gradually by about 6 °C over that span.
The relatively cool late Paleocene ended with the Thanetian Thermal Event and then the PETM.
Global mean surface temperature in the latest Paleocene, about 57 Ma, is estimated at 22.3–28.3 °C.
Plant diversity at both poles rose through the Paleocene, especially at its end, as the world warmed.

entries.title: The Hiawatha impact under Greenland's ice

facts.text: A metallic asteroid about 1.5 km wide left a 31 km crater now buried under Greenland's Hiawatha Glacier.
Argon–argon and uranium–lead dating of zircons in its melt rock give 57.99 ± 0.54 Ma, in the late Paleocene.
The impact has no clear climatic effects, and its age rules out a link to the Younger Dryas.

entries.title: The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum

facts.text: At the end of the Paleocene, about 2,500–4,500 billion tonnes of carbon poured into the air and oceans, spiking temperatures and acidifying the sea.
Global average temperature rose about 5–8 °C during an event lasting about 200,000 years; mid-latitude and polar regions may have topped today's tropical temperatures.
Proposed carbon sources include magma sills baking organic-rich sediments in the North Atlantic Igneous Province, seafloor methane clathrates and kimberlite eruptions at Lac de Gras, Canada.
Its onset may have taken anywhere from a few decades to several thousand years.
It wiped out 30–50% of deep-sea benthic foraminifera, which had come through the K–Pg extinction unscathed, and is linked to one of the smaller mass extinctions.
