entries.text: At the end of the Paleocene, Earth released carbon at a pace that rivals the burning of fossil fuels. About 2,500–4,500 billion tonnes of carbon poured into the air and oceans. Temperatures spiked and the sea turned more acidic. Global average temperature rose about 5–8 °C during an event that lasted about 200,000 years. Mid-latitude and polar regions may have been warmer than today's tropics. The source of the carbon is still debated. Candidates include magma sills baking organic-rich sediments in {{ref:pale-030}}, methane clathrates on the seafloor and kimberlite eruptions at Lac de Gras, Canada. How fast it began is uncertain too: anywhere from a few decades to several thousand years. Deep-sea life took the hit. The event wiped out 30–50% of deep-sea benthic foraminifera, bottom-dwelling shelled microbes that had come through the K–Pg extinction unscathed. The PETM is linked to one of the smaller mass extinctions, and it marks the start of the Eocene.

entries.title: Oxygen in the air roughly doubles

facts.text: At about the beginning of the Eocene the amount of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere more or less doubled.

entries.text: At about the start of the Eocene, roughly 56 million years ago, the air itself changed. The amount of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere more or less doubled. Every breath taken by an early Eocene animal held far more oxygen than the air of only a short while before. The shift came just as the new, hot epoch began.

entries.title: Modern mammal orders burst onto the scene

facts.text: The PETM warming brought more modern mammal groups into North America while many Paleocene forms declined.
The oldest fossils of most modern mammal orders appear within a brief early Eocene window, among them artiodactyls, perissodactyls and hyaenodontids.
Odd-toed ungulates seem to have arisen in Asia: Cambaytherium from western India dates to roughly 54.5 million years ago.
The new mammals had long thin legs, grasping hands and feet, and teeth differentiated for chewing.
All were small, under 10 kg; Eocene mammals were only about 60% the size of the Paleocene mammals before them.

entries.text: Most of the major branches of today's mammals show up in the rocks almost at once. The warming of {{ref:pale-048}} brought more modern mammal groups into North America while many Paleocene forms declined. The oldest fossils of most modern mammal orders appear within a brief early Eocene window. Among them are artiodactyls, the even-toed hoofed mammals, and perissodactyls, the odd-toed ones. Hyaenodontids, meat-eaters, arrived too. The odd-toed ungulates seem to have arisen in Asia: Cambaytherium, from western India, dates to roughly 54.5 million years ago. The newcomers shared a new body plan. They had long thin legs, grasping hands and feet, and teeth shaped for chewing. All were small, under 10 kg. In fact, Eocene mammals were only about 60% the size of the Paleocene mammals before them.

entries.title: The Fur Formation, a Danish fossil treasure

facts.text: In northern Denmark, about 60 m of diatom-rich clay with up to 180 volcanic ash layers settled on the earliest Eocene seafloor.
Deposited just after the PETM, its tropical to subtropical flora points to a climate about 4–8 °C warmer than today.
It preserves abundant fish, insects, reptiles, birds and plants, one of the richest Eocene fossil insect faunas.

entries.title: Champsosaurs, the last crocodile look-alikes, die out

facts.text: Champsosaurus and its crocodile-like neochoristodere relatives, survivors of the K–Pg extinction, died out in the early Eocene.
Their loss coincides with the mammal turnover linked to PETM warmth.
Only the small lizard-like Lazarussuchus carried the choristodere line on, in Europe, until the Miocene.

entries.title: The first true primates

facts.text: Archicebus achilles, from about 55 million years ago, is the earliest known ancestor of primates.
In North America, tarsier-like omomyids and lemur-like strepsirrhines replaced the archaic plesiadapiforms at the start of the Eocene.
Primates were exchanged between North America and Asia around 55.8 million years ago.
Primates split into strepsirrhines (lemurs, lorises) and haplorhines (tarsiers, anthropoids) and diversified by about 50 million years ago.

image.caption: Andrea Jagher, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

entries.text: The oldest ancestor of every monkey, ape and human known so far was a tiny animal called Archicebus achilles. It lived about 55 million years ago, and it is the earliest known ancestor of primates. At the start of the Eocene, true primates spread fast. In North America, tarsier-like omomyids and lemur-like strepsirrhines replaced the archaic plesiadapiforms of {{ref:pale-018}}. Primates moved between North America and Asia around 55.8 million years ago, across the land links of the time. Then the family tree branched. Primates split into strepsirrhines, the lemurs and lorises, and haplorhines, the tarsiers and anthropoids. The anthropoids are the branch that would one day include monkeys, apes and people. By about 50 million years ago, both branches had diversified.

entries.title: Songbirds, parrots and loons appear

facts.text: Many modern bird orders first appeared in the Eocene: the first songbirds, parrots, loons, swifts and woodpeckers.
The oldest known stem loon, Nasidytes, comes from England's London Clay, about 55 million years old.
The first perching birds (passerines) appear around 52.5 million years ago.
The woodpecker order dates from the early Eocene and the kingfisher order from the middle Eocene.

entries.title: India hits Asia and the Himalayas begin to rise

facts.text: India's collision with the Eurasian plate is most often dated to about 55–50 million years ago, though the exact timing is debated.
India's northwestern corner touched Eurasia first, about 55 Ma; contact along the Yarlung–Zangbo suture began around 50 Ma.
India's plate slowed from about 18–19.5 cm a year to about 4.5 cm a year around 55 Ma, circumstantial evidence of the collision.
The collision closed the Tethys Ocean there and began thrusting up the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau.
Rival models have a microcontinent colliding first, with India itself arriving only around 40 Ma or even at the end of the Oligocene.

entries.title: The Pyrenees take shape

facts.text: Iberia and Europe, converging since about 100 million years ago, collided in the Eocene and Oligocene.
From about 55 million years ago the Pyrenees underwent very strong crustal compression, which set up the range's present structure.
This main phase lasted until about 47 million years ago, shortening the crust by about 4 mm a year and stacking thrust sheets.

entries.title: The North Atlantic splits Greenland from Europe
entries.article: Opening of the North Atlantic Ocean

facts.text: Seafloor spreading crept north from the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay and, by about 54 million years ago, split Greenland from Eurasia.
The opening of the North Atlantic finally broke the old northern continent Laurasia in two.
By 56 million years ago Greenland was already its own plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift.
The North Atlantic Igneous Province's break-up volcanism ran from about 56 to 54 million years ago, forming the Iceland Plateau and Greenland's Skaergaard intrusion.
Extension between North America and Eurasia also opened the Eurasian Basin across the Arctic.

entries.title: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum

facts.text: The EECO was a long spell of extreme greenhouse warmth, the warmest sustained interval of the Cenozoic Era.
It was set off by a series of intense early Eocene hyperthermals, including ETM-2 and ETM-3.
Global mean surface temperature is estimated at about 23–30 °C; the 56–47 Ma hothouse ran about 14 °C warmer than today.
Antarctic summers reached about 25 °C, alligators and amphibians lived north of the Arctic Circle, and palms grew in Alaska.
Climate models struggle to reproduce its warm poles and mild polar winters, the so-called equable climate problem.

entries.title: Eocene Thermal Maximum 2, nicknamed Elmo

facts.text: ETM-2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after the PETM.
It left a smaller drop in carbon-13 than the PETM and was less severe.
It came exactly 4.5 long orbital-eccentricity cycles after the PETM, and orbital forcing may have triggered it.
Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they ushered in the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

entries.text: After the PETM, the Earth ran a second, smaller fever. ETM-2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after {{ref:pale-048}}. It left a smaller drop in carbon-13 and was less severe. Its timing is strikingly regular: it came exactly 4.5 long orbital-eccentricity cycles after the PETM. Eccentricity is how stretched Earth's orbit is, and it changes on a slow rhythm. That pattern suggests orbital forcing may have triggered it. Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they led into the warmest part of the Eocene.
entries.text_plain: After the PETM, the Earth ran a second, smaller fever. ETM-2, also called H-1 or Elmo, was a brief burst of global warming, the second major hyperthermal after The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. It left a smaller drop in carbon-13 and was less severe. Its timing is strikingly regular: it came exactly 4.5 long orbital-eccentricity cycles after the PETM. Eccentricity is how stretched Earth's orbit is, and it changes on a slow rhythm. That pattern suggests orbital forcing may have triggered it. Smaller hyperthermals followed within about a million years, and together they led into the warmest part of the Eocene.

It is perhaps the best record of Cenozoic freshwater communities, with fish, crocodilians, birds and mammals.
Frost-free climate let crocodiles live there among sycamore forests, as the moist early Eocene turned slightly drier.

entries.title: Eohippus and the first horses

facts.text: The first equids lived in North America by the earliest Eocene, with early equoids of unclear affinity in Europe.
Eohippus appeared about 52 million years ago, and one of its species branched out into various new types of horse.
Thousands of complete skeletons of these early horses come from Eocene layers, mainly in Wyoming's Wind River basin.
About 50 million years ago Eohippus graded into Orohippus, which gave rise to Epihippus, with better grinding teeth, about 47 million years ago.
Their European cousins, the palaeotheres, arose later in the early Eocene.

entries.title: The great Eocene cooling begins

facts.text: Around 49 million years ago the warming climate turned to cooling, a slow trend that lasted until about 34 million years ago.
Changing geography and ocean circulation, as Australia and South America drew away from Antarctica, drove the drop.
Cold-water diatoms suggest winter sea ice formed in the Arctic, and Antarctica shows glaciation by about 37 million years ago.
Falling carbon dioxide, drawn down by organic productivity and weathering of new mountains, kept the cooling going; models suggest CO2 mattered more than ocean isolation.
The cooling that began in the middle Eocene ultimately led to the ice ages of the Quaternary.

entries.title: The Azolla event: a fern that cooled the world

facts.text: With the Arctic Ocean almost cut off from the wider oceans, warm waters and high carbon dioxide let the floating fern Azolla grow rapidly across it.
With modest warmth and 20 hours of polar summer daylight, the fern can double its biomass in two to three days.
Dead ferns sank to the stagnant seafloor and were buried in sediment over about 800,000 years, building large Azolla deposits that locked away carbon.
Carbon dioxide fell catastrophically, from about 3,500 ppm in the early Eocene to 650 ppm during the event.
The drawdown is believed to have ended the early Eocene warmth about 48.5 Ma; temperatures fell rapidly 49-47 Ma, and glacial dropstones then became common in Arctic sediments.

entries.title: The Messel Pit

facts.text: A lake at Messel, in Hesse, Germany, preserved over 1,400 taxa of plants and animals about 47 million years ago, the best record of its time.
Near the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, the site had a mean annual temperature of 22 °C, with maar lakes ringed by lush subtropical forest; it lay 10° farther south.
Animals sank into deep, oxygen-poor water without scavengers, so whole skeletons survive, some even with fur, feathers and 'skin shadows'.
Bursts of toxic volcanic gas from the lake, like Lake Nyos in 1986, may have killed the animals; other researchers blame toxic cyanobacterial blooms.
Its fossils, from pygmy horses and early primates to bats, keep yielding major discoveries about the early evolution of mammals and birds.

entries.title: The Tasmanian Passage opens

The general consensus is that the two continents had fully separated by 60 million years ago; 45 Ma is a minority estimate.

entries.title: Basilosaurus, the giant fully marine whale

facts.text: Basilosaurus, a large predatory archaeocete whale, lived from about 41.3 to 33.9 million years ago.
At 17–20 m and up to 15 tonnes, it was one of the largest animals of the Paleogene.
A top predator of shallow seas, it ate sharks, large fish and other marine mammals, especially the smaller whale Dorudon.
By the end of the Eocene, whales such as Basilosaurus had become fully aquatic.
Its extinction coincides with the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, which ended almost all other archaeocetes.

entries.title: The Drake Passage begins to open

entries.title: The Middle Eocene Climatic Optimum

facts.text: From about 40.5 to 40.0 million years ago, a spell of very warm climate briefly reversed the long Middle–Late Eocene cooling.
The warming was globally synchronous; mean surface temperature reached about 23 °C and Tethys sea surfaces 32–36 °C.
Carbon dioxide, not methane, drove it; one estimate puts CO2 at 4,000 ppm, though other studies find a smaller rise.
A coinciding minimum in two orbital eccentricity cycles, around 40.2 million years ago, likely helped sustain the warmth.
Planktonic foraminifera turned over: acarinids dwindled and morozovellids went extinct.

entries.title: The mid-Tertiary ignimbrite flare-up

facts.text: From about 40 to 25 million years ago a dramatic burst of volcanic eruptions swept the western United States.
Its andesite-to-rhyolite eruptions produced about 500,000 km³ of explosive and 5 million km³ of effusive volcanic rock.
It followed the end of Laramide compression, as the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion changed.
Volcanoes of Colorado's San Juan field became active 40–35 million years ago; New Mexico's Mogollon-Datil field began erupting about 36.2 million years ago.
In Mexico's Sierra Madre Occidental, the flare-up's Oligocene ash flows stacked ignimbrite sheets covering the largest area of any known series, with ten calderas.

Around 35 million years ago, glaciers merged into the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It buried the Gamburtsev Mountains, which remain hidden under the ice. A brief glaciation, the Late Eocene Event, followed about 34.4 million years ago.

entries.title: The White River fauna

facts.text: In North America's Chadronian age, from 37 million years ago, the White River fauna was in full swing.
Modern rodent families such as beavers, squirrels and gophers replaced older tropical ones, alongside early relatives of bears, peccaries and rabbits.
Rabbit relatives, first found in East Asia, reached North America in the late Eocene.

entries.title: Popigai, a giant crater in Siberia

facts.text: A large bolide blasted a 100 km crater in northern Siberia in the late Eocene.
It is tied as the fourth-largest verified impact structure on Earth.
It may be linked to the Eocene–Oligocene extinction, and may have struck at the same time as the Chesapeake Bay and Toms Canyon impacts.

entries.title: The Chesapeake Bay impact

facts.text: A bolide about 3 km wide struck the eastern shore of North America, then lined with rainforest and shallow limy seas.
It left a crater about 85 km wide, now buried beneath the mouth of Chesapeake Bay.
It is one of the best-preserved marine-target craters, and sediment slumping over its rubble helped shape the bay.
The nearby Toms Canyon crater, and possibly Siberia's Popigai, may have formed in the same event.

entries.title: The Laramide orogeny ends

facts.text: The Laramide orogeny, which raised mountains across western North America from the Late Cretaceous, ended sometime between 55 and 35 million years ago.
Compression gave way to crustal extension that ultimately formed the Basin and Range Province.
As convergence slowed the Farallon slab steepened and plate motion turned oblique, and volcanism flared across the Basin and Range.
In New Mexico, Laramide deformation lasted until about 40 million years ago.
The orogeny's exact start and end dates are in dispute.

entries.title: EOT-1: the first step into the ice age

facts.text: Long cooling crossed a threshold around 34 million years ago, and a large ice sheet formed in East Antarctica as carbon dioxide fell.
Antarctica glaciated in two steps; the first and smaller, EOT-1, came about 34.1–33.9 million years ago, at the boundary itself.
By the boundary an ice sheet in western Antarctica reached the ocean, and glaciers had appeared in Greenland.
Glaciers sliding off the Gamburtsev Mountains are thought to have seeded the East Antarctic Ice Sheet.
At the Eocene–Oligocene transition, about 34 million years ago, deep overturning circulation shifted from the Pacific to the Atlantic as the Arctic–Atlantic gateway closed.

entries.title: Toothed and baleen whales go separate ways

facts.text: The ancestors of toothed and baleen whales split around 34 million years ago, as the southern oceans' climate changed with the opening of the Drake Passage.
The earliest known mysticete, Mystacodon, 37 to 33 million years old, still had teeth and fed by suction.
Later forms carried both baleen and teeth, then lost their teeth and became full filter feeders, as all living baleen whales are.
Toothed whales are defined by features for echolocation, such as a fatty melon; Oligocene Squalodon skulls give the first hypothesized evidence of it.

entries.title: The Eocene–Oligocene extinction

facts.text: The Eocene ends with a major extinction and faunal turnover, called the Grande Coupure in Europe, spanning about 33.9 to 33.4 million years ago.
It accompanied Earth's shift from greenhouse to icehouse: sharp cooling, a big sea-level drop and rapid growth of the Antarctic ice sheet as CO2 fell to about 750–800 ppm.
The extinction of hantkeninid planktonic foraminifera marks the boundary; Basilosaurus and nearly all other archaic whales died out.
Cooling turned over snails, amphibians and reptiles in central North America; some sites show extinctions drawn out over millions of years, starting in the early Priabonian.
Its causes are debated and not fully understood; the large Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts may also be involved.

entries.text: The Eocene closed with the planet flipping from greenhouse to icehouse, and life paid the price. A major extinction and faunal turnover, called the Grande Coupure, or 'great break', in Europe, spanned about 33.9 to 33.4 million years ago. It came with sharp cooling, a big drop in sea level and rapid growth of the Antarctic ice sheet. Carbon dioxide fell to about 750–800 ppm. In the sea, hantkeninid planktonic foraminifera went extinct, and their disappearance marks the boundary. {{ref:eoce-061}} and nearly all other archaic whales died out. In central North America, the cooling turned over snails, amphibians and reptiles. Some sites show extinctions drawn out over millions of years, beginning in the early Priabonian. The causes are debated and not fully understood. The large Popigai and Chesapeake Bay impacts may also have played a part.

entries.title: Antarctica freezes and an ice age begins

facts.text: Ice began to build up on Antarctica about 33.9 million years ago, opening the Late Cenozoic Ice Age that still continues.
The Eocene–Oligocene boundary marks Earth's switch from its last greenhouse climate to the present icehouse.
Falling carbon dioxide, past a tipping point of about 600 ppm, was the main driver of Antarctic glaciation.
For the first time in the Phanerozoic, both poles fell well below freezing.
Ice-rafted debris shows glaciers had also appeared on Greenland by the start of the Oligocene.

entries.text: The ice age you live in today began about 33.9 million years ago, when ice started to build up on Antarctica. That moment opened the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, and it has never ended. The Eocene–Oligocene boundary marks the switch: Earth left its last greenhouse climate and entered the present icehouse, a world with permanent ice at the poles. The main driver was falling carbon dioxide. Once it dropped past a tipping point of about 600 ppm, the Antarctic ice could grow and persist. The north was not spared. Ice-rafted debris, rock dropped on the seafloor by melting icebergs, shows that glaciers had also appeared on Greenland by the start of the Oligocene. For the first time in the Phanerozoic, both poles fell well below freezing at once. Much of what follows in this chapter, from falling seas to spreading grasslands, traces back to this cold turn.

entries.title: Grasses leave the wetlands as forests shrink

facts.text: Grasslands expanded around the world while tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt.
By the early Oligocene, North American and Eurasian tropical forests had given way to dry woodland and wide grasslands.
Grasses spread out of their wetland-edge habitats into open country; in South America the cooler climate spread savanna.
Falling carbon dioxide favored C4 photosynthesis, typical of grasses, yet even by the epoch's end grass was not common enough for modern savannas.
Cooling and spreading grassland favored the evolution of larger mammals.

entries.text: As the planet cooled, the forests lost ground. Tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt, and grasslands expanded around the world. By the early Oligocene, tropical forests in North America and Eurasia had given way to dry woodland and wide grasslands. In South America the cooler climate spread savanna, open country with scattered trees. Grasses themselves changed address. They moved out of their old habitats at the edges of wetlands and into open land. Falling carbon dioxide favored C4 photosynthesis, a way of fixing carbon typical of grasses that works well when the gas is scarce. Even so, by the end of the epoch grass was still not common enough to make modern savannas. The open landscapes shaped the animals living in them. Cooling and spreading grassland favored the evolution of larger mammals, a trend that would run on through the Miocene.
entries.text_plain: As the planet cooled, the forests lost ground. Tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt, and grasslands expanded around the world. By the early Oligocene, tropical forests in North America and Eurasia had given way to dry woodland and wide grasslands. In South America the cooler climate spread savanna, open country with scattered trees. Grasses themselves changed address. They moved out of their old habitats at the edges of wetlands and into open land. Falling carbon dioxide favored C4 photosynthesis, a way of fixing carbon typical of grasses that works well when the gas is scarce. Even so, by the end of the epoch grass was still not common enough to make modern savannas. The open landscapes shaped the animals living in them. Cooling and spreading grassland favored the evolution of larger mammals, a trend that would run on through the Miocene.

entries.title: The Obik Sea drains and Europe meets Asia

facts.text: The Obik Sea, which had separated Europe from Asia, retreated early in the Oligocene and left a lasting land connection.
Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait across it, opening Europe to Asian mammals.

entries.title: Oi-2 glaciation drops the sea to a record low

facts.text: Several pulses of glaciation struck in the middle Oligocene, around the Oi-2 oxygen isotope shift.
Growing Antarctic ice caused the largest sea-level drop of the past 100 million years, about 75 metres.
Rivers cut into exposed continental shelves, leaving gaps in marine rock records around the world.
Lesser turnovers of animal life coincided with the Oi-2 event.

entries.title: Paratethys turns into a giant airless sea

facts.text: In the Oligocene a northern arm of the Tethys, the Paratethys, covered much of central and eastern Europe.
A sea-level drop and the uplift of Alpine mountain chains partly cut it off from the Tethys.
Poorly connected to the world ocean, it became stratified and turned into a giant anoxic sea.
Sand from rising mountains buried organic matter in the Maykop Suite, now a source of hydrocarbons around the Black Sea.
The Menilite Formation preserves its deep-sea fish and microbial mats.

entries.title: The Grande Coupure: Asia's mammals overrun Europe

facts.text: Around 33.5 million years ago, Europe's mammal fauna turned over sharply as Asian species arrived; the French name means 'great break'.
Asian animals replaced most European mammals, except some endemic rodent and marsupial families.
Falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait, letting Asian rhinos and ruminants into Europe, where they drove native species extinct.
Before it, Europe was dominated by native artiodactyls, palaeothere perissodactyls, and adapid and omomyid primates.
The break brought widespread extinction; the first Asian immigrants appear about 350,000 years later in northwest European records.

entries.text: Around 33.5 million years ago, Europe's mammals turned over so sharply that the event got a French name meaning 'great break': the Grande Coupure. Before it, Europe had its own cast. The sources differ slightly on placement: the Oligocene's own account puts it at the very start of the epoch.

entries.title: The Atacama begins its long drought

facts.text: A proto-Humboldt Current, set up with the Tasmania–Antarctic passage about 33 million years ago, began the Atacama's drying; it may be Earth's oldest desert.
Humid air was generally lacking there after 33 million years ago, apart from brief wetter spells.

entries.title: Greenland stops drifting and an Arctic orogeny ends

facts.text: About 33 million years ago, seafloor spreading in the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay ceased and shifted to the northeast Atlantic.
The end of spreading brought the Eurekan orogeny of the Arctic to a close.
Until then, Greenland had moved as a separate plate, drifting north and rotating anticlockwise.
By the late Oligocene the North America–Eurasia boundary ran along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, with Greenland rejoined to North America.

entries.title: The Tasman Gateway opens a southern seaway

facts.text: The Tasman Gateway between Australia and Antarctica opened at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, about 33 million years ago, bringing abrupt cooling.
Shallow channels south of Tasmania opened in the Eocene; deep-ocean routes followed from the mid Oligocene.
Australia had drifted slowly from Antarctica since the Jurassic; one estimate puts a deep channel in place by the end of the early Oligocene.
Southeastern Australia then became a land of high rainfall and swamps.

On land, southeastern Australia became a place of high rainfall and swamps.

entries.title: Aegyptopithecus and the primates of the Fayum

facts.text: Aegyptopithecus, a howler-monkey-sized catarrhine predating the ape–Old World monkey split, lived in Egypt's Fayum about 30.2–29.5 million years ago.
Its Jebel Qatrani Formation spans the Eocene–Oligocene boundary and records tropical forests, swamps and rivers draining north into the Tethys Sea.
The formation holds over a dozen primate genera and early elephants such as Phiomia and Moeritherium, key to the early evolution of modern mammal groups.

entries.title: A current wraps Antarctica in cold water

facts.text: A steady current circling Antarctica probably did not form until about 30 million years ago.
Once the gateways opened, the current kept cold water circling Antarctica and strengthened the formation of Antarctic Bottom Water.
A shallow flow at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary may have started a proto-current, but it was too shallow for a true circumpolar current.
Deep-sea cores south of New Zealand show cold deep currents by the early Oligocene.
Fossil evidence places the current's full establishment about 23 million years ago, once the Drake Passage opened fully and the Tasman Gateway deepened.

entries.contested_note: Its timing depends on the disputed opening of the Drake Passage, and how much it drove Oligocene cooling is debated.

entries.text: A ring of ocean now spins endlessly around Antarctica, and it may have started spinning about 30 million years ago. A steady circumpolar current probably did not form before then. A shallow flow at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary may have started a proto-current, but it was too shallow to circle the continent in earnest. Deep-sea cores south of New Zealand show cold deep currents by the early Oligocene. Once the gateways around Antarctica opened, the current kept cold water circling the continent. It also strengthened the formation of Antarctic Bottom Water, the cold, dense water that sinks to the ocean floor. Fossil evidence places its full establishment later, about 23 million years ago, after the Drake Passage opened fully and the Tasman Gateway deepened. The timing is disputed because it rests on the contested opening of the Drake Passage, described in {{ref:olig-048}}. Researchers also still debate how much the current drove Oligocene cooling.

entries.title: Ethiopian Traps flood the Horn of Africa with lava

facts.text: Flood basalts poured across Ethiopia, northeast Sudan and southwest Yemen as the Afar mantle plume hit the base of Africa's lithosphere.
About 350,000 cubic kilometres of lava erupted around 30 million years ago.
Layer upon layer of fissure-fed lava built the flood-basalt plateau of the Ethiopian Highlands.
The eruptions coincided with the start of rifting along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
From 30 to 10 million years ago, shield volcanoes added another 1,000–2,000 m on top.

entries.title: Arabia begins to tear away from Africa

facts.text: The Arabian plate, part of the African plate for most of the Phanerozoic, began to split away in the Oligocene.
Rifting of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden began around 30 million years ago, alongside the Ethiopian flood basalts.
Rifting began in the southern Red Sea in the mid Oligocene and spread along the whole Red Sea–Gulf of Suez system in the late Oligocene.
The Gulf of Suez Rift was active from about 28 million years ago to the end of the Miocene.

entries.title: A spreading ridge meets California and the San Andreas is born

facts.text: The San Andreas Fault began to form about 30 million years ago, as the Pacific–Farallon spreading ridge reached North America's subduction zone.
The arrival of the Murray and Mendocino fracture zones at the subduction zone started strike-slip motion and Basin and Range extension.
It also ended volcanism south of the Cascades and rotated many western North American terranes clockwise.
The first ridge segment entered the subduction zone near Baja California about 28 million years ago.

entries.title: La Garita, one of Earth's greatest eruptions

facts.text: The eruption that formed La Garita Caldera in Colorado was among the largest and most powerful known in Earth's history.
It blasted out the Fish Canyon Tuff, about 5,000 cubic kilometres of ash-flow deposit, and the caldera formed by collapse.
It was one of many calderas of a huge ignimbrite flare-up across Colorado, Utah and Nevada from 40 to 18 million years ago.
Sanidine crystals from the tuff, astronomically dated to 28.175 million years, are a reference standard for argon–argon dating.

entries.title: The Drake Passage parts South America from Antarctica

facts.text: Seafloor spreading along the Scotia Ridge finally parted South America from Antarctica by 28 million years ago, forming the Drake Passage.
South America became an island continent and drifted north toward North America.
Published estimates for the opening range from 49 to 17 million years ago; one study finds deep-water flow possible by about 31 million years ago.
Together with the Tasmanian Gateway, the opening reshaped Oligocene ocean currents.
It may have helped trigger Antarctic glaciation, though models suggest falling carbon dioxide mattered more.

entries.contested_note: Sources disagree on when the passage opened, from the early Eocene to the Miocene, and on whether it happened at the start or near the end of the Oligocene.

This hornless rhino relative weighed up to 15–20 tonnes; giant indricotheres like it stood up to 6 metres at the shoulder in Eurasia.
They bucked a general trend for Oligocene mammals to be much smaller than Eocene ones.

entries.title: A late Oligocene warm spell

facts.text: The late Oligocene, 26.5 to 24 million years ago, probably warmed despite low carbon dioxide, though the change varied by region.
Global temperatures rose slightly but stayed well below earlier Paleogene levels, and Antarctica stayed heavily glaciated.
Pollen from the Tibetan Plateau records the warming.
Lanternfish, until then confined to shelf seas, spread into the open ocean during the warm interval at the end of the Oligocene.

entries.title: The Farallon Plate breaks up

facts.text: About 26 million years ago the Farallon Plate broke up into the Cocos and Nazca plates.
Subduction sped up, reviving volcanism in the Central Andes and broadening the volcanic arc to about 250 km.
Volcanic activity rose sharply along the Andes, and the modern volcanic arc and tectonic regime took shape.
At the Paleogene–Neogene boundary, Pacific–Farallon spreading stopped and the plate split again into today's Nazca and Cocos plates.

entries.title: Tibet rises and the South Asian monsoon strengthens

facts.text: Around 25.8 million years ago, the South Asian monsoon intensified sharply as the Tibetan Plateau rose.
Tibetan pollen shows the monsoon had already developed by the late Oligocene.

entries.text: The South Asian monsoon intensified sharply around 25.8 million years ago. The trigger was the rising Tibetan Plateau. The monsoon itself was not new. Tibetan pollen shows it had already developed by the late Oligocene, and the plateau's growth turned it up. A higher plateau meant a stronger seasonal swing in the winds, and the same link between Tibet and the monsoons returns throughout the Miocene.

entries.title: Rukwapithecus and the earliest apes and monkeys

facts.text: Tanzania's Nsungwe Formation in the Rukwa Rift, about 25.2 million years old, yields Rukwapithecus, interpreted as the earliest known ape (hominoid).
The same beds hold Nsungwepithecus, an early Old World monkey, so apes and Old World monkeys had already split by then.
That fits molecular estimates of the split at about 25–30 million years ago, though early catarrhine relationships remain uncertain.
The finds extend both groups into a poorly sampled interval; tectonic changes in East Africa may have influenced their diversification.

entries.title: East Africa starts to split open

facts.text: The East African Rift began to develop around the start of the Miocene, 25–22 million years ago.
Rifting and volcanism began in northern Kenya around 30 million years ago, reaching southern Kenya by 12 and northern Tanzania by 8 million years ago.
Volcanism started on the central Ethiopian plateau around 30 million years ago, long before rifting.
Mount Elgon, at least 24 million years old, is East Africa's oldest known extinct volcano.

entries.text: Mount Elgon, at least 24 million years old, is East Africa's oldest known extinct volcano, and it stands at the start of a great tearing. The East African Rift began to develop around the start of the Miocene, 25–22 million years ago. Its fires began earlier. Volcanism started on the central Ethiopian plateau around 30 million years ago, long before any rifting there. In northern Kenya, rifting and volcanism began around the same time. Then the crack worked its way south. It reached southern Kenya by 12 million years ago and northern Tanzania by 8 million years ago. The rift would go on to reshape the landscape of eastern Africa, the setting for much of the human story later in this course.

facts.text: A deep glaciation lasting 400,000 years at the Oligocene–Miocene boundary is recorded at McMurdo Sound and King George Island, Antarctica.
The boundary is set not at one clear global event but at regional shifts from the warmer late Oligocene to the cooler Miocene.
The Miocene opened with the Mi-1 cool event around 23 million years ago, during a major expansion of Antarctica's ice sheets.

entries.title: Africa's plants lose ground to the seasons

facts.text: Africa's plant diversity fell sharply at the start of the Miocene, probably because seasons became more pronounced.
Africa's equatorial forest belt broke apart and rejoined repeatedly through the Miocene.

entries.text: Africa's plant life took a sharp hit as the Miocene began. Plant diversity fell steeply, probably because the seasons became more pronounced, with stronger swings between wet and dry. Species suited to steady conditions lost out. The great equatorial forest belt did not simply shrink. Through the whole Miocene it broke apart and rejoined again and again, splitting forest populations and then reconnecting them.

entries.title: Apes spread across the Old World

facts.text: Apes first evolved in the early Miocene (Aquitanian and Burdigalian), diversified and became widespread across the Old World.
After Afro-Arabia met Eurasia, hominoids and proboscideans dispersed from Africa into Eurasia.
The earliest claimed upright spine and vertical body plan belongs to Morotopithecus, about 21.6 million years ago.
Later waves reached Eurasia: Griphopithecus in Turkey and Slovakia 15–13.5 million years ago, and Dryopithecus in Europe by 12.5 million years ago.
An 'Out-of-Europe' idea holds that several great ape species evolved in Eurasia during the Miocene.

entries.text: Morotopithecus, about 21.6 million years old, carries the earliest claimed upright spine and vertical body plan of any ape. It belongs to a group just finding its feet. Apes first evolved in the early Miocene, in the Aquitanian and Burdigalian ages, and then diversified and spread across the Old World. Geography made the spread possible. Once Afro-Arabia met Eurasia, hominoids, the ape group, and proboscideans, the elephant group, could walk out of Africa. Apes crossed in waves. Griphopithecus lived in Turkey and Slovakia 15–13.5 million years ago, and Dryopithecus had reached Europe by 12.5 million years ago. One proposal, the 'Out-of-Europe' idea, holds that several great ape species evolved in Eurasia during the Miocene. The crossing itself is the subject of {{ref:mioc-037}}, and the later story of the apes runs through {{ref:mioc-046}} to the split of human and chimpanzee lines.

entries.title: Himalayan rubble builds the Bengal Fan

facts.text: Sediment eroded from the rising Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, carried mostly by the Ganges and Brahmaputra, built the Bengal Fan.
The oldest sediments recovered from the fan so far are of Early Miocene age, so the fan is at least that old.
Their minerals and chemistry show Himalayan origin, so the Himalaya was already a major mountain range 20 million years ago.
It is the largest submarine fan on Earth, about 3,000 km long, 1,430 km wide and up to 16.5 km thick.
Changes in its sediments show Himalayan uplift slowed in the Late Pliocene.

entries.title: The daisy family takes off

facts.text: The geologic time scale lists the daisy family (Compositae) as appearing and diversifying rapidly in the Early Miocene, triggering radiations of rodents, snakes and songbirds.
The family went through a significant adaptive radiation in the Neogene, though its oldest fossil pollen, from Antarctica, is 76-66 million years old.
With over 32,000 species, about 10% of flowering plants, it rivals the orchids as the largest plant family.

entries.title: The East Asian summer monsoon takes modern shape

facts.text: Global cooling led the East Asian Summer Monsoon to begin taking its modern form in the Early Miocene.
Major phases of Himalayan geology during the Miocene affected Asian monsoon patterns, which were linked to northern glacial periods.

entries.text: Global cooling led the East Asian Summer Monsoon to begin taking its modern form in the Early Miocene. The mountains mattered too. Major phases of Himalayan geology during the Miocene changed Asian monsoon patterns. Those patterns were tied in turn to glacial periods in the north, so ice far away and rock nearby both shaped the rain. The link between rising Tibet and stronger monsoons, first seen in {{ref:olig-063}}, keeps returning through the Neogene.

entries.title: Tian Shan and Altai rise in Central Asia

facts.text: The geologic time scale lists the Tian Shan and Altai Mountains of Central Asia as forming in the Early Miocene, as part of the Himalayan orogeny.
Both lie in the belt deformed by India's collision with Eurasia; the Siberian Altai is the northernmost region that collision affected.
The Tian Shan rose sharply again in the Late Miocene, blocking westerly winds from the Tarim Basin and drying it.

entries.title: The Andes rise fastest in the Miocene

facts.text: Head-on subduction of the new Nazca Plate under South America lifted the Andes, with the greatest effect in the Miocene.
The Altiplano began rising in the Miocene and was a high plateau, second in size only to Tibet, by about 13–11 million years ago.
From the Late Miocene the Altiplano region rose from low elevations to over 3,000 m, and Peru's Western Cordillera, paused since the Oligocene, rose sharply after about 10 Ma.
The Principal Cordillera east of Santiago rose about 20–8 Ma; Colombia's Eastern Ranges exhumed faster 12–3 Ma; the Western Cordillera near Misti rose 9–4 Ma with large ignimbrites.
Atacama Fault movement raised the Chilean Coast Range, an island arc collided with northwestern South America, and Quechua phases (9–8, 7–5 Ma) deformed northern Peru.

entries.title: Whales and dolphins at their most diverse

facts.text: Whales and dolphins were at their most diverse in the Miocene, with over 20 baleen whale genera against six living today.
Raptorial sperm whales appeared during this baleen whale radiation, apparently evolving to prey on baleen whales.
From around 15 million years ago, modern cetaceans began to reach enormous sizes.

entries.text: The Miocene ocean held over 20 genera of baleen whales. Only six survive today. Whales and dolphins were at their most diverse in this epoch. The boom in baleen whales brought its own hunters: raptorial sperm whales, toothed whales with large biting teeth, apparently evolved to prey on them. From around 15 million years ago, modern cetaceans began to reach enormous sizes. One of those whale-hunters, Livyatan, appears in {{ref:mioc-125}}.

entries.title: The Fram Strait opens a door to the Arctic

facts.text: The Fram Strait opened in the Miocene and became the only route for Atlantic water into the Arctic Ocean until the Quaternary.
Uplift of the continental shelf kept that water from passing through the Barents Seaway.

entries.title: Grass takes over the world

facts.text: As in the Oligocene, grasses kept spreading through the Miocene and came to dominate much of the world while forests dwindled.
Early Miocene forests gave way to mixed forest-grassland in the Middle Miocene; Oregon was savanna by 12 Ma, and grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma.

Fibrous, fire-tolerant grasses co-evolved with herds of high-crowned grazers, which displaced woodland and browsers; by the Hemingfordian, savanna dominated North America and grazing horses outnumbered browsers.
Ants, termites, grassland mammals and snakes diversified; a cooler, drier climate and spreading open landscapes were a major cause of perissodactyl decline.
Deep grassland soils buried carbon and held water, and grass raised albedo, helping make the climate cooler and drier.

entries.text: Grass did not just spread in the Miocene. It changed the climate that let it spread. As in the Oligocene, grasses kept advancing and came to dominate much of the world while forests dwindled. Early Miocene forests gave way to mixed forest and grassland in the Middle Miocene. Oregon was savanna by 12 Ma, and grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma. The new grasses were fibrous and fire-tolerant. They co-evolved with herds of grazers that had high-crowned teeth, and those herds displaced woodland and browsing animals. By the Hemingfordian age, savanna dominated North America and grazing horses outnumbered browsers. Ants, termites, grassland mammals and snakes diversified. A cooler, drier climate and open landscapes were a major cause of the decline of perissodactyls, the odd-toed hoofed mammals. Then came the feedback. Deep grassland soils buried carbon and held water, and pale grass raised albedo, the share of sunlight reflected. Both helped make the climate cooler and drier still.

Oregon was savanna by 12 Ma, and grasslands and savannas were established by about 10 Ma. The new grasses were fibrous and fire-tolerant. entries.title: Kelp forests rise in Miocene seas

facts.text: Kelp forests first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems.
With grasslands, kelp forests were one of two new biomes that supported much of Miocene life.

entries.text: Two new biomes carried much of Miocene life. One was the grassland. The other grew underwater. Kelp forests, dense stands of giant brown seaweed, first appeared in Miocene seas and soon became one of Earth's most productive ecosystems. On land and in the sea, then, the epoch built new kinds of habitat at the same time, each feeding a great range of animals.

facts.text: Clearly recognisable dabbling ducks, plovers, typical owls, cockatoos and crows appear in the Miocene.
Crows of the genus Corvus are first recorded about 17 million years ago.
By the end of the epoch, all or nearly all modern bird groups are thought to have been present.

entries.title: Snakes boom in North America

facts.text: Snakes, once a minor part of North American fauna, rose sharply in number and diversity during the Miocene.
Vipers and elapids first appeared in North America, and colubrids diversified into many modern genera.

entries.title: The Ogallala spreads its gravels over the Plains

facts.text: As the Rockies rose, rivers carried eroded rock east and dumped vast sand and gravel on the gentle plains as overlapping alluvial fans.
These Miocene to early Pliocene deposits form the Ogallala Formation of the central High Plains.
They hold the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the world's largest, under about 450,000 km2 of eight states; it supplies about 30% of US irrigation groundwater.

entries.title: Riversleigh's rainforest animals

facts.text: Riversleigh, in Queensland, is Australia's most famous fossil site, with mammals, birds and reptiles of Oligocene and Miocene age.
Its Faunal Zone B dates to the Early Miocene, when the area was very wet rainforest; uncompacted limestone keeps bones three-dimensional.
Later Middle Miocene layers hold a 15-million-year-old platypus relative, Obdurodon, and the oldest modern bandicoots and bilbies.

entries.title: The Central Andes begin erupting ignimbrites

facts.text: Large-scale ignimbrite volcanism began in the Central Andes about 23 million years ago and continues today.
North of 21 degrees S, the Oxaya Formation erupted 23 to 18 million years ago.
Calderas of the Altiplano-Puna complex have since produced about 15,000 cubic km of mostly dacitic ignimbrite.
One early eruption, the Verde Ignimbrite from Aguas Calientes caldera 17.2 million years ago, released 140–300 cubic km.
In southern Peru the Chuquibamba (Huaylillas) Ignimbrite came from a VEI 7 super-eruption 14.3 to 13.2 million years ago.

entries.text: Ignimbrite is rock made from a glowing avalanche of volcanic ash that welds as it settles. In southern Peru, the Chuquibamba Ignimbrite came from a VEI 7 super-eruption 14.3 to 13.2 million years ago.

entries.title: Megalodon, the giant shark, appears

facts.text: The giant shark megalodon evolved around 23 million years ago.
Megalodon and the sperm whale Livyatan were among the large predators that dominated Neogene oceans.
Its first appearance is disputed: some remains are reported from the Late Oligocene, about 28 million years ago, while other estimates are as young as 16 million years.

facts.text: East Antarctica probably held some glaciers during the early to mid Miocene, 23 to 15 million years ago.
The Ross Sea margin of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet advanced and retreated often during the Early Miocene.

entries.title: Granites melt inside the High Himalaya

facts.text: Granites of early Miocene age, about 22 million years old, intruded the High Himalayan Crystalline Sequence in many places.
That 30-km-thick metamorphic sequence belongs to the Central Himalayan Domain, the backbone of the orogen with its highest peaks.
The Himalayan orogeny is among the continental collisions that produced leucogranites, pale granites melted from sediment-derived rock in thickened crust.

entries.text: Deep inside the growing Himalaya, rock melted. Granites about 22 million years old intruded the High Himalayan Crystalline Sequence in many places. That metamorphic sequence is 30 km thick and forms the backbone of the range, holding its highest peaks. Many of these were leucogranites, pale granites melted from sediment-derived rock in crust thickened by collision.

entries.title: New Zealand almost drowns

facts.text: About 22 million years ago only 18% of present-day New Zealand stood above sea level.
This drowning was very important in the radiation of the moa.

Isolation on scattered patches of land mattered for evolution. This drowning was very important in the radiation of the moa.

facts.text: After sinking about 900 m between 25.5 and 21.6 million years ago, the Tibetan Plateau rose by 500 to 1,000 m.
This rise took place between 21.6 and 20.4 million years ago.

facts.text: Watering-hole deposits in Nebraska hold mass-death assemblages of small rhinos with bear dogs, entelodonts, camels and chalicotheres.

entries.title: Lake Pebas floods western Amazonia

facts.text: The Pebas Formation of western Amazonia records the Pebas Mega-Wetland, or Lake Pebas, from about 21 to 8 million years ago.
The formation covers about 1,000,000 square km.
Its fauna correlates with those of La Venta in Colombia and Urumaco in Venezuela.

entries.text: For millions of years, western Amazonia held a giant wetland. The Pebas Formation records this Pebas Mega-Wetland, or Lake Pebas, from about 21 to 8 million years ago. Its end came as the Amazon took a new course, told in {{ref:mioc-099}}.

facts.text: Around 20 million years ago the western flank of the East African Rift rose, cutting the Great Lakes region off from the Congo basin.
Lake Victoria did not yet exist, and Ethiopian and Ugandan rivers did not yet feed the Egyptian Nile.

facts.text: In the Early Miocene the Arabian part of Africa collided with Eurasia, cutting the Mediterranean off from the Indian Ocean.
The first step of the seaway's closure, about 20 million years ago, cut water exchange by 90%.
The Atlantic–Indian Ocean link closed as Africa-Arabia moved north and sea level fell while the Antarctic Ice Sheet grew.
By the mid-Burdigalian the collision had built a land bridge joining the two landmasses.

entries.title: A land bridge sets animals crossing both ways

facts.text: A land bridge between Afro-Arabia and Eurasia, formed around 20 million years ago, set off the Great Old World Biotic Interchange.
Until then the open Tethyan seaway had kept most animals from crossing between the two landmasses.
Animals crossed both ways; at least 37 Eurasian lineages entered Afro-Arabia during the Burdigalian.
Gomphotheres and deinotheres were the first to leave Africa, reaching India by about 18.3 and Iberia by 18 million years ago.
Perissodactyls reached Africa for the first time when it joined Eurasia.

Models link it to plumes from a sinking Tethys slab spreading low-density material beneath the Indian Ocean.

entries.title: Most open-ocean sharks vanish

facts.text: About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared.
Neogene oceans came to be ruled by large predators such as megalodon and Livyatan.

entries.text: About 19 million years ago, roughly 70% of all open-ocean shark species disappeared. Seven in ten kinds of shark that roamed the high seas were simply gone. It is New Zealand's only Cenozoic land fossil record, with early moa, kiwi and adzebills, tuatara relatives, crocodiles, turtles and many bats.
Later cooling and drying wiped out its subtropical members.

facts.text: Volcanoes built the Vogelsberg in Hesse, Germany, mainly in the Middle Miocene; potassium-argon dates span 18.5-10 million years ago, peaking 17-15 million years ago.
It is Central Europe's largest basalt formation and contiguous volcanic region, about 2,500 km2 of many overlapping volcanoes, not one shield.
Its volcanism was tied to fault-block movement, and it ranks among the largest volcanic centres of the European Cenozoic Rift System.

facts.text: Rifting in Ethiopia began about 18 million years ago at the south end, about 11 near the Afar and perhaps 8–6 in the centre.
The rift formed as the Nubian and Somali plates began to separate along the East African rift system.
Opening of the Gregory rift caused the Afar triple junction to form.

In the Middle Miocene the Red Sea rift broke apart along its length, with motion shifting to the Dead Sea Transform; seafloor spreading followed.

entries.title: Iceland rises above the waves

facts.text: Iceland, thought to have been built by the Iceland mantle plume, first rose above the ocean about 18-16 million years ago.
The oldest rocks formed above sea level in today's Iceland date to 16.5 million years ago.
The island sits where the Eurasian and North American plates pull apart, above the plume, giving it repeated volcanism and geysers.

The double setting gives it repeated volcanism and geysers.

entries.title: Great apes and gibbons go separate ways

facts.text: Great apes and gibbons are estimated to have split about 18 to 12 million years ago.
Molecular evidence puts the ape ancestral to the modern hominid clade at 18 to 13 million years ago; fossils are too scarce to name it.

entries.title: The Basin and Range begins to stretch

facts.text: By the Early Miocene most of the Farallon plate had been consumed and the Pacific-Farallon Ridge neared North America.
Crustal stretching that began about 17 million years ago created the province's landscape of ranges and basins.
Tension thinned and dropped the land west of the Grand Canyon region, forming the province.
Since extension began, parts of the province have moved 60 to 300 km sideways, more in the south than the north.

entries.title: The Middle Miocene Climatic Optimum

facts.text: Between roughly 17 and 14 million years ago the climate was about 3 °C warmer than today.
Benthic foraminifera put its onset at 16.9 Ma, peak warmth at 15.3 Ma and its end at 13.8 Ma.
Around 15 million years ago, the warmest part of the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, global temperature averaged about 18.4 °C and the Antarctic ice cap shrank.
A positive carbon isotope shift, the Monterey Carbon Excursion, began just before the optimum and ended just after it.
Columbia River flood basalts, helped by volcanic degassing at plate margins, are seen as the main driver, but cannot explain warming before 16.3 Ma.

entries.contested_note: Whether the Columbia River Basalts drove the Middle Miocene warming is debated: warming began about 16.9 Ma, before their main pulse, and they cannot explain warming before 16.3 Ma.

entries.title: The Columbia River basalts flood the Northwest

facts.text: In the mid-Miocene, lava flooded the Columbia Plateau and Oregon; this large igneous province emitted 95% of its lava between 16.7 and 15.9 Ma.
The province, linked to the Yellowstone hotspot, totals about 210,000 cubic km; its Roza Member alone held at least 1,500 cubic km.
A mantle plume is the most widely accepted cause, though the question is still debated.
The flood basalts ended the Western Cascades period; Cascade volcanism stayed at a low point from 17 to 9 Ma.
The eruptions are often blamed for the Middle Miocene warming, though that warming began earlier, around 16.9 Ma.

entries.title: The Yellowstone hotspot's first calderas

facts.text: The Yellowstone hotspot is thought to have arrived under North America in the Miocene and is still active.
Calderas including McDermitt and Virgin Valley formed 16.5 to 15.5 million years ago as the Steens flood basalts waned.
McDermitt Caldera, made by the hotspot about 16.4 million years ago, formed when a rhyolite lava dome collapsed.
Eruptions such as the Longridge Caldera's, 15.6 million years ago, produced up to 400 cubic km of tuff.

entries.title: Cooling ends the warm Miocene's tropical Europe

facts.text: A wave of extinctions on land and in the sea, the Middle Miocene disruption, followed the warm optimum about 14.8 to 14.5 Ma.
Monitor lizards, chameleons, cordylid lizards, alligators and giant turtles had lived in central Europe during the warm optimum.
The crocodilians Gavialosuchus and Diplocynodon vanished from northern latitudes between 14 and 13.5 Ma.
Cooling wiped out the coral reefs of the Paratethys Sea.
Desmostylians, an order of marine mammals, began a terminal decline after the optimum.

entries.title: The great Middle Miocene cooling

facts.text: A major, permanent cooling step between 14.8 and 14.1 Ma, the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, ended the warm optimum.
Cold Antarctic deep water increased and the East Antarctic Ice Sheet expanded, reaching roughly its present size by 14 Ma.
Antarctic summers cooled by at least 8 °C; around 13.94 Ma Transantarctic glaciers turned cold-based as annual temperatures fell 25–30 °C.
A flip in the 41,000-year obliquity cycle around 14.0–13.8 Ma is read as a signal of the ice expansion.
The resulting change in ocean circulation is thought to have caused the Miocene Carbonate Crash in the early Tortonian.

entries.text: Antarctic summers cooled by at least 8 °C. Around 13.94 Ma, annual temperatures in the Transantarctic Mountains fell 25–30 °C, and their glaciers froze to their beds. This was the Middle Miocene Climate Transition, a major and permanent cooling step between 14.8 and 14.1 Ma that ended the warm optimum. Cold Antarctic deep water increased. The East Antarctic Ice Sheet expanded, reaching roughly its present size by 14 Ma. The rocks carry a signal of the change in Earth's orbit. A flip in the 41,000-year obliquity cycle, the slow nodding of Earth's tilt, around 14.0–13.8 Ma is read as a sign of the ice expansion. The cold reached the deep sea too. The resulting change in ocean circulation is thought to have caused the Miocene Carbonate Crash in the early Tortonian. From here, the Miocene world turns steadily colder and drier.

entries.title: Tibet nears its modern height

facts.text: East–west rift valleys in the Lhasa and Himalaya terranes suggest the plateau was close to its modern altitude by about 14 to 8 Ma.
Sudden mafic volcanism and faster uplift 14 to 11 Ma point to delamination of the lithosphere, as seen beneath Tibet.
India kept pushing into Asia through the Neogene, building the Himalayas.
Major phases of Himalayan geology in the Miocene affected Asian monsoon patterns.
Accounts differ: the plateau may have neared its present height by the late Oligocene, yet some suture zones stayed tropical lowlands into the early Miocene.

entries.title: The Badenian Salinity Crisis

facts.text: Midway through the Middle Miocene, rising central European mountains and falling sea level cut the Paratethys off from the ocean.
Around 13.8 Ma closure of the Bârlad Strait turned the Eastern Paratethys into a saltwater lake.
Starved of fresh water, the Central Paratethys laid down evaporites until about 13.4 Ma, like the later Messinian crisis.
Growing isolation wiped out most small and mid-sized deepwater and open-ocean sharks there.

entries.title: Ashfall: a waterhole buried by a distant eruption

facts.text: Ash from the Bruneau-Jarbidge supereruption, on the Yellowstone hotspot in Idaho, drifted about 1,600 km east and buried animals at a Nebraska waterhole, creating famous mammal bone beds.
Rhino-like Teleoceras, three-toed and one-toed horses, camels and birds lie articulated; one rhino holds an unborn fetus. They died of lung failure from inhaled ash.
The Lagerstätte captures a snapshot of a savanna of grassland and trees under a milder climate than today's.

facts.text: Bullock Creek in Australia's Northern Territory preserves complete marsupial skulls, the crocodile Baru, an early kangaroo and the horned tortoise Meiolania.

entries.title: The Eridanos, a lost river, builds a giant delta

facts.text: By about 12 Ma (a minimum age) the Eridanos, flowing from Lapland across the Baltic region, had reached the North Sea area.
Its sediments built an immense delta, reckoned comparable in size to the modern Amazon's.

entries.title: The Paratethys becomes a brackish megalake

facts.text: Around 12 Ma the Paratethys sea became a megalake of over 2.8 million km², reaching from the eastern Alps to Kazakhstan.
Its water was brackish, with salinity mostly 12–14‰.
Tectonically trapped and cut off from the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean, it became an isolated inland sea that gradually disappeared.

entries.title: Pliohippus and the rise of the grazing horses

facts.text: Pliohippus arose from Calippus around 12 Ma; Hipparion, Protohippus and Pliohippus all descend from Merychippus.
Around 10 Ma horses grew larger and developed high-crowned teeth.
Hipparion and its relatives proliferated in North America, and at least one migrated to Asia and Europe.

entries.text: Around 10 Ma, horses grew larger and developed high-crowned teeth built for grinding tough grass. The family tree behind them branched from Merychippus, the ancestor of Hipparion, Protohippus and Pliohippus. Pliohippus itself arose from Calippus around 12 Ma. Hipparion and its relatives multiplied in North America. At least one of them migrated to Asia and Europe, carrying the grazing horse lineage across the northern continents.

entries.title: Supereruptions build the Snake River Plain

facts.text: The western Snake River Plain began forming around 12–11 Ma with eruptions of rhyolite lava and ignimbrite.
The Yellowstone hotspot's Picabo caldera erupted the Arbon Valley Tuff about 10.2 Ma; the Twin Falls field was active 10–8.6 Ma.
Two VEI 8 supereruptions followed: McMullen at 8.99 Ma (at least 1,700 km³) and Grey's Landing at 8.72 Ma (at least 2,800 km³).
From 6.6 Ma the Heise field in eastern Idaho produced four big caldera eruptions, starting with 1,500 km³ of Blacktail Tuff at 6.62 Ma.
Oregon's High Lava Plains propagated west from about 10 Ma while the Snake River Plain advanced east.

entries.title: The deep seaway between the Americas closes

facts.text: Deep-ocean links between the Pacific and the Caribbean through Central America had closed by 12–9.2 Ma; a shallow link lasted until 2.45 Ma at the latest.
The first phase of uplift of the Isthmus of Panama is dated to around 12 Ma.
Islands began forming between the Americas in the Late Miocene, letting ground sloths such as Thinobadistes island-hop north.
Colombia's La Venta fauna is the last purely South American assemblage before the Great American Biotic Interchange.
Zircons in middle Miocene bedrock of northern Colombia suggest a full isthmus, rather than islands, may already have formed by 10 Ma.

entries.title: The Amazon runs across a continent

facts.text: Between 11.8 and 11.3 Ma the Amazon began flowing as a river across the whole continent.
In the Cretaceous the proto-Amazon had flowed west, as part of a river system draining from Africa.

entries.title: The Benguela Upwelling begins

facts.text: The cold, nutrient-rich Benguela Upwelling began in the late Miocene, likely feeding the phytoplankton behind the rich marine fossils of Hondeklip Bay.
Today the cold Benguela Current along the coast helps keep the Namib Desert arid.

In Iberia, grazers diversified while browsers declined as the climate dried.

entries.title: South America's giant crocodilians vanish

facts.text: Giant native crocodilians, including the caiman Purussaurus and the gharial Gryposuchus, died out in the late Miocene, probably as northern South America's wetlands vanished.
Purussaurus was the largest of these Miocene crocodilians.

entries.title: Danuvius, an ape that may have walked upright

facts.text: Danuvius guggenmosi, a great ape from the Hammerschmiede clay pit in southern Germany, is dated magnetostratigraphically to 11.62 million years ago.
Its discoverer argues it both hung in trees and walked upright along branches, an 'extended limb clambering' that may have preceded human bipedalism.
Other researchers say the fragmentary remains differ too little from other fossil apes to show how bipedalism began.

entries.contested_note: Whether Danuvius walked upright, and what it says about the origin of bipedalism, is disputed.

The last was Lazarussuchus, a European genus and the group's only survivor since the early Eocene.
Its last definite remains are Early Miocene, from the Czech Republic; possible remains from southern Germany date to about 11.6 Ma.

entries.title: The Late Miocene Cool Interval begins

facts.text: About 11 Ma the Middle Miocene Warm Interval ended and the much cooler Late Miocene Cool Interval began.
Through the Late Miocene, Earth's climate became increasingly like today's.
Desmostylians, cold-adapted marine mammals, declined during the Middle to Late Miocene cooling, which may have been harsher than earlier cold spells.

entries.title: The elephant family arises in Africa

facts.text: Around 10 Ma the first members of the elephant family, Elephantidae, arose in Africa from gomphotheres.
From the Late Miocene many proboscideans evolved ever larger tusks and shortened lower jaws.
Late Miocene climate change drove groups such as amebelodontids and choerolophodontids into decline and extinction.
The first members of modern elephant genera appeared around 6–5 Ma, at the Miocene–Pliocene transition.

entries.title: Greenland's rising edges make room for ice

facts.text: Around 10 Ma Greenland's western margin began to rise, later forming plateaus 2,000–3,000 m high; the eastern uplands followed about 5 Ma.
This uplift made a single coherent Greenland ice sheet possible.
Greenland may have had large glaciers as early as 8–7 Ma, though forests survived there into the Pliocene.

entries.title: Ground sloths island-hop to North America

facts.text: Megalonychid and mylodontid ground sloths had island-hopped to North America by about 10–9 Ma (minimum ages), via islands forming between the Americas before any land bridge.
The earliest North American megalonychid, Pliometanastes, lived in the southern US about 9 Ma.
Some large North American herbivores may have reached South America 10–9 Ma over an incomplete land bridge.
These crossings were an early phase of the Great American Biotic Interchange.

facts.text: Uplift of the Carpathians around 10 Ma isolated the Pannonian Sea from the rest of the Paratethys.

entries.title: Baja California tears away from Mexico

facts.text: Rifting began opening the Gulf of California 10–6 Ma, tearing the Baja California peninsula northwest from mainland Mexico.
The gulf's opening around 6 Ma let a large river cut its way northeast from it; by 5.5–5 Ma streams had merged into one major river.
Geologists widely interpret the gulf itself as coming into being around 5.3 million years ago, as rifting tore Baja California off the North American plate.
The East Pacific Rise propagated up the middle of the gulf, forming the Gulf of California Rift Zone.

The East Pacific Rise, a mid-ocean spreading ridge, pushed up the middle of the gulf, forming the Gulf of California Rift Zone. The new gulf changed the rivers around it. Its opening around 6 Ma let a large river cut its way northeast. By 5.5–5 Ma, streams there had merged into one major river, the subject of {{ref:plio-010}}.

entries.title: The Altiplano–Puna ignimbrite flare-up

facts.text: From about 10 Ma calderas of the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex erupted felsic ignimbrites in four pulses separated by quieter spells.
About 10,000 km³ of ignimbrite erupted between 10 and 1 Ma, over crust 70 km thick.
Mafic magma injected into the lower crust, and an overturn before 10.6 Ma melted crust and started the ignimbrite volcanism.
Volcanism peaked 8–4 Ma with huge eruptions at Cerro Panizos, Coranzulí, Vilama, Cerro Guacha and La Pacana.

entries.title: Humans and chimpanzees go separate ways

facts.text: Gibbons, then orangutans, then gorillas branched off before the lines leading to chimpanzees and humans separated; their last common ancestor was probably a small African ape.
A 2026 meta-analysis found that genome-based estimates fitting the fossil record put the split at about 8 Ma, almost certainly more than 7 Ma.
Other molecular estimates range from 10–13 Ma (1998) and 9.3–6.5 Ma (2016) to 6.6–4.7 Ma (2022) and 6.3–5.5 Ma (2025).
Hominin fossils such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin were at odds with older molecular dates of 6–4 Ma.
The two lineages may have kept exchanging genes as late as 6.3–5.4 Ma.

entries.contested_note: Molecular and fossil-based estimates of the split disagree, ranging from about 13 to 4.7 Ma.

verification.title: Parting ways: Pan-Homo divergence revisited

entries.text: Your closest living relative is the chimpanzee, and the question of when the two lines parted has no settled answer. The order of branching is clear. Gibbons split off first, then orangutans, then gorillas, before the lines leading to chimpanzees and humans separated. Their last common ancestor was probably a small African ape. The date is the hard part. A 2026 meta-analysis found that genome-based estimates fitting the fossil record put the split at about 8 Ma, almost certainly more than 7 Ma. Other molecular estimates scatter widely: 10–13 Ma in 1998, 9.3–6.5 Ma in 2016, 6.6–4.7 Ma in 2022 and 6.3–5.5 Ma in 2025. Fossils pushed back on the youngest numbers. Hominins such as Sahelanthropus and Orrorin did not fit older molecular dates of 6–4 Ma. The parting may not have been clean either. The two lineages may have kept exchanging genes as late as 6.3–5.4 Ma. Researchers still disagree, with estimates running from about 13 to 4.7 Ma.

entries.title: The world dries out

facts.text: Global cooling cut the atmosphere's moisture, driving a worldwide trend towards aridity, especially after 8–7 Ma.
Uplift of East Africa helped shrink its rainforests, and Australia dried as it entered a low-rainfall zone, though its southwest grew wetter 12–8 Ma.
Uplift of the Tian Shan blocked westerly winds and dried the Tarim Basin.
In Kenya's Great Rift Valley aridity rose gradually, with wet episodes still recurring.
One theory links the Sahara's drying to a monsoon weakened when the Tethys Sea dried up around 7 Ma.

entries.title: C4 grasses take over the grasslands

facts.text: C4 grasses, which use CO2 and water more efficiently than C3 grasses, became ecologically significant between 7 and 6 Ma, though not yet in the north.
As CO2 fell, C4 plants came to dominate grasslands over the last 10 million years.
Silica-rich C4 grasses drove worldwide extinctions of herbivores that lacked high-crowned teeth.
Proposed drivers include falling CO2, or rising seasonality and aridity with monsoon-fed wildfires.
The spread left its imprint on the global carbon cycle, visible in carbon isotope records.

entries.text: Grass is tough to eat, and a new kind made it tougher. C4 grasses use carbon dioxide and water more efficiently than C3 grasses, the older type. Between 7 and 6 Ma they became ecologically significant, though not yet in the north. As carbon dioxide kept falling, C4 plants came to dominate grasslands over the last 10 million years. They changed who could eat. Silica-rich C4 grasses wore down teeth, and herbivores without high-crowned teeth went extinct worldwide. The cause of the spread is still argued over. Some point to falling carbon dioxide. Others point to rising seasonality and aridity, with wildfires fed by the monsoons. The shift was large enough to mark the whole planet. It left its imprint on the global carbon cycle, visible in carbon isotope records.

entries.title: The sharp Late Miocene cooling

facts.text: Between 7 and 5.3 Ma temperatures fell sharply, most likely from declining CO2 and a smaller swing in Earth's axial tilt.
Ocean temperatures dropped to near-modern values; extratropical sea surfaces cooled by about 7–9 °C.
Antarctic ice neared its present size, and significant glaciation from 6.26 to 5.50 Ma was paced by 41,000-year obliquity cycles, dominant since 7.7 Ma.
A cold spell around 6 Ma advanced glaciers, lowered sea level and helped start the Messinian salinity crisis.
Around 6 Ma the carbon cycle reorganised: continental carbon stores stopped growing during cold spells.

When the sea refilled, the gorge became a gulf that slowly filled with sediment.

entries.title: The Messinian crisis: the Mediterranean dries out

facts.text: From 5.96 to 5.33 Ma the Mediterranean Sea dried out in cycles of partial or nearly complete desiccation, with evaporites piling up across its floor.
The crisis began basin-wide at 5.96 ± 0.02 Ma, when the Betic corridor and the precursor of the Strait of Gibraltar closed, sealing the sea from the Atlantic.
Causes include plate motion at the Gibraltar Arc, mountain uplift in the western Mediterranean, and glacial sea-level falls of about 10 m from about 6.14 Ma.
After a last closure around 5.6 Ma the basin dried almost completely within a thousand years, and erosion cut canyons on the scale of the Grand Canyon.
Native marine fauna suffered major extinctions; from 5.5 Ma river water diluted the brines into brackish 'Lago Mare' lakes, until the Strait of Gibraltar reopened 5.33 Ma.

entries.title: The Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean

facts.text: Atlantic water broke through at the Strait of Gibraltar and refilled the dried-out Mediterranean, ending the Messinian salinity crisis.
About ninety percent of the basin may have filled within months to two years, with sea level at times rising over 10 metres a day.
Peak discharge is estimated at about 100 million cubic metres per second, roughly a thousand times today's Amazon.
Seawater flooded the deep canyon cut by the ancestral Nile up to at least Aswan; the modern Nile then began filling it with sediment.
The reconnection marks the start of the Zanclean age, the first age of the Pliocene.

entries.title: The Pliocene extinction of big sea animals

facts.text: A marine megafauna extinction in the Pliocene wiped out 36% of large marine species, including 55% of marine mammals, 35% of seabirds, 9% of sharks and 43% of sea turtles.
It struck warm-blooded and partly warm-blooded animals harder than cold-blooded ones, pointing to a shrinking food supply.
Plio-Pleistocene sea-level swings, the largest of the Cenozoic and driven by growing polar ice, damaged coastal habitats and may have helped cause several marine megafauna extinctions.
After the Central American Seaway closed, tropical whales declined in diversity and abundance.

Sea level also swung more in the Plio-Pleistocene than at any other time in the Cenozoic, driven by growing polar ice. Those swings damaged coastal habitats and may have helped cause several extinctions. After the Central American Seaway closed, tropical whales declined too.

entries.title: Mount Kenya, a volcano once taller than Kilimanjaro

facts.text: Mount Kenya, a large stratovolcano on the shoulder of the East African Rift, was active in the Plio-Pleistocene.
Its original summit was probably over 6,000 m high, perhaps 7,000 m, taller than Kilimanjaro is today.
Since it went extinct, glaciers have eroded it; its remains are Africa's second-highest mountain, topped by Batian at 5,199 m.

entries.title: The Pliocene Warm Interval

facts.text: From about 5.3 to 2.7 Ma a warm interval, the Pliocene Warm Interval, interrupted the long-term cooling trend.
The Pliocene opened with warmer global temperatures than the cooler Messinian before it.
Carbon dioxide levels were similar to today's, so the interval is often treated as an analogue for near-future warming.
Ice-sheet collapses were much more common in the early to mid Pliocene, between 5 and 3 Ma.
The oceans stayed relatively warm, though they kept cooling.

The chain's volcanoes get younger to the southeast, as the plate carries each one west-northwest away from the hotspot.

entries.title: The Colorado Plateau and River take their modern shape

facts.text: About 5 million years ago the Colorado Plateau reached its present height and the Colorado River took a course close to today's.
Plateau uplift and the opening of the Gulf of California by 5 Ma rearranged the drainage of the Colorado and its tributaries.
About 4 million years ago the Colorado River began reaching the Salton Trough, still connected then to the Gulf of California.

facts.text: Thylacoleo, the marsupial lion, first appeared in the Pliocene; its early species T. crassidentatus, about 5 million years ago, was the size of a large dog.
Its later species grew to lioness weight and the genus became Australia's apex predator, the only one of its family until the end of the Pleistocene.

entries.title: The Paratethys breaks into inland seas

facts.text: From about 5 million years ago the Paratethys Sea grew steadily shallower and largely dried out.
During the Pliocene it split into a few inland seas that were at times fully cut off from each other.
The Black, Caspian and Aral seas are its remnants; the Pliocene Caspian was a small lake without an outlet.

entries.title: A Pliocene burst of ignimbrites in the Puna

facts.text: Between 5 and 3.8 Ma, large-scale ignimbrite eruptions struck the arc front of the northern Puna, part of a magma pulse around 4 Ma.
The Puripicar ignimbrite of about 4.2 Ma alone held some 1,500 cubic kilometres.
Later giants include the 3.49-million-year-old Tara ignimbrite (800 km3) and the 2.89-million-year-old Pastos Grandes ignimbrite (1,500 km3).

entries.title: The Gray Fossil Site, a Tennessee sinkhole

facts.text: Between 4.9 and 4.5 million years ago a sinkhole pond in a warm, wet forest in Tennessee trapped plants and animals.
It is the first site of its age known from Appalachia, yielding new species of red panda, rhinoceros, pond turtle and hickory.
Its fossils show eastern North America still shared a biogeographic link with Eurasia in the Early Pliocene.
