entries.title: The Kilgore Tuff supereruption

facts.text: The Kilgore Tuff eruption in eastern Idaho, rated VEI 8, blasted out about 1,800 cubic kilometres of ash and left a caldera 80 by 60 km.
It was the last caldera-forming eruption of the Heise volcanic field, active for over 2 million years above the Yellowstone hotspot.
Between 5 and 3.3 Ma, the Picabo and Heise centres subsided as the hotspot track moved northeast.

entries.title: Ardi, a skeleton caught between trees and ground

facts.text: The early hominin Ardipithecus ramidus lived in the Afar region of Ethiopia about 4.4 million years ago.
Its most complete specimen is 'Ardi', a 4.4-million-year-old female skeleton.
Ardi's pelvis shows bipedal walking was well under way by then, though her hands and limbs could still climb trees.
Fossils of at least nine more individuals from As Duma in the Afar date to 4.51-4.32 million years ago.
The older A. kadabba is considered its direct ancestor.

entries.title: Australopithecus anamensis, the first australopith

facts.text: Australopithecus anamensis, the oldest known Australopithecus species, lived roughly 4.3 to 3.8 million years ago.
Its first fossils came from Kanapoi and Allia Bay in northern Kenya; the Allia Bay finds give the earliest evidence of a bipedal gait.
Australopithecus probably arose in eastern Africa around 4 Ma, later spread across the continent, and died out somewhat after 2 Ma.
A nearly complete 3.8-million-year-old skull from Ethiopia shows it overlapped in time with A. afarensis.

The much smaller Toconao ignimbrite erupted at almost the same time, with no sign of a pause between the two.

entries.title: Australopithecus afarensis walks East Africa

facts.text: Australopithecus afarensis lived in East Africa from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago.
The 3.58-million-year-old Kadanuumuu skeleton suggests the species already walked fully upright by 3.6 Ma, though not all researchers agree.
Selam, a three-year-old girl from Dikika, Ethiopia, dates to 3.3 Ma, about 100,000 years before Lucy.
Tooth chemistry shows a flexible diet, from forest plants to open savanna plants.
Africa then held more large carnivores than today, including hyenas and saber-toothed cats, which likely preyed on australopithecines.

entries.title: A green North Africa

facts.text: North Africa went through an extended humid period from about 3.8 to 3.3 million years ago.
Tropical forests in northwestern Africa reached as far as Cape Blanc until around 3.5 Ma.
A significant Saharan river flowed until 3.35 Ma, when trade winds began to dominate.

entries.title: Footprints in the ash at Laetoli

facts.text: At Laetoli in Tanzania, early hominins, probably Australopithecus, left footprints in fresh volcanic ash about 3.7 million years ago.
Soft rain then cemented the powdery ash into tuff, preserving the prints.
The tracks were made by three individuals, one walking in the footprints of another.
With the leg bones, the trackways suggest A. afarensis was a competent biped, though less efficient at walking than humans.
Dated to 3.7 million years ago within the upper Laetolil Beds (3.8-3.6 Ma), the prints were then the oldest known evidence of hominin bipedalism and closely resemble modern human footprints.

The prints closely resemble modern human footprints. They were then the oldest known evidence of hominin bipedalism. Together with leg bones, the trackways suggest A. afarensis walked well on two legs, though less efficiently than humans.

entries.title: Little Foot, the most complete early hominin

facts.text: Little Foot, an Australopithecus skeleton from the Sterkfontein caves of South Africa, is about 90% complete, the most complete early hominin skeleton known.
A 2015 radioisotopic date of 3.67 million years makes it the earliest known South African australopith, contemporary with A. afarensis.
Its dating is controversial, with estimates from 2.2 to 3.67 million years, and whether it belongs to A. africanus or another species is disputed.

entries.title: Megalodon disappears

facts.text: Megalodon, a giant shark estimated at 14-24 m long and among the most powerful predators ever, hunted worldwide from about 23 million years ago.
A 2019 statistical reanalysis of its fossil record moved its extinction back to about 3.6 million years ago, earlier than the long-assumed 2.6 million years.
Cooling seas, falling sea levels that shrank its warm nursery waters, and the decline of small baleen whales probably combined to finish it.
Competition from early killer whales, once blamed, now looks unlikely; rivalry with white sharks may have played a part instead.
Its loss let great white sharks spread into waters it had held, and baleen whales grew markedly larger afterwards.

entries.title: Mammoths and Asian elephants leave Africa

facts.text: The elephant genera Elephas and Mammuthus (mammoths) migrated out of Africa in the late Pliocene, around 3.6 to 3.2 million years ago.
Elephants, gomphotheres and stegodonts thrived in Asia, though proboscidean diversity fell sharply during the Late Pliocene.
By 3.2 million years ago mammoths had dispersed into Eurasia via the Sinai Peninsula, entering Europe around 3 million years ago.
In Africa, mammoths became confined to the north of the continent by the Late Pliocene.

entries.title: Australopiths reach Central Africa

facts.text: Jaw fossils from Koro Toro in Chad, about 3.5 million years old, are the first and only australopiths known from Central Africa.

They lived in lakeside grassland with sparse trees by an expanded 'Lake Mega-Chad', apparently eating mostly savanna foods.

entries.title: Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced rival

facts.text: Kenyanthropus, a flat-faced, small-toothed hominin, lived by Lake Turkana in Kenya; its type skull, lying between tuffs of 3.57 and 3.4 Ma, is about 3.5 million years old.
Its fossils span about 3.5 to 3.2 Ma and show that more than one hominin lineage lived in the Middle Pliocene alongside A. afarensis.
It shared a lakeside or floodplain mix of forest and grassland, and may have made the Lomekwian stone tools found at the same site.

entries.title: Camels in the High Arctic

facts.text: Fragmentary camel remains, referred to Paracamelus, come from Ellesmere Island inside the Arctic Circle and are about 3.4 million years old.
Global temperatures were then 2-3 °C warmer than today, and the island was covered in boreal forest.
Collagen sequences confirm these High Arctic camels were close relatives of modern Camelus.

entries.title: Dikika's disputed cut marks

facts.text: At Dikika, Ethiopia, a rib from a cow-sized hoofed animal and a juvenile bovid femur bear cut marks, the rib also some crushing.
If made by stone tools, they would be the oldest evidence of butchering with sharp-edged tools, at 3.4 million years, attributable to Australopithecus afarensis.
The claim is disputed: the bones lay in sandstone, where abrasive sand and gravel also scratched them.

entries.title: Lomekwi: the oldest stone tools

facts.text: The oldest known stone tools, from Lomekwi 3 in West Turkana, Kenya, date to 3.3 million years ago.
Their makers are unknown; Kenyanthropus platyops, a 3.5-3.2-million-year-old hominin from Lake Turkana, may have been the earliest tool user.
Cut-marked animal bones about 3.4 million years old from Ethiopia's Lower Awash Valley may be even older, indirect evidence of tool use.
The Paleolithic, which covers almost all of humanity's prehistoric technology, begins with the first stone tools about 3.3 million years ago.
The Lomekwian tools are simple flakes struck by pounding a core on an anvil or with a hammerstone, made from volcanic rock gathered within 100 m.

entries.title: The Phoenix plate stops sinking

facts.text: About 3.3 million years ago spreading on the Antarctic-Phoenix Ridge stopped, and subduction of the Phoenix plate slowed or ceased after over 100 million years.
The plate's remnant was absorbed into the Antarctic plate.

facts.text: A possible cosmic impact struck Argentina about 3.3 million years ago, at the start of the Marplatan land-mammal age.
It has been suggested as a cause of the turnover of South American fauna, but this remains controversial.

entries.title: The Mid-Piacenzian Warm Period

facts.text: Between 3.3 and 3.0 million years ago, global temperatures were 2-3 °C above today's, with carbon dioxide near 400 ppm, like the year 2000.
This peak of Pliocene warmth is also called the Pliocene Thermal Maximum.
Arctic summers were about 8 °C warmer than today, and Greenland's ice was limited to its highest eastern and southern peaks.
In southeastern European lakes, viviparid snails diversified rapidly as temperatures rose by as much as 10 °C between 3.3 and 2.9 Ma.
Global sea level stood about 25 m higher than today, and models suggest the Arctic above 70°N was 10-20 °C warmer, with little change in the tropics.

entries.title: Australopithecus africanus and the Taung Child

facts.text: Australopithecus africanus lived in South Africa from about 3.3 to 2.1 million years ago; its fossils come from Taung, Sterkfontein, Makapansgat and Gladysvale.
Its first specimen, the Taung Child, a juvenile skull about 2.8 million years old, was the first early hominin ever found.
A competent biped, though less efficient than humans, it kept a more apelike upper body than East Africa's A. afarensis.
It lived in gallery forest bordered by grassland and ate a highly varied diet, including C4 foods such as grasses and seeds.
It probably died out because of strong climatic volatility and perhaps competition with Homo and Paranthropus robustus.

entries.title: Lucy, the skeleton that walked before it thought big

facts.text: Lucy, a female Australopithecus afarensis whose skeleton is about 40% complete, lived at Hadar in Ethiopia's Afar region around 3.2 million years ago.
Ash layers beneath the fossil were argon-dated to 3.22 and 3.18 Ma; the younger lies only one metre below her.
Her small, ape-like skull paired with an upright, bipedal gait shows that walking upright came before larger brains.
Nearby, the 'First Family' site AL 333, about 3.2 million years old, holds at least thirteen individuals of different ages.

entries.title: The eastern Pacific's permanent El Niño ends

facts.text: A permanent El Niño-like state kept the eastern equatorial Pacific warm in the early to mid Pliocene, lowering Earth's reflectivity.
Around 3 million years ago cold surface water appeared there, which may have aided global cooling and changed climate's response to orbital cycles.

The warm water absorbed sunlight and lowered Earth's reflectivity. Around 3 million years ago, cold surface water appeared there. That change may have helped cool the globe. It may also have changed how Earth's climate responded to the slow cycles of its orbit.

entries.title: Savannas spread across East Africa

facts.text: Around 3 million years ago savanna expanded in East Africa as the climate turned cooler and drier.
Pliocene global cooling may have hastened the disappearance of forests and the spread of grasslands and savannas.
One hypothesis holds that walking upright and other hominin traits evolved as Pliocene climate change turned forests into more open savannah.
Moving from dense forest to savanna, where wildfires were common but easier to survive, may have been the first step toward early humans' control of fire.

entries.title: South America's native predators collapse

facts.text: Roughly 3 million years ago South America's native carnivore guild collapsed, including the last sparassodonts, the continent's meat-eating metatherians.
Thylacosmilids last occur about 3 Ma, already rarer before the interchange; terror birds also declined after that.
The collapse did not match the arrival of carnivorans: dogs and weasels reached South America about 2.9 Ma but stayed rare until the Pleistocene.
By the Pliocene only two sparassodont families were left; hathliacynids are last known from the early Pliocene.
The long sparassodont decline from the Late Miocene to the end of the Pliocene may be linked to cooling and the onset of Quaternary glaciation.

facts.text: The South Asian Summer Monsoon grew stronger after 2.95 Ma, probably because the Indonesian Throughflow was reorganized.

entries.text: After 2.95 Ma, the South Asian Summer Monsoon grew stronger. The likely cause lay at sea, in the Indonesian Throughflow, the current that carries water from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean between the islands of Indonesia. That flow was reorganized, and the monsoon responded, another sign of how ocean gateways shaped Asia's rains.

entries.title: Oldowan tools: the first widespread toolkit

facts.text: The Oldowan (Mode I), the first widespread stone-tool industry, was used by hominins across much of Africa from about 2.9 Ma until at least 1.7 Ma.
The oldest known Oldowan tools come from Nyayanga on the Homa Peninsula in Kenya, dated to about 2.9 million years ago.
Thousands of artifacts at Gona, Ethiopia, are firmly dated to 2.6 Ma by radioisotopes and magnetostratigraphy.
Sharp-edged tools of about 2.6 Ma at Ledi-Geraru may be the work of early Homo; Australopithecus garhi is another candidate maker.
The tools served mainly for butchering: 2.5-million-year-old tools lay beside cut-marked bones, and Homo habilis made Oldowan tools from about 2.3 Ma.

entries.title: The Isthmus of Panama joins the Americas

facts.text: South America became attached to North America through the newly formed Isthmus of Panama around 2.8 million years ago.
Raised at a convergent plate margin, partly by volcanism, it closed the last strait outside the polar regions linking the Pacific and Atlantic.
Surface-water exchange through the seaway may already have been fading by 4.6-4.2 Ma; the closing cut Pacific nutrients off from the Caribbean 4.5-3 Ma.
Closure ended the last remnant of a circum-equatorial current that had flowed since the Cretaceous, and pushed more heat and salt toward the North Atlantic.
Strengthened Gulf Stream and Humboldt currents cooled the Arctic, eventually leading to the Quaternary ice age glaciations.

entries.title: The Ledi-Geraru jaw, the first Homo

facts.text: The oldest known fossil of the genus Homo, the jawbone LD 350-1 from Ledi-Geraru in Ethiopia's Afar region, dates to 2.8-2.75 million years ago.
Its age suggests Homo may have evolved from Australopithecus afarensis around this time.
Homo is assumed to have emerged by about 2.8 Ma, most likely from australopithecine ancestors in East Africa's Rift Valley.
Teeth from Koobi Fora, Kenya, dated 3-2.7 Ma, may belong to the same species.
The origin of Homo 2.8-2.5 Ma coincided with climatic changes, but too few fossils are known to tell whether climate was the cause.

entries.title: The Great American Interchange

facts.text: From around 2.7 million years ago the new land bridge set off the last and largest wave of migration between the Americas.
Cats, condors, raccoons and camelids moved south; armadillos, hummingbirds and opossums moved north.
Ground sloths and glyptodonts reached North America; xenarthrans were among South America's most successful emigrants.
Horses and tapirs entered South America, where competition from northern hoofed mammals helped push native ungulates toward extinction.
The exchange was lopsided: extinction rates were much higher in South America, and North American groups diversified greatly there.

Crossings had begun earlier, as {{ref:mioc-118}} shows, but the land bridge turned a trickle into a flood.

entries.title: Ice spreads across the Northern Hemisphere

facts.text: Around 2.7 million years ago temperatures dropped and glaciation began in the Northern Hemisphere.
Greenland's separate ice caps merged into one ice sheet covering most of the island once carbon dioxide fell to 280-320 ppm, 2.7-2.6 Ma.
Ice-rafted cobbles on North Atlantic and North Pacific seabeds and an abrupt shift in oxygen isotopes mark the new Arctic ice.
Suggested causes include falling carbon dioxide and a stronger North Atlantic circulation after Panama closed, which carried moisture north.
A weakening Indonesian Throughflow cut heat transport toward Antarctica, cooling Earth in a self-reinforcing loop as sea levels fell.

entries.text: Around 2.7 million years ago temperatures dropped, and glaciation began in the Northern Hemisphere. The evidence lies on the seafloor. Ice-rafted cobbles, dropped by melting icebergs on North Atlantic and North Pacific seabeds, and an abrupt shift in oxygen isotopes mark the new Arctic ice. Greenland's separate ice caps merged into one ice sheet covering most of the island, once carbon dioxide fell to 280-320 ppm, 2.7-2.6 Ma. Several causes are suggested. One is falling carbon dioxide. Another is a stronger North Atlantic circulation after Panama closed, which carried moisture north to feed the ice. A weakening Indonesian Throughflow also cut the heat carried toward Antarctica. As sea levels fell, that cooling fed on itself in a self-reinforcing loop.

entries.title: Paranthropus, the robust hominins, appear

facts.text: The robust hominin genus Paranthropus evolved around 2.7 million years ago.
Paranthropus aethiopicus is known from Lake Turkana, Kenya, and the genus was still present at the start of the Pleistocene.
Its earliest species, P. aethiopicus, lived in East Africa about 2.7-2.3 Ma; the oldest remains, from Ethiopia's Omo Kibish Formation, date to 2.6 Ma.

entries.title: Supernovae leave iron-60 on the seafloor

facts.text: Radioactive iron-60, which only supernovae can make, points to a large influx about 2.6 million years ago, recorded in ancient seabed deposits.
A scattered excess over 10 million years suggests several relatively close supernovae, perhaps from the passing Scorpius-Centaurus OB association.
So close an explosion could have damaged Earth's ozone layer and killed some ocean life.

entries.text: Only supernovae, exploding stars, can make radioactive iron-60. Ancient seabed deposits record a large influx of it about 2.6 million years ago. A scattered excess over 10 million years suggests several fairly close supernovae, perhaps from the passing Scorpius-Centaurus group of young stars. So close an explosion could have damaged Earth's ozone layer and killed some ocean life.

entries.title: The magnetic flip that starts the Quaternary

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field flipped from normal polarity (the Gauss Chron) to reversed polarity (the Matuyama Chron) about 2.58 Ma.
The reversal marks the base of the Gelasian and so the start of the Pleistocene and the Quaternary; the boundary stratotype is at Monte San Nicola, Sicily.
It coincides with a minor extinction of calcareous nannofossils, including Discoaster pentaradiatus and Discoaster surculus.
The weakened field may have left Earth's surface unshielded for about 15,000 years from the radiation of an early Pleistocene supernova.
In 2009 the boundary was moved down to 2.58 Ma to match key changes in Earth's climate, oceans and life at that time.

entries.text: About 2.58 Ma, Earth's magnetic field flipped. It went from normal polarity, the Gauss Chron, to reversed polarity, the Matuyama Chron. Geologists use the flip as a marker. It defines the base of the Gelasian, and so the start of both the Pleistocene and the Quaternary, with the reference section at Monte San Nicola in Sicily. In 2009 the boundary was moved down to 2.58 Ma to match key changes in climate, oceans and life at that time. The flip coincides with a minor extinction of calcareous nannofossils, tiny chalky plankton, among them Discoaster pentaradiatus and Discoaster surculus. The weakened field may have left Earth's surface unshielded for about 15,000 years from the radiation of a supernova.

entries.title: The Quaternary ice age begins

facts.text: Around 2.58 Ma ice sheets began to spread across the Northern Hemisphere, starting the Quaternary glaciation, which is still going on.
The Quaternary's start is tied to the formation of the Arctic ice cap; Greenland had been icing over since the late Pliocene.
Glacials and interglacials then alternated, with mean temperatures falling and the swings between them growing through the Pleistocene.
At the height of glacials, ice sheets at least 4 km thick covered parts of Europe, North America and Siberia.
In the first Pleistocene glacial, Patagonian ice reached the present Argentine coast.

entries.text: At the height of the glacials, ice at least 4 km thick covered parts of Europe, North America and Siberia. That world began around 2.58 Ma, when ice sheets started to spread across the Northern Hemisphere. This was the start of the Quaternary glaciation, and it is still going on. The start of the Quaternary is tied to the formation of the Arctic ice cap. Greenland had been icing over since the late Pliocene, as {{ref:plio-058}} describes. From then on, glacials and interglacials, cold spells and warmer breaks, alternated. Through the Pleistocene, mean temperatures fell and the swings between the two grew larger. The south felt it too. In the first Pleistocene glacial, Patagonian ice reached the present Argentine coast.

entries.title: Mastodons and gomphotheres vanish outside the Americas

facts.text: During the Early Pleistocene all non-elephantid proboscideans outside the Americas died out, including mammutids, gomphotheres and deinotheres; only Stegodon survived.

entries.text: The elephant's relatives had once roamed widely across the Old World. During the Early Pleistocene, every proboscidean outside the Americas that was not a true elephant died out. Mammutids, gomphotheres and deinotheres all disappeared. Only Stegodon survived. Outside the Americas, the trunked mammals were reduced to the elephant family and that one holdout. It was a sharp narrowing for a group that had spread out of Africa in {{ref:mioc-037}}.

entries.title: The Eltanin asteroid strikes the deep ocean

facts.text: An asteroid about 1–4 km wide hit the deep ocean at the edge of the Bellingshausen Sea, about 1,500 km southwest of Chile.
It struck sea floor 4–5 km deep and left no known crater; the site was found from an iridium anomaly in sediment cores.
The impact probably vaporised about 150 km³ of water and raised tsunami waves hundreds of metres high.

entries.title: Ice at both poles dries the planet

facts.text: Bipolar glaciation dried the globe, speeding a long decline in the functional diversity of hoofed mammals around 2.5 Ma.
In Africa a cooling and drying trend about 2.5 Ma coincided with the rise of thick-molared Homo rudolfensis and Paranthropus.
In Australia an aridification event at 2.56 Ma may be linked to the onset of continental glaciation in the Arctic.
Around 2.5 Ma the Omo–Turkana Basin mixed forest, woodland, grassland and bushland, with grasslands spreading through the Early Pleistocene.

verification.title: Two major ecological shifts shaped 60 million years of ungulate faunal evolution

entries.text: With ice now at both poles, the globe dried out. That drying sped up a long decline in the functional diversity of hoofed mammals around 2.5 Ma, the range of different ways they made a living. Africa cooled and dried about 2.5 Ma, at the same time as the rise of thick-molared Homo rudolfensis and Paranthropus. In Australia an aridification event at 2.56 Ma may be linked to the start of Arctic glaciation. Around 2.5 Ma, the Omo–Turkana Basin held a mix of forest, woodland, grassland and bushland, and its grasslands kept spreading through the Early Pleistocene.

entries.title: Early Homo and robust australopithecines branch out

facts.text: About 2.5 Ma hominin fossils in East Africa become extraordinarily diverse, with robust australopithecines and early Homo appearing first in the Turkana Basin.
This apparent adaptive radiation of hominins straddles the Pliocene–Pleistocene boundary.
The first Homo species appeared about 2.5 Ma; earlier hominins had kept their tree-climbing habits until then.
Brain size rose quickly, and by 2 Ma the first animals classed in the genus Homo had appeared.
Paranthropus and early Homo coexisted at the start of the Pleistocene, but only Homo erectus remained for much of it.

entries.title: Ethiopian waters join the Nile

facts.text: About 2.5 Ma waters from Ethiopia flowed north for the first time and joined the ancestral Egyptian Nile.
Uplift of the Rwenzori Mountains turned paleolake Obweruka's drainage east and began forming Lake Victoria, which did not yet drain north.

entries.title: Smilodon and the short-faced bear appear

facts.text: The earliest species of the sabre-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus evolved about 2.5 Ma.
The earliest species, S. gracilis, lived from 2.5 million to 500,000 years ago and probably evolved from Megantereon; it reached northern South America in the Great American Interchange.
Smilodon lived in the Americas until at latest 8,200 years ago and was perhaps the last of the sabre-toothed cats.

entries.title: Paranthropus boisei shares Africa with early Homo

facts.text: Paranthropus boisei, a robust australopithecine, lived in East Africa about 2.5 to 1.15 million years ago; its oldest remains, from Malema, are about 2.3 million years old.
It is found at Koobi Fora and in Olduvai Gorge Beds I and II, persisting after H. habilis gave way to H. erectus around 1.6 Ma.
The 1.7-million-year-old skull KNM-ER 406, with a 510 cc brain, shows several hominin species shared Africa at once.

entries.title: Lake Bungunnia dams the Murray

facts.text: Earth movements blocked the Murray River near Swan Reach, creating vast freshwater Lake Bungunnia, which lasted from 2.5 to 0.5 Ma.
The damming followed more than 250 m of uplift in the Grampians of Victoria about 2.5 Ma.

entries.title: Pre-Illinoian ice reaches Kansas and Missouri

facts.text: North America went through repeated Pre-Illinoian glacial and interglacial periods from about 2.5 to 0.2 million years ago.
Researchers found 11 distinct glaciations in this span, not the two once assumed, and discarded the old Nebraskan, Aftonian, Kansan and Yarmouthian stages.
The Laurentide Ice Sheet reached as far south as the Missouri and Ohio river valleys, and to Douglas County, Kansas.
Later Illinoian ice sheets pushed farther south still, to near Carbondale, Illinois.
Patchy Pre-Illinoian glacial drift more than 500,000 years old survives in parts of the Driftless Area of the upper Mississippi.

entries.text: Researchers once counted two great glaciations in North America's early ice age. They now count 11. From about 2.5 to 0.2 million years ago, the continent went through repeated Pre-Illinoian glacial and interglacial periods. The old named stages, the Nebraskan, Aftonian, Kansan and Yarmouthian, were discarded. The Laurentide Ice Sheet reached as far south as the Missouri and Ohio river valleys, and to Douglas County, Kansas. Later Illinoian ice sheets pushed farther still, to near Carbondale, Illinois. Patchy glacial drift, debris dumped by the ice, more than 500,000 years old survives in parts of the Driftless Area of the upper Mississippi.

entries.title: The last seaway across Panama closes

facts.text: The last shallow, temporary sea connection through the Central American Seaway ended no later than 2.45 Ma.
Deep-ocean connections had already closed between 12 and 9.2 Ma, after a collision that began about 25 Ma.
Surface-water exchange that kept Atlantic and Pacific salinities alike ended about 4.6 Ma; a last definite temporary breach came as recently as 2.45 Ma.

entries.title: The Amazon settles into its present course

facts.text: The Amazon, a transcontinental river since 11.8–11.3 Ma, took its present shape about 2.4 million years ago.

entries.text: The Amazon had already been a transcontinental river since 11.8–11.3 Ma, as {{ref:mioc-099}} describes. It took its present shape later, about 2.4 million years ago. So the river that crosses the continent is old, but its present layout is young. Its shape settled in the same cold, dry stretch that saw ice spread across the north.

entries.title: Wind-blown dust builds the Loess Plateau

facts.text: Crustal movement and a cold climate started loess deposition on the Loess Plateau about 2.4 Ma.
Tibetan uplift had set up the East Asian monsoon, and the drier Quaternary climate weathered out the silt that became loess.

entries.text: About 2.4 Ma, crustal movement and a cold climate started laying down loess on China's Loess Plateau. Loess is fine, wind-blown silt that piles up in thick blankets. Several causes lined up. Tibetan uplift had set up the East Asian monsoon, as {{ref:mioc-007}} describes. Then the drier Quaternary climate weathered out the silt. The winds carried it away and dropped it, layer upon layer, over the plateau.

entries.title: Sundaland emerges and mammals reach Java

facts.text: Sundaland emerged around 2.4 Ma; before then Java had no mammals.
As sea level fell, animals such as the dwarf elephant relative Sinomastodon bumiajuensis colonised Sundaland from mainland Asia.

entries.text: Before about 2.4 Ma, Java had no mammals. Then Sundaland, the shallow shelf of Southeast Asia, emerged as sea level fell. Animals walked across from mainland Asia, among them Sinomastodon bumiajuensis, a dwarf elephant relative, and colonized the newly exposed land.

entries.title: Oldowan tools spread across and out of Africa

facts.text: Oldowan stone tools flourished in eastern Africa and spread to southern Africa between 2.4 and 1.7 million years ago.
Securely dated Oldowan artefacts 2.4–1.9 million years old at Ain Boucherit, Algeria, carry the industry into North Africa.
At Swartkrans, South Africa, Oldowan tools of 2.2–1.8 Ma lie with Paranthropus robustus fossils; a polished bone point there dates to 1.8–1.5 Ma.
Oldowan toolmakers also left Africa: by 1.8 Ma early Homo with Oldowan tools lived at Dmanisi, Georgia.
Acheulean tools appeared about 1.7 Ma, yet Oldowan assemblages went on being made beside them; other traditions supplanted the Oldowan only by about 0.25 Ma.

entries.title: Homo habilis, the 'handy man'

facts.text: Homo habilis, the 'handy man', lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago.
Its brain ranged from about 500 to 900 cm³, and it may still have climbed trees like the australopithecines.
It made Oldowan stone tools and, unlike australopithecines, ate much meat, probably scavenged.
Around 2 Ma it may have built the first structures, stones propping up branches; a 1.75 Ma stone circle at Olduvai is the oldest claimed architecture.
Whether it was the direct ancestor of Homo erectus is now debated.

entries.text: Homo habilis, the 'handy man', lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago. Its brain ranged from about 500 to 900 cm³, and it may still have climbed trees like the australopithecines. It made Oldowan stone tools. Unlike australopithecines, it ate much meat, probably scavenged. Around 2 Ma it may have built the first structures, stones propping up branches. A 1.75 Ma stone circle at Olduvai is the oldest claimed architecture. Whether it was the direct ancestor of Homo erectus is now debated.

entries.title: Shangchen: stone tools in China before Dmanisi?

facts.text: Possible stone artefacts at Shangchen, central China, are dated by magnetostratigraphy to 2.12 Ma, about 300,000 years before Dmanisi.
If confirmed, they are the oldest known stone tools outside Africa.
Pebble tools are also reported from Yiron, Israel, at 2.4 Ma, Riwat, Pakistan, at 2.0 Ma and Renzidong, China, at over 2 Ma.
They suggest Homo habilis or an ancestral species may have spread across Asia.
Tools perhaps 2.48 million years old from the Zarqa Valley, Jordan, could likewise mean a hominin earlier than H. erectus left Africa.

entries.title: Huckleberry Ridge, Yellowstone's greatest eruption

facts.text: Yellowstone volcanism began 2.15 Ma; its first and largest cycle climaxed in the eruption of the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff.
The VEI 8 eruption produced about 2,450–2,500 km³ of material and left the Island Park Caldera, roughly 80 by 65 km.
It made about 2,500 times as much ash as Mount St. Helens in 1980; the ash is found from southern California to St. Louis.
Part of the tuff records the Huckleberry Ridge geomagnetic excursion and is dated very precisely to 2.0773 ± 0.0034 Ma.

entries.title: Homo erectus appears in Africa

facts.text: The oldest identified Homo erectus is DNH 134, a 2.04-million-year-old skull from Drimolen, South Africa, which lived alongside Paranthropus robustus.
Other early fossils include the roughly 1.9-million-year-old KNM-ER 2598 and the cranium KNM-ER 3733 from Koobi Fora, Kenya.
Its populations spread through grassland and woodland savannas, which were expanding with global aridification at the onset of the Quaternary glaciation.
H. ergaster, often treated as African H. erectus, was the first human with a slender, modern body plan.
Most H. erectus fossils date from 1.8 to 1 Ma; the species lasted until about 0.6 Ma and was long the only hominin.

entries.title: Homo spreads out of Africa
entries.article: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

facts.text: The earliest hominins outside Africa date to close to 2 million years ago, at the start of expansions led by Homo erectus.
In the Early Pleistocene archaic Homo arose in Africa and spread throughout Afro-Eurasia, in waves known together as Out of Africa I.
Key early sites are Riwat in Pakistan (about 2 Ma), Dmanisi in the Caucasus (1.81 Ma) and Ubeidiya in the Levant (1.5 Ma).
Favourable climate swings probably opened the Levantine corridor to the adaptable Homo erectus, perhaps only at times.
The dispersal has been linked to the Saharan pump around 1.9 Ma; by 2.0–1.5 Ma hominins were settling southern Europe and Asia.

entries.text: The earliest hominins outside Africa date to close to 2 million years ago. They mark the start of expansions led by Homo erectus. entries.title: Homo rudolfensis in East Africa

facts.text: Homo rudolfensis lived in East Africa about 2 million years ago; most of its fossils come from Koobi Fora and date to 1.9–1.85 Ma.
Fossils from Ethiopia and Malawi dated 2.5–2.4 Ma could make it the earliest known Homo, but which specimens belong to it is disputed.
Its molar enamel was almost as thick as that of Paranthropus.

entries.title: Kap København: a lost Greenland world in DNA

facts.text: Environmental DNA from the Kap København Formation in northern Greenland is at least two million years old, from the Early Pleistocene.
It records mastodons, Arctic hares, geese, poplar, birch and willow trees, horseshoe crabs and corals; mastodons evidently ranged much farther north than once thought.
The site's average minimum temperature is reconstructed at more than 10 °C warmer than today.

entries.title: South America's native predators fade further

facts.text: The sabre-toothed thylacosmilids, among South America's only large mammalian carnivores in the Pliocene, died out about 2 Ma.
Placental counterparts such as dogs, weasels and sabre-toothed cats entered South America only in the early Pleistocene.
The terror bird Titanis, which had crossed into North America, died out there about 1.8 Ma, perhaps outcompeted by carnivorans.
Bears, cats and skunks reached South America by about 1 Ma, when the short-faced bear Arctotherium first appears there.

entries.title: The Acheulean: a toolkit for a million years

facts.text: Acheulean technology, derived from the Oldowan, first developed about 2 million years ago; finds from Ethiopia date to 1.95 Ma.
Homo erectus is credited with inventing it by 1.95 Ma, inheriting Oldowan technology and refining it.
Early Acheulean tools from West Turkana, Kenya, date to about 1.76 Ma, and those at Kokiselei to 1.7–1.6 Ma.
It spread from Africa to Asia, the Middle East and Europe between 1.5 Ma and about 800,000 years ago, reaching southern India by 1.51 Ma.
Its end is poorly defined; counting the Sangoan, it lasted until as late as 130,000 years ago.

entries.title: Dmanisi: the oldest human bones outside Africa

facts.text: Hominins lived at Dmanisi, Georgia, from about 1.8 Ma; their fossils are the oldest human skeletal remains known outside Africa.
Fossils and tools span 1.85 to 1.77 million years, the earliest well-dated hominin fossils in Eurasia; argon dating gives 1.81 ± 0.03 Ma.
The site yielded five skulls, including Skull 5, the first complete adult hominin skull from the Early Pleistocene, plus stone tools and animal fossils.
The fossils, classed as Homo erectus georgicus, resemble early African Homo so much that all early Homo may be one species.
One toothless elderly skull has been read as early evidence of care for the old or disabled.

entries.title: A magnetic flip marks the start of the Calabrian

facts.text: The Olduvai subchron, a spell of normal magnetic polarity within the reversed Matuyama chron, lasted from about 1.95 to 1.77 Ma.
The Calabrian Age begins at 1.8 Ma, just above the top of the Olduvai chronozone and the extinction of the nannofossil Discoaster brouweri.
Its reference section is at Vrica, near Crotone in Calabria, southern Italy.
Before 2009 this level, then dated 1.806 Ma, was the base of the Pleistocene.

entries.text: Compasses would have pointed the other way for most of the early Pleistocene. Earth's magnetic field sat in a reversed state called the Matuyama chron, broken by short spells of normal polarity. One of these, the Olduvai subchron, lasted from about 1.95 to 1.77 million years ago. The Calabrian Age begins at 1.8 million years ago, just above the top of the Olduvai layers. Before 2009 this level, then dated to 1.806 million years ago, marked the very base of the Pleistocene.

entries.title: The wolf event spreads Canis across Eurasia

facts.text: Around 1.8 Ma Canis evolution exploded across Eurasia in what is called the wolf event.
The large wolf C. falconeri appeared abruptly in Europe, and C. borjgali lived at Dmanisi 1.8–1.75 Ma.
Coyote and wolf lineages split about 1.5 Ma; the first coyotes appear about 1.0 Ma and the first wolves about 810,000 years ago.

entries.title: Charred bones hint at the first use of fire
entries.article: Control of fire by early humans

facts.text: Charred bones deep in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, beyond the reach of wildfires, show human use of fire about 1.79 million years ago.
Other early claims include blackened bones at Yuanmou, China, about 1.7 Ma, and reddened, heated sediment at Koobi Fora, Kenya, about 1.5 Ma.
Some studies read Homo erectus' smaller molars as a sign of cooking by about 1.8 Ma; in Africa people may have scavenged fire from frequent wildfires by 1.6 Ma.

entries.text: Deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, beyond the reach of wildfires, lie charred bones. They have been read as human use of fire about 1.79 million years ago. Some studies read the smaller molars of Homo erectus as a sign of cooking.

entries.title: Diprotodon, the largest marsupial ever

facts.text: The earliest Diprotodon fossils, indirectly dated, come from the Nelson Bay Formation in New South Wales and are 1.77 million to 780,000 years old.
Diprotodon was the largest marsupial that ever lived and the largest herbivore in Australia.
Most specimens are younger than 110,000 years; the oldest directly dated fossils, from Floraville, are about 340,000 years old.

entries.title: Homo erectus reaches China and Java

facts.text: Homo erectus was at Yuanmou in southern China by 1.7 Ma and at Sangiran on Java by 1.66 Ma.
A Lantian cranium dates to 1.63 Ma, and stone tools in northern China's Nihewan basin to 1.7–1.6 Ma.
Yunxian Man in China is dated to 1.77 Ma; Java's Mojokerto child, once put at 1.81 Ma, is now dated to at most 1.49 Ma.
By 1.3 Ma Oldowan tools had reached as far north as the 40th parallel at Xiaochangliang.
By 1 Ma Homo erectus had spread across Eurasia, mostly south of the 50th parallel.

entries.title: Two blasts build the Valles Caldera

facts.text: In New Mexico's Jemez Mountains, the Toledo eruption 1.61 Ma laid down the Otowi member of the Bandelier Tuff.
It produced 216–550 km³ of dense rock; the larger estimate puts it at the low end of supereruptions (VEI 8).
A second great eruption about 1.25 Ma laid down the Tshirege member and formed the Valles Caldera, one of the best-studied resurgent calderas.

entries.text: New Mexico's Jemez Mountains hide the scar of two enormous eruptions. The first, the Toledo eruption 1.61 million years ago, laid down the Otowi member of the Bandelier Tuff, a rock made of welded volcanic ash. It produced 216 to 550 km³ of dense rock, and the larger estimate makes it a small supereruption, VEI 8. A second great eruption about 1.25 million years ago laid down the Tshirege member and formed the Valles Caldera. It is one of the best-studied resurgent calderas, craters whose floors later bulged back up.

entries.title: Turkana Boy, the most complete Homo erectus

facts.text: Turkana Boy (KNM-WT 15000), a Homo erectus youth who lived 1.6–1.5 Ma near Lake Turkana, Kenya, is the most complete H. erectus skeleton ever found.
Some authorities assign it to Homo ergaster.
Its spinal column could not have supported the well-developed breathing muscles needed for speech.

entries.title: The first Missoula floods scour the Scablands

facts.text: The oldest Pleistocene Missoula floods swept through the Channeled Scablands sometime before 1.5 million years ago.
The age rests on interglacial calcretes between flood deposits, magnetostratigraphy and luminescence dating.

Magnetic dating of the layers and luminescence dating, which measures when grains last saw light, back it up.

entries.title: Mammoths cross into North America

facts.text: Mammoths migrated into North America around 1.5 Ma, while gomphotheres spread into South America in the Great American Interchange.
Their spread south of Alaska, about 1.4 Ma, is often used to end the Blancan and start the Irvingtonian land-mammal age.
Mammoths had left Africa in the late Pliocene, about 3.6–3.2 Ma.
The steppe mammoth arose in East Asia around 1.7 Ma and crossed the Bering Land Bridge 1.5–1.3 Ma, giving rise to the Columbian mammoth.
DNA from a 1.1–1.65-million-year-old Siberian tooth reveals the Krestovka lineage, probably the first mammoths to colonise the Americas.

entries.title: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition stretches the ice ages

facts.text: Between about 1.25 and 0.7 Ma, glacial cycles lengthened from about 41,000 years to asymmetric 100,000-year cycles, making climate swings more extreme.
Afterwards, long cold spells built thick, higher and less slippery ice sheets, which ended in rapid jumps to warm interglacials.
Around 850,000 ± 50,000 years ago, orbital eccentricity replaced axial tilt as the main pacemaker of the ice ages.
Models reproduce the shift with falling atmospheric CO2 and glaciers gradually scraping regolith off the northern continents.
The severe glacial MIS 22 brought widespread aridity to Africa and may have caused a bottleneck in human ancestors about 1 Ma.

entries.text: The rhythm of the ice ages changed, and the swings grew wilder. Between about 1.25 and 0.7 million years ago, glacial cycles lengthened from about 41,000 years to lopsided cycles of about 100,000 years. This shift is the Mid-Pleistocene Transition. Afterwards, long cold spells built ice sheets that were thicker, higher and less slippery. Each cycle then ended in a rapid jump to a warm interglacial. Around 850,000 ± 50,000 years ago, the stretch of Earth's orbit, its eccentricity, replaced the tilt of its axis as the main pacemaker of the ice ages. What caused the change is still worked out with models. They reproduce it with two slow trends: falling carbon dioxide in the air, and glaciers gradually scraping loose rock and soil off the northern continents. The new climate reached people too. A severe glacial stage, MIS 22, brought widespread drought to Africa. It may have squeezed human ancestors into a population bottleneck about 1 million years ago.

entries.title: Homo antecessor, the pioneer of Western Europe

facts.text: Homo antecessor, 'pioneer man', is recorded at Spain's Sierra de Atapuerca from 1.2 to 0.8 Ma, among the first people to settle Western Europe.

Once proposed as the last common ancestor of modern humans and Neanderthals, it is now seen as a side branch splitting just before them.

entries.title: Kilimanjaro's Kibo and Mawenzi cones awaken

facts.text: Kibo and Mawenzi, two of Kilimanjaro's three volcanic cones, began erupting about 1 million years ago; the older Shira centre had been active since 2.4 million years ago.

Kilimanjaro, at 5,895 m the highest peak in Africa, is a dormant stratovolcano; Kibo still has gas-emitting fumaroles in its crater.

facts.text: Earth's field briefly returned to normal polarity within the reversed Matuyama chron, usually dated from 990,000 to 950,000 years ago.
Some studies start it at 1.07 Ma instead; the causes of such short reversals are still disputed.
A proposed link to the Bosumtwi impact has been called highly speculative and refuted.

entries.title: Footprints on the Norfolk shore

facts.text: Hominin footprints pressed into sediment at Happisburgh, Norfolk, between about 950,000 and 850,000 years ago are the oldest known outside Africa.
They are the first evidence of early humans this far north, alongside flint tools from the same deposits.
The makers may have been Homo antecessor; the beds lie between the Jaramillo and Brunhes–Matuyama reversals.

entries.title: A hidden impact scatters glass across Australasia

facts.text: About 790,000 years ago a large impact scattered tektites across the enormous Australasian strewnfield.
Its crater has not been found; one about 100 km wide in Indochina, perhaps under Tonlé Sap in Cambodia, has been suggested.
Artifacts found with its tektites tie a Homo erectus population to the impact and its aftermath.
A link to the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal is highly speculative; the two probably only happened around the same time.

entries.title: Cooking fish at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov

facts.text: Around 780,000 years ago, hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in northern Israel left traces of fire and the oldest likely evidence of cooking, mainly heated fish teeth.
It is the oldest established continuous fire site outside Africa; H. erectus or H. ergaster is claimed to have controlled fire there 790,000–690,000 years ago.
Its inhabitants gathered and ate 55 kinds of fruits, vegetables, seeds, nuts and tubers.

entries.title: The Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, Earth's last magnetic flip

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field last reversed, ending the Matuyama chron (C1r) and opening the present Brunhes chron (C1n).
Estimates of the flip's length range from within a human lifetime to several thousand years, or about 22,000 years.
Its apparent duration at any one site can vary tenfold with geomagnetic latitude and local quirks of the field.
The reversal marks the GSSP for the base of the Chibanian Stage at the Chiba section in Japan, ratified in 2020.
It is a standard tie-point for dating ocean sediment cores and volcanic rocks.

entries.text: About 774,000 years ago, a compass needle would have swung around to point the way it points today. Earth's magnetic field last reversed then, ending the Matuyama chron, known as C1r, and opening the present Brunhes chron, C1n. Nobody knows quite how long the flip took. Estimates range from within a single human lifetime to several thousand years, or about 22,000 years. Part of the confusion is local. The apparent length of the flip at any one site can vary tenfold with geomagnetic latitude and local quirks of the field. Because it shows up worldwide in rock, the reversal is a precious marker. It is a standard tie-point for dating ocean sediment cores and volcanic rocks. In 2020 it was ratified as the golden spike, the GSSP, for the base of the Chibanian Stage, at the Chiba section in Japan.

entries.title: A turnover of mammals at the Middle Pleistocene

facts.text: With Sinomastodon's extinction in East Asia, gomphotheres vanished from Afro-Eurasia, though they survived in the Americas into the Late Pleistocene.
A major extinction of European carnivorous mammals, including the giant hyena Pachycrocuta, occurred around the same transition.
True horses migrated out of North America into Eurasia at the Early–Middle Pleistocene boundary.
In Europe the mammoth Mammuthus meridionalis died out and was replaced by the Asian steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii.
The elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread from Africa into Eurasia, including the first straight-tusked elephants (Palaeoloxodon antiquus).

entries.text: As the Early Pleistocene gave way to the Middle, the cast of big mammals reshuffled. Sinomastodon died out in East Asia, and with it gomphotheres vanished from Africa and Eurasia, though they survived in the Americas into the Late Pleistocene. Many European carnivores died out, including the giant hyena Pachycrocuta. True horses migrated from North America into Eurasia. In Europe the mammoth Mammuthus meridionalis gave way to the Asian steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii. Out of Africa came Palaeoloxodon, including the first straight-tusked elephants, Palaeoloxodon antiquus.

entries.title: The Bishop Tuff eruption opens Long Valley Caldera

facts.text: A VEI-7 eruption in eastern California released about 600 km³ of material, which cooled into the Bishop Tuff.
Draining the magma chamber caused collapse, leaving Long Valley Caldera, about 32 by 18 km and one of Earth's largest calderas.
Pyroclastic flows burned and buried thousands of square miles, and ash blanketed much of the western United States.

entries.text: About 760,000 years ago, eastern California exploded. A VEI 7 eruption released about 600 km³ of material, which cooled into a rock called the Bishop Tuff. Pyroclastic flows, avalanches of scorching gas and ash, burned and buried thousands of square miles. Ash blanketed much of the western United States. With its magma chamber drained, the ground above collapsed. The hole left behind, Long Valley Caldera, measures about 32 by 18 km and is one of the largest calderas on Earth.

entries.title: The 100,000-year ice-age rhythm takes hold

facts.text: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition, under way since about 1.25 million years ago, was complete by about 0.7 million years ago.
Ice-age rhythm shifted from 41,000-year cycles to asymmetric, high-amplitude cycles averaging 100,000 years, making climate swings more extreme.
Interglacials after the transition had more atmospheric carbon dioxide than those before it.
Since about 600,000 years ago, six major glacial periods have lowered sea level by up to 120 m, exposing continental margins.

entries.text: By about 700,000 years ago, Earth's climate had settled into the beat it still keeps. The Mid-Pleistocene Transition, under way since about 1.25 million years ago, was complete. Before it, ice ages came and went in cycles of about 41,000 years. Afterwards they followed lopsided, high-amplitude cycles averaging 100,000 years. Ice built up slowly over long cold spells, then melted fast, so the climate swings became more extreme. The warm spells changed too. Interglacials after the transition had more carbon dioxide in the air than those before it. The ice sheets of the new cycles locked up enormous amounts of water. Since about 600,000 years ago, six major glacial periods have lowered sea level by up to 120 m. Each time, the shallow edges of the continents were laid bare as dry land.

Late Acheulean culture, usually tied to the dispersal of Homo heidelbergensis, spread across Europe and Africa by the beginning of the Middle Pleistocene.

entries.title: The Eridanos, a lost river of Europe, dies

facts.text: During the first glacial stage of the Cromerian Complex, sedimentation by the Baltic River System in the Netherlands ended, marking the end of the Eridanos.
Repeated Scandinavian ice caps destroyed its source area and gouged the basin where the Baltic Sea later formed.
At its height about 2 Ma, the Eridanos ran some 2,700 km from Lapland across the Baltic region to a vast delta in western Europe.

entries.title: The Lava Creek supereruption at Yellowstone

facts.text: Yellowstone's third-cycle climactic eruption produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera.
Rated VEI 8, it ejected more than 1,000 km³ of rock, dust and volcanic ash.
Its ash bed spread over 3–4 million km², and debris up to two metres deep covered a large part of North America.
It capped several hundred thousand years of rhyolitic volcanism and struck near the shift from glacial MIS 16 to interglacial MIS 15.
Eruptions of this size happen somewhere on Earth about every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

entries.text: About 631,000 years ago, Yellowstone tore itself open. Its third cycle peaked in a climactic eruption that produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera. Rated VEI 8, the top of the scale, it ejected more than 1,000 km³ of rock, dust and volcanic ash. Debris up to two meters deep covered a large part of North America, and the ash bed spread over 3 to 4 million km². The blast capped several hundred thousand years of rhyolitic volcanism, the explosive kind fed by sticky, silica-rich magma. It struck near the shift from the glacial MIS 16 to the interglacial MIS 15. Such events are rare on a human scale but common on a geological one. Eruptions this size happen somewhere on Earth about every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

entries.title: Homo heidelbergensis, the muddle in the middle

facts.text: Homo heidelbergensis evolved about 600,000 years ago in Africa as a derived form of Homo erectus.
Fossils from the MIS 15 interglacial (621–563 ka) include Heidelberg Man and the Bodo cranium.
It was the likely ancestor of Denisovans and Neanderthals, and perhaps of modern humans.
Some scholars place the first symbolic communication with this species.
It is a controversial, poorly defined species; the tangle of Middle Pleistocene Homo forms is nicknamed the 'muddle in the middle'.

entries.title: The woolly mammoth evolves in Siberia

facts.text: The woolly mammoth evolved from the steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii, in Siberia by around 600,000–500,000 years ago.
Its lineage had begun to diverge about 800,000 years ago; molars with 26 ridges, the woolly mammoth's mark, appeared about 400,000 years ago.
Siberian mammoths over a million years old already carried many of the woolly mammoth's genes for tolerating cold.
Columbian mammoths descend half from woolly mammoths and half from the Krestovka lineage, which hybridised more than 420,000 years ago.
Woolly mammoth numbers crashed around 280,000 years ago, then recovered.

entries.title: Tautavel Man in the Arago Cave

facts.text: Archaic humans lived in the Caune de l'Arago, a limestone cave at Tautavel in France, from about 550,000 to 400,000 years ago.

The landscape swung repeatedly between temperate forest and cold, dry grassy steppe.

Homo erectus lived at Trinil 540,000–430,000 years ago, part of a long occupation of Java that began at Sangiran 1.51–0.93 million years ago.

entries.title: MIS 13, a Cromerian warm spell

facts.text: MIS 13 was an interglacial covering the late Cromerian in Britain, about 524,000–474,000 years ago.
It began with birch, pine and spruce, and followed the relatively warm glacial MIS 14 before the cold MIS 12 glacial.
Boxgrove then lay on the coast, below chalk cliffs, amid mudflats that gave way to woodland and grassland.

entries.title: Homo heidelbergensis settles Europe

facts.text: Around 500,000 years ago, early humans often called Homo heidelbergensis came to Europe from Africa and eventually evolved into Neanderthals.
Boxgrove in Sussex, about 500,000 years old, is the earliest site in Britain with fossils of Homo.
These humans pushed north beyond the 50th parallel, to Boxgrove and Eartham Pit.
Populations had dispersed into Europe by 700,000 years ago, spreading Late Acheulean tools, and more permanent groups settled north of 45°N about then.
Settlements became more permanent by 500,000 years ago, and occupation grew much more frequent afterwards.

entries.title: The Anglian–Elster glaciation buries northern Europe

facts.text: The Elster glaciation, the Anglian in Britain, was the oldest ice age to glaciate North Germany and much of Europe on a large scale.
MIS 12 was globally the stronger glacial of its era, ranking with MIS 16 among the two largest Quaternary ice volumes.
An ice sheet filled much of the North Sea, with a large proglacial lake to its south fed by the Rhine, Scheldt and Thames.
Great Britain was widely glaciated, and the glaciation ended the long, relatively warm Cromerian Complex.

entries.title: The mammoth steppe is born

facts.text: The steppe-tundra biome first emerged during the MIS 12 glacial, uniting animals of the northern tundra and Central Asian steppe.
It would repeatedly expand and contract with later glacial cycles.

entries.text: During the MIS 12 glacial, about 460,000 years ago, a new kind of landscape appeared. The steppe-tundra biome, also called the mammoth steppe, first emerged. It joined animals of the northern tundra with those of the Central Asian steppe into one community. Cold, dry grassland stretched where the two had once been separate. This biome was not fixed. It grew with every later glacial cycle and shrank in each warm spell, again and again.

entries.title: A megaflood cuts Britain loose from France

facts.text: An ice dam to the north backed river water into a vast lake in the southern North Sea, held by a chalk ridge from the Weald to Artois.
During the Anglian glaciation the lake broke through, the first of two megafloods that cut through the Weald–Artois Anticline.
The flood diverted the Rhine into the English Channel; sonar shows deeply gouged channels and streamlined islands on the seabed.
It ended the land bridge between Britain and France, though links returned at low sea level.

entries.text: Britain became an island in a catastrophe. During the Anglian glaciation, about 450,000 years ago, an ice dam to the north backed river water into a vast lake in the southern North Sea. The lake was held in by a chalk ridge running from the Weald in England to Artois in France. Then the lake broke through. Sonar shows deeply gouged channels and streamlined islands on the seabed. The land bridge between Britain and France was broken, though links returned whenever sea level fell low.

entries.title: MIS 11, the super-interglacial

facts.text: MIS 11 was the longest and warmest interglacial of the last 500,000 years, possibly twice as long as others.
It saw the highest-amplitude deglacial warming of the last 5 million years.
South Greenland nearly fully deglaciated, adding 4.5–6 m of sea-level equivalent around 410,000–400,000 years ago.
High-latitude seas were warm, thermohaline circulation strong, sea level higher than now, and coral reefs expanded.
It matches the Hoxnian in Britain, Holsteinian in Central Europe and Yarmouthian in North America; Swanscombe Man dates from it.

entries.text: Between about 424,000 and 374,000 years ago, Earth went through an unusually long, warm spell. MIS 11 was the longest and warmest interglacial of the last 500,000 years, possibly twice as long as the others. It began with the highest-amplitude deglacial warming of the last 5 million years. The north felt it most. South Greenland nearly lost its ice entirely around 410,000 to 400,000 years ago, adding 4.5 to 6 m to sea level. High-latitude seas were warm and the thermohaline circulation, the deep ocean conveyor driven by heat and salt, ran strong. Sea level stood higher than today, and coral reefs expanded. The same warm spell carries different names on land. It is the Hoxnian in Britain, the Holsteinian in Central Europe and the Yarmouthian in North America. Swanscombe Man, a fossil human from England, dates from it.

entries.title: Humans learn to keep fire for good
entries.article: Control of fire by early humans

facts.text: Reliable evidence of regular fire use appears in the archaeological record about 400,000 years ago; before that, fire use was sparse.
The shift may mark true domestication of fire and fire-starting technology, or simply better ways of keeping fires alight.
The oldest definitive fire-making, about 400,000 years ago at a Neanderthal site in eastern England, left burnt soil, fire-cracked handaxes and pyrite for striking sparks.
European caves show no regular fire before 400,000–300,000 years ago; good evidence follows the MIS 9 interglacial, about 340,000 years ago.
Fire became widespread in the Middle Paleolithic, and humans were cooking food by about 250,000 years ago.

Fire became widespread in the Middle Paleolithic, and humans were cooking food by about 250,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Saale glaciation complex

facts.text: The Saale complex, the middle of northern Europe's three great Scandinavian ice-sheet glaciations, spanned about 400,000 to 130,000 years ago.
It spans several glacial cycles separated by warmer periods, opening with the Fuhne cold phase and the Dömnitz interglacial.
Its latter part coincides with the global Penultimate Glacial Period.
Britain's equivalent, the Wolstonian, lasted about 374,000–130,000 years ago; the Alpine Riss is paralleled by MIS 10, 8 and 6.

They lived across Europe and the Near East from about 300,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Whakamaru supereruption shakes New Zealand

facts.text: A VEI-8 eruption sequence, lasting under a thousand years, produced 1,200–2,000 km³ of tephra on New Zealand's North Island.
It created the Whakamaru Caldera, about 30 by 40 km, just north of today's Lake Taupō.
It opened a burst of under 100,000 years in which the Taupō Volcanic Zone erupted over 4,000 km³ in total.
This was part of an ignimbrite flare-up from about 350,000 to 240,000 years ago.

It produced 1,200 to 2,000 km³ of tephra, the fragments a volcano hurls out. The collapse left the Whakamaru Caldera, about 30 by 40 km, just north of today's Lake Taupō. This was only the start. In a burst of under 100,000 years, the Taupō Volcanic Zone went on to erupt over 4,000 km³ in total. That burst belonged to an ignimbrite flare-up lasting from about 350,000 to 240,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Schöningen spears, oldest complete wooden weapons

facts.text: Ten wooden weapons of spruce and pine from a lignite mine at Schöningen, Germany, are the oldest complete wooden weapons known, found with butchered horse bones.
Probably used for both throwing and thrusting, they were made by Homo heidelbergensis or early Neanderthals and point to sophisticated hunting and forward planning.
Their age is disputed: first put at 400,000–380,000 years, then 337,000–300,000 by thermoluminescence, and about 200,000 years by a 2025 study.

entries.title: Homo naledi in the Rising Star Cave

facts.text: Homo naledi, a small-brained archaic human, lived in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system 335,000–236,000 years ago, in the Middle Pleistocene.
Because its brain was so small, the fossils were first assumed to be 1–2 million years old; its line branched from other Homo by 900,000 years ago.
The Dinaledi Chamber holds over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, the largest find of a single hominin species in Africa.
Some researchers suggest it deliberately placed its dead in the remote chamber, a claim still debated.

entries.title: The Middle Stone Age begins

facts.text: Africa's Middle Stone Age began around 300,000 years ago and is linked to anatomically modern or nearly modern Homo sapiens.
Its European counterpart, the Middle Paleolithic, broadly spans 300,000 to 50,000 years ago.
The Chibanian thus spans the Lower-to-Middle Paleolithic transition.
At Pinnacle Point, South Africa, Middle Stone Age Homo sapiens cooked shellfish and heat-treated silcrete in fire to improve their tools by about 164,000 years ago.
Evidence of hafting, in both Europe and Africa, becomes much more common after 300,000 years ago.

entries.title: Gigantopithecus, the giant ape, dies out

facts.text: Gigantopithecus, a giant Asian relative of the orangutan, died out about 300,000 years ago.
The great ape lived in central and southern China from about 2 million years ago; its youngest remains, from Shuangtan and Gongjishan Caves, are 295,000–215,000 years old.
After about 400,000 years ago it survived only in Guangxi; retreating subtropical forest, and perhaps archaic humans, likely drove it extinct.

entries.title: Denisovans in Siberia and Tibet

facts.text: Early Middle Paleolithic tools, including cores and scrapers, were left in Denisova Cave, Siberia, about 287,000 years ago.
Denisovan DNA from the cave's sediments dates back to 217,000 years ago.
Child hand- and footprints at Quesang, Tibet, dated 226,000–169,000 years ago, may be Denisovan and are the plateau's oldest human traces.
A 200,000-year-old Denisovan molar carries about 5% of its genome from a previously unknown Neanderthal population.
Denisovans ranged across Asia from about 200,000 to 32,000 years ago.

Its sediments trapped and buried Pleistocene animals, including 58 Columbian and 3 woolly mammoths.

entries.title: Woolly mammoths take over from steppe mammoths

facts.text: The woolly mammoth emerged in the mid-to-late Middle Pleistocene and replaced its forerunner, the steppe mammoth Mammuthus trogontherii.
In Europe, woolly mammoths had fully replaced steppe mammoths by around 200,000 years ago.
In North America, woolly mammoths were among the northern specialists that spread south of Alaska with bison during the Rancholabrean.
Neanderthals lived alongside mammoths and used their bones for tools and building, as at La Cotte de St Brelade about 200,000 years ago.

entries.title: Steppe bison cross into North America

facts.text: Steppe bison, ancestors of the American bison, crossed the Bering land bridge into North America around 195,000–135,000 years ago.
Their arrival marks the start of the Rancholabrean faunal stage, defined by the presence of Bison.
Bison first appeared in northwestern North America during the Illinoian, then spread across the continent in the Sangamonian.
They expanded south of Alaska alongside caribou, muskoxen, moose and woolly mammoths.

entries.title: The Penultimate Glacial Period, MIS 6

facts.text: The Penultimate Glacial Period ran from about 194,000 years ago, at the end of the MIS 7 interglacial, to about 135,000 years ago.
Its maximum, around 140,000 years ago, was Eurasia's most extensive glaciation in 400,000 years; a thick ice sheet over northern Europe slashed vegetation.
High latitudes were colder, and the tropics warmer, than at the Last Glacial Maximum.
It is the coldest, last part of the Saale/Wolstonian complex; in North America the Illinoian Stage, OSL-dated to MIS 6, matches it.
The Bull Lake glaciation of the Rocky Mountains, about 200,000–130,000 years ago, was concurrent.

entries.text: The ice age before the last one was in some ways the harsher. The Penultimate Glacial Period ran from about 194,000 years ago, as the MIS 7 interglacial ended, to about 135,000 years ago. Its peak, around 140,000 years ago, brought Eurasia's most extensive glaciation in 400,000 years. A thick ice sheet over northern Europe slashed plant cover. High latitudes were colder than at the later Last Glacial Maximum, while the tropics were warmer. It is the coldest, final part of the Saale and Wolstonian complex. In North America the Illinoian Stage matches it, and the Bull Lake glaciation of the Rocky Mountains, about 200,000 to 130,000 years ago, ran at the same time.

entries.title: A second megaflood makes Britain an island

facts.text: A second megaflood broke through the Weald–Artois chalk ridge during the Saalian/Wolstonian glaciation (MIS 6).
Cohen and Hijma date the ridge's final destruction to the Saalian peak around 160,000 years ago, ending with a second meltwater lake about 130,000 years ago.
A lake held back in the Doggerland region burst through, cutting the Strait of Dover.
Afterwards Britain became an island whenever sea level was high.

entries.title: A green Sahara opens a road out of Africa

facts.text: The exceptionally intense Eemian humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than the Holocene's African humid period.
It opened pathways for early humans to cross Arabia and northern Africa.
Modern humans dispersed via North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago at least.
The Red Sea coastal route was extremely arid before 140,000 and after 115,000 years ago.
Such humid phases come with interglacials and precession minima, while glacial stages bring dry periods.

entries.text: The Sahara was not always a barrier. During the Last Interglacial, an exceptionally intense humid period greened northern Africa, more strongly than its later Holocene counterpart. Modern humans dispersed through North Africa and the Arabian Peninsula at least between 130,000 and 115,000 years ago. Timing mattered. The Red Sea coastal route was extremely dry before 140,000 and after 115,000 years ago. Such humid phases come with interglacials and with precession minima, points in the slow wobble of Earth's axis, while glacial stages bring dry spells.

entries.title: The Eemian, the Last Interglacial

facts.text: The Last Interglacial followed the Penultimate Glacial Period and lasted until about 115,000 years ago; it corresponds to Marine Isotope Stage 5e.
It was one of the warmest spells of the last 800,000 years, up to about 2 °C warmer than the Holocene, with CO2 near 280 ppm.
Warmth peaked about 128,000–123,000 years ago; around 125,000 years ago forests grew at North Cape, Norway, today tundra.
Arctic summers ran about 2–4 °C warmer than in 2011; abrupt cold spells around 120,000 years ago followed shifts in the North Atlantic Current.
The end of the Riss (Penultimate) glaciation and start of this interglacial is the proposed beginning of the Late Pleistocene.

entries.title: Hippos wallow in northern England

facts.text: Interglacial warmth let hippos range as far north as Stockton-on-Tees in northern England, though rarely east of the Rhine outside southern Europe.
Europe's temperate landscapes held straight-tusked elephants, Merck's and narrow-nosed rhinos, Irish elk, aurochs, cave lions and cave hyenas.
Warmer seas let tropical 'Senegalese' marine snails, such as cone shells, colonise the Mediterranean.

entries.title: Seas rise as West Antarctic ice collapses

facts.text: At its peak, sea level stood probably 6–9 m above today's, with Greenland, thermal expansion and Antarctica all contributing.
The West Antarctic Ice Sheet appears to have collapsed around 125,000 years ago, when temperatures resembled the early 21st century's.
Seas may have risen as fast as 2.5 m per century; East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin lost ice worth about 0.5 m.
High seas made Fennoscandia and Jutland islands and flooded much of northwestern Europe and the West Siberian Plain.
Fossil coral reefs from this highstand, now stranded above sea level, are common in the Caribbean and along the Red Sea.

entries.text: The last time Earth was about as warm as the early 21st century, the West Antarctic Ice Sheet appears to have collapsed. That was around 125,000 years ago. East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin alone lost ice worth about 0.5 m. Seas may have risen as fast as 2.5 m per century. The high water made islands of Fennoscandia and Jutland and flooded much of northwestern Europe and the West Siberian Plain. Fossil coral reefs from that highstand are now stranded above the sea, common in the Caribbean and along the Red Sea.

entries.title: Modern humans reach Arabia

facts.text: Stone tools at Jebel Faya (Faya-1) in the United Arab Emirates show modern humans in Arabia at least 125,000 years ago.
Groups may have left Africa by two routes: the Nile, Sinai and Levant, and across the Bab-el-Mandeb strait when seas were low.
Tools on a raised 125,000-year-old reef at Abdur, Eritrea, suggest coastal foragers ate shellfish over 100,000 years ago.
These early migrations do not seem to have led to lasting colonisation and had receded by about 80,000 years ago.

entries.title: Giant long-horned bison evolve

facts.text: At the start of the Last Interglacial, about 130,000 years ago, steppe bison spread from Alaska into central North America as the Laurentide ice melted.
There they gave rise to the giant long-horned bison, Bison latifrons, first known from Colorado's Snowmass site about 120,000 years ago.
By 60,000 years ago long-horned bison had given rise to Bison antiquus, widely considered the ancestor of the modern American bison.

entries.title: Neanderthals hunt elephants at Neumark-Nord

facts.text: At Neumark-Nord in Germany, remains of at least 57 straight-tusked elephants date to the Last Interglacial, about 120,000 years ago.
Systematic butchery there and at Lehringen, Taubach and Gröbern points to widespread Neanderthal hunting of these elephants in Eemian Germany.
Neanderthals at Neumark-Nord hunted elephants regularly, perhaps every 5 to 6 years, and may have rendered fat from their bones.

entries.title: Solo Man, the last Homo erectus

facts.text: Solo Man, the youngest known Homo erectus population, lived beside the Solo River in Java about 117,000–108,000 years ago.
It closed a long Homo erectus presence on Java that began 1.51–0.93 million years ago at Sangiran.
By 125,000 years ago a much wetter climate had made Java an island and let tropical rainforest spread.
The species probably died out as rainforest replaced the savannas it depended on.
It long predates modern humans, who reached the region roughly 55,000–50,000 years ago, and left no living descendants.

entries.title: The Last Glacial Period begins

facts.text: About 115,000 years ago the Last Interglacial ended and the Last Glacial Period began; it lasted until 11,700 years ago.
Average temperatures dropped markedly, and warmth-loving woodland species were displaced in northern Europe.
It is the Würm in the Alps, the Devensian in Britain and the Weichselian in northern Europe, broadly matched by North America's Wisconsin.
Temperatures fell gradually through the glacial, reaching their lowest at the Last Glacial Maximum.
Lower seas exposed much of Sundaland and left most of the Persian Gulf dry land for most of the glacial.

entries.text: About 115,000 years ago the warmth ended. The Last Interglacial gave way to the Last Glacial Period, which lasted until 11,700 years ago. Temperatures fell gradually through the glacial, reaching their lowest at the {{ref:late-096}}. Each region has its own name for this ice age. It is the Würm in the Alps, the Devensian in Britain and the Weichselian in northern Europe, broadly matched by the Wisconsin in North America. With so much water locked in ice, the seas fell. Much of Sundaland, the shelf linking Southeast Asia's islands, became dry land. So did most of the Persian Gulf, for most of the glacial.

entries.title: Dansgaard–Oeschger events: sudden glacial warmings

facts.text: Dansgaard–Oeschger events, rapid climate fluctuations, occurred 25 times during the Last Glacial Period.
They are best recorded in Greenland ice cores, which reach back to the end of the Eemian, about 115,000 years ago.
In sharp cases Greenland warmed about 8 °C within 40 years; a 5 °C rise over 30–40 years was more typical.
They arose when ice volume and CO2 were intermediate, a window in which the Atlantic overturning circulation was bistable.
Each nudged CO2 up about 5 ppm and weakened the Indonesian–Australian monsoon; a 1,470-year rhythm is proposed but debated.

entries.title: Woolly mammoths cross into North America

Isotopes show Siberia stayed more uniformly cold and dry than the New World side of the Bering land bridge.

Its ice dammed lakes 90,000–80,000 and 60,000–50,000 years ago, rerouting rivers such as the Yenisei, Ob, Pechora and Mezen that now flow north.

entries.title: Heinrich events: armadas of icebergs

facts.text: In Heinrich events, great fleets of icebergs broke from the Laurentide ice sheet and drifted through Hudson Strait into the North Atlantic.
They are especially well documented for the Wisconsin glaciation, about 75,000 to 11,000 years ago.
Melting icebergs dropped rock debris as Heinrich layers and poured fresh water into the North Atlantic, likely altering ocean circulation.
Iceberg discharges between 21,000 and 11,500 years ago coincided with subtropical droughts.
Why the ice sheet became unstable is still debated.

entries.title: Mastodons and giant beavers retreat from the north

facts.text: American mastodons, which had lived in North America's far north in Last Interglacial forests, were extirpated there about 75,000 years ago as the Wisconsin glaciation (MIS 4) set in.
This happened long before people arrived, and confined mastodons to lands south of the North American ice sheets.
Giant beavers likewise vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago as conditions grew more hostile.

entries.title: Toba, the great supereruption

facts.text: Toba in Sumatra erupted around 74,000 years ago, a VEI 8 supereruption and one of the largest known in the Cenozoic.
It released about 2,800 km3 of magma, left the caldera now filled by Lake Toba, and covered India in about 5 cm of ash.
It struck during the rapid cooling into MIS 4; whether it sped that cooling is debated, and Arabian Sea records suggest not.
The Toba catastrophe theory ties it to a human population bottleneck, but that causal link remains highly controversial.
Eruptions of this size happen somewhere on Earth every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

entries.article: Recent African origin of modern humans

facts.text: People outside Africa today descend mainly from a single expansion of Homo sapiens from Africa about 70,000–50,000 years ago.
A small group carrying mitochondrial haplogroup L3, perhaps under 1,000 people, crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Arabia.
They followed the coasts around Arabia and Persia to South Asia before 55,000 years ago, and on toward Southeast Asia and Oceania.
Around 50,000 years ago others entered Eurasia via the Zagros Mountains, some heading for the Central Asian steppes.
Human-driven extinctions began as people spread out of Africa over 60,000 years ago.

entries.text: Almost everyone whose family roots lie outside Africa descends from one small band of travelers. People outside Africa today come mainly from a single expansion of Homo sapiens, about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. A small group carrying the maternal lineage called mitochondrial haplogroup L3, perhaps fewer than 1,000 people, crossed the Bab-el-Mandeb strait into Arabia. From there they followed the coasts. They worked their way around Arabia and Persia and reached South Asia before 55,000 years ago. Their descendants pressed on toward Southeast Asia and Oceania. Not everyone kept to the shore. Around 50,000 years ago, others entered Eurasia through the Zagros Mountains, and some headed for the steppes of Central Asia. The expansion had a shadow. Extinctions driven by humans began as people spread out of Africa over 60,000 years ago.

entries.title: A brief modern human visit to Mandrin Cave

facts.text: Modern human teeth, including a baby's molar, and Neronian tools in layer E of Mandrin Cave, in France's Rhône valley, date to 56,800–51,700 years ago.
