entries.title: The Flores hobbit vanishes

facts.text: Homo floresiensis, the small 'Hobbit' human of Flores, lived on the island until modern humans arrived about 50,000 years ago.
Its bones at Liang Bua date from 100,000 to 60,000 years ago; the youngest stone tools are about 50,000 years old.
A drying trend intensified around 61,000 years ago, shrinking fresh water and the dwarf Stegodon it may have hunted.
At Liang Bua, bones of the dwarf Stegodon florensis, 80,000–50,000 years old, lie with H. floresiensis stone tools, a few bearing cut marks.
The dwarf Stegodon's last records also date to about 50,000 years ago, around the time modern humans reached Flores.

entries.title: The great megafauna die-off begins

facts.text: From around 50,000 years ago most large land animals outside Africa died out, an extinction unprecedented for its bias toward large species.
About 65% of megafaunal species vanished worldwide, 72% in North America, 83% in South America and 88% in Australia.
Losses began in Sahul about 50,000 years ago and in the Americas about 13,000 years ago, each as modern humans arrived.
Hunting, climate change or both are blamed; the balance is long debated, though most scholars accept some human role.
Africa was affected less than other continents; mammal diversity lost since could take 5–7 million years to recover.

entries.contested_note: Scientists still argue over how much hunting and how much climate change caused the losses; most think humans played at least some part.

entries.title: Meteor Crater blasted into Arizona

facts.text: A nickel-iron meteorite about 50 m across blasted out Meteor Crater about 50,000 years ago.
The Colorado Plateau was then cooler and damper: open grassland and woods roamed by mammoths and giant ground sloths.
It is called the best-preserved meteorite crater on Earth.

entries.title: Procoptodon, the giant short-faced kangaroo

facts.text: Procoptodon goliah, the largest known kangaroo, stood about 2 m tall, weighed up to 240 kg, and may have been the largest hopping mammal ever.
It died out about 50,000–45,000 years ago, though some evidence suggests it survived until 18,000 years ago.
Its loss coincided with human arrival in a fairly stable climate; hunting, human burning of vegetation and drought have all been proposed.

entries.title: The Upper Paleolithic: a burst of new tools and art

facts.text: The Upper Paleolithic began between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago, as Africa's Middle Stone Age ended around 50,000 years ago.
Around 50,000 years ago artifacts became markedly more diverse; before then, stone tools were much alike everywhere.
Artifacts of modern behaviour are unambiguous from 40,000–50,000 years ago, though whether a sudden 'Great Leap Forward' occurred is debated.
Art followed: Spanish cave paintings and the Lion-man figurine date to around 40,000 years ago.
The Aurignacian culture flourished in Europe and southwest Asia from 43,000 to 26,000 years ago.

entries.title: Genyornis, the last of the giant dromornithid birds

facts.text: By the Late Pleistocene the flightless Genyornis newtoni, 2–2.5 m tall, was the only surviving dromornithid, a family once diverse in the Miocene.
It lived until around 50,000–40,000 years ago; at Lake Callabonna its population died about 50,000 years ago as the lake dried.
Eggshells 53,900–43,400 years old suggest people collected and cooked its eggs in the millennia before it vanished.

entries.contested_note: Drying lakes and human predation are both proposed causes, part of the long-running debate over the causes of the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions.

entries.title: Australia loses its giants

facts.text: All forms of megafauna on the Australian mainland died out in the same rapid window, about 46,000 years ago.
Most Australian megafauna vanished considerably earlier than on other continents, including every mammal over 1,000 kg.
Victims included Diprotodon, the largest marsupial known, and the giant monitor lizard Megalania; Diprotodon was last recorded at South Walker Creek about 40,100 years ago.
The losses followed human arrival, not known climate shifts; climate then resembled today's, and drying is judged an unlikely cause.
How much people contributed remains controversial; a Zygomaturus from New South Wales, 33,000–37,000 years old, is the latest known survivor.

entries.title: Fire-stick farming reshapes Australia

facts.text: People were deliberately using fire to shape Australia's environment 46,000 years ago; Coral Sea ash shows fire was already significant there over 100,000 years ago.
Fire becomes abruptly more common about 45,000 years ago, a rise one geologist attributed to Aboriginal fire-stick farming of forests and grasslands.
One account holds that dense forest became open sclerophyll forest and open forest grassland, favouring eucalyptus, acacia and grasses; links to ecological collapse remain hard to prove.

entries.contested_note: How far early burning changed Australian vegetation, and whether it helped drive the megafauna extinctions, is debated.

entries.title: Modern humans reach Europe

facts.text: Modern humans had reached northwestern Europe by 45,000 years ago; remains in Germany date to 45,000–47,000 years ago.
Finds in Italy and Britain date to 43,000–45,000 years ago, and by 45,000 years ago people lived at 61°N.
They came from Central Asia and the Middle East, adapted to hunting the big game of the glacial steppe.
Settling Europe may have taken 15,000–20,000 years; from 40,000 to 16,000 years ago it held only some 4,000–6,000 people.
Substantial interbreeding with Neanderthals seems to have ended before modern humans entered Europe, by 47,000 years ago.

Settling it may have taken 15,000 to 20,000 years, and from 40,000 to 16,000 years ago it held only some 4,000 to 6,000 people. Most of their mixing with Neanderthals had ended before they arrived, by 47,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Châtelperronian, a Neanderthal toolkit

facts.text: The Châtelperronian, about 44,500 to 33,000 years ago, was the earliest Upper Palaeolithic industry in central and southwestern France and northern Spain.
It is the only Upper Palaeolithic industry attributed to Neanderthals, perhaps adopting modern human techniques; it made curved-backed flint knives.
Its existence and authorship are debated; critics see it as a mix of Mousterian and Aurignacian layers.

entries.title: The straight-tusked elephant's last stand

facts.text: Palaeoloxodon antiquus, whose bulls averaged 4 m tall and 13 tonnes, was among the largest land mammals ever.
After the Last Interglacial ended about 115,000 years ago it retreated from northern Europe to southern refugia, perhaps lingering in Britain until 87,000 years ago.
Its youngest confirmed remains, from Iberia, are about 44,000–43,000 years old; footprints may extend its record to 28,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Laschamp excursion: a brief magnetic flip

facts.text: Earth's magnetic field briefly reversed between 42,200 and 41,500 years ago, during the Last Glacial Period.
The flip took about 250 years and the field stayed reversed about 440 years, falling to 5% of today's strength in transition.
More cosmic rays reached Earth, raising beryllium-10 and carbon-14 production, thinning ozone and altering atmospheric circulation.
A fossil kauri tree from New Zealand, alive 42,500–41,000 years ago, recorded the event.
Claimed links to megafauna and Neanderthal extinctions and to cave art lack corroborating evidence.

entries.title: The Neanderthals disappear

facts.text: Neanderthals disappeared from the fossil record about 40,000 years ago, and their distinctive tools vanished with them.
Modern humans spreading from Africa replaced them across Eurasia; they survived until about 40,000 years ago in Iberia.
Possible late holdouts lived in Iberia 37,000 years ago and at Byzovaya in the Urals, near the Arctic, about 33,000–32,000 years ago.
A small amount of Neanderthal DNA survives in people today.
A 2021 recalibration dates their extinction to 40,700 ± 200 years ago; they had vanished from northwestern Europe by 44,200–40,600 years ago.

entries.title: The last marsupial lions

facts.text: Thylacoleo, the carnivorous 'pouch lion' of Australia, lived from the late Pliocene until around 40,000 years ago.
Since the Pliocene it had been the only surviving genus of its family, the Thylacoleonidae.
It vanished at essentially the same time as most Australian megafauna; how much climate change or newly arrived people were to blame is debated.

entries.title: The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption near Naples

facts.text: The Archiflegreo volcano at the Campi Flegrei near Naples produced the Campanian Ignimbrite; argon–argon dating puts the eruption at 39,850 ± 140 years ago.
It erupted about 200 km3 of magma (500 km3 bulk), the largest event in the Campi Flegrei's history.
Its tephra, the Y-5 ash layer, spread over about 3,000,000 km².
It coincided with a suite of Late Pleistocene biocultural changes in and beyond the Mediterranean.
One theory blamed it for the Neanderthals' extinction, but a 2021 recalibration puts their disappearance at 40,700 ± 200 years ago, before the eruption.

entries.title: The paintings of Chauvet Cave

facts.text: Chauvet Cave in southeastern France holds some of the world's best-preserved figurative cave paintings, with remains and prints of animals, some now extinct.
Radiocarbon dates show two occupations, 37,000–33,500 and 31,000–28,000 years ago; most black drawings are from the first, the oldest painted about 36,500 years ago.
A collapsing cliff sealed the cave entrance about 29,000 years ago.

entries.title: Stegodon fades from mainland Asia

facts.text: Stegodon, an elephant relative of the extinct family Stegodontidae, persisted across South, Southeast and East Asia after dying out in Africa.
Its last mainland records date to perhaps 35,000–30,000 years ago in India and at least 30,000–20,000 in China; Holocene claims are unsubstantiated.
The harsh Last Glacial Maximum may have contributed to its decline, while Asian elephants, with more flexible diets, survived.

entries.title: The Gravettian spreads across Europe

facts.text: The Gravettian succeeded the Aurignacian about 33,000 years BP and reached as far as Estremadura in Portugal; Venus figurines are among its hallmarks.
At Pavlov I in Moravia, its most complete site, clay fragments bear impressions of woven textiles dated about 26,980–24,870 BP.
It had mostly disappeared by about 22,000 BP, near the Last Glacial Maximum, though some elements lasted until about 17,000 BP.

entries.title: Disputed early sites in the Americas

facts.text: Stones from Chiquihuite Cave in Zacatecas, Mexico, thought to be artifacts, are dated to 26,000 years ago and possibly as far back as 33,000.
Bluefish Caves in the Yukon may record people 24,000 years ago, though the dates are contested; Old Crow Flats mammoth bones, apparently butchered, date to 25,000–40,000 BP.
Sceptics note that the oldest sites with many artifacts in undisturbed layers are in eastern Beringia, 14,200–13,000 BP.

facts.text: Megafauna were most abundant in Europe around 27,000–21,000 years ago, thanks to the cold stadial climate.

A mammoth steppe then stretched from Spain across Eurasia and Beringia into Alaska and the Yukon.

A mammoth steppe stretched from Spain across Eurasia and Beringia into Alaska and the Yukon. But as cold peaked in the Last Glacial Maximum, around 23,000 years ago, Europe's top predators began to die out.

entries.title: The Last Glacial Maximum

facts.text: Ice sheets reached their greatest extent of the Last Glacial Period between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago.
They had begun advancing about 33,000 years ago in both hemispheres.
Ice up to 3 km thick covered much of northern Europe, Asia, North America, Greenland and Antarctica.
Around 21,000 years ago the global average temperature was about 6 °C colder than today.
Northern Hemisphere people and animals retreated to refugia, sheltered areas where they survived until the ice withdrew.

entries.title: Oruanui, the world's most recent supereruption

facts.text: Taupō Volcano erupted about 25,700 years ago in the world's most recent supereruption, rated VEI 8.
The largest phreatomagmatic eruption known, it produced about 530 km3 of magma: fall deposits, ignimbrite and intracaldera fill.
It burst through a lake system, destroying Lake Huka and forming the caldera that now holds Lake Taupō.
It may have deepened Last Glacial Maximum cold in New Zealand and the nearby Pacific.
Afterward Lake Taupō filled to about 75 m above today's level before cutting through its ignimbrite dam, less than 22,500 years ago.

The Patagonian Ice Sheet covered all of Chile south of Puerto Montt and crossed into Argentina, where the dry climate halted it.

entries.title: The Laurentide ice sheet at its maximum

facts.text: North America's ice reached its maximum about 25,000–21,000 years ago, the Late Wisconsin.
After retreating 52,000–40,000 years ago, the Laurentide Ice Sheet grew fast, covering Canada east of the Rockies to the Missouri and Ohio rivers and Manhattan.
Ice sheets reached to about the 45th parallel north.
In the Rockies the Pinedale glaciation peaked 23,500–21,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Mal'ta boy and the Ancient North Eurasians

facts.text: A boy buried about 24,000 years ago at Mal'ta, near Lake Baikal in Siberia, was laid to rest with artifacts and a Venus figurine.
His people, the Ancient North Eurasians, were important genetic contributors to Native Americans, Siberians and Europeans.
Mal'ta, the oldest known site in eastern Siberia, had bone-walled houses and about thirty female figurines, a type previously found only in Europe.

entries.title: The cave bear dies out

facts.text: The cave bear, a Pleistocene bear of Europe and Asia, died out about 24,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum.
Ancient DNA shows its numbers falling steeply from about 40,000 years ago, as the Aurignacian began and modern humans arrived.
By around 35,000 years ago it was no longer abundant in Central Europe.

entries.title: The White Sands footprints

facts.text: Seeds in the sediment layers date human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, to 23,000–21,000 years ago.
If correct, they are possibly the oldest evidence of people in the Americas, from the Last Glacial Maximum.
Sceptics say the seeds took up old groundwater carbon, putting the maximum age at only 15,500–13,500 years.
Pollen and quartz-grain dating in 2023, and mud dating in 2025, supported the older ages, but the debate continues.
The site holds perhaps hundreds of thousands of human and animal tracks, recording people alongside ice-age megafauna.

facts.text: The Fennoscandian Ice Sheet reached the mid-Norwegian shelf edge by about 26,000 years ago, then merged with Barents Sea and British ice.
It first reached its maximum extent in Denmark, Germany and western Poland about 22,000 years ago, and in Lithuania and Belarus about 19,000.
Ice buried the entire Scandinavian Mountains and spread into Denmark, Germany, Poland and the former USSR.
Its margin began to retreat 22,000–17,000 years ago.

The paintings were the work of many generations.

entries.title: The Solutrean toolmakers of glacial Europe

facts.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, about 22,000–17,000 years ago, the Solutrean flint industry flourished in France, Spain and Portugal, succeeding the Gravettian.
Its people lived west of the Alps in a glacial refuge, between forest steppe and steppe tundra.
Its toolmaking used techniques not seen before and not rediscovered for millennia; with earlier traditions it gave rise to the Magdalenian.

Lower seas exposed the Bering land bridge between Siberia and Alaska and the Bassian Plain linking Tasmania to Australia.
On the Great Barrier Reef, reef growth moved seaward, farthest from today's coast around 20,700–20,500 years ago.

entries.title: Xianren Cave: the oldest pottery

facts.text: Pottery sherds from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, radiocarbon-dated to 20,000–19,000 years ago, are the earliest pottery yet known anywhere.
Mobile foragers made the pots during the last glacial maximum, long before farming; scorch marks suggest they were used for cooking.
Pottery had been thought to begin with the Neolithic, around 10,000 years ago.

entries.title: The last deglaciation begins

facts.text: Ice sheets were largest 26,000–20,000 years ago; northern ice began to retreat around 19,000 years ago, and the retreat sped up around 15,000 years ago.
At the onset a brief event, lasting at most 500 years, may have raised sea level by as much as 10 m (meltwater pulse 19ka).
Antarctica had warmed abruptly by about 6 °C around 22,000 years ago; northern warming began near 20,000 years ago but stayed limited until about 14,600 years ago.
Over the whole deglaciation global mean temperature rose about 5 °C, high latitudes over 10 °C, and sea level more than 120 m.
The melting was neither steady nor simultaneous: ice still covered most of Great Britain until about 16,000 years ago.

entries.text: Antarctica felt the thaw first. Around 22,000 years ago it warmed abruptly, by about 6 °C. The ice sheets had been largest between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Northern warming began near 20,000 years ago, and northern ice began to retreat around 19,000 years ago. The start may have been sudden. A brief event, lasting at most 500 years, may have raised sea level by as much as 10 m, a surge called meltwater pulse 19ka. Northern warming stayed limited until about 14,600 years ago, and the retreat sped up around 15,000 years ago. The melting was neither steady nor simultaneous. Ice still covered most of Great Britain until about 16,000 years ago. The totals were vast. Over the whole deglaciation, global mean temperature rose about 5 °C and high latitudes over 10 °C. Sea level climbed more than 120 m.

entries.title: The Southern Ocean breathes out carbon dioxide

facts.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, CO2 was low because extra carbon was stored in the deep ocean, held by stratification in the Southern Ocean.
Ice cores show CO2 at 180–210 ppm during ice ages, rising to 280–300 ppm in warm interglacials.
Over the deglaciation, about 19,000–11,000 years ago, deep Southern Ocean overturning, driven by stronger winds and retreating sea ice, may have released the stored carbon.
The rise came in three abrupt pulses and halted during the Antarctic Cold Reversal, 14,700–13,000 years ago.
Rising CO2 warmed the globe out of the glacial maximum; its rapid increase eased about 11,500 years ago as the deglaciation ended.

entries.text: Where did the carbon go during the ice age, and how did it come back? Ice cores show carbon dioxide at 180 to 210 ppm during ice ages, rising to 280 to 300 ppm in warm interglacials. During the Last Glacial Maximum, the extra carbon was stored in the deep ocean, held down by layering in the Southern Ocean. Over the deglaciation, about 19,000 to 11,000 years ago, stronger winds and retreating sea ice may have stirred the deep Southern Ocean and released it. The rise came in three abrupt pulses. It paused during the Antarctic Cold Reversal, 14,700 to 13,000 years ago. Rising carbon dioxide warmed the globe out of the glacial maximum. Its rapid increase eased about 11,500 years ago, as the deglaciation ended.

entries.title: The Oldest Dryas and Heinrich event 1

facts.text: The Oldest Dryas, a cold stadial that interrupted the last glacial retreat, lasted from about 18,000 to 14,700 years ago.
Heinrich event 1 cooled the North Atlantic and weakened the Atlantic overturning circulation, pushing rain belts south and drying northern Africa.
Europe was treeless, dry, grassy tundra; brown bears and other species began returning from refugia in the Carpathians, Italy, Spain and Greece.
Iberian mountain glaciers that had nearly vanished readvanced, surging into valleys 16,800–16,500 years ago.
Globally, rising CO2 still warmed the planet about 2 °C, nearly half of it in the stadial's last centuries.

entries.title: The Southern Hemisphere thaws fast

facts.text: In southern Chile rapid warming from 17,800 years ago brought interglacial temperatures within about 1,000 years, as glaciers retreated and Valdivian rainforest spread.
A 2017 study tied stratospheric ozone depletion about 17,700 years ago to abruptly accelerated Southern Hemisphere deglaciation.
The Patagonian Ice Sheet peaked about 18,000–17,500 years ago, covering about 480,000 km² with over 500,000 km³ of ice.
Its northern edge then melted rapidly, freshening the nearby ocean and altering its circulation, with ecological effects near and far.
Glacial retreat on Antarctica's Alexander Island began around 18,000 years ago, when valley glaciers also melted from New Zealand's Tongariro.

The dog was the only domesticated animal of the Pleistocene, and people brought dogs into North America.

entries.title: The Bonneville flood

facts.text: Lake Bonneville, covering about 83,000 km² of northern Utah, reached its highest level about 17,400 calendar years ago.
It breached a natural dam of alluvial fans at Red Rock Pass, sending a 120 m flood crest toward the Snake River.
Peak flow of about 930,000 m³/s scoured the Snake River Canyon and created Shoshone Falls.
The flood drained about 5,000 km³ of water, lowering the lake 107 m to the Provo shoreline.
Unlike the repeated Missoula floods, the Bonneville flood happened only once.

entries.title: The Pacific coast opens a path south

facts.text: Retreating glaciers on the Alaska Peninsula opened access from Beringia to the Pacific coast by around 17,000 BP, after which the coastal corridor became habitable.
The ice barrier between interior Alaska and the coast broke up from about 16,200 BP; the coast range was fully ice-free by 16,000–15,000 BP.
Kelp forests, estuaries and other sea-level habitats along the deglaciated coast could have formed an unobstructed migration corridor.

entries.title: A proposed Caspian flood into the Black Sea

The overflow would have raised the Black Sea by 60–70 m, flooding land once used for settlement or hunting.

entries.title: Woolly mammoths and rhinos retreat to the far north

facts.text: Woolly rhinos vanished from Europe 17,000–15,000 years ago; their youngest reliable bones, from the Urals and northeast Siberia, are about 14,200–14,000 years old.
Bølling–Allerød warmth likely brought more rain and snow, turning the rhinos' low grass and herb habitat into shrubland and woods.
Woolly mammoths disappeared from most of Europe by 14,000 years ago, and from Alaska and Yukon about 13,300 years ago, roughly 1,000 years after people arrived.
From about 15,000 years ago wet tundra and forest replaced most of Siberia's mammoth steppe; by the Younger Dryas mammoths survived only in its far north.
DNA shows a final mammoth population crash about 12,000 years ago, near the ice age's end, from which the species never recovered.

entries.contested_note: Whether warming habitat loss or human hunting mattered more is part of the long-running debate over the causes of the Late Pleistocene megafauna extinctions.

entries.title: People spread through the Americas

facts.text: Scholars agree the first Americans came from Siberia and spread widely after the Last Glacial Maximum, around 16,000–13,000 years ago.
Ice sheets blocked inland routes until about 16,000 years ago, though a Pacific coastal route may have opened by 17,000 years ago.
The northern and southern Native American genetic branches split around 16,000 years ago.
Widely accepted pre-Clovis sites include Cooper's Ferry, Idaho (c. 15,800 BP), Page-Ladson, Florida (c. 14,550 BP) and Paisley Caves, Oregon (c. 14,200 BP).
Humans reached South America around 15,000 years ago, before its megafauna extinctions.

entries.title: The Missoula floods scour the Scablands

facts.text: Glacial Lake Missoula, dammed by ice on the Clark Fork River, held up to about 2,500 km³ of water.
The dam failed and re-formed repeatedly, unleashing dozens of floods, about one every 55 years, between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago.
The largest discharged about 10 km³ an hour, sweeping across eastern Washington and into Oregon's Willamette Valley.
Together the floods stripped about 210 km³ of loess, sediment and basalt from the Channeled Scablands.

entries.title: Magdalenian hunters return to the north

facts.text: The Magdalenian reindeer hunters, 21,000–13,000 years ago, descended mainly from Gravettian groups who had retreated to southwestern Europe during the Last Glacial Maximum.
Around 15,000 years ago, after the harsh Oldest Dryas, they moved north to recolonise northern Europe, reaching Britain and, eastward, Poland.
From about 14,000 years ago Epigravettian-linked Western Hunter-Gatherers spread north across the Alps, largely replacing them.

entries.title: The cave lion dies out

facts.text: Cave lions died out almost simultaneously across their range about 15,000–14,000 years ago, lingering roughly 1,000 years longer in North America.
A population bottleneck between 47,000 and 18,000 years ago, probably driven partly by climatic instability, had already cut their genetic diversity.
The cause is unknown; climate change, shrinking prey and competition with other carnivores and humans have all been suggested.

entries.title: The Antarctic Cold Reversal

facts.text: While the north warmed, the Southern Hemisphere south of 40°S underwent intense atmospheric and oceanic cooling between 14,700 and 13,000 years ago.
Temperatures fell, atmospheric CO2 stopped rising and glaciers readvanced, as in New Zealand's Southern Alps; Tasmania records a matching cold spell.
It is thought to have been caused by a meltwater pulse, probably from the Antarctic or Laurentide ice sheet.
It may have pushed the southern polar front north and increased precipitation in the Andes.
After about 13,000 years ago warming resumed and glaciers withdrew abruptly from the moraines they had built.

entries.title: The Bølling–Allerød warming

facts.text: The Bølling–Allerød interstadial, about 14,690 to 12,890 years ago, opened with abrupt warming in the Northern Hemisphere.
Greenland's NorthGRIP ice core records its onset at 14,600 years ago, and atmospheric methane rose about 14,700 years ago.
A stronger Atlantic overturning circulation carried heat north while the Southern Hemisphere cooled, a 'polar seesaw'.
The Allerød phase lifted northern Atlantic temperatures almost to present-day levels.
The warmth let people repopulate Eurasia from glacial refuges; in Beringia shrub tundra replaced dry steppe after 14,000 years ago.

entries.title: Meltwater pulse 1A: the fastest sea-level rise

facts.text: Global sea level rose 16–25 m in about 400–500 years, at roughly 40–60 mm a year.
These are the fastest known rates of post-glacial sea-level rise, attributed to the rapid collapse of continental ice sheets.
The pulse began with, or just after, the abrupt Bølling–Allerød warming recorded in Greenland ice.
The West Antarctic ice sheet shrank between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, matching an abrupt sea-level rise around 14,500 years ago.
It is the most widely recognised and least disputed of the named meltwater pulses.

entries.text: In about 400 to 500 years, global sea level rose 16 to 25 m. That is roughly 40 to 60 mm a year, the fastest known rate of rise since the ice age. This surge, meltwater pulse 1A, is blamed on the rapid collapse of continental ice sheets. It began with, or just after, the abrupt Bølling–Allerød warming recorded in Greenland ice. The West Antarctic ice sheet shrank between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, matching an abrupt rise around 14,500 years ago. Of all the named meltwater pulses, it is the most widely recognized and least disputed.

entries.title: The African humid period begins

facts.text: North Africa turned wetter about 14,600–14,500 years ago, as Heinrich event 1 ended and the Bølling–Allerød warming began.
Summer sunshine at least 4% above today's, with vegetation, dust and greenhouse-gas changes, strengthened the African monsoon.
Lake Victoria, dry around 15,000 years ago, refilled and overflowed, and Lakes Albert and Tana spilled into the White and Blue Nile.
The Nile took its current form about 15,000 years ago.
Lakes such as Lake Chad formed or grew, glaciers grew on Kilimanjaro, and the Sahara shrank.

entries.title: Monte Verde, a camp at the end of the Americas

facts.text: Monte Verde II in southern Chile, about 14,500 years old, is one of the widely accepted sites older than Clovis.
Its level II held a tent-like structure about 20 feet long, built of wood and animal hides.
Its people were probably territorial, living in their river basin most of the year alongside late Pleistocene megafauna.

entries.title: The Natufians settle down before farming

facts.text: The Natufian culture of the Levant, radiocarbon-dated to 12,500–9,500 BC, supported sedentary or semi-sedentary communities before agriculture.
Its settlements were larger and more permanent than earlier ones, some with round stone buildings, as at Ain Mallaha, and the first evidence of food storage.
Natufians harvested wild cereals and hunted gazelles; the cold, dry Younger Dryas pushed early settled groups back toward a more mobile life.

entries.title: Paisley Caves and the oldest DNA in North America

facts.text: Human coprolites from Oregon's Paisley Caves, radiocarbon dated to about 14,300–14,400 years ago, hold the oldest human DNA found in North America.
The DNA ties these pre-Clovis people to Siberia or Asia; they ate plants, seeds, rodents, fish and insects.
Critics question whether the coprolites are human and whether their dates hold, suspecting contamination by leached human DNA.

facts.text: The Great Lakes began forming around 14,000 years ago, as retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved and meltwater filled them.

entries.title: The Older Dryas cold snap

facts.text: The Older Dryas was a brief cold stadial between the Bølling and Allerød warm phases, about 14,000 years ago.
Its dates vary by about 400 years between methods, but it lasted only a century or two.
Ice readvanced in places, as in the Littleton–Bethlehem readvance and Canada's Shulie Lake phase.

entries.title: The Americas lose their megafauna

facts.text: North American extinctions clustered around 13,800–11,400 years ago, with the Younger Dryas onset and Clovis; across the Americas they spanned 3,000 years at most.
About 72% of North American and 83% of South American megafaunal species died out, including every mammal over 1,000 kg.
Ground sloths, litopterns and the last notoungulates vanished from the mainland around 12,000 years ago, with most other large mammals.
Losing the American megafauna is estimated to have cut methane production by about 9.6 million tons a year.
Butchered bones, such as an Ohio ground sloth dated 13,738–13,435 BP, show people hunted megafauna, but the causes remain debated.

entries.contested_note: Whether human hunting, climate change or both caused the extinctions is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least a contributory human role.

entries.title: An ice-free corridor opens east of the Rockies

facts.text: By 21,000 BP the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets had merged east of the Rocky Mountains, closing a route into North America's interior.
A gap between them opened about 13,800 ± 500 years ago by 2022 estimates; older studies put it at 13,000–12,000 BP.
That is later than the earliest widely accepted archaeological sites, so the corridor could not have carried the first people south.

entries.title: The Clovis culture spreads across North America

facts.text: The Clovis culture spanned about 13,050–12,750 years ago; its type site, Blackwater Draw in New Mexico, held tools alongside Columbian mammoth remains.
Its hallmark was the fluted Clovis point, a large lanceolate projectile point also used for cutting.
Mobile hunter-gatherers, Clovis people relied on big game, especially mammoths, and may have contributed to megafauna extinctions, a controversial idea.
A 2022 study found the ice-free corridor impassable until about 13,800 years ago, long after people had reached lands south of the ice.
From about 12,750–12,600 years ago Clovis gave way to regional cultures such as Folsom.

entries.title: The Laacher See eruption

facts.text: A VEI 6 Plinian eruption, comparable to Pinatubo in 1991, expelled about 6 km³ of magma and left the Laacher See crater lake in western Germany.
Its tephra dammed the Rhine into a 140 km² lake; when the dam broke, an outburst flood left deposits as far as Bonn.
Dated to 13,006 ± 9 calibrated years ago, it preceded the Younger Dryas by over a century, though 1990s research had proposed it as a trigger.

entries.title: Lake Agassiz, the giant meltwater lake

facts.text: Fed by meltwater from the retreating Laurentide Ice Sheet, Lake Agassiz spread over parts of Manitoba, Ontario, Minnesota, North Dakota and Saskatchewan around 13,000 years ago.
At its greatest extent it may have covered 440,000 km², more than any lake today and about the area of the Black Sea.
From about 13,500 BP it overflowed south through Glacial River Warren toward the Mississippi; at times it drained east to Lake Superior or northwest to the Arctic.
A drainage about 13,000 years ago may have caused the Younger Dryas, long the most supported explanation for that cold spell.
Its huge freshwater releases are thought to have disrupted ocean circulation and affected climate and sea level.

entries.title: The Champlain Sea floods the St. Lawrence

facts.text: Land still pressed down by ice let rising seas flood the St. Lawrence and Ottawa valleys, forming the Champlain Sea from about 13,000 years ago.
About 12,000 years ago the ice dam holding Lake Vermont failed, dropping the lake 91 m within hours or days before salt water swept in.
The sea shrank steadily as the land rebounded, lasting until about 10,000 years ago.

entries.title: Hunter-gatherers reach Cyprus

facts.text: Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 11,000–10,000 BC; the Aetokremnos site may record hunting of dwarf hippos and dwarf elephants.
They introduced wild boar to the island around 12,000 years ago.
Cyprus's dwarf elephant and pygmy hippopotamus later vanished, and the genet Genetta plesictoides died out after humans and invasive species arrived.

entries.title: The Irish elk's brief return

facts.text: The Irish elk's range collapsed during the Last Glacial Maximum: few remains date between 27,500 and 14,600 years ago, and none between 23,300 and 17,500.
It recolonised northern Europe in the Bølling–Allerød; most Irish remains date to the Allerød, around 13,000 years ago.
Its range shrank again in the Younger Dryas, and it had vanished from northern Europe by that period's end.

By the end of that period, it had vanished from northern Europe.

entries.title: Pygmy mammoths of the Channel Islands

facts.text: Columbian mammoths that reached California's Channel Islands evolved into the pygmy mammoth, under half mainland size, living there 80,000–13,000 years ago.
Their youngest records, about 13,000 years old, coincide with rising seas shrinking the islands, the first people there and declining conifer forests.
The people of Arlington Springs Man, on Santa Rosa Island, are thought to have hunted them.

entries.title: The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis

facts.text: A fringe hypothesis claims a comet or meteor impact or airburst about 12,900 years ago disrupted Atlantic circulation and set off the Younger Dryas.
Richard Firestone and colleagues introduced it in 2007, also blaming the impact for megafaunal extinctions.
Most relevant experts reject it for lack of clear evidence, and the Hiawatha crater, once linked to it, proved to be 58 million years old.

entries.title: The Younger Dryas: one last cold snap

facts.text: The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, was the last cold phase of the Last Glacial Period, a return to glacial conditions.
Annual temperatures fell about 3 °C in North America, 2–6 °C in Europe and up to 10 °C in Greenland, where cooling took 3 years or less.
Scientists agree a severe weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation caused it; a Lake Agassiz meltwater flood or a volcanic trigger are proposed explanations.
The Southern Hemisphere warmed, drought hit the African humid period region, and Altiplano lakes reached a peak.
It ended as rapidly as it began, with dramatic warming over about 50 years that closed the Pleistocene.

entries.title: Arctodus, the short-faced bear, dies out

facts.text: Arctodus simus, averaging about 625 kg and reaching 957 kg, was one of the largest land carnivorans ever and ranged across North America.
It vanished from Beringia about 23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum, possibly from sharp cooling tied to Heinrich event 2.
Elsewhere it died out about 12,800 years ago; vegetation shifts that cut its food supply and competition with brown bears are suggested causes.

entries.title: The last scimitar-toothed cats

entries.title: The last Columbian mammoths

facts.text: The Columbian mammoth, up to 4.2 m tall and 12.5 tonnes, ranged from southern Canada to Costa Rica and outsized the woolly mammoth.
Its latest calibrated date, from Colorado's Dent site, is 12,705–12,124 years ago, as the Younger Dryas began; no Holocene survival is recorded.
Clovis people hunted or scavenged it; its extinction is blamed on climate-driven habitat loss, human hunting, or both.

entries.title: Lake Lahontan at its highest

facts.text: At its Sehoo highstand about 12,700 years ago, Lake Lahontan covered over 22,000 km² of the Great Basin, centred on today's Carson Sink.
It was about 270 m deep near Pyramid Lake, one of North America's largest lakes of the last glacial period.
Climate change near the end of the Pleistocene then began its gradual drying.

entries.title: Castoroides, the giant beaver, dies out

facts.text: Castoroides, a bear-sized beaver of about 90–125 kg, was the largest known beaver and North America's largest Pleistocene rodent.
It vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago; its last populations lived in the lowlands south of the Great Lakes.
The youngest specimens, from New York, date to about 12,050–11,501 years ago and overlap Paleo-Indian artifacts by up to a thousand years.

entries.title: Macrauchenia, among the last litopterns

facts.text: Macrauchenia, a long-necked hoofed mammal, was one of the last members of the Litopterna, an order native to South America for over 60 million years.
It died out around 12,000 years ago with most large mammals of the Americas, after people reached South America at least 14,500 years ago.
At Paso Otero 5 in the Argentine Pampas its burned bones lie with Fishtail spear points among other extinct megafauna.

entries.title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Warming from 11.7 ka coincides with the earliest farming in the Fertile Crescent, where crop growing and herding opened the Neolithic.
Sheep, goats, cattle and later pigs were domesticated there, along with cereals such as wheat and barley, and legumes.
Barley was domesticated in the Near East around 11,000 years ago, and domesticated emmer wheat appears in Iran by 9,800 BP.
Between 8500 and 7000 BC people in the Fertile Crescent took up the systematic husbandry of plants and animals.
Neolithic settlers had reached Cyprus by 8800–8600 BC.

entries.title: The Younger Dryas ends and the Holocene begins

facts.text: The Younger Dryas cold spell, which began about 12,800 years ago, ended about 11,700 years ago, closing the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene.
The boundary is a GSSP sample in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland, matched to the end of the Younger Dryas; it was ratified in 2008.
Greenland's average yearly temperature rose by about 8 °C within 40 years, in three steps of five years each.
After this sudden jump, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace through the Greenlandian.
Earth has stayed in this interglacial ever since; in the American Southwest the cool, wet pluvial climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

It ended the Younger Dryas, a cold spell that began about 12,800 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. After the sudden jump, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace through the Greenlandian. Earth has stayed in this interglacial ever since. In the American Southwest, the cool, wet pluvial climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

entries.title: Forest and wetland swallow the mammoth steppe

facts.text: At the start of the Holocene, mossy forests, tundra, lakes and wetlands displaced the vast mammoth steppe.
Higher temperatures and rainfall shrank its habitat, fragmenting animal populations and then driving them extinct.
By about 10,000 years ago patches of closed larch and pine forest had developed in northern Siberia.
As the climate turned warmer and wetter, forests replaced much of the open habitat of the large grazers.
Only from about 10,000 years ago did forbs decline, as woody plants and grasses came to dominate.

entries.title: Ice Age wolf lineages collapse

facts.text: Ancient wolves lost most of their genetic diversity at the start of the Holocene in Alaska, Siberia and Europe, overlapping little with modern wolves.
In North America a population bottleneck almost erased ancient wolf diversity.
The Japanese wolf turned out to be the last of the Siberian Pleistocene wolves.

entries.title: The Baltic Ice Lake gives way to the Yoldia Sea

facts.text: The Baltic Ice Lake ended close to the start of the Holocene.
The Yoldia Sea stage, about 11,700–10,700 years BP, began when the lake fell to sea level and salt water could flow into the basin.
Pine and birch pollen rose sharply around the basin from 11,500 BP, and people lived on its Estonian shores by 11,200–10,200 BP.

entries.title: The megafauna keep dying into the Holocene

facts.text: Many megafauna species died out during the Greenlandian, keeping up the extinction rate of the end of the Late Pleistocene.
From the Late Pleistocene into the early Holocene most animals over 45 kg vanished, including 80% of those over a tonne, collapsing faunal density and diversity.
In the Colombian Andes, dung-fungus spores record a second wave of megafaunal extinction around 10,990 BP.
Human activity is blamed for an ongoing mass extinction, the Holocene extinction, that began roughly 10,000 years ago.
Climate change is one main explanation; the balance of human and climatic causes is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept some human role.

entries.title: The early Holocene sea rises 60 meters

facts.text: Sea level jumped about 60 m in the early Holocene, between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago.
The rise was fast while continental ice sheets melted, then slowed from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm a year by 4,200 years ago.
Background rates of about 6–10 mm a year were broken by brief bursts of 30–60 mm a year.
Rising seas drowned vast lowlands and turned parts of continents into islands, cutting off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania.
In Brazil's Bahia region mangroves spread inland as the sea rose.

entries.text: Between about 12,000 and 7,000 years ago, sea level jumped about 60 m. The water came from the continental ice sheets as they melted away, as {{ref:gree-009}} describes, and the rise ran fastest while they melted. Background rates of about 6–10 mm a year were broken by brief bursts of 30–60 mm a year. Then the pace slackened, from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm a year by 4,200 years ago. The rising water drowned vast lowlands and turned parts of continents into islands. It cut off the British Isles, Indonesia, New Guinea and Tasmania from the lands they had joined, a story told in {{ref:gree-028}} and {{ref:nort-011}}. Along Brazil's Bahia coast, mangroves followed the shoreline and spread inland as the sea rose. The modern map of coasts and straits is largely the work of these few thousand years.

entries.title: Northern ice sheets melt fast

facts.text: The abrupt warming that opened the Holocene, around 9700 BC, set off rapid melting of the remaining ice sheets in North America and Europe.
The Laurentide ice sheet's surface mass balance turned negative only in the early Holocene, once radiative forcing and summer temperatures rose.
In northern British Columbia the Cordilleran ice sheet had essentially melted away by about 11,000 years ago.
Most of the ice-sheet melting and sea-level rise of the last deglaciation came after about 11,000 years ago.
From 8,500 BP, ice pouring from the collapsing Laurentide ice sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic.

entries.title: Meltwater pulse 1B: a burst that may not have been

facts.text: Meltwater pulse 1B is a proposed burst of rapid post-glacial sea-level rise between 11,500 and 11,200 years ago, just after the Younger Dryas.
One study put the rise at 13 m in 300 years, about 40 mm a year; others cut it to 7.5 m or less than 6 m.
Barbados coral cores were read as a 28 m rise in about 500 years around 11,300 years ago.
A peak in Antarctic iceberg discharge about 11,300 years ago, matching the Barbados record, suggests Antarctica contributed significantly.
Some researchers found it was at best a modest speed-up, and at worst no different from steady rise between 11,500 and 10,200 years ago.

entries.contested_note: Its size and even its existence are debated: estimates run from a 28 m rise to no clear departure from steady sea-level rise.

entries.title: Hunter-gatherers raise the pillars of Göbekli Tepe

facts.text: Göbekli Tepe, in Upper Mesopotamia in today's Turkey, was built around 9500 BCE and used until about 8000 BCE, at the dawn of the world's first permanent settlements.
Its circular enclosures hold large stone pillars, among the oldest known megaliths, many carved with reliefs of wild animals; the early circles date to c. 9000 BCE.
Its builders were hunter-gatherers who hunted gazelle and ground much cereal; sources differ on whether any of that cereal was domesticated.

entries.title: The Sahara turns green

facts.text: Between 11,000 and 10,000 BP, perihelion fell at the June solstice, raising summer sunlight by about 8% and pushing a stronger African monsoon farther north.
From 11,000 years ago a giant Lake Mega-Chad covered more than 350,000 km² of the Chad Basin.
Grasses, trees and lakes covered much of the Sahara; the humid period had begun about 14,600 years ago.
Lake Kivu began overflowing into Lake Tanganyika by about 10,500 BP, and lakes formed in Arabia's Rub' al Khali 9,000–7,000 years ago.
People moved into the greening Sahara: Takarkori was first occupied 10,000–9,000 years ago, and the Kiffian culture flourished 10,000–8,000 years ago.

Grasses, trees and lakes covered much of the Sahara, in a humid period that had begun about 14,600 years ago. Lake Kivu began overflowing into Lake Tanganyika by about 10,500 BP, and lakes formed in Arabia's Rub' al Khali 9,000–7,000 years ago. People moved into the greening desert: Takarkori was first occupied 10,000–9,000 years ago, and the Kiffian culture flourished 10,000–8,000 years ago.

entries.title: North America loses its sloths, horses and short-faced bears

facts.text: Around 11,000 years ago short-faced bears vanished from North America, the last giant ground sloths died out there, and all native horses disappeared.

Horses had evolved largely in North America; they died out there and were reintroduced only in the 15th century.

Ground sloths lingered on Caribbean islands until about 4,000 years ago.

entries.title: Glyptodon and its armored kin die out

facts.text: Glyptodon, a giant plant-eating armadillo relative that had lived in South America since about 3.2 million years ago, died out around 11,000 years ago.
A wetter post-glacial climate replaced C3 grasses with C4 grasses and southern beech, killing off grazing specialists like glyptodonts and toxodonts; human hunting may also have contributed.
Its relatives Doedicurus and Panochthus survived on the Argentine Pampas into the early Holocene, living alongside people for at least 4,000 years.

entries.title: The first livestock: goats, sheep, pigs and cattle

facts.text: Zooarchaeology shows that goats, pigs, sheep and taurine cattle were the first livestock, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent 11,000–10,000 years ago.
The earliest dates in northern Mesopotamia are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, c. 8500 BCE for pigs and c. 8000 BCE for cattle.
The milder climate after the Younger Dryas set the stage; by 10,000 years ago hunters were culling young males and sparing females to breed.
Domestication began a rapid shift in the evolution, ecology and demography of people and of many animal and plant species.
In Eurasia domestic animals then overtook other primates as the main source of new human infections.

entries.title: The Ancylus Lake fills the Baltic basin

entries.title: The last mainland woolly mammoths

facts.text: Woolly mammoths survived in mainland Siberia until around 10,000 years ago; a small population lived on Wrangel Island much longer.
The youngest European mammoth remains come from the Southern Urals, 9650 BCE, and Cherepovets in Russia, 9290–9180 BCE.
In Eurasia, cold-adapted giants such as the woolly mammoth and woolly rhinoceros were generally the last of the megafauna to go, around 10,000 BP.
The youngest mainland fossils come from Siberia's Kyttyk Peninsula and are 9,650 years old.
Trackways at St. Mary Reservoir in Canada show a mammoth herd of adults, subadults and young still roaming there 11,300–11,000 years ago.

entries.title: Doggerland drowns beneath the North Sea

facts.text: In the early Holocene, Doggerland linked eastern Britain to northern France, the Low Countries, north-west Germany and Jutland.
By 9000 BCE a large tidal bay had formed between eastern England and Dogger Bank, and rapid sea-level rise followed.
Between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago rising seas broke Doggerland into low islands and then submerged it completely.
Dogger Bank became an island, and Britain was finally cut off from the European mainland around 6500 BCE.
Most evidence of people living there dates to the Mesolithic of the early Holocene.

entries.title: Farming rises far beyond the Fertile Crescent

facts.text: Between 10,000 and 7,000 BP plants and animals were rapidly domesticated in tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa and Central America.
Drainage ditches at Kuk Swamp in highland New Guinea show taro and other crops cultivated by about 11,000 BP, perhaps by 8000 BCE.
The Near East was not the only cradle of farming: maize was domesticated in Mesoamerica from about 7000 BCE, and rice in the Far East.
Mehrgarh in Balochistan, South Asia's earliest Neolithic site with wheat, barley and herding, is dated variously from 8500 to 6500 BCE.
Cereal farming and herding reached the eastern Sahara by about 7000 BC.

entries.title: The Holocene Climatic Optimum begins

facts.text: The Holocene Climatic Optimum was a warm period lasting roughly from 9,500 to 5,500 years BP.
Northern Hemisphere heating peaked about 9,000 years ago, when axial tilt was 24° and perihelion fell in northern summer.
In New Zealand and Antarctica the warmest stretch, often called the Early Holocene Climatic Optimum, came earlier, roughly 10,500 to 8,000 years ago.
The Amery Ice Shelf in Antarctica retreated about 80 km landward during that southern warm interval.
North-western North America peaked 11,000–9,000 years ago while the Laurentide ice sheet still chilled eastern Canada.

entries.title: Sapropel S1 darkens the eastern Mediterranean floor

facts.text: The latest eastern Mediterranean sapropel, a dark, organic-rich mud laid down when bottom waters lose oxygen, formed between 9,500 and 5,500 years ago.
This S1 layer is tied to the African humid period: greater Nile and other river discharge freshened the sea, stratifying it and making it eutrophic.
Sapropels recur about every 21,000 years, following Earth's orbital cycles; when Nile discharge fell, deposition off its delta stopped.

entries.title: Did the Mediterranean pour into the Black Sea?

facts.text: A catastrophic inflow of Mediterranean seawater is proposed to have flooded the Black Sea, then a freshwater lake.
The flood was first dated to about 7,600 years ago, then redated in 2003 to 8,800 years ago, c. 6800 BCE.
The hypothesis is controversial; other authors argue for a gradual inundation of the basin.
Opponents cite water flowing out of the basin as late as 15,000 years ago and sill sediments building up from before 10,000 years ago.

entries.title: Kurile Lake caldera blasts Kamchatka

facts.text: In 6460–6414 BCE a very large eruption formed the present Kurile Lake caldera and its ignimbrite, dropping ash up to 1,700 km away.

It ranks with Fisher, Kikai and Mazama among the largest eruptions around the Pacific Ring of Fire, during an especially active spell in 6600–6400 BCE.

entries.title: The 8.2-kiloyear cold snap

facts.text: Global temperatures dropped abruptly around 8,200 years ago, and the cool spell lasted two to four centuries.
In Greenland the temperature fell 3.3 °C below the decadal average in under 20 years; the coldest phase lasted about 60 years.
A meltwater pulse, probably from glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway draining into the North Atlantic, may have weakened Atlantic overturning by 55–62%.
Cave records from Eurasia to South America and southern Africa show it; methane fell 15%, and North and East Africa turned drier.
Its signal in the NGRIP1 Greenland ice core is the GSSP for the base of the Northgrippian, set at 8,236 years before 2000.

entries.text: In Greenland, the temperature fell 3.3 °C below the decadal average in under 20 years. Around 8,200 years ago global temperatures dropped abruptly, and the cool spell lasted two to four centuries; its coldest phase lasted about 60 years. The likely cause was a flood of fresh water. A meltwater pulse, probably from glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway draining into the North Atlantic, may have weakened Atlantic overturning by 55–62%. That overturning is the ocean circulation that carries warm surface water north, so slowing it chilled the lands around the Atlantic. The event shows up far beyond the North Atlantic. Cave records from Eurasia to South America and southern Africa show it. Methane fell 15%, and North and East Africa turned drier. Its signal in the NGRIP1 Greenland ice core is the GSSP for the base of the Northgrippian, set at 8,236 years before 2000. The drainage itself is told in {{ref:nort-002}}.

entries.title: Lakes Agassiz and Ojibway drain into the sea

facts.text: As the last Hudson Bay ice melted, Lake Agassiz drained almost completely in its final major drainage shift.
Neighbouring Lake Ojibway, comparable in size, likely drained at the same time, perhaps in two floods through a broken ice dam and beneath the ice.
The final drainage raised global sea level by an estimated 0.8 to 2.8 m.
The freshwater flood is the leading suspected trigger of the 8.2-kiloyear cooling.
Lake Agassiz refilled as the ice withdrew north of today's Canada–US border around 10,000 years ago, and abandoned its southern outlet by about 9400 BP.

entries.title: The Storegga Slides send a tsunami across the North Atlantic

facts.text: Three submarine landslides at the edge of Norway's continental shelf moved about 3,500 km³ of debris along 290 km of shelf, among the largest known.
The slides set off large tsunamis in the North Atlantic; waves up to 20 m high hit Scotland and the Faroe Islands.
Tsunami sediment in Scotland lies up to 29 km inland and 4 m above today's normal tide level.
An earthquake that destabilised methane clathrate is thought to have triggered the collapse.
The tsunami may have flooded Doggerland's last low-lying land, though its impact there is debated.

entries.title: Did early farmers warm the planet?

facts.text: William Ruddiman argues that forest clearing by early farmers began raising greenhouse gases about 8,000 years ago.
CO2 rose markedly from about 8,000 years ago, and methane some 3,000 years later.
Critics counter with data from an earlier interglacial, and say all interglacials differ.

entries.title: The Holocene's warmest centuries

facts.text: The warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP.
After the 8.2 ka cold snap the climate warmed to the highest temperatures of the Holocene, and polar ice caps shrank to their Holocene minimum.
The warmest 200 years, around 6,500 years ago, were about 0.7 °C warmer than the 19th century.
Rain belts shifted: Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo valley got up to twice today's rainfall, and a stable climate fostered farming in China.
The warmth was followed by a slow decline of 0.1–0.3 °C per millennium until about two centuries ago.

entries.text: The warmest 200 years of the Holocene, around 6,500 years ago, were about 0.7 °C warmer than the 19th century. The warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP, and polar ice caps shrank to their Holocene minimum. Rain belts moved with the heat. The warmth was followed by a slow decline of 0.1–0.3 °C per millennium until about two centuries ago, a long cooling traced in {{ref:nort-022}}. Only the warming described in {{ref:megh-090}} broke that trend.

entries.title: Rising seas cut off Tasmania and New Guinea

facts.text: Post-glacial sea-level rise flooded the Bassian Plain, forming Bass Strait and making Tasmania an island.

entries.title: The Laurentide Ice Sheet's final collapse

facts.text: About 8,000 years ago the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split into two lobes, over Quebec–Labrador and Keewatin.
Central Asia stayed at near-glacial temperatures until the ice sheet collapsed around 8,000 BP.
Its final melting, between 8 and 7 ka, was followed by a much slower rate of global sea-level rise.

entries.title: The Mississippi and Rhine deltas take shape

facts.text: As sea-level rise slowed, the modern Mississippi River delta plain began to build around 8,000–7,500 years ago.

By switching course every 1,000–1,500 years, the Mississippi built six delta complexes; such deltas became major farming and population centres.

entries.title: The last Irish elk

facts.text: The Irish elk, or giant deer, survived in western Russia until around 7,700 years ago as Ice Age megafauna losses continued.
Its latest dated remains include finds at Kamyshlov and Maloarkhangelsk, Russia, from the 6th millennium BCE; it likely died out soon after.
By the early Holocene its range had shrunk dramatically; its youngest eastern records, near Lake Baikal, date to 10,700–10,400 BP.

entries.title: Mount Mazama blows apart and leaves Crater Lake

facts.text: Oregon's Mount Mazama, active again after 20,000 quiet years, ended in a VEI 7 eruption whose collapse left the caldera now holding Crater Lake.
A 48 km ash column reached the stratosphere; ash fell across eight western US states and three Canadian provinces.
The USGS has called it the largest explosive eruption in the Cascades in the past million years.
Its orange Mazama Ash covers at least 900,000 km² of the northern Great Plains and reaches Greenland's ice sheet, making it a standard dating marker.
Aerosols may have cooled mid- to high northern latitudes by 0.6–0.7 °C for one to three years; ashfall drove people out, leaving one Alberta site empty for about 200 years.

entries.title: Farming spreads into Europe

facts.text: Fast sea-level rise, the 8.2 ka cooling and loss of coastal land may have helped push the Neolithic Revolution into Europe.
In Central Europe human impact first shows in pollen records from 7,500 BP, and becomes substantial after 6,300 BP.
An Early Neolithic lakeshore village at La Marmotta, Italy, dates to about 5700 BC.
From about 7,500 years ago European Neolithic farmers also crossed from Iberia into Northwest Africa.
Farming took about 2,500 years, 8500–6000 BP, to spread from the Aegean, where it appears by c. 6500 BCE, to Britain; the Baltic followed around 5500 BP.

entries.title: Kikai-Akahoya: the Holocene's biggest eruption

facts.text: Japan's submarine Kikai Caldera produced the Akahoya eruption, a VEI 7 event and one of only six confirmed eruptions of its size in the Holocene.
Pyroclastic flows crossed the sea to southern Kyushu, up to 100 km away, and ash fell as far as Hokkaido.

entries.title: Neoglacial cooling sets in

facts.text: About 6,000 years ago the post-glacial warming trend ended and a long cooling trend began.

entries.title: The sea stops rising

facts.text: Global sea level, rising steadily since 20,000 years ago, levelled off about 6,000 years ago and has been fairly stable since.
In places sea level overshot today's: off Santa Catarina, Brazil, it peaked about 2.1 m above present 5,800–5,000 BP.
Rising water drowned the last land bridges, such as the southern Kuril link to Hokkaido around 6,000 BP.
The rate of rise fell from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm, ushering in some 4,000 years of near-stable sea level.

entries.title: The green Sahara dries into desert

facts.text: The African humid period ended about 6,000–5,000 years ago, often put at 5,500 BP, and the green Sahara began turning into desert.
North of the monsoon belt drying came in one step within 500 years; dust off Mauritania rose sharply within a few centuries.
Orbital shifts cut rainfall and raised temperatures; overgrazing has also been proposed as a trigger.
Lakes dried, vegetation vanished, and dust from basins like Bodélé, now Earth's largest dust source, grew; shrinking wetlands lowered atmospheric methane.
North Africa's population fell within a millennium, and many inner-Arabian settlements were abandoned about 5,300 years ago.

entries.title: The 4.2-kiloyear drought topples empires

facts.text: A severe drought began about 4,200 years ago; starting around 2200 BC it probably lasted the whole 22nd century BC, among the Holocene's harshest climate events.
Intense aridity is recorded from North Africa and the Middle East to Arabia, India and midcontinental North America; the East Asian summer monsoon weakened sharply.
Models link it to a major weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation, and the tropical rain belt (ITCZ) shifted abruptly south.
It is thought to have helped topple Egypt's Old Kingdom, the Akkadian Empire and China's Liangzhu culture, as Nile floods failed and irrigated fields salted up.
A Mawmluh Cave stalagmite in India marks it as the Meghalayan's base, 4,250 years before 2000; critics argue the drought was neither global nor neatly timed.

entries.contested_note: Its use as the Meghalayan's base is debated, since critics say the drought was neither global nor confined to a clear timeframe.

entries.title: The humid period ends across East and equatorial Africa

facts.text: A major pan-tropical environmental change took place about 4,000 years ago; drying in East Africa peaked around then.
Blue Nile discharge fell noticeably, and its sediment load rose as vegetation thinned in the catchment from 4,000–3,600 years ago.
In the Sahara, Lake Teli dried out completely about 4,200 years ago, and groundwater-fed Lake Yoa turned hypersaline by 4,000 years ago.
Nearer the equator the humid period ended later, between 4,000 and 2,500 years ago; West Africa had a long dry phase 3,500–1,700 years ago.
South of the equator, at Lake Malawi, drying began only about 1,000 years ago.

entries.title: The Kaali craters form on Saaremaa

entries.title: The Homeric solar minimum

facts.text: A deep, persistent grand solar minimum, the Homeric Minimum, lasted from about 800 to 600 BC.
It is linked to the Homeric Climate Oscillation, or 2.8 kyr event, when western North America and Europe grew colder; whether wetter or drier is debated.
Germany's Meerfelder Maar records a lasting shift to colder, wetter, windier weather, and the Göschenen I glacier advance in the Alps relates to it.

entries.title: The central Sahara becomes a lasting desert

facts.text: By 2,700 years ago the central Sahara had become a desert, which it has remained ever since.
At Libya's Wadi Tanezzuft, water stored in dunes and the Tassili mountains kept rivers flowing until 2,700 years ago, when they finally stopped.
Arabia's long drying trend, under way since 7,000–5,000 years ago, continued until 2,700 years ago.
Brief humid spells still returned, as in Roman North Africa and around the Dead Sea between 500 BCE and 300 CE.
At the Tanezzuft oasis, the drying trend after 1,600 years ago helped end the Garamantian civilisation.

entries.title: The Roman Warm Period

Alpine glaciers show AD 100–400 was markedly warmer than the centuries around it, and Iceland had a warm spell from 230 BC to AD 140.
A 2019 analysis of a much larger proxy dataset found it was a regional phenomenon, not a globally coherent episode.

entries.title: Madagascar loses its giants after people arrive

facts.text: At least 17 giant lemur species vanished, nearly all after people colonised Madagascar about 2,000 years ago; cut-marked bones show humans by 350 BCE, Bornean Austronesians by 500 CE.
The largest animals vanished soon after people arrived; others fell to prolonged hunting as settlers spread about 1,000 years ago, when areas now lemurless held 20 or more lemur species.
Malagasy hippos and elephant birds are thought to have died out in 750–1050 AD; the youngest Aepyornis maximus remains date to 1040–1380 CE, hippos to 1,000–400 years ago.
Giant lemurs survived into modern times: Megaladapis to 630 ± 50 BP, Palaeopropithecus to 510 ± 80 BP, making this one of history's most recent megafaunal extinctions.
Aridification began nearly 3,000 years ago, and human-set fires deforested the island; on Nosy Be, rainforest became fire-disturbed grassland and woodland 1,300–1,000 years ago.

entries.title: Okmok and the cold of 43 BCE

facts.text: Alaska's Okmok volcano had its second Holocene caldera-forming eruption, rated VEI 6, in 43 BCE.
It sent about 15–16 teragrams of sulfur into the stratosphere, cooling the Northern Hemisphere by 0.7–7.4 °C.
With another eruption a year or two earlier, it made 43 BCE and the next two years among the coldest of the last 2,500 years.
Cold, famine and failed Nile floods followed; this may have helped end Ptolemaic Egypt amid Rome's crisis, though a direct link is unproven.
Its tephra is a time marker in Greenland ice cores, and a lake filled the new caldera within a decade.

Some evidence once made Ilopango the source of the 539/540 eruption of the Late Antique Little Ice Age. A newer study dates it to 431 instead.

entries.title: The volcanic winter of 536

facts.text: Extreme weather in 535–536 CE ranks among the notable climate events in Earth history.
It is attributed to a large eruption of unknown source around 536, rated VEI 6–7.
Its climate impact is compared with Tambora in 1815, Samalas in 1257 and the 1452/1453 mystery eruption.
A violent eruption of Krakatoa in 535 was once proposed as the cause, but drilling in the Sunda Strait ruled out an eruption there that year.
Tree rings show the sharpest cold in mid-July to early August 536 across North America and Eurasia; European summers fell up to 2.5 °C below normal.

entries.title: The Late Antique Little Ice Age

facts.text: A century-long Northern Hemisphere cooling lasted from AD 536 to about 660, beginning with the volcanic winter of 536.
It coincided with three large eruptions, in 535/536, 539/540 and 547; one study suggests a global cooling of 2 °C.
The second eruption cut European summer temperatures by up to 2.7 °C in 539–540; sea-ice feedback and a deep solar minimum in the 600s prolonged the cold.
Scandinavia may have lost up to half its population, and the cooling coincided with the Plague of Justinian, which began in 541.
It strained the Eastern Roman and Sassanid empires and contributed to the migrations of the Lombards and early Slavs.

entries.title: The Medieval Warm Period

facts.text: A warm spell, the Medieval Warm Period or Medieval Climate Anomaly, lasted from about 950 to 1250, just before the Little Ice Age.
The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool stayed warm and saline from 1000 to 1400, with temperatures close to today's, then cooled.
Reconstructions show warmth in the eleventh and early fifteenth centuries, though the twentieth century was warmer still.
Evidence does not show globally synchronous warmth, so the term has limited use for hemispheric or global trends.
The warmth may have sent extra fresh water into the North Atlantic, possibly disrupting ocean circulation ahead of the Little Ice Age.

entries.title: Samalas erupts and buries a city on Lombok

facts.text: In 1257 Samalas, on the Indonesian island of Lombok, erupted catastrophically with a VEI of 7, one of the Holocene's largest eruptions.
Eruption columns rose 38–43 km; pyroclastic flows buried much of Lombok, destroyed the city of Pamatan and left the 6–7 km Segara Anak caldera.
Ice cores worldwide record a large sulfate spike; the aerosols caused a volcanic winter, cooling by about 0.7 °C in 1258 and 1.2 °C in 1259.
Cold, wet weather brought floods, crop failures and famine in Europe and Japan in 1258–1259, though the scale of the anomalies is still debated.
It may have helped trigger the Little Ice Age; global sea level dipped afterwards, recovering between 1250 and 1400.

entries.title: Quilotoa wakes after 14,000 years

entries.title: The Little Ice Age

facts.text: A period of regional cooling, strongest around the North Atlantic, ran from about 1300 to about 1850; it was not a true global ice age.
Hemispherically it was a modest Northern Hemisphere cooling of under 1 °C relative to late twentieth-century levels.
Mountain glaciers advanced in Europe, Alaska, New Zealand and Patagonia; Atlantic pack ice grew from about 1250, though regional maxima came at different times.
Proposed causes include volcanism, low solar activity, ocean circulation changes and human depopulation; climate models point to volcanism as the main driver.
Onset was between 1200 and 1400 in the north and about two centuries later in the south; it ended in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century.

entries.title: Moa hunted to extinction

facts.text: Moa, nine species of wingless birds up to about 3.6 m tall, were New Zealand's largest land animals and dominant herbivores until the Māori arrived.
Hunting, and to a lesser degree forest clearance, wiped them out, probably within 100 years of human settlement.
By 1445 all moa were gone, along with Haast's eagle, the giant raptor that had preyed on them.
Middens hold huge numbers of moa bones; ovens near the Waitaki River mouth alone held an estimated 29,000–90,000 birds.

entries.title: The 1452/1453 mystery eruption

With Samalas and Tambora, it was among the strongest cooling events of the last millennium.

entries.title: The Grindelwald Fluctuation

facts.text: From the 1560s to the 1630s, glaciers at Grindelwald, Switzerland, expanded markedly, part of a worldwide glacial expansion.
Temperatures ran 1–2 °C below twentieth-century averages, among the lowest of the Holocene.
Eruptions of Colima (1585), Nevado del Ruiz (1595) and Huaynaputina (1600) likely contributed, though cooling began about 15 years before the first.

entries.title: Huaynaputina, South America's largest witnessed eruption

facts.text: On 19 February 1600 Huaynaputina in southern Peru began the largest eruption ever witnessed in South America, rated VEI 6.
It killed perhaps 1,000–1,500 people, buried the surrounding land under 2 m of volcanic rock and coated nearby El Misti in ash.
Its sulfur cut sunlight by about 1.9 W/m²; the summer of 1601 was among the Northern Hemisphere's coldest of the last six centuries.
Frosts and harvest failures followed from Sweden to China and Japan, probably including Russia's famine of 1601–1603.
With Samalas and the 1452/1453 eruption, it may have helped bring on the Little Ice Age's coldest phase.

entries.title: A carbon dioxide dip around 1610

facts.text: Atmospheric carbon dioxide fell around 1610; mass deaths in the Americas after European arrival may explain it, though Huaynaputina's eruption may have contributed.
Conquest and disease killed as many as 90% of Indigenous Americans, and around 50 million hectares of farmland may have returned to forest.
Regrowth of tropical American forests from 1500 to 1650 may have stored 2–5 Pg of carbon; the CO2 drop shows at Law Dome, Antarctica.
Critics argue pre-Columbian farming did not clear forest on a modern scale, so regrowth should have had little effect.
A 2015 report suggested 1610 as one possible start of the Anthropocene.

entries.title: The last wild aurochs dies in Poland

Hunting, forest clearance, competition with livestock and cattle diseases left one herd in Poland's Jaktorów forest, where the last died in 1627.

entries.title: The Maunder Minimum

facts.text: From 1645 to 1715 solar activity was very low, the Maunder Minimum: sunspots were minimal and carbon-14 and beryllium-10 deposition rose.
It fell in the coldest part of the Little Ice Age; one of three especially cold intervals began about 1650.
Northern Hemisphere cooling began before the minimum, and climate models make volcanism the larger driver.

entries.title: The dodo vanishes from Mauritius

facts.text: The dodo, a large, flightless relative of pigeons found only on Mauritius, was last seen in 1662 and may have vanished from the main island by the 1640s.
Sailors ate many, but introduced pigs and other species likely did more harm; the dodo became an early poster species for human-caused extinction.
Other Mascarene birds followed, including the Réunion rail (last recorded 1674), Rodrigues rail (1726) and Réunion ibis (1763).

entries.title: The 1700 Cascadia earthquake and its orphan tsunami

facts.text: Around 9 pm on 26 January 1700, a magnitude 9.0 earthquake ruptured the 1,000 km Cascadia subduction zone off North America's Pacific coast.
Coasts from British Columbia to Oregon dropped up to 2 m and were buried by tsunami sand, leaving drowned 'ghost forests'.
Its tsunami crossed the Pacific and struck Honshu, Japan, about ten hours later, where it was recorded as an 'orphan tsunami'.
Oral traditions of several coastal peoples recall earthquakes and saltwater floods; it remains the zone's last megathrust earthquake.
Drowned red cedars in Oregon and Washington have outermost rings from 1699, the last growing season before the earthquake.

entries.title: Methane climbs 2.6-fold

facts.text: Since about 1750 atmospheric methane rose from 722 ppb to 1,936 ppb by 2025, a 2.6-fold increase to the highest level in at least 800,000 years.
Human activities caused almost all of the rise; methane is 3% of greenhouse emissions by mass but about 23% of climate forcing.
After a decade of near-zero growth, methane began climbing again in 2007, with sharp rises in 2015–2019 and a record annual jump in 2021.
Isotopes suggest recent growth comes mainly from microbial sources such as wetlands and agriculture rather than fossil fuels.
From 2010 to 2019 methane caused about 0.5 °C, roughly 30%, of observed global warming.

After a decade of near-zero growth, methane began climbing again in 2007, with sharp rises in 2015–2019 and a record annual jump in 2021. Isotopes suggest recent growth comes mainly from microbial sources such as wetlands and agriculture rather than fossil fuels. From 2010 to 2019, methane caused about 0.5 °C, roughly 30%, of observed global warming.

facts.text: On 1 November 1755 the Great Lisbon earthquake struck, one of the most destructive in history, killing around 100,000 people.
It heads the list of large earthquakes and tsunamis the Azores–Gibraltar fault zone has produced since records began in the 1700s.

entries.title: The Industrial Revolution starts the greenhouse rise

facts.text: With the Industrial Revolution, around 1780 and the steam engine, large-scale greenhouse gas emissions began to warm Earth.
Carbon dioxide had stayed near 280 ppm for 10,000 years before the mid-18th century; it has since risen 54%.
Antarctic ice cores record the highest greenhouse gas levels from the Industrial Revolution on; the IPCC takes 1750 as its pre-industrial baseline.
Warm decades became more common, and recorded extinctions mounted: over 322 species are often cited as lost to humans since then.
It is one proposed start of the Anthropocene, though humans had already reshaped much of Earth's landscape.

entries.title: The Laki fissure poisons Iceland

facts.text: From June 1783 to February 1784 the 40 km Laki fissure in Iceland poured out about 15 km³ of lava, one of history's largest effusive eruptions.
Its lava fields cover 565 km² of southeast Iceland.
In Northern Hemisphere ice cores its sulfate signal exceeds even Samalas's, and the sulfur caused substantial cooling.
Fluorine and chlorine poisoning devastated farming, and about a fifth of Iceland's people died.
It released about 120 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide; famine cost Egypt a sixth of its people in 1784, and hardship in Europe may have fed the French Revolution.

entries.title: Tambora, the most powerful eruption on record

facts.text: In April 1815 Tambora, on Sumbawa in Indonesia, produced the most powerful eruption in recorded history, a VEI 7 that ejected 37–45 km³ of material.
Its climax on 10 April drove a column 45 km high; it is the most recent confirmed VEI-7 eruption.
About 10,000–11,000 people died directly, and 49,000–90,000 more from famine and disease on Sumbawa, Lombok and Bali.
Its sulfur dioxide formed a stratospheric sulfate veil, seen in 1815 as a persistent 'dry fog' that dimmed the Sun.

entries.text: On 10 April 1815, an eruption column rose 45 km over the Indonesian island of Sumbawa. Tambora was at its climax. entries.title: 1816, the Year Without a Summer

facts.text: Tambora's aerosols lowered global temperatures by about 0.4–0.7 °C, and 1816 became the 'Year Without a Summer' across the Northern Hemisphere.
Frost and snow struck New England and Quebec in June 1816, ruining most North American crops.
Harvests failed across Europe in the worst famine of the nineteenth century; India's monsoon failed and a new cholera strain spread from Bengal.
1816 was the Northern Hemisphere's second-coldest year since about 1400 and the 1810s the coldest decade on record, aided by an eruption around 1809.
It also fell during the Dalton Minimum, a period of unusually low solar radiation.

entries.title: The 1831 eruption traced to Zavaritski Caldera

entries.title: Glaciers retreat as the Little Ice Age ends

facts.text: Glaciers began a strong retreat after about 1850, as the Little Ice Age ended in the late nineteenth century.
Since 1850 Austria has lost 40% of its glacier cover and Switzerland 30%; Pyrenean glaciers have also retreated greatly.
Alpine glaciers shrank from 1,817 km² in 1876 to 1,342 km² by 1973, reducing river run-off.
By 1879 the ice of Alaska's Glacier Bay had retreated 77 km.
Photographs show glaciers retreating markedly since 1850; only 27% of Glacier National Park's 1850 ice cover remained by 1993.

entries.title: Modern sea-level rise begins

facts.text: Sea level was nearly stable for the last 3,000 years until its rise accelerated, an onset variously dated between 1850 and 1900.
Tide gauges, later joined by satellites, show global mean sea level rose 19.5 cm between 1870 and 2004, about 1.44 mm a year.
Between 1901 and 2018 global sea level rose 15–25 cm, faster than in any century for at least 4,000 years, climbing 2.3 mm a year since the 1970s.
