entries.title: Krakatoa explodes

facts.text: On 26–27 August 1883 Krakatoa, in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, exploded in one of history's most violent eruptions, VEI 6, ejecting about 25 km³ of rock.
The blasts were heard 4,800 km away on Rodrigues, and the pressure wave was recorded on barographs worldwide seven times.
Tsunamis with a 41 m run-up killed at least 36,417 people, and two-thirds of the island was destroyed, leaving a caldera.
Ash rose 80 km, and Northern Hemisphere summer temperatures fell by an average of 0.4 °C that year.
The sterilised islands became a classic case of ecosystems rebuilding from scratch; Anak Krakatau rose from the caldera from 1927.

entries.title: Extinctions soar above the background rate

facts.text: Since 1900, extinctions have run at over 1,000 times the background rate, and the rate is still rising.
Humanity has entered what is sometimes called Earth's sixth major extinction, at perhaps 100 to 1,000 times the background rate, though the exact rate is disputed.
Over 322 species are often cited as lost to human activity since the Industrial Revolution, perhaps 500 vertebrates alone, mostly after 1900.
Islands suffer most: 95% of bird extinctions since the late 15th century were of island species.

entries.title: Santa María erupts in Guatemala

facts.text: In October 1902 Santa María in Guatemala had its first recorded eruption, a VEI 6 that ejected about 5.5 km³ of magma over two days.
It ranks with Novarupta (1912) and Pinatubo (1991) among the three largest eruptions of the 20th century; 7,000–13,000 people died.

entries.title: The Tunguska explosion flattens a Siberian forest

facts.text: On 30 June 1908 a huge explosion over the Siberian taiga near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River flattened about 2,150 km² of forest.
Scientists attribute it to the air burst of a 50–60 m meteoroid 5–10 km up, releasing about 10–15 megatons; whether asteroid or comet is debated.
The shock wave killed at least three people and was detected worldwide; bright nights followed across western Eurasia.
Models suggest it made nitric oxide that cut ozone by 35–45% in early 1909 and tripled ground UV-B at 30°N.
It is the most violent impact event recorded in modern times; nearby Lake Cheko may be a fragment's crater, though sediment studies disagree.

entries.title: Novarupta, the 20th century's largest eruption

facts.text: Beginning 6 June 1912, Novarupta on the Alaska Peninsula produced the 20th century's largest eruption, a 60-hour VEI 6 blast of 13–15 km³ of ash.
Magma drained from beneath Mount Katmai, whose summit collapsed; deep pyroclastic flows filled the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.
No one died directly, but the most ash-buried Native villages were abandoned.

It was declared extinct in 1914 when Martha, the last known bird, died at the Cincinnati Zoo, 20 years after the species vanished from the wild.

entries.title: Is the Atlantic overturning slowing?

facts.text: Reconstructions suggest that by 2015 the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation was weaker than before the Industrial Revolution, by roughly 15–20% since the mid-twentieth century.
One analysis found it weaker in 1975–1995 than at any time in the past millennium; another estimates a slowdown of 0.46 sverdrups per decade since 1950.
Ocean warming and Greenland meltwater may be weakening it, but some studies find no overall decline, and the share of natural variability is debated.

entries.title: The ocean turns more acidic

facts.text: Average ocean-surface pH fell from about 8.15 to 8.05 between 1950 and 2026, roughly a 26% rise in hydrogen-ion concentration.
Human carbon dioxide is the main cause: from 1850 to 2022 the ocean absorbed 26% of all anthropogenic emissions.
Present-day surface pH, and its rate of change, are unprecedented for at least 26,000 years.
Interior ocean pH has also fallen everywhere over the last 20–30 years, and open-ocean surface pH has dropped about 0.017–0.027 units per decade since the late 1980s.
Falling pH lowers carbonate saturation, speeding dissolution of the calcium carbonate that molluscs, foraminifera and other shell-builders need.

entries.title: Rapid global warming since the mid-20th century

facts.text: Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels have caused planetary-scale climate change; warm decades became ever more common after the Industrial Revolution.
The global average temperature was 14 °C for 1951–1980 and 15 °C for 2013–2017.
The ocean is about 0.7 °C warmer than in 1950, warming that has contributed more than 15 cm of sea-level rise.
The Arctic warmed faster than most regions and land twice as fast as ocean; Antarctica warmed after 1957, the South Pole at triple the global rate after 1990.
Effects include more extreme weather, thawing permafrost, marine heatwaves, ocean deoxygenation and acidification.

entries.title: The 1952 Kamchatka earthquake

facts.text: A magnitude 9.0 megathrust earthquake struck off Kamchatka, one of the four most powerful quakes measured since the 1930s.
It ruptured the Kuril–Kamchatka subduction zone, which has produced several giant quakes, including those of 1737 and 2025.
Just after the quake, Tao-Rusyr Caldera in the Kuril Islands had its only historical eruption, building a small lava dome.
On 5 November 1952 the Mw 8.8–9.0 quake raised a tsunami that struck the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka, with waves 15–18 m high at Severo-Kurilsk.
It remains Russia's most powerful recorded earthquake, fifth worldwide since 1900, and Russia's deadliest and most damaging tsunami.

entries.title: The Great Acceleration and the bomb spike

facts.text: After World War II, population, economic growth, pollution and resource use all began rising at a dramatic rate, the so-called Great Acceleration.
Since about 1950 humans have doubled Earth's fixed nitrogen, opened an ozone hole with CFCs, and cut off almost a fifth of river sediment from the sea.
Atomic-bomb tests scattered radionuclides such as caesium-137, strontium-90 and plutonium around the globe, embedding them in sediments and glacial ice.
Sediments of Crawford Lake, Ontario, record a plutonium spike from hydrogen-bomb tests at 1952, with carbon particles and nitrates from fossil fuels and fertilizers.
Global radionuclide levels peaked around 1965, and bomb carbon-14 entered atmospheric CO2 and the biosphere.

entries.title: West Antarctica warms and sheds ice

facts.text: West Antarctica warmed by about 2.4 °C between 1958 and 2012, a change attributed to rising greenhouse gases.
Warming seawater melts its ice shelves, and coastal glaciers, above all Thwaites, Pine Island and Smith, have retreated substantially since at least the 1990s.
Ice loss rose from 53 Gt a year in 1992 to 159 Gt a year in 2017, adding about 7.6 mm to global sea level.

entries.title: The Keeling Curve climbs at Mauna Loa

facts.text: Continuous measurements on Mauna Loa from March 1958 gave the first significant evidence of rapidly rising atmospheric carbon dioxide.
CO2 climbed steadily from 313 ppm in March 1958 to 406 ppm in November 2018, by then rising about 2.5 ppm a year.
Air in ice cores shows Holocene CO2 stayed between 275 and 285 ppm until it began rising sharply early in the nineteenth century.
The accelerating rise comes from burning fossil fuels; the curve also swings about 6 ppm each year with Northern Hemisphere plant growth.
On 9 May 2013 daily CO2 at Mauna Loa passed 400 ppm, a level probably not reached since the mid-Pliocene, 2 to 4 million years ago.

entries.title: Valdivia 1960: the largest earthquake ever recorded

facts.text: The largest earthquake ever recorded, of moment magnitude 9.4–9.6, struck southern Chile on 22 May 1960.
It ruptured the subduction zone where the Nazca plate sinks beneath southern Chile, a boundary with a long history of massive earthquakes.
Two days after the main shock, the Cordón Caulle volcano began erupting along its southern flank.
Its tsunami reached 25 m on the Chilean coast and 10.7 m at Hilo, Hawaii, 10,000 km away; between 1,000 and 6,000 people died.
Similar great earthquakes struck the region in 1575 and around 1800 BC, the latter dated from tsunami debris in the Atacama Desert.

entries.title: The 1964 Alaska earthquake

facts.text: A magnitude 9.2 megathrust earthquake struck southern Alaska, one of the four most powerful recorded since the 1930s.
The shaking collapsed weak clay beds left by ancient Lake Atna, setting off catastrophic landslides in Anchorage.
Its seismic waves set water sloshing in seiches as far away as Puerto Rico.
Lasting 4 minutes 38 seconds, the Mw 9.2–9.3 quake is the most powerful recorded in North America and second worldwide since 1900.
Land rose across 520,000 km², by 13–15 m on Montague Island; tsunamis ran up 67 m, and about 139 people died.

entries.title: Wildlife populations plunge since 1970

facts.text: Monitored vertebrate wildlife populations fell by almost 70% on average after 1970, driven mainly by agriculture and fishing.
Land-use change, overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species all contributed; migratory freshwater fish declined by 76%.
In 1987 the death of the last Kauaʻi ʻōʻō ended an entire bird family, the Hawaiian honeyeaters.
In the Yangtze, the Chinese paddlefish was last recorded in 2003, and the baiji river dolphin was declared extinct in 2006, the loss of a whole genus.

entries.title: A chytrid fungus kills off frogs

facts.text: Chytridiomycosis, a fungal disease spread by travel and the wildlife trade, has caused steep declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions.
Victims include Australia's gastric-brooding frogs, gone by the mid-1980s, and Costa Rica's golden toad, last seen in 1989.
The chytrid Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, a main driver of the worldwide amphibian decline, has spread across Australia, New Zealand, Central America and Africa.

entries.title: Arctic sea ice shrinks

facts.text: Arctic sea ice, tracked by satellite since 1979, has declined by over 50%, the loss accelerating to 4.7% per decade in the early 21st century.
The September minimum hit a record 3.39 million km² in 2012, beating the 2007 record of 4.16 million km².
Ice at least four years old fell from 26% of the cover in 1988 to 7% by 2013, and ice thickness dropped 66% over six decades.
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average, and the melt season has lengthened five days per decade.
Sea ice lost between 1979 and 2011 caused radiative forcing equal to a quarter of CO2 emissions over the same years.

entries.title: Mount St. Helens erupts in 1980

facts.text: Mount St. Helens erupted catastrophically on 18 May 1980, a VEI 5 event of about 1.2–1.3 km³, the most significant in the contiguous US in recorded history.
Its flank collapsed into a huge debris avalanche, which became the reference case for recognizing collapses at volcanoes such as Mount Bandai and Parinacota.
Ash dusted land from British Columbia to Manitoba, and ferns recolonized the devastated ground first, a 'fern spike' like the one after the dinosaur extinction.

entries.title: The ozone layer thins and a hole opens

facts.text: From the late 1970s stratospheric ozone thinned worldwide, with a far deeper springtime loss over the poles, the Antarctic 'ozone hole'.
Manufactured chlorofluorocarbons, halons and related refrigerants, solvents and propellants were the main cause.
Antarctic spring ozone fell by up to 70%, first reported in 1985; inside the polar vortex over half the lower-stratospheric ozone is destroyed each spring.
Mid-latitude total ozone fell below pre-1980 values between 1980 and 1996; Arctic losses reached 30% in the coldest winters and springs.
Stronger ultraviolet-B under depleted ozone cuts plant productivity by about 6%, and the hole has at times reached parts of Australia, Chile and Argentina.

entries.title: El Chichón warms the northern winter

facts.text: Long-dormant El Chichón in Chiapas, Mexico, produced three Plinian eruptions within a week in spring 1982.
The VEI 5 eruption put 7 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and 20 million tonnes of particles into the stratosphere, which circled Earth in three weeks.
Its aerosols brought winter warming to North America, Europe and Siberia in 1982–83, while Alaska, Greenland and China ran colder than normal.

entries.title: Pinatubo cools the world in 1991

facts.text: Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted on 15 June 1991, a VEI 6 event and the second-largest land eruption of the 20th century after Novarupta in 1912.
Its ash column rose 35 km, and it put more particles into the stratosphere than any eruption since Krakatoa in 1883.
Aerosols spread a global sulfuric-acid haze; world temperatures fell about 0.5 °C in 1991–1993, and ozone depletion temporarily rose sharply.
The summit collapsed into a 2.5 km caldera, later filled by Lake Pinatubo, and rain-driven lahars flooded the surrounding lowlands.
It released 17–20 megatonnes of sulfur dioxide, and 1992 brought a 'Summer that Wasn't', with odd weather and cooling across the United States.

entries.title: Sea-level rise speeds up in the satellite era

facts.text: Satellite altimeters, flying since TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992, measured 7.5 cm of rise from 1993 to 2017, and the rate reached 4.62 mm a year in 2013–2022.
From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers supplied 44% of the rise and thermal expansion of warming seawater 42%.
Greenland's contribution grew from 0.07 mm a year in 1992–1997 to 0.68 mm a year in 2012–2017.
Flooding of Bramble Cay in 2016 wiped out its melomys, the first mammal lost to human-caused sea-level rise, declared extinct in 2019.

entries.title: Greenland's ice loss accelerates

facts.text: Jakobshavn Isbræ, Greenland's largest outlet glacier, switched to rapid mass loss after 1997 as warming North Atlantic water melted glacier fronts from below.
Annual ice loss from the whole sheet accelerated to about 187 Gt in 2000–2010 and 286 Gt in 2010–2018.
In July 2012 melt reached 97% of the ice sheet's surface, a melt unmatched since 1889, and that year's net loss of 464 Gt set a record.
An even larger melt in 2019 brought a record net loss of 586 Gt, with about 600 Gt of ice lost in just two months.
During another record melt in 2021, rain fell for 13 hours at the 3,216 m Summit Station, where it had never rained before.

entries.title: 1998: the first global coral bleaching

facts.text: In 1998 the first globally recognized coral bleaching event struck, with 21% of reefs under bleaching-level heat stress.
A very strong 1997–98 El Niño drove it, warming Indian Ocean waters by 2 °C; 1998 became the warmest year then on record.
Belize's barrier reef had its first recorded mass bleaching, and the Great Barrier Reef its first major bleaching event.
Mass bleaching has grown sharply in frequency and severity worldwide since the early 1980s, driven by marine heatwaves.

facts.text: From 1998 to 2013, negative phases of the Pacific decadal and Atlantic multidecadal oscillations briefly slowed surface warming.
The slowdown is less pronounced in current observational datasets than in those available in 2012.
It ended after 2012: every year from 2015 on was warmer than any before, and 2024 exceeded 1.5 °C.

entries.title: Mass bleaching returns to the Great Barrier Reef

facts.text: Marine heatwaves caused mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef in 1998, 2002, 2006, 2016, 2017 and 2020, with another event confirmed in March 2022.
Over half of the reef's coral cover was lost between 1995 and 2017, and many breeding adults died in the 2016–17 bleaching.
Warming is already bleaching coral reefs worldwide, habitats that sustain high biodiversity.

entries.title: The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

facts.text: On 26 December 2004 the boundary between the Indian and Burma plates slipped off Sumatra in a megathrust earthquake of magnitude 9.1–9.3.
More than 1,600 km of the fault ruptured, lifting the seafloor up to 5 m and shifting it 11 m sideways within seven minutes.
The tsunami reached 35 m near Banda Aceh and killed approximately 229,800 people around the Indian Ocean.
The second- or third-most powerful quake since 1900, it released about one-eighth of all seismic moment from 1906 to 2005.
Deposits on Phra Thong, Thailand, record at least three earlier major tsunamis in 2,800 years, the latest about 700 years ago.

entries.title: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami

facts.text: On 11 March 2011 a magnitude 9.0–9.1 undersea megathrust earthquake struck off Honshu, as the Pacific plate subducted beneath the Okhotsk microplate.
It ranks among the four most powerful earthquakes measured since the 1930s, and the worst-hit areas of Tōhoku shook for about six minutes.
Its seismic waves crossed 8,000 km in under 30 minutes, raising seiches about 1.5–1.8 m high in Norway.
Its tsunami reached up to 40.5 m at Miyako and swept up to 10 km inland; 19,759 people died, and three Fukushima Daiichi reactors melted down.
Japan's most powerful recorded quake, it released about 93% of the moment estimated to have built up there since 1926.

entries.title: The Chelyabinsk airburst

facts.text: On 15 February 2013 an asteroid about 20 m across exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in an airburst of around 500 kilotons.
The largest airburst observed with modern instruments, it shattered windows, injured over 1,000 people and scattered meteorites.
Its similar dynamics reinforced the view that the Tunguska blast was a meteoroid exploding high in the air.

entries.title: The global coral bleaching of 2014–2017

facts.text: Record ocean heat during the 2014–2017 El Niño caused the longest and most destructive coral bleaching event then known.
Bleaching in 2014–2016 killed coral on an unprecedented scale; reefs making up three-quarters of the world's reef systems were severely bleached.
In 2016 bleaching killed 29 to 50% of the Great Barrier Reef's coral; near Port Douglas over half the bleached corals died.

entries.title: Reykjanes wakes after 800 years

facts.text: After nearly 800 years of quiet, volcanic and earthquake activity resumed on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula from 2020; Fagradalsfjall erupted on 19 March 2021.
A 15 km magma intrusion in late 2023 opened a subsiding graben beneath Grindavík, forcing the town's evacuation; nine Sundhnúkur fissure eruptions followed through August 2025.
The eruptions were small and effusive (VEI 1), but experts suggested the activity may mark the start of decades of volcanism.

entries.title: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai blows its top
entries.article: 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai eruption and tsunami

facts.text: After erupting from December 2021, the submarine Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai volcano exploded on 15 January 2022, the largest eruption since Pinatubo, rated at least VEI 5.
Its plume reached 58 km into the mesosphere, and the blast, the largest atmospheric explosion recorded by modern instruments, sent pressure waves around the globe.
It lofted 146 million tons of seawater, a tenth of the stratosphere's water vapour, enough to warm Earth's surface temporarily; a Pacific-wide tsunami followed.

entries.title: The fourth global coral bleaching

facts.text: A fourth global coral bleaching event began in February 2023; in April 2024 NOAA confirmed it as the largest yet.
From January 2023 to September 2025 bleaching-level heat reached about 84% of the world's reef area, with bleaching in at least 83 countries and territories.
Great Barrier Reef hard-coral cover fell by up to 30.6% from 2024 to 2025, the largest single-year drops since 1986 in two regions.

entries.title: 2024, the warmest year on record

facts.text: 2024 was the warmest year since regular tracking began in 1850, at +1.60 °C, well above the 1.5 °C mark.
It followed 2023, already 1.48 °C above the 1850–1900 average and declared the warmest year on record as soon as it ended.
The years 2015–2025 included all eleven warmest since 1850, and the 2016–2025 decade averaged 1.26 °C above pre-industrial.
The global ocean was the warmest ever recorded in 2022.
NOAA data rank 2025 as the third-warmest year on record, behind 2024 and 2023.

entries.title: The Anthropocene epoch is voted down

facts.text: In 2024, after 15 years of deliberation, stratigraphers voted down by a wide margin the proposal to make the Anthropocene a formal epoch after the Holocene.
Its shallow sediment record and very recent start date weighed against it; the ICS and IUGS then confirmed the rejection by a near-unanimous vote.
The term stays in wide informal use for human impact on the Earth system, though its validity as a scientific term remains disputed.

meiofauna.text: Tiny animals that live among the grains of the seafloor.

siphuncle.text: A tube running through the chambers of a cephalopod shell.

bentonite.text: A clay formed from altered volcanic ash.

disaster taxon.text: A species that booms in the wreckage of a mass extinction, spreading widely while competitors are scarce.

plastron.text: The flat bony belly shell of a turtle; the upper shell is the carapace.

tuff.text: Rock made of volcanic ash that has settled and hardened.

konservat-lagerstätte.text: A fossil site of exceptional preservation, where soft tissues and delicate imprints survive.

hyperthermal.text: A rapid, short-lived episode of global warming.

planktic foraminifera.text: Tiny single-celled organisms with shells that drift in the open sea.

polarity reversal.text: A swap of Earth's magnetic north and south poles.

tektite.text: A droplet of natural glass formed from rock melted and thrown out by an impact.

fern spike.text: A sudden burst of fern spores in the fossil record.

diatom.text: A single-celled alga with a glassy shell.

bone conduction.text: Hearing through vibrations carried by the skull bones rather than the eardrum.

maar.text: A crater left by a volcanic explosion, often filled by a lake.

echolocation.text: Sensing the surroundings by sending out sounds and listening for their echoes.

loess.text: Fine, wind-blown silt that piles up in thick blankets.

calcrete.text: A hard, limy crust that forms in soil.

biface.text: A stone tool flaked on both faces, such as a hand axe.

marine isotope stage.text: A numbered warm or cold stage of the ice ages, read from chemical signals in seafloor shells.

thermohaline circulation.text: The deep ocean conveyor driven by differences in heat and salt.

tephra.text: The fragments of rock and ash a volcano hurls into the air.

hafting.text: Fixing a stone point or blade to a handle or shaft.

fire-stick farming.text: The deliberate burning of forest and grassland to shape the landscape.

refugium.text: A sheltered area where species survive a harsh period such as a glacial maximum.

phreatomagmatic eruption.text: An eruption driven by steam where magma meets water.

polar seesaw.text: A pattern in which one hemisphere warms while the other cools.

surface mass balance.text: The yearly gain of snow on an ice sheet minus what it loses to melting.

perihelion.text: The point in Earth's orbit where it passes closest to the Sun.

sapropel.text: A dark, organic-rich mud laid down on the sea floor when bottom waters lose oxygen.

post-glacial rebound.text: The slow rise of the Earth's crust after the weight of an ice sheet is removed.

coral bleaching.text: The whitening of heat-stressed corals that expel the algae living in them.

hade-001.q: What seeded the region where Earth formed with heavy elements?
hade-001.a: A supernova shock wave in a dense part of the Milky Way.

hade-005.q: How did runaway accretion build Earth?
hade-005.a: Dust and debris from the solar nebula clumped into ever larger bodies.

hade-009.a: Anorthosite, which separated from the magma below about 100 million years after the Moon formed.

hade-014.a: That it solidified about 100 million years after Earth formed.

hade-019.q: In some models, what covered the Hadean Earth?
hade-019.a: A global ocean; models disagree on how much continental crust existed.

76ce00527f13.title: Geologic time scale
76ce00527f13.sentence: Hadean | Earth consolidates from solar nebula over 10-30 million years. Collision with Theia (proto-planet) forms Moon from debris. Core differentiates. Magma ocean cools, releasing CO 2 and water to give CO 2 -rich atmosphere. Icy asteroids also contribute water. Mantle convection begins with rapid, shallow plate tectonics or stagnant lid tectonics. Decline in meteorite impacts with last ocean-vaporising impact c. 4.3 Ga. Probable emergence of life after this. Evidence for oldest crust from detrital zircon c. 4.37 Ga. Acasta gneiss complex contains oldest recorded rocks c. 4.03 Ga. | 4567.3 ± 0.16

510284fcea37.title: Precambrian
510284fcea37.sentence: The supercontinent Kenorland was formed c. 2.72 Ga ago and then broke sometime after 2.45–2.1 Ga into the proto-continent cratons called Laurentia, Baltica, Yilgarn craton and Kalahari.

cfb4126bcdf3.title: Witwatersrand
cfb4126bcdf3.sentence: The "Central Rand Group" of deposits was brought to an abrupt end by massive outpourings of lava, which form the Ventersdorp lavas which erupted 2.715 billion years ago.

0a61e88f7f95.title: Witwatersrand
0a61e88f7f95.sentence: The cause of these lava outpourings is a matter of speculation.

4b3d05d23705.title: Witwatersrand
4b3d05d23705.sentence: It might be related to the collision of the Kaapvaal craton with the Zimbabwe Craton, eventually to become knitted together to form a single continental unit.

3b8d06c92446.title: Craton
3b8d06c92446.sentence: The 30 to 40 per cent partial melting of mantle rock at 4 to 10 GPa pressure produces komatiite magma and a solid residue very close in composition to Archean lithospheric mantle.

fa82970401c4.title: Archean
fa82970401c4.sentence: The pulses of increased oxygenation at 2,700 and 2,501 Ma have both been considered by some as potential start points of the Great Oxygenation Event, which most scholars consider to have begun in the Palaeoproterozoic (c. 2,400 Ma).

9036e7c6ea3e.title: Paleoclimatology

9036e7c6ea3e.sentence: In the late Archaean eon, an oxygen-containing atmosphere began to develop, apparently from photosynthesizing cyanobacteria (see Great Oxygenation Event) which have been found as stromatolite fossils from 2.7 billion years ago.

616843d98661.title: Cambrian explosion
616843d98661.section: Precambrian life > Evidence of animals around one billion years ago
616843d98661.sentence: Stromatolites, stubby pillars built by colonies of microorganisms, are a major constituent of the fossil record from about 2,700 million years ago, but their abundance and diversity declined steeply after about 1,250 million years ago.

beaf2b19dd68.title: Fossil
beaf2b19dd68.sentence: The earliest stromatolite of confirmed microbial origin dates to 2.724 billion years ago.

5d3831854fa4.title: Archean
5d3831854fa4.sentence: Stromatolites are found throughout the Archean and become common late in the Archean.

eeae505dc90a.title: Archean
eeae505dc90a.sentence: Only at the end of the Archean did the continents likely emerge from the ocean.

1ccef0b028e3.title: Archean
1ccef0b028e3.sentence: The Earth during the Archean was mostly a water world: there was continental crust, but much of it was under a superocean deeper than today's oceans.

b515bebeaf9b.title: Archean
b515bebeaf9b.sentence: The Archean ocean was enriched in heavier oxygen isotopes relative to the modern ocean, though δ18O values decreased to levels comparable to those of modern oceans over the course of the later part of the eon as a result of increased continental weathering.

e1265d2fe07d.title: Geologic time scale
e1265d2fe07d.sentence: Proterozoic | Paleoproterozoic | Siderian | 2.5 – 2.42 Ga massive banded iron formations (BIFs) precipitated across most continents. Increasing atmospheric oxygen leads to Great Oxidation Event (c. 2.4––2.3 Ga) and Huronian glaciations as global temperatures drop. | 2500

4458f700aec1.title: History of Earth
4458f700aec1.sentence: The oxidized iron appears as red layers in geological strata called banded iron formations that formed in abundance during the Siderian period (between 2500 Ma and 2300 Ma).

d27c7052ba19.title: Banded iron formation
d27c7052ba19.sentence: They are relatively undeformed and form extensive topographic plateaus, such as the Hamersley Range.

dd8de53683f8.title: Banded iron formation
dd8de53683f8.sentence: The banded iron formations here were deposited from 2470 to 2450 Ma and are the thickest and most extensive in the world, with a maximum thickness in excess of 900 meters (3,000 feet).

7f53cd32e113.title: Proterozoic
7f53cd32e113.sentence: The first surge in atmospheric oxygen at the beginning of the Proterozoic is called the Great Oxygenation Event, or alternately the Oxygen Catastrophe – to reflect the mass extinction of almost all life on Earth, which at the time was virtually all obligate anaerobic.

9b63842bb98c.title: Extinction event
9b63842bb98c.section: Uncertainty in the Proterozoic and earlier eons
9b63842bb98c.sentence: The Oxygen Catastrophe, which occurred around 2.45 billion years ago in the Paleoproterozoic, is plausible as the first-ever major extinction event.

25b5866238f5.title: Extinction event
25b5866238f5.section: Uncertainty in the Proterozoic and earlier eons
25b5866238f5.sentence: It was perhaps also the worst-ever, in some sense, but with the Earth's ecology just before that time so poorly understood, and the concept of prokaryote genera so different from genera of complex life, that it would be difficult to meaningfully compare it to any of the "Big Five" even if Paleoproterozoic life were better known.

2878e4855018.title: Extinction event
2878e4855018.section: Uncertainty in the Proterozoic and earlier eons
2878e4855018.sentence: For this reason, well-documented extinction events are confined to the Phanerozoic eon – with the sole exception of the Oxygen Catastrophe in the Proterozoic – since before the Phanerozoic, all living organisms were either microbial, or if multicellular then soft-bodied.

695acf1c08f4.title: Extinction event
695acf1c08f4.sentence: The "Big Five" of the Phanerozoic Eon were anciently preceded by the presumed far more extensive mass extinction of microbial life during the Great Oxidation Event (also known as the Oxygen Catastrophe) early in the Proterozoic Eon.

5cc7432401fe.title: History of life
5cc7432401fe.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Fossil evidence
5cc7432401fe.sentence: Fungi-like fossils were found in vesicular basalt dating back to the Paleoproterozoic Era around 2.4 billion years ago.

ce225ae0f0c6.title: History of Earth
ce225ae0f0c6.sentence: The earliest fossils possessing features typical of fungi date to the Paleoproterozoic era, some 2.4 Ga ago; these multicellular benthic organisms had filamentous structures capable of anastomosis.

2cce067c51c6.title: Proterozoic
2cce067c51c6.sentence: The earliest fossils possessing features typical of fungi date to the Paleoproterozoic Era, some 2.4 Ga; these multicellular benthic organisms had filamentous structures capable of anastomosis.

e582af3ef620.title: Ice age
e582af3ef620.sentence: Correlative Huronian deposits have been found near Marquette, Michigan, and correlation has been made with Paleoproterozoic glacial deposits from Western Australia.

af1626ab26c3.title: Ice age
af1626ab26c3.sentence: Rocks from the earliest well-established ice age, called the Huronian, have been dated to around 2.4 to 2.1 billion years ago during the early Proterozoic Eon.

aafba4e4082b.title: Paleoclimatology
aafba4e4082b.sentence: - The Huronian glaciation is the first known glaciation in Earth's history, and lasted from 2400 to 2100 million years ago.

158950045143.title: Precambrian
158950045143.section: Planetary environment and the oxygen catastrophe
158950045143.sentence: A number of glacial periods have been identified going as far back as the Huronian epoch, roughly 2400–2100 Ma.

c825955d68bf.title: History of Earth
c825955d68bf.sentence: Glacial deposits found in South Africa date back to 2.2 Ga, at which time, based on paleomagnetic evidence, they must have been located near the equator.

cd8be5f4caab.title: Geologic time scale
cd8be5f4caab.sentence: Proterozoic | Paleoproterozoic | Rhyacian | Massive rise in atmospheric oxygen leads to expansion of life and increased burial of organic matter (Lomagundi carbon isotope excursion) (2.3 to 2.1 Ga). First red beds deposited. Eruptions of Bushveld Magmatic Province (from 2.25 Ga). Orogenies in South America and West Africa mark beginning of Columbia supercontinent. Yarrabubba impact structure (c. 2.23 Ga). | 2300

86b13183aa53.title: Impact event
86b13183aa53.section: Impacts and the Earth > Earth impacts in history > Precambrian
86b13183aa53.sentence: In 2020, scientists discovered the world's oldest confirmed impact crater, the Yarrabubba crater, caused by an impact that occurred in Yilgarn craton (what is now Western Australia), dated at more than 2.2 billion years ago with the impactor estimated to be around 7 kilometres (4.3 mi) wide.

6891a974d6a8.title: Proterozoic
6891a974d6a8.sentence: Red beds, which are colored by hematite, indicate an increase in atmospheric oxygen 2 Ga.

7eba965f8a66.title: History of life
7eba965f8a66.sentence: The earliest evidence of eukaryotes (complex cells with organelles) dates from 1.85 Ga, likely due to symbiogenesis between anaerobic archaea and aerobic proteobacteria in co-adaptation against the new oxidative stress.

5cce04603b2a.title: History of life
5cce04603b2a.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Fossil evidence
5cce04603b2a.sentence: The controversial Francevillian biota fossils, dated to 2.1 Ga, are the earliest known fossil organisms that are clearly multicellular, if they are indeed fossils.

a99da59289b1.title: Geologic time scale
a99da59289b1.sentence: Proterozoic | Paleoproterozoic | Orosirian | 2.0–1.8 Ga Columbia supercontinent assembles during collisional events including Trans-Hudson orogeny (North America), Limpopo Belt (South Africa), Capricorn orogeny (Australia) and Trans-North China orogeny. Drop in atmospheric oxygen as increased volcanism releases carbon dioxide. Grypania represents a possible early eukaryote. Sudbury Impact (1.85 Ga). | 2050

88ffd8ca9c5a.title: Impact event
88ffd8ca9c5a.section: Impacts and the Earth > Earth impacts in history > Precambrian
88ffd8ca9c5a.sentence: The Vredefort impact event, which occurred around 2 billion years ago in Kaapvaal craton (what is now South Africa), caused the largest verified crater, a multi-ringed structure 160–300 km (100–200 mi) across, forming from an impactor approximately 10–15 km (6.2–9.3 mi) in diameter.

ad8185e895e8.title: Witwatersrand
ad8185e895e8.sentence: Thus, it is possible that if it had not been for the Vredefort asteroid strike 2 billion years ago, humanity would either never have discovered the rich gold deposits beneath the Southern African surface, or they would have been eroded away during the uninterrupted removal of a several kilometres thick layer of deposits from the surface of the Southern African Plateau in the relatively recent geological past: i.e. the past 150 million years, but especially during the last 20 million years.

039144938673.title: Witwatersrand
039144938673.sentence: A final event that had a major impact on the geology of the Witwatersrand Basin and its exposure in the Johannesburg region, was a massive meteor impact 110 km to the south-west of Johannesburg 2.02 billion years ago.

389336e7a02e.title: History of life
389336e7a02e.section: Diversification of eukaryotes > Chromatin, nucleus, endomembrane system, and mitochondria
389336e7a02e.sentence: Fossils of the algae Grypania have been reported in 1.85 billion-year-old rocks (originally dated to 2.1 Ga but later revised), indicating that eukaryotes with organelles had already evolved.

748bc9eef9cf.title: Proterozoic
748bc9eef9cf.sentence: Their accumulation ceased after 1.9 Ga, after the iron in the oceans had all been oxidized.

9522731beb4a.title: Banded iron formation
9522731beb4a.section: Origins > Formation processes > Absence of oxygen or hydrogen sulfide
9522731beb4a.sentence: An asteroid (estimated at 10 km (6.2 mi) across) impacted into waters about 1,000 m (3,300 ft) deep 1.849 billion years ago, coincident with the pause in BIF deposition.

e2ee49c4188e.title: Impact event
e2ee49c4188e.section: Impacts and the Earth > Earth impacts in history > Precambrian
e2ee49c4188e.sentence: The Sudbury impact event occurred on the Nuna supercontinent (now Canada) from a bolide approximately 10–15 km (6.2–9.3 mi) in diameter approximately 1.849 billion years ago Debris from the event would have been scattered across the globe.

0e5bd5325f32.title: Geologic time scale
0e5bd5325f32.sentence: Proterozoic | Paleoproterozoic | Statherian | Columbian supercontinent continues to grow along its margins by subduction-related magmatism and terrane accretion. Extension and rift zones begin to develop from c. 1.6 Ga. Eukaryotic red algae appear. Vredefort impact event (2.19 Ga). | 1800

3406e3b70bdb.title: History of life
3406e3b70bdb.sentence: At around 1.7 Ga, multicellular organisms began to appear, with differentiated cells performing specialized functions.

4eb3e1e6f7c5.title: History of life
4eb3e1e6f7c5.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Fossil evidence
4eb3e1e6f7c5.sentence: Another early multicellular fossil, Qingshania, dated to 1.7 Ga, appears to consist of virtually identical cells.

7649e5bb2180.title: Mesoproterozoic
7649e5bb2180.sentence: Though the biota of the era was once thought to be exclusively microbial, recent finds have shown multicellular life did exist during the Mesoproterozoic.

f77fab67289b.title: History of life
f77fab67289b.sentence: Around 1.6 Ga, some eukaryotes gained the ability to photosynthesize via endosymbiosis with cyanobacteria, and gave rise to various algae that eventually overtook cyanobacteria as the dominant primary producers.

5d0f65333d76.title: History of life
5d0f65333d76.sentence: The symbiosis evolved around 1.5 Ga and enabled eukaryotes to carry out oxygenic photosynthesis.

b454756be25b.title: History of life
b454756be25b.section: Diversification of eukaryotes > Chromatin, nucleus, endomembrane system, and mitochondria
b454756be25b.sentence: A diverse collection of fossil algae were found in rocks dated between 1.5 and 1.4 Ga.

bae75b1e499f.title: Mesoproterozoic
bae75b1e499f.sentence: The supercontinent of Columbia broke up between 1500 and 1350 million years ago, and the fragments reassembled into the supercontinent of Rodinia around 1100 to 900 million years ago, on the time boundary between the Mesoproterozoic and the subsequent Neoproterozoic.

8edb89cc819a.title: History of life
8edb89cc819a.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Fossil evidence
8edb89cc819a.sentence: The "string of beads" organism Horodyskia, found in rocks dated from 1.5 Ga to 900 Ma, may have been an early metazoan; however, it has also been interpreted as a colonial foraminifera.

c62a6ed2dcd5.title: Fossil
c62a6ed2dcd5.sentence: Stromatolites are a major constituent of the fossil record for life's first 3.5 billion years, peaking about 1.25 billion years ago.

e9a8d70fa787.title: Proterozoic
e9a8d70fa787.sentence: The blossoming of eukaryotes such as acritarchs did not preclude the expansion of cyanobacteria – in fact, stromatolites reached their greatest abundance and diversity during the Proterozoic, peaking roughly 1.2 Ga.

1342f4afd014.title: Cambrian explosion
1342f4afd014.sentence: Earlier still, predatory pressure has acted on stromatolites and acritarchs since around 1,250 million years ago.

6f1ef7fd2e16.title: Fossil
6f1ef7fd2e16.sentence: The most widely supported explanation is that stromatolite builders fell victims to grazing creatures (the Cambrian substrate revolution), implying that sufficiently complex organisms were common over 1 billion years ago.

cd7751a09251.title: Mesoproterozoic
cd7751a09251.sentence: This era was also the high point of the stromatolites before they declined in the Neoproterozoic.

6b16ec53c1b1.title: History of life
6b16ec53c1b1.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Fossil evidence
6b16ec53c1b1.sentence: The red algae called Bangiomorpha, dated at 1.2 Ga, is the earliest known organism that certainly has differentiated, specialized cells, and is also the oldest known sexually reproducing organism.

45a38bc99629.title: History of life

45a38bc99629.sentence: The earliest known fossils of fungi date from 1.43 Ga.

c98318553e68.title: History of life
c98318553e68.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Fossil evidence
c98318553e68.sentence: The 1.43 billion-year-old fossils interpreted as fungi appear to have been multicellular with differentiated cells.

26abf58ebdf7.title: History of life
26abf58ebdf7.section: Sexual reproduction and multicellular organisms > Multicellularity
26abf58ebdf7.sentence: The available evidence indicates that eukaryotes evolved much earlier but remained inconspicuous until a rapid diversification around 1 Ga.

0491b54e610b.title: Tonian
0491b54e610b.sentence: The first large evolutionary radiation of acritarchs occurred during the Tonian.

0ce45a7184d1.title: History of life
0ce45a7184d1.sentence: By about 1 billion years ago, eukaryotes, including multicellular forms, inhabited freshwater environments.

940f7f18fbad.title: History of Earth
940f7f18fbad.sentence: The oldest fossils of land fungi and plants date to 480–460 Ma, though molecular evidence suggests the fungi may have colonized the land as early as 1000 Ma and the plants 700 Ma.

1823e1f5f4cb.title: History of Earth
1823e1f5f4cb.sentence: Although the division between a colony with specialized cells and a multicellular organism is not always clear, around 1 billion years ago, the first multicellular plants emerged, probably green algae.

85cfa912627e.title: Tonian
85cfa912627e.sentence: Even earlier sponge-like fossils have been reported in reefs dating back to 890 Ma, but their identity is highly debated.

2fee46b15821.title: Tonian
2fee46b15821.sentence: The first putative metazoan (animal) fossils are dated to the middle to late Tonian (c. 890 to 800 Ma).

a855a271ae25.title: Tonian
a855a271ae25.sentence: Fossils of Otavia antiqua, which has been described as a primitive sponge by its discoverers and numerous other scholars, date back to about 800 Ma.

26ba90942df2.title: Neoproterozoic
26ba90942df2.sentence: The earliest fossils of complex life are found in the Tonian period in the form of Otavia, a primitive sponge, and the earliest fossil evidence of metazoan radiation are found in the Ediacaran period, which included the namesaked Ediacaran biota as well as the oldest definitive cnidarians and bilaterians in the fossil record.

8b81d8941905.title: Neoproterozoic
8b81d8941905.sentence: Molecular phylogeny suggests that animals may have emerged even earlier in the Neoproterozoic (early Tonian), but physical evidence for such animal life is lacking.

c3d6f80ee33e.title: Proterozoic
c3d6f80ee33e.sentence: A second, later surge in oxygen concentrations is called the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event, occurred during the Middle and Late Neoproterozoic and drove the rapid evolution of multicellular life towards the end of the era.

c36fa5a79faf.title: Neoproterozoic
c36fa5a79faf.sentence: The Huainan biota (of late Tonian age) consists of small worm-shaped organisms.

f4ad6ef9eb94.title: Cambrian explosion
f4ad6ef9eb94.section: Possible causes > Changes in the environment > Increase in oxygen levels
f4ad6ef9eb94.sentence: Around 800 million years ago, there was a notable increase in the complexity and number of eukaryotes species in the fossil record.

6635eac0598b.title: Cambrian explosion
6635eac0598b.section: Possible causes > Changes in the environment > Increase in oxygen levels
6635eac0598b.sentence: Oceanic sulfide levels decreased around 800 million years ago, which supports the importance of oxygen in eukaryotic diversity.

2c63beec0b7b.title: Cambrian explosion
2c63beec0b7b.sentence: Older (~750 Ma) fossils indicate that mineralization long preceded the Cambrian, probably defending small photosynthetic algae from single-celled eukaryotic predators.

0c4a89ecce00.title: Neoproterozoic
0c4a89ecce00.sentence: The widespread proliferation of marine algae during the Neoproterozoic caused an increased flux of algal particulate matter to benthic environments, stimulating the evolution of microbial eukaryotic predators.

0b5eb298e0ed.title: Triassic
0b5eb298e0ed.sentence: Before the Permian extinction, Archaeplastida (red and green algae) had been the major marine phytoplanktons since about 659–645 million years ago, when they replaced marine planktonic cyanobacteria, which first appeared about 800 million years ago, as the dominant phytoplankton in the oceans.

8a9a071bda02.title: Geologic time scale
8a9a071bda02.sentence: Proterozoic | Neoproterozoic | Ediacaran | As Rodinia breaks up Gondwana begins to assemble with the Pan-African (Africa and South America), East African (Africa, India and Arabia) and Kuungan (India, eastern Antarctica and western Australia) orogenies. First cnidarians (jellyfish and sea pens). 580 Ma Gaskiers glaciation, followed by rise in atmospheric oxygen levels. Ediacaran biota, deep water, soft-bodied organisms. First trace fossils including simple burrows and first evidence of bilateral symmetry. | ~635 *

0abeb5df7a21.title: History of Earth

be33cfa552fa.title: Cambrian explosion
be33cfa552fa.sentence: At the start of the Ediacaran period, much of the acritarch fauna, which had remained relatively unchanged for hundreds of millions of years, became extinct, to be replaced with a range of new, larger species, which would prove far more ephemeral.

899c33c4a9f6.title: Earth
899c33c4a9f6.sentence: During the Ediacaran period (approximately 620 Ma), for example, there were 400±7 days in a year, with each day lasting 21.9±0.4 hours.

e2fb2f5f6d5c.title: Earth
e2fb2f5f6d5c.sentence: Due to their tidal interaction, the Moon recedes from Earth at the rate of approximately 38 mm/a (1+1⁄2 in/year).

cbe3f62f5fdf.title: History of life
cbe3f62f5fdf.sentence: In November 2019, researchers reported the discovery of Caveasphaera, a multicellular organism found in 609-million-year-old rocks, that is not easily defined as an animal or non-animal, which may be related to one of the earliest instances of animal evolution.

297faff04e01.title: History of Earth
297faff04e01.sentence: The supercontinent Pannotia formed around 600 Ma and then broke apart a short 50 million years later.

a76c9641b0f9.title: History of life
a76c9641b0f9.sentence: Nonetheless, the earliest widely accepted animal fossils are the rather modern-looking cnidarians (the group that includes jellyfish, sea anemones and Hydra), possibly from around 580 Ma, although fossils from the Doushantuo Formation can only be dated approximately.

427f9f948e9f.title: Cambrian explosion
427f9f948e9f.sentence: Since fossils of rather modern-looking cnidarians (jellyfish-like organisms) have been found in the Doushantuo lagerstätte, the cnidarian and bilaterian lineages must have diverged well over 580 million years ago.

4a61fcedbadc.title: Trace fossil
4a61fcedbadc.sentence: The first evidence of burrowing which is widely accepted dates to the Ediacaran (Vendian) period, around 567.3 million years ago, from lower Blueflower Formation.

dd6f689a46d2.title: Cambrian explosion
dd6f689a46d2.sentence: The traces of organisms moving on and directly underneath the microbial mats that covered the Ediacaran sea floor are preserved from the Ediacaran period, about 565 million years ago.

76b1a616d4d7.title: Paleozoic
76b1a616d4d7.sentence: Ediacaran trace fossils are simple, sub-horizontal feeding traces.

a428e9ac5ef5.title: History of life
a428e9ac5ef5.sentence: Ediacara biota appeared during the Ediacaran period, and bilaterians—animals with bilateral symmetry—were present by 555 Ma (million years ago).

4bcb9c7ac3d8.title: Precambrian
4bcb9c7ac3d8.sentence: Tracks from an animal with leg-like appendages have been found in what was mud 551 million years ago.

94cc1342390a.title: Cambrian explosion
94cc1342390a.sentence: At least some may have been early forms of the phyla in the Cambrian explosion, having been interpreted as early molluscs (Kimberella), echinoderms (Arkarua) and arthropods (Spriggina, Parvancorina, Yilingia).

0637790114c0.title: Fossil
0637790114c0.sentence: These 543-million-year-old embryos support the emergence of some aspects of arthropod development earlier than previously thought in the late Proterozoic.

b7cc0f545485.title: Mollusca
b7cc0f545485.sentence: Kimberella, from about 555 million years ago, has been described by some paleontologists as "mollusc-like", but others are unwilling to go further than "probable bilaterian", if that.

d63d7a8e3d10.title: History of life
d63d7a8e3d10.sentence: However, there seems little doubt that Kimberella was at least a triploblastic bilaterian animal, in other words, an animal significantly more complex than the cnidarians.

ad184bcb2aef.title: Cambrian explosion
ad184bcb2aef.sentence: If the Ediacaran Kimberella was a mollusc-like protostome (one of the two main groups of coelomates), the protostome and deuterostome lineages must have split significantly before 550 million years ago (deuterostomes are the other main group of coelomates).

690cce655e29.title: Trace fossil
690cce655e29.sentence: The potential mollusc related Kimberella is associated with scratch marks, perhaps formed by a radula, further traces from 555 million years ago appear to imply active crawling or burrowing activity.

bb9b275347b5.title: Cambrian explosion
bb9b275347b5.sentence: The mineralized tubes of Cloudina, Namacalathus, Sinotubulites and a dozen more of the other organisms from carbonate rocks formed near the end of the Ediacaran period from 549 to 542 million years ago, as well as the triradially symmetrical mineralized tubes of anabaritids (e.g. Anabarites, Cambrotubulus) from uppermost Ediacaran and lower Cambrian.

a380d8f7171f.title: Trace fossil
a380d8f7171f.sentence: Quantitative analyses of trace fossils suggest an increase in body aspect ratio, from ovoid forms to more elongated body plans, with body lengths exceeding eight times body width by the terminal Ediacaran.

21fc2418f088.title: Trace fossil
21fc2418f088.sentence: Terminal Ediacaran tracemakers also exhibited the ability to produce tightly looping and space-filling trajectories, such as those preserved in Parapsammichnites.

cfd0b0444370.title: Trace fossil
cfd0b0444370.sentence: These observations have been cited as evidence that some behavioural and sensory innovations commonly associated with the Cambrian Information Revolution may have originated during the terminal Ediacaran.

310cfb640580.title: History of Earth
310cfb640580.sentence: It was a form of adaptive radiation, where vacant niches left by the extinct Ediacaran biota were filled up by the emergence of new phyla.
